# CHAPTER 156

## THE ADVOCATE

Forty-three lines was not forty-three lines.

This was the first lie.

I discovered it before I got back upstairs.

Iven took the pages from me, spread them across the bakery table, and
crossed out six.

"What are you doing?"

"Helping."

"You removed them."

"Yes."

"Those are my lines."

"Not anymore."

He crossed out another.

I took the charcoal from him.

"Stop."

"The joke is bad."

"That is not the point."

"It is one point."

The sick man who had been the Advocate sat wrapped in a blanket near the
ovens. His name was Lorn. I had learned that because Rinna had asked
whether Lorn wanted broth and he had said no before coughing for long
enough to reconsider.

He leaned over the pages.

"Keep the magistrate."

I looked at him.

"Which magistrate?"

Iven pointed.

"That."

"Why?"

Lorn said, "Otherwise Orin comes in for no reason."

I looked at Orin's name farther down the page.

"What reason does he come in?"

"To arrest the Chancellor."

"Why?"

Lorn and Iven answered at the same time.

"Forgery."

"Treason."

They looked at each other.

I said, "Excellent."

Iven tapped the page.

"Forgery first. Treason later."

Lorn said, "No. Treason accusation first. Forgery proves it."

"You've been saying it backward."

"I've been saying it for six months."

"Backward for six months."

Lorn coughed.

Then raised one finger.

"Paid."

I liked him.

The Advocate, as far as I could tell, existed because everyone else in
the play had committed too many crimes to explain them efficiently.

He entered after the Princess accused the Chancellor of falsifying a
royal order. The Advocate represented someone called the Merchant
Council, which had apparently lost three wagons because of the false
order. He brought a copy of the order, identified a seal, accused the
Chancellor of forgery, then argued with the King about whether the crown
could prosecute its own officer.

Later he returned to establish that the Chancellor had also redirected
soldiers away from a bridge.

That allowed Orin, playing the magistrate, to enter and arrest him.

Except Orin said treason.

Except Iven said forgery.

Except the pages contained both.

I read them again.

The words moved.

Not magically.

Tiredly.

"Who is the Merchant Council?"

Iven said, "Doesn't matter."

Lorn said, "Matters to me."

"You are the Advocate."

"Was."

"Fine. Why do I care about them?"

"You don't."

"Then why am I advocating?"

"Money."

Iven nodded.

Finally, a character I understood.

Lorn pointed at a paragraph.

"This matters."

It was eleven lines.

"All of it?"

"No. Seal. Three wagons. Bridge."

"The bridge is later."

"Right."

He closed his eyes.

Iven said, "Go to bed."

Lorn said, "I'm helping."

"You're dying on the bread."

"I am not."

Rinna put a bowl of broth in front of him.

He looked at it.

Then at her.

"Traitor."

"Drink."

He drank.

Iven took the charcoal back from me.

"First entrance. You need the order. You need the seal. You need the
wagons. You need to make Marek refuse to act."

"Why?"

"So Serra can force him."

"Why?"

"Because that is the scene."

"Useful."

He crossed out two more lines.

"Stop doing that."

"You won't learn them."

"I might."

"No."

That irritated me enough to try.

I took the pages upstairs.

Pell was asleep.

The red dress watched me from the chair.

I sat on my bed and learned the first page.

Not all of it.

I learned the beginning.

"Your Majesty, I appear on behalf of the merchants of the eastern road,
whose goods were seized under an order bearing your seal."

Good.

Again.

"Your Majesty, I appear on behalf of the merchants of the eastern road,
whose goods were seized under an order bearing your seal."

Again.

Then the next line.

Then the next.

The Advocate had too many nouns.

Merchants.

Order.

Seal.

Wagons.

Chancellor.

Authority.

Bridge.

Council.

Crown.

I learned a sentence about the seal and forgot which wagons had been
seized.

Three.

Three wagons.

I remembered three because Lorn had said three.

Then I forgot whether they carried wool or grain.

The page said wool.

The next page said grain.

I stared.

Pell snored.

I went downstairs.

Lorn was asleep at the table.

Iven was gone.

Rinna was gone.

The bakery woman was shaping dough.

"Wool or grain?"

She looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

I went back upstairs.

Page one said wool.

Page three said grain because they were different wagons.

Of course.

I hated the Advocate.

I learned until the words became shapes.

At some point I woke with my cheek on the second page.

Morning had happened.

Pell was gone.

The red dress was gone.

I sat up too fast.

My neck hurt.

My mouth was dry.

The pages had lines from my face pressed into them.

I checked the window.

Gray light.

No hard rain.

Good.

Then I remembered forty-three lines.

Bad.

Downstairs, the bakery was full of people who had apparently decided to
have a day without waiting for me.

Nessa stood near the door drinking tea.

Serra was eating bread.

Marek was arguing with Bessa about tickets.

Davin carried a coil of rope through the room.

Teren was not there.

Iven saw me.

"First line."

I stopped on the last stair.

"Your Majesty, I appear on behalf of the merchants of the eastern road,
whose goods were seized under an order bearing your seal."

"Second."

"That was one sentence."

"Second line."

I knew it.

I absolutely knew it.

Nothing happened.

Iven waited.

Serra ate bread.

Marek continued arguing about whether ninety people could become
ninety-two.

I said, "The order was presented at the south gate by men acting under
the Chancellor's authority."

Iven shook his head.

"North gate."

"Fuck."

"Doesn't matter."

"Then why correct me?"

"Because you asked."

"I did not."

He handed me bread.

"Eat."

Lorn was not there.

"Where is he?"

"Bed."

"Here?"

"Bessa's sister."

"Who is Bessa's sister?"

Iven looked at me.

"Exactly."

He left.

I ate.

The hall roof had mostly held.

That was the morning report.

Mostly.

One bucket remained near the left rear stage, but the canvas was gone.
The boards underneath were damp rather than wet. The gray-haired roof
man stood onstage in muddy boots while Teren pressed a heel against the
floor.

"Dry by evening," the man said.

Teren looked at the bucket.

"Mostly."

"Bucket's for confidence."

"Whose?"

"Mine."

Teren accepted this.

The left entrance might reopen.

Might.

Nobody restored the moved bench.

Bessa had sold eleven more tickets.

Fifty-three.

Marek knew before I did.

"Money," he said.

"People," Bessa corrected.

"People with money."

"People with tickets."

"Which were money."

"Yesterday."

Marek looked at me.

"She is difficult."

Bessa said, "You are standing in my hall."

"Beautiful hall."

"You called it a bucket with walls."

"That was before sales."

I went to the stage.

The route through the house remained open.

Good.

I could enter either way depending on whether the boards dried.

Bad.

Two possible entrances meant I now had two possible places to forget I
was supposed to enter.

Serra came up behind me.

"Advocate."

"Yes."

"Show me the order."

"What?"

"Your prop."

I looked around.

"I don't have it."

"Then you cannot accuse anyone of forging it."

"Where is it?"

She pointed toward props.

I went.

There were three rolled papers on the table.

One had a red ribbon.

One had blue wax.

One was blank.

I chose blue wax.

Pell, from the floor behind the table, said, "No."

I looked down.

He was sewing a shoe.

"Which?"

"Red ribbon."

"Why?"

"Blue is marriage contract."

"Whose?"

"No idea."

I took red.

Serra was gone when I returned.

Of course.

I put the order in my belt.

Then remembered the Advocate probably did not carry it in his belt.

I found Iven.

"Where do I keep this?"

He looked at the paper.

"Hand."

"For the entire scene?"

"Yes."

"What do I do with my crutches?"

He stopped.

That was useful.

We went back to the stage.

The Advocate had been written for Lorn, who had two legs and apparently
fewer logistical objections.

I could not carry the order and use both crutches while entering.

Iven tried tucking the paper under my arm.

It fell.

He tried my coat.

Wrong costume.

He tried rolling it tighter.

Nessa shouted from across the hall, "No."

We stopped.

She came over, took the order, and shoved it inside the front of my
Advocate coat.

I was wearing only the shirt.

"There."

"It will wrinkle."

"It is forged."

"Fair."

She left.

Iven said, "First line."

I said it.

"Seal."

I said the seal line.

"Wagons."

"Three wagons of wool were seized at the north gate under the
Chancellor's authority."

"Good."

"That is not the actual line."

"Good."

I looked at him.

He pointed toward the stage.

"King refuses."

I said the next part.

Wrong.

I made the King agree.

Iven stopped me.

"No. He refuses."

"I know."

"You just made him prosecute."

"I said he should."

"You said he did."

"Difference."

"Yes."

I tried again.

This time I forgot the Merchant Council.

Iven let me.

We reached the bridge.

I accused the Chancellor of diverting soldiers to the bridge.

"From," Iven said.

"What?"

"From the bridge."

I looked at the page.

That was worse.

If I said it wrong in the show, the Chancellor would have protected the
bridge instead of exposing it.

"Fuck."

"Yes."

I circled FROM with charcoal.

Then I circled NORTH.

Then THREE.

Then SEAL.

My pages began to look diseased.

Teren passed.

"How is he?"

Iven said, "Bad."

Teren kept walking.

I said, "Thank you."

"You asked?"

"No."

"Then why are you upset?"

Marek found out I had forty-three lines.

He was delighted.

Not because he wanted me to succeed.

Because he had fewer.

"How many do you have?"

"Enough."

"How many?"

"No."

"Orin does that."

"Good man."

"Help me."

"I am helping."

"You are drinking tea."

"Morale."

He drank.

I said, "King refuses to prosecute Chancellor."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"Chancellor is his cousin."

I looked at the page.

"No, he isn't."

Marek frowned.

"Brother?"

"No."

"Then why do I care?"

"You are the King."

"You think I read the whole play?"

I stared.

He laughed.

"Ask Serra."

Serra was unavailable because someone had finally put her in the red
dress.

I knew because she came through the dressing-room door wearing it while
Nessa walked behind her staring at the hem.

Nobody celebrated.

Nobody announced completion.

The dress simply existed on a person.

Pell knelt, adjusted one pin, stood, and said, "Done."

Nessa said, "No."

Pell closed his eyes.

Serra looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You're staring."

"The dress."

She looked down.

"Oh."

Apparently she had suffered less from it than everyone else.

"Why does the King refuse to prosecute the Chancellor?"

"Because if he admits the order is false, he admits he lost control of
his own seal."

That made sense.

"Also the Chancellor is his cousin."

I turned slowly toward Marek.

He raised his tea.

"I knew."

Serra walked away.

The day continued without respecting my problem.

Tickets reached sixty-one.

The roof man removed the confidence bucket, then put it back when a
brief shower came through.

Bessa swore at the sky.

Davin moved the long box from the office to a dry rear corner after the
office man demanded his desk back.

Rinna bought lamp oil.

I knew because I saw her pay two copper and complain about the price.

A local baker sent over a tray of small rolls because we were sleeping
above his ovens and apparently actors made his daughter laugh the night
before in another town.

That explanation made no sense.

Nobody refused the rolls.

Marek ate three.

A woman who had bought tickets brought Bessa a basket of pears "for the
players."

That was the phrase.

For the players.

Bessa took two pears as management tax.

The rest reached backstage.

I put one in my bag for later.

Five copper per show was money.

Pears were also money, in the sense that I did not have to buy a pear.

This seemed obvious enough not to require philosophy.

By afternoon I knew perhaps twenty-five lines exactly.

That number was misleading.

I knew another ten if someone gave me the first word.

I knew five in the wrong order.

I knew one from a completely different scene.

The remaining lines hated me personally.

Iven crossed out four more.

"You cannot keep removing the role."

"We are shortening."

"Teren know?"

"No."

"Teren!"

From across the hall:

"What?"

"Iven is cutting the Advocate."

"Good."

Iven crossed out another.

"Traitor," I said.

Teren shouted, "Gregory."

"Yes?"

"Learn less."

I hated everyone.

The sick Advocate's forty-three lines became thirty-two.

Then thirty-one because Orin refused to wait through a legal argument he
called "three minutes of furniture."

"It establishes jurisdiction," I said.

Orin stared.

"You have been Advocate for twelve hours."

"Thirteen."

"Dangerous."

He crossed out the jurisdiction.

I put it back.

He crossed it out again.

I let it die.

At some point, Bessa asked Teren whether we could add seats.

He said no.

She added four.

Teren removed two.

They settled on two.

Sixty-eight tickets.

The rain stopped.

The roof man climbed up once more.

The confidence bucket remained empty.

At five, Teren gathered us on the stage.

Not for rehearsal.

"Left is open unless it rains."

That was the meeting.

Nessa asked, "If it rains?"

"House route."

Orin said, "Rear cross?"

"Open."

Davin said, "No scenery on west brace."

Teren nodded.

Bessa said, "Seventy-one."

Marek smiled.

Teren said, "Good."

Then everyone left.

I stood there.

"That's it?"

Teren looked back.

"What?"

"We don't run anything?"

"Do you want to?"

I looked at the pages.

No.

"Yes."

"No time."

"Why did you ask?"

He walked away.

Doors in ninety minutes.

I ate stew.

Not enough.

Then too much.

I changed.

The Advocate coat was dark brown, too broad through the shoulders, and
smelled faintly of Lorn.

Nessa pinned one side so it did not bunch under my arm.

"Order."

I showed her.

"Good."

"Do I look like an Advocate?"

"No."

"Useful."

"You look nineteen."

"I am nineteen."

"That is the problem."

She went away.

I looked in the mirror.

She was right.

The Advocate probably should have looked like a man entrusted by
merchants to accuse royal officers of treason.

I looked like someone entrusted with holding a lantern.

Fine.

I tried the first line again.

Perfect.

Second.

Perfect.

Third.

North gate.

Three wagons.

Seal.

King refuses.

Crown cannot prosecute itself without admitting seal compromised.

Serra forces question.

Chancellor denies.

Forgery.

Bridge.

FROM the bridge.

Orin enters.

Arrest.

I could hold the shape.

Maybe.

The actual words remained less cooperative.

Doors opened.

I heard the audience enter.

Not all at once.

Feet.

Voices.

Wet coats.

Benches scraping.

Bessa telling someone no, their ticket did not include the front because
there was no front ticket.

Marek appeared beside me in costume.

"Money."

"How many?"

"Seventy-six."

"You asked?"

"Obviously."

"Is that good?"

"Yes."

"Why?"

"More than seventy-five."

He left.

Iven came past.

"Order."

I showed him.

"Bridge."

"From."

"Good."

"King."

"Refuses."

"Seal."

"Compromised."

"Wagons."

"Three."

"Wool."

"North."

He nodded.

That was the most useful thing anyone had done all day.

Then he said, "You enter second scene."

"I know."

"You said third earlier."

I went cold.

"No, I didn't."

"Yes."

"When?"

"Lunch."

"I was wrong at lunch."

"Yes."

"Second."

"Yes."

"Fuck."

He left.

I stood behind the right wing.

The left entrance was open.

Dry enough.

The confidence bucket had been removed.

The first scene began.

I knew this part.

Not my part.

Good.

Marek entered.

Audience laughed at something he did before his first line.

Serra entered in the red dress.

It moved correctly.

Somewhere backstage, Pell whispered, "Done."

Nessa said, "Quiet."

I smiled.

Then remembered I was Advocate.

Second scene.

I checked the order.

Red ribbon.

Good.

The first scene ended.

People moved.

A prop table shifted.

Someone nearly knocked over a lamp.

Davin caught it.

I waited.

My entrance came after Serra's accusation.

I knew that.

I absolutely knew that.

Onstage, Serra accused the Chancellor of using the King's seal to seize
merchant wagons.

That was my entrance.

I did not move.

I was listening to the line.

Not entering.

Iven shoved my shoulder.

"Go."

I went.

Late.

Not terribly late.

Late enough that Serra had to look toward the wing as if summoning me.

I crossed onto the stage.

The hall looked different with people in it.

Seventy-something faces.

Warm lamps.

Wet coats steaming.

A child near the front.

Bessa against the rear wall.

My crutch struck the board once.

Too loud.

Marek looked at me.

King.

Right.

I reached into my coat.

The order stuck.

For one horrible second I fought my own costume.

Then it came free.

Wrinkled.

Forged.

Fine.

I looked at Marek.

First line.

Gone.

Completely.

The first line I had said perhaps fifty times.

Nothing.

The audience waited.

Marek waited.

Serra did not look at me.

I had the shape.

Merchants.

Order.

Seal.

I held up the paper.

"Your Majesty, three wagons belonging to the merchants of the eastern
road were seized at the north gate under an order carrying your seal."

Not the line.

Everything necessary.

Marek leaned back.

"And you have come to complain about my handwriting?"

The audience laughed.

That was not his line either.

Fine.

I said, "I have come because your handwriting is apparently stealing
wool."

Better laugh.

Dangerous.

I wanted the laugh again.

No.

Seal.

I broke the wax.

I was not supposed to break the wax.

Too late.

I held it out.

"This seal is yours."

Marek looked at it.

"Was."

What?

Serra moved slightly.

I saw it.

Not rescue yet.

My next line accused the Chancellor.

I knew it.

I said it.

Correctly.

The Chancellor denied it.

Good.

Marek refused to act.

Good.

Serra stepped in.

Good.

We were in the scene.

Then I said the wagons carried grain.

I knew immediately.

Wool.

The Chancellor actor looked at me.

Tiny pause.

He said, "Yesterday they were wool."

Audience laughed.

I stared at him.

Yesterday?

He had given me something.

I said, "Yesterday they were in our possession."

More laughter.

Not enough.

Necessary information still wrong.

I added, "Today the wool is gone, which is the complaint."

There.

Wool restored.

The Chancellor shrugged.

"Then perhaps you should advocate for better locks."

The scene moved.

I could feel my pages inside my coat.

Useless.

I could not read them.

I could not stop.

Marek refused.

Serra forced.

Seal compromised.

The first part survived.

Then I reached the bridge.

This mattered.

Soldiers had been diverted FROM the bridge.

I opened my mouth.

"To the bridge."

Fuck.

Orin was waiting somewhere.

The Chancellor smiled.

"Indeed. To defend it."

No.

I had reversed the crime.

The audience had no idea.

Everyone onstage did.

Serra looked at me.

Not panic.

Waiting.

I said, "They were ordered to the bridge."

The Chancellor said, "You just said that."

"Yes."

I could hear Iven backstage swearing.

I continued.

"They were ordered to it from the south road, then ordered away before
they arrived."

Was that the plot?

No idea.

Could become the plot.

The Chancellor actor said, "By whom?"

I held up the broken seal.

"You."

Silence.

Then Serra said, "Which is why the bridge stood empty when the
magistrate arrived."

There.

She had put the destination back where it belonged.

Orin entered.

Late or on time.

I did not know anymore.

He looked at the Chancellor.

Then at me.

Then at the broken seal.

"That was evidence."

I said, "It remains evidence."

"It is in two pieces."

"More evidence."

The audience laughed.

Orin took it from me.

"Stop helping."

That laugh was bigger.

I wanted to answer.

I did not.

Good.

Orin arrested the Chancellor.

The scene survived.

Not the scene on the page.

A scene.

When I came offstage, Iven caught me by the coat.

"From."

"I know."

"You said to."

"I know."

"You said it twice."

"I know."

"Good."

Serra passed us.

She was already going toward another entrance.

Without stopping, she said, "You owe me a bridge."

Then she was gone.

I looked at Iven.

"Is that bad?"

"Yes."

"How bad?"

He listened to the stage.

"Later."

He shoved the next prop into my hand.

I looked down.

A sword.

Not me.

An actual sword.

"What is this?"

"King."

"Why do I have it?"

"Because Marek needs it in twenty seconds."

"Why am I giving it to him?"

"You aren't. Put it on the table."

"Which table?"

Iven was already gone.

There were three.

The show continued.

Apparently the Advocate was only one of my problems.

# CHAPTER 157

## THE TABLE

There were three tables.

One held cups.

One held a crown, two folded letters, a wooden bird, and something that
might have been a dead fish.

The third was empty.

I put the sword on the empty one.

Pell appeared from nowhere.

"No."

"Fuck."

"Other."

"Which other?"

He pointed at the table with the fish.

"Why?"

"King."

"The King keeps his sword with a dead fish?"

"Not dead."

The fish moved.

I stared.

It was carved wood attached to a spring.

"Why does it move?"

Pell took the sword from me.

"Later."

"There is a later?"

He put it beside the crown.

"Hopefully."

Then he ran.

I had been offstage perhaps thirty seconds.

My Advocate coat was still pinned wrong under one arm. The broken order
was in Orin's possession. I had no idea where my pages were. Somewhere
onstage the Chancellor was being arrested for a crime I had nearly
transformed into public service.

Marek needed the sword.

I listened.

Wrong scene.

Not yet.

Good.

I leaned against the wall.

Iven came back.

"Why are you standing?"

"I am resting."

"Shopkeeper."

"When?"

He looked toward the stage.

"Two."

"Two what?"

"Scenes."

"That is not time."

"It is theatre."

He handed me a cloth cap.

I stared at it.

"Shopkeeper doesn't wear this."

"Tonight he does."

"Why?"

"Your Advocate hair."

I touched my hair.

It was hair.

Apparently it had become legally distinct.

I put on the cap.

Iven took it off.

"Wrong way."

"It's a cap."

"Yes."

He turned it and put it back.

I hated theatre.

The sword disappeared from the table.

Marek had apparently collected it without me noticing.

Good.

I started removing the Advocate coat.

Nessa caught the sleeve before I pulled.

"Pins."

"What?"

She reached inside and removed two pins.

"Do you want blood?"

"Not particularly."

"Then stop undressing like an animal."

She took the coat.

I stood in my shirt while she passed it to Pell.

"Shopkeeper coat."

Pell looked around.

Nessa said, "Pell."

"I know."

He did not know.

Neither did I.

The Shopkeeper coat was hanging behind the curtain because somebody had
moved the costume rail away from the leaking window. I found it after
Pell found something else.

He held up a gray coat.

"That is Marek."

"No."

"It was yesterday."

"Today it's Orin."

"Why?"

"Rain."

I stared at him.

He stared back.

Neither of us knew how rain had changed ownership of the gray coat.

Nessa shouted, "Shopkeeper!"

I found mine.

By the time I had it on, the audience was laughing.

I stopped.

Listened.

Still one scene before me.

Fine.

My body had begun doing something unpleasant where every sound from the
stage felt like a missed cue.

A door shut.

Was that mine?

No.

Audience laugh.

Mine?

No.

Serra spoke.

Definitely not mine.

I breathed.

I had done Shopkeeper four times.

This should have been easier than Advocate.

That thought was obviously a mistake.

Iven appeared in debtor clothes.

No coat again.

"Don't."

"I haven't said anything."

"You were looking at my coat."

"You don't have one."

"Exactly."

"Why are you telling me not to ask about something you don't have?"

"Because now you're going to."

"I wasn't."

"You are now."

Fuck him.

We waited.

The hall was quieter than the eastern-town night crowd. Not silent. More
attentive. They laughed, but they did not shout over the play. Wet
weather had apparently produced people willing to sit indoors and watch
carefully.

I preferred the drunk ones.

They were less likely to notice legal errors.

Iven looked toward the wing.

"Go."

"Not yet."

"Correct."

"Why did you say go?"

"Testing."

"Fuck you."

He smiled.

Then our cue came.

We went.

Shopkeeper began well.

Not brilliantly.

Well.

Iven entered complaining about debt.

I asked how much he had.

He said less than yesterday.

I almost said, "Under whose authority?"

The words reached my teeth.

I stopped them.

The pause was too long.

Iven looked at me.

The audience looked at me.

I said, "That is an impressive way to answer without using a number."

A few laughs.

Not many.

Move.

Iven offered half.

I said, "Half is what people offer when they have all."

That was written.

I think.

He said he had expenses.

I asked whether I was one.

He said, "Increasingly."

Better.

Then I used the word jurisdiction.

I do not know why.

"Your poverty is outside my jurisdiction."

Silence.

Iven blinked.

I heard someone backstage choke.

I said, "Pay me."

That worked.

Not huge.

Enough.

Iven leaned closer.

"What is jurisdiction?"

"Expensive."

That worked better.

Fine.

Apparently the Shopkeeper had attended law school between towns.

The scene moved.

No uncle.

No aunt.

No coat.

No constable error.

Different room.

Different people.

At the end Iven tried to leave.

I said, "Where are you going?"

"To find a cheaper creditor."

"Bring him here."

"Why?"

"I have jurisdiction."

The audience laughed.

I hated myself.

Iven did too.

I could tell because he was trying not to smile.

Backstage he said, "Never again."

"Agreed."

"Jurisdiction?"

"I have been poisoned."

"By advocacy."

"Apparently."

He handed me water.

I drank.

The next scene was already moving.

Marek came offstage without the sword.

"Where is it?"

"What?"

"Sword."

"Gregory."

"No. Actual sword."

"Oh."

He looked back toward the stage.

"On throne?"

There was no throne in this hall.

There was a chair.

I looked.

The sword was not there.

Pell ran past.

"Sword?"

"Which?"

"Actual."

"Prop."

"Yes."

"Table."

"Which?"

He kept running.

I found the table.

No sword.

The wooden fish jumped.

I nearly hit it.

"Stop that."

The fish did not.

Iven appeared.

"Sword."

"I know."

"Where?"

"I don't know."

"Good."

"How is that good?"

"Now two of us know."

Serra came offstage in the red dress.

"What are you doing?"

"Looking for a sword."

She pointed.

It was under Marek's chair.

Of course.

"Why?"

Marek, from onstage, shifted his foot.

He had kicked it.

I retrieved it.

Serra took it from me.

"You need to be Sword."

"I know."

"You are holding Sword."

"That is different."

She shoved the prop into Iven's hands.

"King."

Then to me:

"Wall."

I went to the wall.

My Sword position had changed because the left entrance was open again
but the bench was still moved. The mounting board stood farther right
than in the eastern hall. My crutches went behind the flat. My body went
where it fit.

Someone strapped the decorative belt across me.

Not tightly enough.

I said, "Again."

The local worker tightened it.

"Good."

The scene before Sword ended.

I heard applause.

Then movement.

Serra entered.

Red dress.

Different room.

Different Princess.

Not because she had decided to become a new person, I thought. Because
the dress changed how she moved.

Or maybe I was making that up because I was tired.

She took me from the wall.

The belt caught.

For half a second, Sword refused to be stolen.

Serra pulled harder.

I came free.

Audience laughed.

She looked at me.

"Stubborn."

I said, "Evidence."

Wrong role.

A laugh anyway.

Serra's eyes changed.

Barely.

I knew.

I had brought Advocate onto Sword.

I corrected.

"I mean legendary."

Nothing.

Worse.

I should have left evidence.

Too late.

Serra said, "You are badly mounted."

"I was resisting theft."

"Poorly."

"I am a sword."

"That is your defense?"

"No. Apparently I need an advocate."

The audience laughed.

Fuck.

I had done it again.

Serra let the laugh pass.

Then:

"I have one. He's terrible."

Bigger.

I laughed.

Actually laughed.

Wrong.

She waited.

I stopped.

We continued.

Marek entered with the actual prop sword.

For one horrifying instant there were two swords in the scene, one of
them me and one of them sharp-looking wood.

He was not supposed to have it.

I knew because Serra looked at it.

Marek looked at it.

Then he looked at me.

"I found another."

Serra said, "Keep that one."

Marek looked at me again.

"Why?"

"This one talks."

Marek considered the prop.

He raised it to his ear.

The audience laughed.

He said, "This one has better manners."

I said, "That one has no jurisdiction."

Serra closed her eyes.

Iven made a noise backstage.

I had promised never again approximately six minutes earlier.

Marek said, "Neither do you."

Correct.

The scene continued.

The extra sword should have ruined something.

Instead Marek carried it until a servant character entered, then handed
it over without explanation.

The servant accepted it.

Gone.

Problem removed.

Later Serra gave me a line I knew.

I answered with the next line instead.

She looked at me.

I knew immediately.

I had skipped the setup.

The line I had said required her to have threatened the King.

She had not.

Audience silence.

Serra said, "I haven't threatened him yet."

Laugh.

I said, "I know you."

Bigger.

Then she threatened him.

We continued.

Backstage, she unstrapped me.

"You owe me two things."

"Bridge and threat."

"Good."

"Do I get credit for remembering?"

"No."

She left.

The rain started again during Orin's next scene.

I knew because everyone backstage looked upward at once.

Not audience.

Company.

A few drops hit the confidence bucket behind the left curtain.

Ping.

Pause.

Ping.

The roof man, who had stayed for the show, stood from his place near the
rear wall.

He watched the ceiling.

Ping.

Nothing.

Nothing.

Ping.

He sat back down.

Confidence restored.

The audience did not care.

One child turned around to look.

Bessa turned the child back by pointing at Orin.

Orin was in the middle of accusing somebody of poisoning somebody else.

He forgot the poison.

Not the accusation.

The object.

He reached toward the prop table.

No cup.

No jar.

Nothing.

I could see his hand from the wing.

He could see the empty space.

Pell whispered, "Blue."

I whispered, "Where?"

"Blue."

That was not location.

Iven looked under the table.

Nessa looked behind a trunk.

Orin continued speaking with his empty hand.

The other actor said, "You have no proof."

Orin looked at his hand.

Then at him.

"I had proof."

Audience laughed.

"Where is it?"

Orin looked toward the wing.

We all froze.

He said, "Stolen."

The other actor said, "Convenient."

"Crime often is."

They continued.

The blue poison jar was found thirty seconds later inside a boot.

Nobody knew why.

Pell blamed Marek.

Marek was onstage and therefore unavailable to defend himself.

Reasonable.

My second Advocate entrance came too soon.

Everything came too soon.

I had changed out of Sword but still had the Sword shirt under the
Advocate coat.

Nessa looked at it.

"No time."

"Good."

"No, bad. Go."

I had the pages this time.

I could not take them onstage.

I looked once.

Bridge.

From.

Seal.

Magistrate already knew.

This second entrance was shorter after the cuts. I returned to challenge
the King's attempt to dismiss the case after the Chancellor's arrest.
The Advocate had to establish that the forged order had caused actual
loss and that arresting one man did not restore the wagons or the
undefended bridge.

I knew the facts.

I knew them so hard I forgot the character.

I entered on time.

Excellent.

"Your Majesty, the soldiers were diverted FROM the bridge."

Too loud.

Too early.

That was not my first line.

Marek stared.

Audience stared.

I had walked onstage and announced a preposition.

Somewhere backstage Iven died.

Marek said, "I had gathered that."

Laugh.

I held the order.

Still broken.

"Good."

Another laugh.

I had no idea why.

My actual first line returned.

"The Chancellor is arrested, but the merchants remain without their
wool, the crown remains without its bridge, and your seal remains
compromised."

Correct.

Flat.

Completely flat.

I had delivered it like a list of roof repairs.

Marek answered.

I said the next necessary thing.

Correct.

Flat.

The audience listened.

No laughs.

That was fine.

I wanted a laugh.

That was dangerous.

I did not reach for one.

The King tried to dismiss me.

I said the Merchant Council would seek restitution.

Marek said, "From whom?"

"From the crown."

"Which is me."

"Unfortunately."

Small laugh.

Fine.

He said the treasury was empty.

I nearly said pay me.

I did not.

Shopkeeper remained backstage where he belonged.

Instead I said, "Then your Majesty has discovered the merchants'
position."

That got something.

Not much.

Enough.

Orin entered early.

He was not supposed to be in this part.

I knew because Marek's face changed.

Orin crossed the stage carrying the blue poison jar.

Why?

No idea.

He put it on the King's table.

"There."

Marek looked at it.

"So there is proof."

"Different crime."

Audience laughed.

Orin turned to leave.

I said, "Magistrate."

He stopped.

I should not have stopped him.

I had no line for him.

He waited.

I waited.

The audience waited.

I said, "The bridge."

Orin said, "Still there."

Laughter.

"Empty."

"Less good."

He left.

I had accomplished nothing.

Marek said, "Are all your legal arguments this efficient?"

"No."

"Good."

We finished.

Backstage Iven was leaning against the wall.

He looked ill.

Not Lorn ill.

Me ill.

"FROM."

"I said from."

"You entered with from."

"I remembered."

"Too much."

"I know."

"You stopped Orin."

"I know."

"Why?"

"I don't know."

"Good."

"Stop saying good."

"No."

He walked away.

I sat for perhaps forty seconds.

Then Teren pointed at me.

"Bow later."

"What?"

"You're in final."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"Apparently not."

He left.

The final act compressed around fatigue.

Marek lost a line and simply looked at Serra.

She supplied the necessary question herself.

He answered it.

No joke.

No rescue visible.

Just moved.

Iven entered carrying the wrong letter, discovered it halfway across the
stage, turned it over, and announced that the message had become
private.

The audience laughed.

He delivered the information from memory and never opened it.

Pell repaired a fastening on Orin's sleeve while Orin stood behind the
curtain swearing quietly.

Nessa held the curtain because the fastening repair required two hands

The confidence bucket caught five drops.

I counted.

Then stopped because I had a final Shopkeeper appearance that I had
forgotten existed.

It was only three lines.

Thank God.

I entered.

A character owed money.

I said, "Under whose authority?"

Silence.

I closed my eyes.

Not visibly, I hoped.

The actor said, "Yours?"

I said, "Correct."

Then, because I had finally learned something about shutting up, I moved
to the next line.

The audience laughed after I had already moved.

Better.

The last scene ended.

Applause came.

Not the roaring eastern-town night.

Warm.

Full.

Long enough.

We bowed.

Serra in red.

Marek grinning.

Orin pretending not to.

Iven breathing hard.

Me trying to remember whether Advocate bowed as Advocate or whether I
was Sword or Shopkeeper at this point.

Apparently myself was sufficient.

Bessa stood at the back.

She was smiling at the room.

Not us.

The room.

Seventy-something people who had paid to sit under her mostly repaired
roof.

That was fair.

Backstage, the first thing Teren said to me was:

"Bridge."

"I said from."

"You announced it."

"I was correcting yesterday."

"Yesterday was this morning."

That was upsetting.

"Five copper?"

He reached into the purse.

"Five copper."

"Forty-three lines."

"Thirty-one."

"Three roles."

"Same show."

"Fuck you."

He put five copper in my hand.

"Paid actor."

I looked at the coins.

Five.

Same as before.

Advocate had not increased them.

Neither had accidentally destroying evidence.

Neither had becoming a sword with jurisdiction.

Five copper.

I put them in my inner pocket.

Bessa appeared.

"Tomorrow."

Teren looked at her.

"What?"

"Tomorrow night."

Marek, from across the room:

"Money?"

Bessa shouted, "Yes."

Marek raised both arms.

Teren said, "How many?"

"Twenty-three already."

"For tomorrow?"

"I asked tonight."

"You sold them during the show?"

"I sell tickets when people are buying tickets."

Teren looked at the ceiling.

The confidence bucket sat empty.

"Same terms?"

Bessa said, "Better if we pass eighty."

"Better for whom?"

"Me."

"No."

They began.

I stopped listening.

A local woman came through the backstage door with a covered pot.

"For the players."

Rinna intercepted it.

"What?"

"Soup."

"What kind?"

"Hot."

Rinna accepted this as sufficient.

Another man brought a small jug of cider and said his wife had liked the
King.

Marek took personal credit.

The man said, "She liked the woman in red."

Marek gave the jug to Serra.

Serra drank directly from it.

"Correct," she said.

The roof man came backstage only long enough to retrieve his coat.

I asked, "Tomorrow?"

He looked upward.

"Roof?"

"Yes."

"Probably."

"That is not confidence."

He pointed at the bucket.

"That's confidence."

Then he left.

Lorn was still sick.

I learned this because Rinna returned from the bakery with his answer.

"No."

That meant he would not be Advocate tomorrow.

I stared at her.

She stared back.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Good."

She carried the soup away.

Tomorrow.

Again.

Advocate again.

Sword again.

Shopkeeper again.

Five copper again.

Maybe.

I should have been horrified.

I was tired enough that horror required energy.

Instead I took the pear from my bag.

Still there.

I sat on a trunk.

Pell sat on the floor beside me.

He looked at the red dress across the room.

Serra was still wearing it.

"Done?" I asked.

He thought.

"Tonight."

"Good."

We shared the pear.

Around us, Teren and Bessa argued about eighty tickets, Nessa tried to
get Serra out of the dress before she spilled cider on it, Marek
attempted to claim a second bowl of soup, Iven searched for the blue
poison jar again, and somebody put the wooden fish into the wrong crate.

Tomorrow we would do it again.

Apparently that was the good news.

# CHAPTER 158

## THE RETURNER

I woke because Pell was washing a shirt in our drinking water.

I watched him for several seconds.

"That's drinking water."

"Was."

"You have a basin."

"Full."

"Of what?"

"Socks."

I lay back down.

The ceiling smelled like bread.

The room smelled like wet wool, soap, and two men who had spent too much
time in costumes.

Outside, somebody was moving a cart through mud.

Nothing hurt in a new way. My shoulders were sore. My hands had the
familiar rubbed places from the crutches. My residual limb was fine when
I checked it, which made it the least complicated part of the morning.

I cleaned and rewrapped it.

Pell wrung out the shirt.

"Show tonight."

"I know."

"Advocate."

"I know."

"From."

I threw a sock at him.

It was his sock.

That made it less satisfying.

He put it in the basin.

"Thanks."

Downstairs, nobody was waiting for me.

Again.

Marek was eating something fried from a paper twist and arguing with a
boy about whether the King had won last night.

The boy said no.

Marek said the King was still King at the end.

The boy said that was not winning.

Marek looked genuinely troubled by this.

Nessa had three costumes spread over two chairs and half the bakery
counter. Rinna was writing numbers on the back of an old flour invoice.
Iven had coffee or something close enough to coffee that he was
pretending. Orin was absent.

Serra sat by the window with her hair loose, reading a folded note.

She folded it before anyone came near.

Not because of me.

Just because someone came near.

Davin was not there.

Teren was.

That was worse.

He looked rested.

"How?"

He looked at me.

"What?"

"You slept."

"Yes."

"How?"

"Bed."

I hated management.

He pointed toward bread.

"Eat."

"Advocate?"

"Tonight."

"I know tonight."

"Then why ask?"

I took bread.

Bessa came through the front door carrying a board with ticket marks.

Marek stopped arguing with the boy.

"How many?"

"Thirty-seven."

He smiled.

"For tonight?"

"No, Marek. For a funeral next spring."

"Good funeral?"

Bessa walked past him.

"Thirty-seven," he told me.

"I heard."

"Yesterday was twenty-three."

"I remember numbers."

"You forgot three wagons."

"Different numbers."

He accepted this.

Lorn was awake.

I found him in the room above Bessa's sister's shop because Rinna sent
me with bread and because apparently being Advocate meant I had
inherited errands.

Bessa's sister sold candles.

I learned this because the room below Lorn contained enough wax to make
the stairs smell sweet.

Lorn was sitting up in bed under two blankets.

He looked terrible.

Less terrible than last night.

"You're alive."

"Unfortunately."

I gave him bread.

He looked at it.

"Is that payment?"

"No."

"Then good."

His pages were on the chair.

My pages.

His pages.

I had developed opinions about ownership too quickly.

He pointed.

"Bring them."

I did.

He flipped through the marks.

"What happened here?"

"Iven."

"He killed half the role."

"Orin helped."

"Animals."

"You said keep the magistrate."

"I did not say remove jurisdiction."

I stared at him.

"You like jurisdiction?"

"It's the best part."

"Orin called it three minutes of furniture."

"Orin falls down before knives touch him."

Fair.

Lorn found the bridge section.

He looked at my circles.

FROM had been circled enough times that the paper was nearly torn.

"You said to."

"Once."

"Rinna said twice."

"Rinna wasn't onstage."

"Everyone knows."

Excellent.

He read farther.

"You made him angry."

"Who?"

"Advocate."

"I was tired."

"He's not angry."

"He accuses the Chancellor of treason."

"Forgery."

"Both."

"See? You're learning."

"What is he, then?"

Lorn looked at me as if this were obvious.

"Scared."

I waited.

"He walks into a king's hall and says the king's seal is being used to
steal from merchants. If the king decides the seal is fine, Advocate is
calling the king a thief. If the king decides it isn't, Advocate has
just told the room the king can't control his own house."

"That sounds like anger."

"That sounds like wanting to go home alive."

I looked at the first page.

That was irritating.

I had played him like someone who wanted the argument.

Lorn took the bread.

"Don't copy me."

"I wasn't planning to."

"Good. I'm better."

"You're in bed."

"Temporarily."

I left before I started defending a role I had played once to a man who
had played it for six months.

Outside, the rain had stopped.

The town looked better for it.

Not beautiful.

Better.

Mud still ran along the gutters. Water dripped from awnings. People had
opened shutters and put goods back outside.

I had nowhere I was required to be for several hours.

This felt suspicious.

I walked.

Not far.

The market occupied a narrow square three streets from the hall.
Vegetables, cloth, cheap metal goods, paper, cooked food, secondhand
shoes, two cages of chickens, one man selling carved saints, and a woman
selling buttons by weight.

I bought paper.

One sheet cost less than I expected.

Ink cost more.

I bought neither ink nor pen because the paper seller had a writing
table and charged a copper to use both and send a folded letter south
with a carrier leaving before evening.

One copper.

I had more than that now.

Not enough that copper meant nothing.

Enough that I could spend one without having to invent a reason.

I sat.

Lyssa,

The roof did not fall in.

This seemed like the most important opening.

I stared at it.

Then added:

I was not on it. I held a lantern. Completely different employment.

We did a show under it anyway. Then another problem happened and I
became an Advocate with forty-three lines, except apparently lines can
be removed by coworkers if they dislike them. I was paid the same five
copper.

I stopped.

That sounded like complaint.

It was complaint.

Fine.

I wrote about the bridge.

Not all of it.

Enough.

I wrote that I had said to when I meant from and that apparently an
entire criminal case could depend on a direction.

I wrote that the red dress was finally finished.

Then crossed out finally because Lyssa had no idea about the red dress.

Then wrote it again with an explanation that made the red dress sound
more important than the play.

I wrote that the bread was good.

I did not write about Drell.

I thought about him only after noticing I had not.

That was interesting for perhaps one second.

Then a chicken escaped.

The market became more interesting.

A boy caught it against a cabbage stall.

I finished:

We perform again tonight. I think we leave after that, but nobody has
told me anything useful, which may mean I am learning how this works.

I miss you.

Greg

I looked at the last line.

Left it.

Paid the copper.

The paper seller sanded the letter, folded it, tied it, and wrote CARROW
on the outside.

"Name?"

"Lyssa."

"Family?"

"No."

She waited.

I realized this was not enough information to deliver a letter in a
city.

I gave her the street and the place Lyssa usually worked near, plus the
description that would actually help someone find her.

The woman added notes.

"Carrier gets it to Carrow. After that, somebody asks."

"How long?"

"Two days if road's good. Four if not."

"Fine."

She put my letter into a leather pouch with perhaps twenty others.

That was it.

One copper.

I walked away.

At a button stall I saw a narrow brass clasp shaped like two leaves
meeting.

Lyssa would probably call it unnecessary.

It cost two copper.

I walked away.

Then came back.

"One?"

"Two."

"It's small."

"So are buttons."

"One."

"Two."

"One and a button."

She stared at me.

"What button?"

"I don't know. You're the button woman."

"Two."

I paid two.

Apparently theatre money could become brass leaves.

I put the clasp in my inner pocket with the remaining coins.

Not ceremonial.

Just hers, probably.

If she hated it, I could use it to hold Advocate pages together.

Back at the bakery, Orin had appeared.

He had a bruise on his jaw.

Nobody asked.

Marek did.

"What happened?"

"No."

"Was it a person?"

"No."

"A door?"

"No."

"A husband?"

"No."

"Wife?"

"No."

"Animal?"

"No."

"Furniture?"

Orin looked at him.

"No."

Marek smiled.

"Furniture."

Orin took his bread and left.

Serra was gone.

Iven was asleep in a chair.

Nessa had found another problem with the red dress.

Not the dress itself.

A glove.

This was acceptable.

The dress had graduated.

Rinna counted coins into two piles, moved three from one to the other,
then covered both when Marek came near.

"I wasn't."

"You were."

"I was walking."

"Elsewhere."

He walked elsewhere.

I looked at my Advocate pages for perhaps twenty minutes.

Not memorizing.

Mostly.

I restored two lines I liked.

Then removed one because Lorn was right and it made the Advocate sound
too eager.

I practiced the first entrance once with Iven after he woke.

"Your Majesty, I appear on behalf of the merchants of the eastern road."

"Fine."

"Whose three wagons of wool were seized at the north gate."

"Fine."

"Under an order bearing your seal."

"Fine."

"The soldiers were diverted FROM the bridge."

He stared.

"That is later."

"I know."

"Then why?"

"Checking."

"Stop checking."

Good advice.

I ignored it privately.

By late afternoon the confidence bucket was gone.

The roof man had taken it.

Bessa had sold sixty-four tickets.

Marek knew.

Of course.

Teren and Bessa had apparently reached terms because they were no longer
arguing about terms. They had moved on to arguing about whether two
children counted as one seat if they shared.

Bessa said no.

Teren said he did not care.

Bessa said then stop talking.

He did.

I respected her.

The second show began without rain.

That alone changed it.

People arrived less wet and louder.

Some had seen us the night before.

I knew because one man near the front said, "Bridge," when I came out as
Advocate.

Not loudly.

Loud enough.

I heard him.

Fuck.

I entered on time.

Order came free cleanly.

Seal remained unbroken.

First line correct.

North.

Wool.

Three.

Marek looked at me.

"And you have come to complain about my handwriting?"

Same line as yesterday.

He knew I knew it.

The audience from yesterday knew it too.

I had an answer ready.

That was the problem.

I said, "Your handwriting has seized three wagons."

Nothing.

Not dead.

Just nothing.

Yesterday's stealing wool had been better.

I felt the urge to fix it.

Did not.

The Advocate was scared.

Not angry.

I held the order with both hands for half a second before remembering I
needed a crutch.

Awkward.

Real.

"The men at the gate believed this was yours."

Marek's King leaned forward.

"And you do not?"

I looked at the seal.

"I would prefer not to."

That was not written.

The room went quiet.

Not bad quiet.

Different.

Marek stopped smiling.

"Careful."

There.

That was the scene.

For perhaps thirty seconds I forgot about yesterday.

Then I reached the bridge.

I knew FROM.

I knew it so well I nearly smiled.

The Chancellor said the soldiers had been moved for the crown's
protection.

My line.

"They were diverted from the bridge."

Correct.

Normal volume.

Good.

The man in front whispered, "From."

His wife hit his arm.

I almost laughed.

Did not.

Then the Chancellor changed his next line.

Yesterday he had denied issuing the order.

Tonight he said, "And who told you I gave such an instruction?"

That was not my page.

I knew the answer.

The seal.

No.

The witness.

Was there a witness?

I looked at Serra.

She was not in this scene yet.

Marek waited.

The Chancellor waited.

I said, "The man who obeyed it."

Good enough.

"Name him."

Fuck.

I did not know his name.

Maybe he had one.

Maybe not.

I said, "Bring him here and I'll ask."

Audience laughed.

The Chancellor smiled.

"Convenient."

"Very."

Then Marek cut across us.

"Enough."

He restored the scene himself.

Good.

I had preserved bridge and lost witness.

Progress.

Shopkeeper was cleaner.

No jurisdiction.

Not once.

Iven tried to tempt me.

He said, "By what authority do you demand payment?"

I looked at him.

He looked innocent.

Audience waited.

I said, "Mine."

Small laugh.

"Is that legal?"

"Pay me and find out."

Better.

Backstage I hit him with the cloth cap.

"Never again."

"You said that yesterday."

"So did you."

Sword was worse.

Not terrible.

Worse.

I expected the belt to catch.

It didn't.

I expected Serra to call me stubborn.

She didn't.

I expected Marek to enter with the extra sword.

He did not.

The scene felt strangely empty because all my remembered accidents were
absent.

I started anticipating Serra.

She changed the rhythm.

Slower.

I answered too quickly twice.

The second time she simply looked at me.

I stopped.

She waited.

Then gave the line.

I answered after it.

No joke.

No rescue.

Better.

Later, when she asked what sort of legendary sword allowed himself to be
stolen, I had yesterday's advocate joke waiting.

I could feel it.

Apparently I need an advocate.

The line was there.

I did not say it.

I said, "The portable kind."

Audience laughed.

Serra said, "Convenient."

That word again.

Different scene.

Different actor.

I laughed inside.

Not outside.

The second Advocate entrance went almost correctly.

Almost.

I did not announce FROM.

I did not stop Orin.

I did not break evidence.

I delivered the important facts.

I also played the Advocate so carefully afraid of the King that the
Merchant Council sounded as though they had sent a nervous clerk.

Backstage Lorn was not there to complain.

I could hear him anyway.

The final Shopkeeper appearance came.

I remembered it.

That alone felt suspicious.

I entered.

Three lines.

All correct.

Nobody laughed.

Not once.

I came offstage.

Iven said, "Good."

I stared.

"Nothing happened."

"Exactly."

I wanted to argue.

Then the final scene needed him and he left.

The show ended.

Applause.

Louder than last night.

More people.

I did not know how many.

Marek did.

"Eighty-two."

Of course.

Bessa was already smiling before the bows finished.

Teren was not.

That meant money was happening.

Backstage, people drank water and changed clothes and found missing
things.

The blue poison jar was exactly where it belonged.

Nobody trusted it.

Pell checked the boot anyway.

Empty.

Nessa removed Serra's glove and announced it salvageable.

Apparently the glove had nearly become the new red dress.

Teren paid.

Five copper.

I counted because I was tired.

Still five.

"Advocate improved," he said.

I looked at him.

That was dangerously close to praise.

Then he added, "Sword worse."

There.

Balance restored.

"Five copper."

"Yes."

"Eighty-two people."

"Not your eighty-two."

"Some of them liked me."

"Some liked the roof."

"Roof didn't perform."

"It stayed up."

Fair.

Bessa came over.

"Tomorrow."

Teren said, "No."

She stopped.

Marek stopped.

I stopped.

Bessa said, "Eighty-two."

"I know."

"Ninety tomorrow."

"Maybe."

"Same show."

"No."

"Better terms."

"We leave."

"When?"

"Morning."

Marek made a wounded noise.

Bessa ignored him.

"Where?"

Teren looked toward Rinna.

Rinna said, "East road."

That was new.

"Since when?" I asked.

Nobody answered me.

Teren said, "Private house. Afternoon tomorrow if the road holds."

Marek recovered instantly.

"Money?"

"Silver."

The room changed.

Not dramatically.

Enough.

Marek stopped smiling for half a second.

Orin looked over.

Rinna stopped tying a bag.

Even Nessa glanced up.

I said, "How much silver?"

Teren looked at me.

"Not yours."

Of course.

"What do I get?"

"Depends what they want."

"Who are they?"

"People with a house."

"Useful."

Bessa said, "I can beat their gate."

Teren shook his head.

"They already paid half."

Silver.

Half.

That was different.

Bessa looked genuinely annoyed now, not theatrically annoyed.

"Come back."

"Maybe."

"When?"

Teren smiled.

That was cruel.

"Before we leave."

Bessa told him to get out of her hall.

He thanked her.

She did not mean tonight.

Probably.

The company began packing before the audience had fully left.

Not everything.

Enough.

The long box stayed where Davin had put it until he came for it himself.

I did not ask.

I had learned one thing.

Maybe.

A woman from the audience gave Serra a little bunch of white flowers.

No money.

Serra looked surprised.

She smelled them.

Then gave one to Nessa.

Nessa put it behind her ear without stopping her work.

The rest stayed with Serra.

Marek received nothing and complained.

Bessa gave him half a heel of bread.

He accepted.

I put my five copper away.

The brass clasp for Lyssa was still in the same pocket, wrapped in a
scrap of paper.

My letter was already heading south.

Tomorrow we were heading east.

Private house.

Silver, somewhere above my pay.

I should have wanted details.

I did.

But not enough to chase Teren while he was arguing with Davin about
departure time.

I ate soup.

I helped Pell find the wooden fish.

It had been packed with hats.

Nobody knew why.

Then I went upstairs to sleep before someone invented another role.

Apparently we were leaving in the morning.

# CHAPTER 159

## THE PRIVATE PLAYER

Bessa tried again before breakfast.

"Ninety."

Teren was tying a ledger shut.

"No."

"Ninety-five."

"No."

"One hundred if I put benches along the rear wall."

"No."

Marek looked up from a roll.

"One hundred?"

Bessa pointed at him.

"Stay."

Teren said, "No."

Marek looked wounded.

"I have value."

"You have a wagon."

"Less value."

Bessa ignored him and followed Teren through the bakery while he
collected three different things from three different people.

"Better gate."

"Maybe."

"Full house."

"Maybe."

"You know my roof."

"Unfortunately."

"It stayed up."

"So far."

"That's performance."

I looked at Teren.

He did not look at me.

Bessa had stolen my argument.

She finally stopped at the door.

"When you come back, I want first date."

"If we come back."

"When."

Teren opened the door.

Bessa said, "Coward."

"Manager."

Then he went outside.

That appeared to be the end of negotiations.

For perhaps six minutes.

Packing had started before I woke.

I knew this because my bag was no longer beside my bed.

I found it downstairs in the wrong wagon.

Again.

Rinna found me finding it.

"Other."

"I know."

"Then why is it here?"

"I didn't put it here."

She looked at Pell.

Pell was carrying three hats and a loaf of bread.

"No," he said.

Nobody had accused him.

Rinna moved my bag.

I held the wagon flap.

This counted as improvement.

The company came apart from the town in pieces.

Nessa collected the red dress, two gloves, one shoe that belonged to
nobody currently present, and a length of blue ribbon she claimed was
ours.

The baker claimed it was his daughter's.

Nessa returned it immediately.

Rinna settled something with the bakery woman using coins I did not see
clearly. The woman then pushed a sack of yesterday's rolls into Rinna's
arms.

"Stale."

"Food."

"Exactly."

Rinna accepted.

Marek tried to take one.

Rinna slapped his hand.

"Travel."

"I am traveling."

"Later."

Davin arrived with the wagons already harnessed.

I did not know when he had left.

The long iron-cornered box came out last.

Davin and two local men moved it upright, slow and careful. Nobody asked
what was inside. Nobody joked. They secured it against the wagon frame.

I watched the knot.

Did not touch it.

Davin noticed me not touching it.

"Good."

That was all.

Orin was ready before Marek.

This disturbed everyone.

He had a coat today.

Both shoes matched.

The bruise on his jaw had darkened.

Marek stared.

"What happened to you?"

"No."

"You can't answer that with no."

"No."

"Was it furniture?"

"No."

"Was it attractive furniture?"

Orin climbed into the wagon.

"No."

Serra came from somewhere down the street carrying a small wrapped
parcel and the remains of the white flowers. Two blossoms had survived.
One was tucked through a buttonhole in her coat.

She said goodbye to nobody I knew.

A woman across the street raised two fingers.

Serra raised two back.

Then she climbed aboard.

Iven was annoyingly ready.

Pell was not.

Pell was missing.

We discovered this when Teren counted people.

Not loudly.

He looked at the wagons.

"Where is Pell?"

Nessa said, "Bakery."

We checked the bakery.

No Pell.

Rinna said, "Hall."

Marek volunteered to retrieve him.

Teren said, "No."

"Why?"

"You'll disappear too."

"Unfair."

"Accurate."

I went because I could not carry anything useful and therefore
apparently had time.

Pell was at the hall.

He was under the stage.

Of course.

"Why?"

"Fish."

I closed my eyes.

"The wooden fish."

"Yes."

"Why is it under the stage?"

"Don't know."

"Why do we need it?"

"Don't know."

"Then leave it."

He looked offended.

"It's ours."

That was apparently enough.

We found the fish wedged behind a support where someone had pushed it
with a boot.

Its spring still worked.

Pell carried it back like rescued livestock.

Bessa saw us crossing the square.

"One hundred!"

"No," I said.

"I wasn't asking you."

"Good."

We left at nine.

Approximately.

Nine according to Teren.

Marek said it was still morning and therefore exact time was oppressive.

The road east was better than the ridge road for the first hour, then
became worse in a more expensive way.

Stone paving appeared in stretches, cracked where wagon wheels had
broken the edges. Drainage ditches had been dug properly and then
neglected. Large houses appeared farther apart from one another behind
walls, hedges, or fields.

The rain held off.

That helped.

Marek slept.

That also helped.

I sat near the rear of the second wagon with Serra, Pell, and a costume
trunk that smelled faintly of damp wool.

The brass clasp remained in my inner pocket.

I checked once after a hard rut.

Still there.

My money was divided now. Most in the inner pocket. A few copper
somewhere easier to reach. The five from last night had joined the rest.

Serra noticed me checking.

"Rich?"

"No."

"Then stop touching it."

"I wasn't touching money."

She looked at me.

I stopped touching the clasp too.

Pell slept with his head against the costume trunk.

The wooden fish was on his lap.

Every large bump made it twitch.

After the fourth time I covered it with a cloth.

Serra said, "Coward."

"It watches."

"It doesn't have eyes."

I uncovered it.

It had painted eyes.

Serra looked.

"Fair."

We stopped once for water.

Teren spoke with Davin and Rinna away from the wagons. I could not hear.

Orin ate one of the stale rolls.

Marek woke long enough to ask whether we had arrived.

"No," six people said.

He went back to sleep.

By early afternoon the road narrowed between two stone walls.

The house appeared gradually.

First the gate.

Then trees.

Then a long pale roof beyond them.

Not a palace.

Too practical.

The main building had been expanded at least twice. The central portion
was older stone with tall windows and a steep roof. A newer brick wing
extended east. Another lower range connected to stables and service
yards.

I looked at the join between the stone and brick.

Teren, riding ahead, turned in his seat.

"No."

"I didn't say anything."

"You leaned."

"I looked."

"Same thing."

The gatekeeper knew we were coming.

That was new.

At public halls we usually arrived and began proving we belonged there.

Here a man in a dark coat checked a written list.

"The players?"

Teren said, "Yes."

The man counted wagons.

Then people.

His eyes stopped on me for a fraction longer than anyone else.

Not rude.

Recognition.

"Good."

I did not like that word.

He waved us through.

The service yard behind the house was busier than the front had
suggested.

Cooks, stable workers, servants carrying linen, a boy rolling a barrel,
two women stripping leaves from herbs at an outdoor table, three dogs
who believed the wagons were personally offensive.

Nobody stopped working because actors arrived.

A woman in a dark green dress came down the service steps.

Not a servant, I thought.

Then she took a crate from the boy because he nearly dropped it.

Maybe.

She handed it to another worker.

"Teren?"

He climbed down.

"Lady Merra."

There.

Not servant.

Probably.

She was perhaps forty, with gray beginning at her temples and sleeves
plain enough to work in. She looked at the wagons before she looked at
us.

"You're late."

"Road."

"It's dry."

"Now."

She considered that.

"Fair."

Teren said, "Balance first."

She smiled.

"No."

"Then we're early."

"You're already in my yard."

"Still portable."

Marek woke.

He whispered, "Money."

Iven put a hand over his mouth.

Lady Merra heard anyway.

"Your king?"

Teren said, "Unfortunately."

She looked at Marek.

Marek removed Iven's hand.

"Majesty, privately."

"Not yet."

She looked back at Teren.

"Half after setup. Half after performance."

"You paid half already."

"Of the original."

"Which bought travel."

"Which bought arrival."

"Arrival happened."

"Setup hasn't."

Teren's expression changed slightly.

Not angry.

Working.

"What changed?"

"Guest count."

"How much?"

"Thirty-two."

"You said twenty."

"People marry."

Nobody reacted.

I looked at Serra.

She looked at me.

Lady Merra continued.

"My sister's daughter announced her engagement three days ago. The
dinner grew."

There.

Celebration.

Human-sized.

Teren said, "Thirty-two isn't a problem."

"The room is."

"Show me."

She did.

We entered through the service side, not the front.

The house was warm enough that my damp shirt became immediately
uncomfortable.

The performance room had probably never been intended for performance.

Long salon.

Polished floor.

Tall windows.

Fireplace at one end.

A small raised platform at the other, perhaps meant for musicians or
speeches.

Chairs were arranged in two shallow rows with tables behind them.

Too close.

Everything was too close.

I could have reached the front row with a crutch.

Marek whispered, "Excellent."

Serra said, "No."

The ceiling was high.

That was the only generous thing about it.

Teren walked the room once.

"Full play won't fit."

Lady Merra said, "I don't want the full play."

Of course.

"What do you want?"

"The King."

Marek straightened.

"The Princess."

Serra did not.

"The talking sword."

There.

Everyone looked at me.

I looked at the floor.

Lady Merra said, "And the creditor."

"Shopkeeper," I said.

"That."

Teren asked, "Who told you?"

"My nephew saw you in Carrow."

Which nephew?

Not important.

"He said the sword was a man with one leg."

There it was.

Not cruel.

Not even inaccurate enough to argue with.

Still.

Lady Merra looked directly at me now.

"You're Gregory?"

"Greg."

"Can you do both?"

I said, "Apparently."

Marek laughed.

Teren did not.

Lady Merra said, "Good. My father will like you."

That was worse somehow.

"Why?"

"He likes unusual things."

I looked at Teren.

Teren said, "No."

Lady Merra looked at him.

"No what?"

"No handling."

"I wasn't going to handle him."

"Good."

I looked at Teren again.

"Handling?"

"Later."

Lady Merra folded her arms.

"My father is seventy-one, half deaf, rude, and paying for the
engagement dinner. He likes performers who answer him."

"Answering is fine," Teren said.

"If he asks for another scene?"

"Depends."

"If he asks the sword to insult him?"

Marek said, "I can do that."

"No," Teren said.

Marek looked wounded.

Lady Merra smiled.

"What exactly did I buy?"

Teren began counting on his fingers.

"Forty minutes. Selected scenes. Six players. Music between if needed.
One additional piece if requested before we finish."

"An hour."

"Forty-five."

"Fifty."

"Food."

"Already included."

"For everyone."

She looked toward the yard.

"Actors and crew."

"Everyone."

"Fine."

"Wine?"

"For dinner guests."

"Beer?"

"For workers."

Marek whispered, "Workers."

Iven stepped on his foot.

Lady Merra said, "Fifty minutes."

"Forty-five plus one requested piece."

"Done."

"Balance before the requested piece."

She laughed.

"You are tiresome."

"Paid."

"Not yet."

They shook hands.

I had just watched Teren sell us without selling all of us.

That was interesting.

I did not say it.

The house steward appeared.

This man was definitely a steward because he looked offended by the
existence of unlisted objects.

His name was Harl.

He wanted the wagons moved.

Davin wanted the long box kept under cover.

Harl wanted nothing blocking the service arch.

They solved this without me.

The box went into a dry carriage bay, upright.

Nobody recognized it.

Nobody opened it.

Good.

"The actors can eat in the side room," Harl said.

I went with the actors.

Nobody corrected me.

The side room had a long table, bread, cold sliced meat, cheese, apples,
pickled onions, and a pot of something thick with barley.

Marek stopped in the doorway.

"Oh."

Rinna said, "Behave."

"I am."

"You haven't started yet."

The food was better than our last three meals.

Not impossibly better.

Just enough butter to reveal money.

The bread was fresh.

There was meat nobody had brought as a gift after a show.

There was more cheese than twelve people needed.

A servant set down another plate.

Rinna looked at it.

Then at the first plate.

Then at the servant.

"Does that stay?"

"Until dinner."

"And after?"

The servant shrugged.

"Kitchen decides."

Rinna nodded.

She had learned something.

Nessa touched the tablecloth.

Not dramatically.

Two fingers.

Then she looked at the curtains.

Pell followed her eyes.

"No."

"I didn't."

"You did."

"Fabric."

"Not ours."

"Obviously."

Marek had already found the beer.

Teren took it from him.

"After."

"I am a worker."

"Debatable."

Lady Merra entered before we finished eating.

"Change."

Teren looked up.

"What?"

"My father wants the sword at dinner."

"You bought after dinner."

"He wants it during."

"No."

She looked surprised.

Not offended.

Just unused to no arriving so quickly.

"It would amuse him."

"It would put Gregory between tables with people eating."

She looked at me.

I had not considered that.

Crutches, chairs, wine, servants, plates.

Bad.

"He can sit."

Teren looked at the salon again through the open door.

"At the end of the room."

"Near my father."

"End."

"Near."

"Then move your father."

She laughed.

Actually laughed.

"Nobody moves my father."

Teren said, "Then your father waits."

That could have gone badly.

Instead Lady Merra looked delighted.

"I see why my nephew liked you."

"He didn't see me."

"He complained about you."

"Better."

She left.

Marek said, "I want private money forever."

Teren gave him back his bread, not his beer.

Setup took less equipment and more thought.

No scenery.

Nothing tall.

No rear entrance.

The salon had two doors, but one led directly into a corridor guests
would use. The other led toward the side room.

Serra and Marek could use both.

I could not cross behind anything because there was nothing to cross
behind.

For Sword, they put my mounting board beside the fireplace.

I stared.

"Hot."

Davin moved it three feet.

"Better."

For Shopkeeper, a table and chair.

Lady Merra's steward wanted one of the house tables.

Teren said no.

Harl said ours looked poor.

Teren said, "Shopkeeper."

Harl looked at the battered table.

"Fair."

The guests began arriving before we were ready.

That was also different.

Public audiences waited outside.

Private audiences belonged to the building.

They wandered through.

A man with silver at his collar stopped to watch Pell pin a sleeve.

Two girls stared openly at me.

One whispered something.

The other whispered back.

Then both ran away.

A servant carrying wine said, "Sword?"

I said, "Sometimes."

He nodded.

"Good."

Again.

I was beginning to dislike being good before doing anything.

An older man entered using two sticks and no patience.

Seventy-one, presumably.

Lady Merra's father.

He had white hair, a heavy waistcoat, and the expression of someone who
had spent decades discovering that people eventually moved if he
continued forward.

Everyone moved.

He stopped in front of me.

Not close enough to be rude.

Close enough to inspect.

"You're the sword."

"Sometimes."

"One leg."

"Consistently."

He barked a laugh.

Good.

Not mine.

His.

"How'd you lose it?"

There were thirty possible answers.

None belonged in the salon.

I said, "Badly."

He laughed again.

Lady Merra appeared behind him.

"Father."

"What?"

"Don't interrogate the actors."

He looked at her.

"I'm paying them."

Teren appeared from the side room.

"You're paying for a performance."

The old man looked at him.

"Difference?"

"Several silver."

Silence.

Then the old man laughed harder than before.

"Fine."

He pointed one stick at me.

"Insult me later."

Teren said, "If the scene earns it."

The old man looked delighted.

I was less certain.

He walked away.

I said quietly, "Several silver?"

Teren said, "Not yours."

"Still."

"Work."

Then he left.

Forty-five minutes.

Selected scenes.

No Advocate.

Thank every god.

Sword.

Shopkeeper.

Marek's King.

Serra's Princess.

Orin in two short pieces.

Iven in Shopkeeper and another scene.

Music between.

One requested piece after payment balance.

This was not the play.

It was pieces of the play arranged around people who had eaten too much.

Dinner ran late.

Of course.

We waited in the side room dressed and ready while servants carried
plates past us.

The smell became cruel.

Marek ate another apple.

Nessa took it from him after one bite because his costume had pale
cuffs.

He finished it by leaning forward while she held it.

Nobody found this strange.

The household staff moved faster as the guests moved slower.

I watched a young servant balance six plates along one arm.

That was more impressive than anything I had done as Advocate.

When the salon finally cleared enough for chairs to turn toward us, the
guests brought wine with them.

Thirty-two had become thirty-five.

Harl looked offended by arithmetic.

Lady Merra looked pleased.

Teren looked at the room.

Then at us.

"Short."

"How short?" Marek asked.

"Until they stop listening."

"That is not time."

Iven said, "Theatre."

I hated him.

We began with the King.

Not me.

Good.

The guests talked through the first minute.

Not all.

Enough.

Marek pushed louder.

Teren, from the side, shook his head once.

Marek stopped pushing.

Serra entered.

The room changed.

Not silent.

More directed.

She had the red dress.

Apparently rich people liked red too.

Then Sword.

I was mounted beside the fireplace.

Three feet away from an old man holding wine.

Lady Merra's father.

Of course.

Serra took me.

The old man said, "That's him."

Serra looked at him.

Then at me.

"Apparently."

The room laughed.

That was not written.

Fine.

I said, "I was hoping for a less observant audience."

The old man laughed first.

Others followed.

Serra carried me into the scene.

Different distance.

Different danger.

I could see every face.

One woman was still eating a pear.

A man near the window whispered to someone through my line.

A child sat on the floor because chairs were apparently optional when
wealthy.

Serra asked what sort of sword complained about being stolen.

I said, "An expensive one."

Lady Merra's father called, "How expensive?"

There.

Customer.

Audience.

Patron.

Old man.

I looked toward Teren.

He did nothing.

That meant answer.

"More than your daughter told you."

The room exploded.

Lady Merra covered her face.

Her father slapped one stick against the floor.

Teren looked at the ceiling.

I had insulted him.

Apparently the scene had earned it.

We continued.

Not cleanly.

The old man interrupted twice more.

Serra answered one.

Ignored one.

Marek entered and immediately began playing to him.

That worked until it didn't.

The rest of the room started disappearing.

Teren coughed once.

Marek heard.

He turned back into the scene.

Interesting.

Shopkeeper came later.

The table looked poor enough to satisfy Harl.

Iven entered.

Lady Merra's father recognized me without the sword.

"Creditor!"

I said, "Unfortunately."

He said, "Charge him double."

Iven looked at him.

"Why?"

"Because I can afford it."

I said, "Then you're next."

That got him.

The room laughed.

Iven said, "Take him first."

"Older debt."

The old man raised his wine.

Fine.

The scene moved.

Private audiences did not know when to stay out of it because staying
out had never been part of the agreement.

That was the difference.

Or one difference.

A woman asked Iven directly whether his character had a wife.

He answered, "Not anymore."

I had never heard that.

Neither had he, probably.

She asked why.

He pointed at me.

"Debt."

I said, "I don't take wives."

"Good policy."

"Expensive."

Jurisdiction was dead.

Expensive survived.

Fine.

We reached the end.

Applause came from thirty-five people and six servants standing in the
corridor.

The servants were louder.

Marek bowed toward them.

Correct.

Lady Merra approached Teren before anyone could request anything.

She handed him a small purse.

He weighed it.

Opened it.

Counted.

Not secretly.

Silver flashed.

More than one.

Less than a fortune.

Enough that I understood why we had left Bessa's ninety.

Teren closed the purse.

Lady Merra said, "One more."

"One."

"My father wants the sword."

"Of course."

"Five minutes."

"Seven."

She blinked.

"You negotiate upward?"

"He'll interrupt."

She laughed.

"Seven."

Teren looked at me.

"Sword."

I said, "Do I get more?"

Lady Merra looked interested.

Teren said, "Two extra copper."

I stared.

"For seven minutes?"

"For requested piece."

Marek said, "I can be Sword."

"No," three people said.

Lady Merra's father shouted from the salon:

"Bring me the expensive one!"

I held out my hand.

"Two copper."

Teren put two copper into it before the scene.

That was new.

I pocketed them.

"Now?"

"Now."

I went back to the fireplace.

Apparently private money was different.
