Fera watched them.

"You're not blocking that stair."

Teren said, "We won't."

"You are."

We were.

She made us move two benches and the prop basket.

Ten minutes later three passengers came up the stair exactly where the
basket had been.

Local people knew where the future happened.

I was getting used to that.

By afternoon the gallery smelled of lamp oil, horse, beer, and wet wool.

A light rain had started. Not enough to stop coaches. Enough to make
everyone who arrived want shelter.

That helped.

Teren changed the bill.

"King first."

Marek said, "Correct."

"Short."

"Incorrect."

"Widow. Shopkeeper."

"Why King first?"

"People are arriving."

"I can hold them."

"No. You can be loud while they sit down."

Marek considered that.

"Also correct."

The blue lamp was for Widow.

I was not in Widow.

That meant I had a job.

Nessa showed me the ordinary lamp beside it.

"At the turn, Pell shutters this."

Pell touched the shutter.

"Then Rinna cues blue."

Rinna was below arguing with Fera about where the collection bowl could
go.

I said, "What do I do?"

"Nothing."

"I hung it."

"Yes."

"So I'm done."

"Until it slips."

"Does it slip?"

"If you hang it badly."

I looked at the hook.

Nessa walked away.

I looked at the hook harder.

The failed throw blank was in my pocket.

I had taken it out twice on the road that morning.

Not to do anything.

Just to look at the marks.

They were faint and irritating. A shallow line split near the middle,
curved toward the bent end, then stopped. I could not tell whether the
split mattered or whether it was where Varo had decided the piece was
already ruined.

I had tried comparing it to Hessa's diagrams in memory.

That had been useless.

Hessa drew mana.

Varo marked metal.

Nessa hid glass.

Pell used a tube.

All of them could make something happen outside the body.

Only one of those things was the problem Hessa and I had actually been
testing.

I put the blank away.

Marek was practicing nothing.

He stood at the far end of the gallery wearing half his King coat while
eating a meat pie.

"Preparation," he said.

"Food."

"Both."

"Growth."

"Fuck you."

He had bought the pie himself.

I was proud of him.

I did not tell him.

By six, the gallery had thirty people in it.

Then forty.

Some were travelers waiting for coaches. Some were staying at the inn.
Some were locals who had heard there were players. A group of carters
stood along the open rail because they did not want to pay for drinks.

Nobody had paid to see us.

Fera had.

That changed the room.

Teren stood near the stair and watched people settle.

A coach horn sounded outside.

He waited.

The coach came in.

Passengers climbed the stairs.

He waited.

Fera looked at him.

He held up one finger.

A serving girl crossed with six bowls.

Then Teren nodded to Marek.

Marek walked into the middle of the gallery and said, "I have inherited
a kingdom."

A carter said, "Sorry."

Marek looked at him.

"So am I."

The room turned.

Not all at once.

Enough.

The King piece was short.

Marek was good.

That still annoyed me sometimes.

He could take a room that was not interested and make his annoyance seem
like their fault.

Iven joined him.

They did the debt section.

A coachman came up the stairs during it.

Marek moved half a step without looking.

The coachman passed behind him.

No collision.

No pause.

No lesson.

Just work.

The piece ended.

Some people clapped.

A child near the rail asked whether Marek was really a king.

Marek said, "Temporarily."

That got more laughter than the ending.

Widow came next.

Serra entered in dark cloth.

Orin sat on a bench with his head down.

The first part of the piece was ordinary light.

Warm wall lamps.

Rain outside.

People shifting.

A cup dropped downstairs.

Then Serra said, "You left the room warm."

Pell closed the shutter on the ordinary lamp.

Not dark.

Less warm.

Rinna touched the cue mark.

I did not see mana.

I was not looking for it.

The smoky glass changed.

Barely.

The lamp behind it cooled from yellow toward a thin blue-white.

Serra's face changed with it.

Not shape.

Not color exactly.

The shadows under her eyes deepened. The dark cloth stopped looking
brown and became almost black.

Orin lifted his head.

Behind him, Pell pulled a gray cloth away from the wall.

That was all.

A gray cloth.

It revealed pale stone.

The audience went quiet.

I knew the wall was real.

I knew the blue was a prepared glass.

I knew Pell had hidden the pale stone with cloth before the show.

I knew Serra had turned her body so the colder lamp took one side of her
face.

I knew Orin had waited until the room changed before looking up.

The room knew none of that separately.

It knew the room had become colder.

It had not.

That was the strange part.

The rain was real.

The pale stone was real.

Serra's face was real.

The shadow was real.

The lamp was really bluer.

Nothing in front of them needed to be false.

The cold was.

A woman pulled her shawl tighter.

I stared at her.

Nessa hit my arm.

"Hook."

The glass had shifted.

Almost nothing.

One corner had slipped forward.

I reached up and steadied the frame.

Not the prepared line.

The frame.

The edge disappeared again.

The woman kept watching Serra.

Nobody watched me.

That mattered more than I wanted it to.

Widow ended with Serra turning away from Orin.

Pell opened the ordinary lamp shutter.

Rinna released the cue.

Warm yellow returned.

People moved again.

Someone breathed loudly.

A man near the stair said, "Fuck."

Fera smiled.

Not at us.

At the room.

Then she went downstairs because someone was shouting about a horse.

Teren pointed at me.

Shopkeeper.

I had about twelve seconds.

I had been watching the lamp.

I had not put on my coat.

"Fuck."

Pell threw it at me.

I caught one sleeve.

The other folded under.

I went out wearing it wrong.

Iven saw.

His mouth twitched.

I said, "You owe me money."

He said, "You appear to owe your tailor."

The room laughed.

I looked down.

One side of my coat was tucked under my arm.

"Separate account."

More laughter.

Good.

Then I forgot the next line.

Not all of it.

The first three words.

Iven waited.

I could hear the rain.

I could hear somebody downstairs dragging something heavy.

I said, "You have delayed payment."

Wrong line.

Right information.

Iven answered.

We continued.

The scene did not die.

I stopped trying to find the missing words.

The Shopkeeper wanted money.

Iven did not have it.

That was true enough.

Halfway through, a man at the rail said, "Take his boots."

I said, "I have standards."

The man looked at my peg.

I saw him decide whether to say something.

He did not.

Iven said, "Do you?"

I said, "No."

That got him.

He laughed.

Actually laughed.

Then had to turn it into a cough.

The audience saw that too.

We finished.

Teren cut the last planned exchange because another coach horn sounded.

We were off before the passengers came up.

Twenty-three minutes.

Close enough.

Fera paid Rinna fifteen copper.

No argument.

She also sent up the two pitchers.

Marek had already acquired a cup.

Rinna slapped his hand.

"Company."

"I am company."

"Later."

Fera looked at the blue lamp.

"Do that every time?"

Nessa said, "No."

"Why not?"

"Wrong room."

Fera looked around her own gallery.

"What makes this right?"

Nessa pointed at the open rail.

"Rain."

Fera looked at the rain.

Then at the pale stone wall.

Then at Serra.

"Huh."

She went downstairs.

I followed Nessa to the lamp.

"Was the rain important?"

"Yes."

"You didn't make the rain."

"No."

"The stone?"

"Wall."

"Serra's face?"

"Serra."

"The cloth?"

"Pell."

"The blue?"

"Glass."

"And people felt cold."

Nessa looked at me.

"Did you?"

"No."

She waited.

"Maybe."

"Then stop talking."

She took the glass down.

I said, "Nothing was fake."

Pell, carrying the gray cloth, said, "I'm fake."

Nessa said, "You're unpaid if you tear that."

He folded it.

I stood there.

Nothing was fake.

That was not exactly true.

The room had lied.

No.

We had.

No.

We had shown them things that were true and let them make the wrong
thing out of it.

Rain.

Stone.

Blue light.

A widow saying the room had been warm.

A woman tightening her shawl because she already knew rain meant cold.

The effect had not needed to create cold.

It had needed the room to remember cold.

"Greg."

Teren.

I turned.

"Bowls."

"What?"

"Take them down."

There were empty cups and two bowls on the bench.

I took them down.

That was probably healthier.

The kitchen had a flat iron plate with a small red mark worked into one
corner. A cook set a pot on it, touched the mark, and went back to
cutting onions.

The pot began steaming.

I watched for two seconds.

The cook said, "Move."

I moved.

Outside, the rain had thickened.

Davin had put canvas over the wagon loads.

The long box was under it with everything else.

Dry.

Upright.

Uninteresting.

Good.

Rinna found me near the stable.

"Two copper."

She handed me two.

"Show?"

"Rellin."

"Oh."

"Your share."

I looked at the coins.

"Now?"

"Unless you want me to keep them."

"No."

"Then now."

"How much did Marek get?"

"Ask Marek."

"Serra?"

"Greg."

"Fine."

She left.

I put the two copper away.

The failed throw blank clicked against them.

Wrong pocket again.

I moved it.

Marek came out carrying a bowl.

"Hot food."

"Did you buy that?"

"No."

"Steal it?"

"Relationship."

"With who?"

"The cook."

"What's her name?"

He looked at the bowl.

"Soup."

"Strong relationship."

He ate.

We slept in the coach yard for three copper company, wagons and horses
included, no rooms.

The rain stopped sometime after midnight.

In the morning the town smelled washed and metallic.

Davin had us moving early.

Fera sold Rinna bread.

Nessa bought another wick.

Serra returned from somewhere with soap that smelled like pine.

Orin was already at the wagon when I woke.

I did not ask.

At the west fork, the green road marker was dull in daylight.

The letters still said:

CARROW ROAD.

Teren stood beside it.

"One town if we go straight," he said.

Rinna asked, "Work?"

"Maybe."

She looked at him.

He smiled.

She did not.

"Two days?" I asked.

Davin said, "If road."

Everyone looked at him.

He looked back.

"Road."

Marek groaned.

I looked west.

Two days if road.

Maybe three.

Maybe work.

Maybe not.

Lyssa was somewhere at the other end of that direction.

Hessa too.

I touched the failed throw blank through my pocket.

I knew what I wanted to ask Hessa now.

Not how to make a room cold.

We had not made the room cold.

I wanted to know how little had to be real before the rest of it became
true to somebody watching.

That was probably not the right question.

Hessa would frown.

Good.

I had time to make it worse.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 174

## THE RETURNER

We did not perform in the next town.

Teren tried.

That was different.

By noon we had reached a place called Brant, which had one stone bridge,
two inns, a tannery, a smith, and a square too small to deserve the
word. Teren went into the larger inn. Rinna went into the smaller one.
Marek found a woman selling meat pies.

The rest of us waited beside the wagons.

Ten minutes later Teren came out.

"No."

Rinna came out across the square.

"No."

Marek came back with a pie.

"Yes."

Teren looked at him.

"What?"

"Different negotiation."

We kept moving.

That should not have surprised me.

It did.

For most of the trip, every place had become work if we waited long
enough, asked enough people, accepted enough mud, or stood beside enough
cheese.

Brant did not want us.

A man was repairing the bridge rail with a stone-setting tool. It looked
like a short iron mallet with a pale mark down the handle. He tapped
mortar between two stones, touched the mark with his thumb, and the wet
seam tightened darker around the edge.

He did not want us either.

The road west left town between the tannery and a field full of geese.

Pell said, "We could have done the goose piece."

"We don't have a goose piece," I said.

"We could."

"With what goose?"

He pointed at the field.

"That goose."

One of the geese charged the fence.

I said, "No."

Pell laughed.

"What?"

"Real goose."

"So?"

"Bad actor."

"Good goose."

"Exactly."

Nessa, walking ahead of us, said, "Don't steal livestock."

"I wasn't."

Pell said, "He was casting."

"I was not casting."

"Different casting."

I hated him.

The goose followed us along the fence until the road bent away.

For the next hour I thought about the goose more than I should have.

Not magically.

Practically.

If we wanted a goose onstage, a real goose would be the most truthful
possible goose.

It would also shit where it wanted, leave when it wanted, bite Marek,
and refuse every entrance.

A wooden goose would be false and better.

Unless the point was the sound.

Then maybe you did not need a goose at all.

I stopped there.

Mostly because Davin said, "Rear."

I went to the rear wagon.

He had heard something in the left wheel.

I had not.

He crouched beside it while I watched the road.

A freight wagon approached from behind. I moved our water bucket, then
the small prop basket Pell had left too near the wheel.

Davin spun the wheel a fraction.

"Again," I said.

He looked at me.

"What?"

"The sound."

"I know."

Right.

He was not asking me.

I watched the lane.

The freight wagon passed.

Its driver lifted two fingers.

I did the same.

Davin tightened something I could not see.

"Done."

We walked.

By late afternoon, the road had widened enough for two wagons to pass
without negotiation. Old mile stones appeared at intervals. Most were
worn nearly blank.

One still had enough letters.

CARROW 19.

I stopped.

Marek nearly hit me.

"Again?"

"Nineteen."

"I can count."

"Can you?"

"Fuck off."

Nineteen miles was not two days.

Not really.

Not if the road held.

Davin looked at the stone.

"Tomorrow."

Teren said, "Tomorrow."

That moved through me strangely.

Not excitement exactly.

Something less useful.

I checked my coat.

The brass clasp was there.

The failed throw blank was in my trouser pocket.

I checked that too.

Pell saw.

"Still garbage?"

"Yes."

"Good."

"Why good?"

"If it became expensive while you walked, I'd be worried."

We camped that night at a road house six miles past Brant.

Not an inn.

A road house.

The distinction was apparently that an inn had rooms and a road house
had walls you could stand near while paying for everything separately.

The yard cost two copper for both wagons.

Water was free.

Hay was not.

Hot stew was three copper a bowl, which meant none of us bought it
except Marek.

He stood beside the cook fire holding his bowl.

"Personal expenditure."

"You already used that."

"It remains accurate."

Rinna bought bread and a pot of beans for the company.

We ate under a lean-to while rain threatened and failed to happen.

A courier stopped after dark.

His satchel had a waxed flap with a narrow prepared seal stitched into
the leather. When he closed it, the line flashed once and went dull.

I watched.

He noticed.

"No."

"I didn't ask."

"You were going to."

"How does it know it's closed?"

"It doesn't."

That was interesting.

"What does it know?"

He stared at me.

"I don't know. I carry letters."

Then he went inside.

That was probably healthier too.

Serra laughed into her bread.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You laughed."

"I did."

"At me."

"Probably."

She ate.

Across the yard, Pell and Nessa were repairing the hem of Marek's King
coat. Orin sat on an overturned bucket talking quietly with the
road-house owner. Davin had disappeared into the stable. Teren and Rinna
were arguing about whether to leave before sunrise or merely at sunrise.

Nobody was discussing my questions.

I liked that.

I took the failed throw blank out.

Not to use it.

There was nothing to use.

The courier's seal had made me think about the marked line.

That was all.

The preparation marks were easier to see near the fire.

One line.

A branch.

A curve.

Stop.

I knew nothing.

That was becoming clearer.

I had spent weeks learning to draw mana under Hessa's supervision. I
could shape what I felt. I could repeat that much. We had tried to make
something outside me answer.

Three times.

Nothing we could establish.

Varo could mark a piece of metal so that, if she finished it correctly,
a tiny cue would make a sound seem to come from the wrong place.

The troupe could make a room feel cold with rain, stone, cloth, a lamp,
and a woman turning her face.

Pell could make a ghost with a tube.

A real goose was worse than a fake goose.

These did not fit together.

That was probably why I kept trying to fit them together.

Marek sat beside me with his stew.

"You look stupid."

"I'm thinking."

"Same."

"How much did that cost?"

"Do not make this about money."

"Three copper?"

He protected the bowl.

"Leave me."

I did.

Later, I checked the clasp again.

That was worse.

The little brass leaves were still wrapped.

I had bought them days ago.

Long enough that the purchase had stopped feeling like a decision and
started feeling like an object I was responsible for delivering.

I imagined giving it to Lyssa.

Then I imagined explaining why I had carried it halfway across the road
network instead of giving it to her immediately like a normal person.

Then I stopped imagining.

The road house had a loft.

We did not have the loft.

We had the yard.

I slept under the wagon.

In the morning, something screamed in the trees.

I woke hard enough to hit my shoulder on wood.

"What the fuck?"

Pell was already awake.

"Fox."

"That was not a fox."

"Fox."

"No."

Davin, somewhere near the horses, said, "Fox."

I lay back down.

It screamed again.

That was terrible.

I had heard foxes before.

Apparently not that fox.

Marek crawled out from a blanket.

"What died?"

"Nothing," Pell said.

"Then why is it making that sound?"

"Fox."

Marek stared toward the trees.

I said, "Good stage sound."

Pell looked at me.

"No."

"Why?"

"Too ugly."

"That's why."

Nessa threw a rolled stocking at him.

"Pack."

We packed.

The fox screamed once more while we were tying the rear cover.

I listened.

Not because I wanted to reproduce it.

Because I had been wrong about what a fox sounded like.

That felt relevant in a way I did not trust.

If somebody made that sound in a dark theatre and told me it was a woman
dying, I would believe them.

If they told me fox first, I would hear fox.

The sound did not change.

I did.

"Greg."

I looked up.

Rinna held out the Halver money.

"One."

"One what?"

"Copper."

"My share?"

"Yes."

"Only one?"

"You didn't eat company stew because there wasn't any."

"That doesn't seem related."

"It isn't."

I took the copper.

She moved on.

Pell got something too.

I did not count.

The road west was cold and clear.

No rain.

No fair traffic.

No market.

Just people moving.

A farmer with empty baskets.

Two women riding small horses.

A cart carrying glazed tiles.

A man walking six sheep and swearing at all of them equally.

At a low bridge, a prepared counter fixed to the toll post clicked once
for our first wagon and once for the second.

The keeper still looked outside and charged Rinna by hand.

I pointed at the counter.

"What does that do?"

"Counts."

"You count."

"Yes."

"Then why?"

"So I know if I counted."

That was the entire magical system.

I loved it.

We crossed.

Around midday the country began changing.

Not dramatically.

Fields became familiar in the way roads could become familiar before I
remembered why.

A ditch with white stones.

A stand of crooked trees.

A hill I had seen from the other direction.

Then a roadside shrine with one chipped corner.

I knew that shrine.

I stopped.

Serra looked back.

"You all right?"

"Yes."

She followed my eyes.

"Been here?"

"Yes."

She nodded.

Nothing else.

Carrow was no longer a direction.

It was around things I recognized.

We stopped for bread near a cluster of houses.

Teren did not ask for work.

That was when I knew we were actually going home.

Marek did ask whether there was hot food.

There was not.

He took it personally.

By midafternoon, the road grew busier.

Carrow traffic.

I knew that too.

Carts coming out with empty crates.

Workers going in.

A Guild wagon with the bronze mark painted on the side.

Two students in gray coats walking too slowly in the road.

A woman selling prepared lamp stones from a shoulder tray called prices
at passing carts.

Nobody cared that I had been gone.

Good.

Then the city appeared.

Not all of it.

First the outer roofs.

Then smoke.

Then the higher buildings.

Then the road widened.

I had expected something.

I did not know what.

Maybe for it to look smaller.

It did not.

Maybe for me to feel different.

I did.

That was less useful.

Teren called from ahead.

"Hall first."

Rinna said, "Wagons first."

Teren looked back.

"Hall after wagons."

Davin said, "Wagons."

The wagons won.

We entered Carrow through afternoon traffic.

A gate worker waved us through after looking at the company papers.

No recognition.

No problem.

A porter shouted at Marek to move.

Marek shouted back that he was moving.

He was not.

Serra disappeared at the first market turn.

Not metaphorically.

She said, "Later," and walked away.

Orin left two streets after that.

Pell asked where.

Nessa said, "Not your business."

Pell said, "I know."

He still watched Orin go.

I did too.

Then I saw East Market Hall at the end of the street.

That hit harder than the gate.

The building was exactly where we had left it.

Which was unreasonable.

I had crossed half the world.

Not actually.

Enough of it.

The hall had stayed still.

Davin took the wagons around back.

We unloaded.

Not everything.

Company things.

Costume chests.

Prop baskets.

The Sword board.

The long iron-cornered box.

Nobody opened it.

Two workers carried it inside with Davin directing them.

"Other side."

They turned.

"Up."

They lifted.

"Wall."

They put it against the wall.

That was all.

I carried the blue-lamp piece.

Nessa saw.

"Careful."

"I know."

"That's when people drop things."

I carried it more carefully.

Inside the hall smelled like dust, old wood, lamp oil, and somebody
else's lunch.

Home was too strong a word.

Familiar was not.

It was both.

Teren was already talking to someone about tomorrow.

Tomorrow.

Of course.

Rinna was counting something.

Pell had found the wooden fish and was making it bite a rope.

Marek had disappeared toward the kitchen.

I stood with my bag.

Nobody told me what to do.

That was rare enough that I waited.

Nessa walked past.

"Go."

"Where?"

She stopped.

"Wherever you've been trying to get back to."

"Oh."

"Bring your bag."

I looked down.

I still had it.

"Right."

Outside, Carrow kept happening.

I knew the streets.

That was almost inconvenient.

I did not need to ask directions.

I could go to Lyssa.

I could go to Hessa.

One of those choices involved a brass clasp.

The other involved a piece of failed magical garbage and a question I
had spent two days making worse.

I chose Lyssa.

Not because I had become wise.

Because I had been gone too long.

I made it three streets before realizing I was still carrying the
blue-lamp piece.

"Fuck."

I turned around.

At the hall, Pell was in the doorway.

He saw me.

He saw the wrapped glass in my hand.

He laughed so hard he had to hold the frame.

"Shut up."

"You went home with the lamp."

"I noticed."

"Did Lyssa want it?"

"I didn't get there."

"You could give it to her."

"No."

"Romantic."

"Fuck you."

Nessa appeared behind him.

She took the glass.

"Anything else?"

I checked.

Bag.

Clasp.

Throw blank.

Crutches.

Me.

"No."

"Go."

I went.

This time I made it farther.

The streets near Lyssa's usual place were busier than I remembered.

Or maybe I had forgotten.

A fruit seller had moved to the opposite corner. A sign over a tailor's
shop had acquired a tiny glamour that made the painted needle flash
silver when you passed beneath it.

I almost stopped.

I did not.

I reached the door.

Then I stood there.

That was stupid.

I had performed for rooms full of people.

I had argued about money with children.

I had been tied to a board.

I had bought educational garbage from a woman who thought I was an
idiot.

I could knock on a door.

I knocked.

Nobody answered.

Of course.

I waited.

Knocked again.

Nothing.

A woman coming down the street looked at me.

"You looking for Lyssa?"

"Yes."

"She's out."

"Where?"

The woman shifted the basket on her hip.

"North side, I think. Said something about cloth."

That could mean anything.

"When?"

"This morning."

"Right."

She looked at my bag.

"You Greg?"

I stared at her.

"Yes."

"She got your letter."

Then she walked past me.

I turned.

"Which one?"

She looked back.

"What?"

"Nothing."

She kept going.

I stood outside Lyssa's empty door.

She had gotten a letter.

At least one.

Maybe both.

I had come home.

She was somewhere else.

That felt correct.

I sat on the step because my arms hurt.

The brass clasp was still in my coat.

The failed throw blank was still in my pocket.

Hessa was somewhere in Carrow too.

Tomorrow, I could make her frown.

Tonight, apparently, I had to find Lyssa.

I smiled.

Then I got up.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 175

## THE GIFT-GIVER

The woman with the basket had said north side.

That was not an address.

I knew this because I went north and found six streets, two cloth shops,
a dyer's yard, three women carrying folded linen, and no Lyssa.

The first cloth shop had blue bolts stacked to the ceiling and a
prepared measuring cord that crawled flat across the counter when the
shopkeeper tapped one end. I watched it straighten itself.

"Buying?"

"No."

"Then don't lean on the wool."

I moved.

The second shop knew Lyssa.

"She was here."

"When?"

The woman behind the counter looked at the window.

"Before."

That was useful.

"Did she say where she was going?"

"Yes."

I waited.

The woman folded a length of brown cloth.

"Are you going to ask?"

"I thought I did."

"You asked if she said."

"Where did she go?"

"Marra's."

"Where's Marra?"

She pointed with the cloth.

"Two lanes. Green door. Don't knock on the red one."

"Why?"

"That's Sen's."

I did not know Sen.

Apparently that was reason enough.

Marra's green door stood open.

I heard Lyssa before I saw her.

"No, if you cut it there, it will pull when she lifts her arm."

Another woman said, "She doesn't lift her arm."

"Everybody lifts their arm."

"Not like that."

"Marra."

"Fine."

I stopped in the doorway.

Lyssa stood beside a table covered in gray cloth. She had one end pinned
between two fingers while a shorter woman leaned over it with chalk.
Another woman, older, sat by the window unpicking a seam from a dark
green dress.

None of them looked at me.

I had traveled for weeks.

I had performed in markets, mills, halls, yards, and beside livestock.

I had crossed bridges.

I had slept under wagons.

I had come home.

Lyssa was arguing about a sleeve.

Good.

The shorter woman looked up first.

"Door."

"I'm not blocking it."

"You are."

I moved.

Lyssa turned.

She stopped.

Not for long.

Her face changed in a way I could not separate fast enough.

Then she put the cloth down.

"You."

"Me."

"You're back."

"Apparently."

She crossed the room.

I had time to think I should say something.

Then she put both arms around me.

That solved it.

I held her.

My crutch slipped against the floor.

The shorter woman said, "Careful."

Lyssa caught me before I fell.

"Excellent," she said into my shoulder. "You've been home thirty
seconds."

"I was doing well."

"You smell."

"I've been traveling."

"I know."

She pulled back enough to look at me.

Her hands stayed on my arms.

"You look terrible."

"Thank you."

"Not terrible terrible."

"Better."

"Tired."

"I am."

"Thin."

"I ate."

"Did you?"

"Mostly."

The shorter woman cleared her throat.

Lyssa looked over.

"Marra, this is Greg."

Marra looked at me.

"The road one?"

I looked at Lyssa.

She said, "Apparently."

Marra nodded once.

"Don't bleed on the cloth."

"I'm not bleeding."

"Good."

The older woman by the window said, "Yet."

Lyssa laughed.

I had missed that.

That was inconvenient.

"What are you doing?" I asked.

"Helping Marra fix a dress she promised yesterday."

Marra said, "I did not promise yesterday."

"You said tomorrow."

"Yesterday."

"Exactly."

Marra pointed chalk at her.

"You came here voluntarily."

"I know."

The older woman held up the green dress.

"This sleeve is wrong too."

Lyssa closed her eyes.

I said, "I can go."

"No."

"I can wait."

"No."

"You appear busy."

"I am."

That was not the same as wanting me gone.

I understood that now.

Mostly.

Lyssa pointed at a stool near the wall.

"Sit."

I sat.

For the next twenty minutes, nobody asked about my journey.

Marra cut cloth.

Lyssa pinned a sleeve.

The older woman, whose name was Jessa, complained that whoever had sewn
the green dress originally hated shoulders.

I watched.

A little prepared warming plate sat under a pot near the back wall.
Every few minutes Marra put her chalk down, touched the plate, and held
her fingers over it.

That was all the magic in the room.

The rest was needles.

At one point Lyssa glanced at me.

"You're still here."

"I was told to sit."

"Good."

Marra said, "He learns."

"Slowly."

"I've improved."

Lyssa looked at my bag.

"What happened to that?"

"Nothing."

"That seam."

"Serra fixed it."

"Who is Serra?"

"Actor."

Lyssa's eyebrows moved.

"She fixed your bag."

"After I fixed it."

"Ah."

"Mine was structural."

Lyssa smiled.

"What did she call it?"

I stared at her.

"How do you know she called it something?"

"Because I've met you."

"Criminal."

Marra laughed.

"She called the stitches criminal."

Lyssa nodded.

"Correct."

"I had been on the road."

"Needles work on roads."

"Not well."

"Did you try sewing while the wagon was moving?"

"No."

I had.

Not the bag.

Something else.

I decided that did not count.

The dress eventually became acceptable.

Marra paid Lyssa with a folded piece of pale cloth and what looked like
two copper.

Lyssa put both away without showing me.

Good.

She had not been helping for fun.

Outside, the light had started going gold between the buildings.

Lyssa took my bag before I could object.

"I can carry that."

"I know."

"Give it back."

"No."

"I have crutches."

"Yes."

"That is why I have a bag."

"Greg."

"What?"

"You walked here from wherever you came from."

"East Market Hall."

"Before that."

"Halver."

"Before that."

"Rellin."

She looked at me.

"Dast."

"Keep going."

"Kest."

"Give me the bag."

I let her carry it.

We walked south.

Not toward her place at first.

She turned into a food lane.

"I ate."

"When?"

"Morning."

"That's not what I asked."

"Road house."

"What did you eat?"

"Beans."

"And?"

"Bread."

"And?"

"Beans."

She bought two meat buns.

I paid for mine.

She noticed.

"You have money."

"I work."

"Do you?"

"Professionally."

"At what?"

"Waiting, mostly."

She handed me the bun.

I bit it too soon and burned my mouth.

Lyssa watched.

"Professional."

"Fuck you."

"Missed you too."

I nearly choked.

She smiled and kept walking.

That reminded me.

"The letter."

"Which one?"

I stopped.

She took another bite.

"Which one?"

"I got two."

"Both?"

"Unless you sent more."

"No."

"The first one made you sound sensible."

"I was sensible."

"The second one said you didn't share apples with Marek."

"He didn't deserve them."

"I don't know who Marek is."

"Exactly."

She walked.

I caught up.

"You got the Dast one?"

"Yesterday."

"That was fast."

"It was a letter, Greg. Not a wagon."

"It was on a wagon."

"Probably."

"Did you write back?"

"Yes."

I stared at her.

"Where?"

"East Market Hall."

"When?"

"This morning."

I turned my head toward the direction of the hall.

Lyssa caught my sleeve.

"No."

"What?"

"You are not going to chase your own reply across Carrow."

"I wasn't."

"You looked."

"I looked at a building."

"You can't see it from here."

"I looked in its direction."

"Eat."

I ate.

Her reply was probably sitting at the hall I had left less than an hour
ago.

That was irritating.

Also funny.

I had traveled faster than the answer.

We reached her place.

Inside, nothing had arranged itself around my absence.

A cup sat on the table.

A folded shawl lay over the chair.

There were three onions in a bowl and one had gone soft.

A book was open facedown where it should not have been.

I knew better than to say that.

Lyssa put my bag down.

"Bath."

"Now?"

"Yes."

"I just got here."

"You arrived dirty."

"I can sit dirty."

"You can sit after."

I obeyed.

The water was not hot enough to be luxurious.

It was hot enough.

I washed road dust out of places I had stopped noticing road dust could
be.

When I came back, Lyssa had put bread, cheese, and sliced onion on the
table.

"You bought food."

"I own food."

"Right."

"You've forgotten houses."

"Some."

I sat.

My body noticed the chair was not moving.

That was almost unpleasant.

Lyssa sat across from me.

For a while we ate.

Then she said, "How long were you supposed to be gone?"

"I don't remember."

"You told me a few days."

"That sounds wrong now."

"It sounded wrong then."

"I didn't know."

"I know."

No accusation.

That made it worse for a second.

Then she reached across and stole my cheese.

That fixed it.

"There was a goat," I said.

She chewed.

"Of course."

"It ate mounting cloth."

"What is mounting cloth?"

"Cloth for mounting."

"Helpful."

"For the Sword."

"You were the sword."

"Sometimes."

"You wrote that."

"I did?"

"Not clearly."

"That sounds like me."

"You also performed beside cheese."

"Yes."

"And livestock."

"Yes."

"And cider."

"Yes."

"Was any of this intentional?"

"Mostly."

She laughed.

I told her about the north arcade wind.

Not the whole thing.

Just the cheese woman and the carts.

Then the goose came out.

"A real goose is bad theatre," I said.

Lyssa stopped.

"What?"

"We didn't use one."

"You stole a goose."

"We did not steal a goose."

"You tried."

"No."

"Pell tried?"

"He suggested."

"Who is Pell?"

"Props."

"Person or job?"

"Both."

She looked delighted.

I told her about the fox.

That took less time.

"It sounded like someone being murdered."

"Foxes do."

"I know that now."

"You've never heard one?"

"Apparently not correctly."

She frowned slightly.

"What does that mean?"

"I don't know."

That was true.

I ate bread.

Then I remembered the clasp.

Not because of anything romantic.

Because it dug into my chest when I leaned forward.

"Oh."

Lyssa looked at me.

"What?"

"I bought you something."

Her expression changed immediately.

Not softer.

More suspicious.

"Why?"

"I saw it."

"That's not an answer."

"It is the whole answer."

I reached inside my coat and took out the wrapped little packet.

The wrapping looked worse than when I bought it.

Of course it did.

I put it on the table.

Lyssa looked at it.

"Is it alive?"

"No."

"Magic?"

"No."

"Food?"

"No."

"Then why are you nervous?"

"I'm not."

"You've performed tied to a board."

"Mounted."

"Your letter said tied."

"That was editorial simplification."

She opened the wrapping.

The brass clasp lay in her palm.

Two small leaves.

Nothing expensive.

Nothing magical.

Just brass worked carefully enough that the veins showed when the light
caught them.

Lyssa touched one leaf with her thumb.

I suddenly wanted to explain the price.

That would have been terrible.

So I said nothing.

"You carried this the whole way?"

"I bought it after the first northern show."

"That was before Dast."

"Yes."

"Before the mill?"

"I think so."

"You think?"

"There were many places."

She looked at me.

Then at the clasp.

Then she stood.

For one horrifying second I thought she hated it.

She went to the small mirror.

Her hair was loose enough that the clasp was not useful there.

She fastened it instead at the edge of her shawl.

It worked.

She looked at it.

"Good?"

I said, "Yes."

"That's all?"

"What do you want?"

"I don't know. You looked like you were going to give a speech."

"I was trying not to."

"Good."

She came back and kissed me.

That was better than a speech.

Later, I found out I had fallen asleep sitting up.

I knew this because I woke with my neck bent against the wall and
Lyssa's foot under my thigh.

It was dark.

A prepared street lamp outside made a pale bar across the floor.

Lyssa was reading.

"You slept."

"I noticed."

"You snored."

"I don't."

"You did."

"Road damage."

"Permanent."

I shifted.

Everything hurt.

"Bed?"

She closed the book.

"Eventually."

"Why eventually?"

"Because you're awake now."

That was fair.

I looked at the brass leaves at her shoulder.

She had not taken the clasp off.

I liked that more than I intended to.

"What's tomorrow?" she asked.

"The hall."

"What time?"

"I don't know."

"Useful."

"Teren was talking about tomorrow before we finished unloading."

"Of course he was."

"And Hessa."

Lyssa looked at me.

"Tomorrow?"

"Yes."

"Did you practice?"

"No."

"At all?"

"No."

She studied me.

"Good."

"That sounded surprised."

"It was."

"I follow rules."

"You follow rules after arguing with them."

"Still counts."

"What are you taking her?"

I reached for my trousers where I had left them folded badly.

Lyssa said, "No."

"I need the pocket."

"You need sleep."

"There's a thing."

"Tomorrow."

"It's garbage."

"Excellent. Tomorrow."

I lay back down.

"You'll like it."

"I already don't."

"It cost one copper."

"Greg."

"What?"

"Sleep."

I did.

Morning in Carrow was louder than road morning.

Road morning had birds, horses, wagons, people pissing behind things.

Carrow had bells.

Cart wheels.

Vendors.

Somebody below shouting about hot cakes.

A prepared sign across the lane brightened from gray to yellow when the
sun reached it.

Lyssa was already dressed.

The brass clasp was gone from the shawl.

I noticed.

Then I saw it fastened at the side of her hair.

I tried not to look too pleased.

She caught me.

"Don't."

"I didn't say anything."

"Your face did."

"Good clasp."

"Go to work."

I ate one hot cake she bought downstairs.

Then another.

She had somewhere to be.

I did not ask if I could come.

That felt important enough not to think about.

At the corner, she kissed me once.

"When are you done?"

"I don't know."

"Find out."

"Yes."

"Are you leaving again?"

"No."

That came out too fast.

Lyssa looked at me.

I corrected.

"Not today."

"Better."

"Probably not tomorrow."

"Greg."

"I don't know."

"I know."

She touched the clasp once, then pointed at me.

"Find out."

"Yes."

She went east.

I went toward East Market Hall.

The reply letter was there.

Rinna had put it under a cup so Pell would not touch it.

I did not read it immediately.

That was growth.

I put it in my bag.

Teren was in the hall with two actors I did not know and a man arguing
about chairs.

Nessa had half the costume chest open.

Pell was on the floor with the wooden fish.

Davin was not there.

Marek was eating.

Of course.

Teren saw me.

"Tonight."

"What?"

"Show."

"What am I?"

"Shopkeeper."

"Only?"

"For now."

"Good."

He looked at me.

"What?"

"You sound disappointed."

"I'm not."

"You are."

"I have another thing."

"What thing?"

"Guild."

He waved me away.

"Be back by four."

That was the entire negotiation.

I went.

Hessa was not waiting for me either.

She had someone else at her table.

A woman with a wrapped forearm sat in my usual chair while Hessa
examined a row of tiny dark marks on the skin.

I stopped in the doorway.

Hessa looked up once.

"You're back."

"Yes."

"Sit outside."

"Hello to you too."

"Outside."

I sat outside.

For twenty-five minutes.

The woman came out with her arm rewrapped and instructions I did not
hear.

Hessa called, "Greg."

I went in.

The room had not changed enough.

That was becoming a theme.

The suspended-thread apparatus was still shelved.

My old notes were not on the table.

Hessa looked at me.

"You look tired."

"Lyssa said terrible."

"She was being kind."

"Good."

"Did you draw?"

"No."

"Shape?"

"No."

"Test?"

"No."

"Anything I prohibited?"

"No."

She watched me for another second.

"Good."

I sat.

Then I took the failed throw blank from my pocket and put it on her
table.

Hessa looked down.

She did not touch it.

Her mouth tightened.

That was the frown.

"What is that?"

"Educational garbage."

Her eyes lifted to mine.

"That is not a category."

"It was one copper."

The frown got worse.

I smiled.

"I have a question."

"I assumed."

"It's about how little something has to be real."

Hessa looked at the metal again.

Then at me.

"No."

"I haven't asked it yet."

"I know."

"That's unfair."

"Ask it."

I leaned forward.

The failed clasp sat between us.

Completely inert.

Completely useless.

For the first time since I had left Carrow, I was exactly where I was
allowed to make the question worse.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 176

## THE QUESTIONER

"So," I said.

Hessa waited.

There were people who made waiting feel patient.

Hessa made it feel like I had already wasted something.

"The blue lamp makes the light blue."

"Yes."

"You haven't seen it."

"You told me what it does."

"Right. But it doesn't make the room cold."

"I would hope not."

"The room feels cold."

"To whom?"

"The audience."

"Did you ask them?"

"No."

"Then the room felt cold to you."

"It did."

"Good. Continue."

I disliked this already.

"There was rain."

"Inside?"

"Outside."

"Greg."

"The wall was pale. Serra was in the light. The light was blue. It
looked cold."

"So several real things produced an impression."

"Yes."

"That is theatre."

"Some of it."

"What part isn't?"

I pointed at the failed throw blank.

"The magic."

Hessa looked at it.

"The blue lamp uses a prepared piece."

"Yes."

"And this is not the blue lamp."

"No. That's sound."

"This is sound?"

"It was supposed to be."

"Supposed to be is doing a great deal of work."

"It doesn't do anything."

"Good."

"Why is that good?"

"Because I can touch it."

She picked it up.

Varo's failed blank looked smaller in Hessa's hand. She turned it toward
the window, then reached for a little magnifying lens from the shelf
behind her. The lens had a brass rim and no magic that I could see. She
held the blank beneath it.

"Who made this?"

"Varo. Rellin. Blue shutters."

"Profession?"

"Instrument maker. Repairs. Prepared fittings."

"Did she tell you what failed?"

"Channel marked. Bias never set."

Hessa turned the blank.

"That is consistent."

"You can tell?"

"I can tell there is a marked preparation line and no completed bias
structure."

"What's a bias structure?"

"The thing you are not learning today."

"I was asking."

"And I answered."

She put the lens down.

"Anything held in it?"

"No."

"Did she say that?"

"She said it was garbage."

"Good maker."

"Educational garbage."

"Less good."

"One copper."

"I remember."

She put the blank on the table.

"Why did you buy it?"

"So I could look at it."

Hessa's face changed slightly.

Not approval.

Less disapproval.

That was probably the highest available grade.

"And what did looking tell you?"

"That I don't know what I'm looking at."

"Excellent."

"Fuck you."

"Also that."

I leaned back.

The room smelled like old paper, clean metal, and the sharp soap Hessa
used on the table. Outside the door, somebody walked past carrying a
rack of six narrow glass tubes. One glowed faintly amber at the bottom.
Nobody screamed.

I said, "The throw clasp doesn't make another sound."

"According to the maker."

"It changes enough about the sound that you put it somewhere else."

"You think."

"Varo thinks."

"Better."

"And the room helps."

"What room?"

"Her shop."

Hessa looked at me.

"You're changing examples."

"They're connected."

"That is what worries me."

I ignored that.

"The cheap one on her door wasn't very good. Pell heard it wrong."

"Pell?"

"Props."

"Person?"

"Both."

"Of course."

"But the door, the walls, where we were standing, all of that made it
work better. The clasp didn't have to do everything."

Hessa folded her hands.

"And?"

"And the blue lamp doesn't have to make cold. A real goose doesn't have
to be onstage to make a goose."

She blinked.

I kept going because stopping would have made it worse.

"A fox sounds wrong until someone tells you fox."

"What did you think it was?"

"Someone dying."

"Reasonable."

"Then Pell said fox and it sounded like a fox."

"The sound changed?"

"No."

"So."

"So what?"

"You tell me."

"The thing didn't change."

"Correct."

"I did."

"Possibly."

"That's annoying."

"Good."

I looked at the blank again.

"What if the magic only has to do one small real thing?"

Hessa did not answer immediately.

That was different.

I leaned forward.

"Not the whole thing. Not make the room cold. Not make another sound.
Not make a goose."

"Please stop making geese."

"I never made a goose."

"Continue."

"What if I don't need to make something big happen? What if I only need
to make one tiny thing happen, and then everything else is..."

I moved my hand.

Hessa waited.

"Theatre," I finished.

"No."

I stared at her.

"That was the good version."

"It was not."

"Why?"

"Because you have changed questions again."

She pointed at the blank.

"That object is prepared structure. Most of whatever useful behavior a
completed version has was designed into it by someone who knows how to
make one."

She pointed toward the window.

"Your blue lamp changes light."

"Yes."

"The audience's interpretation of that light is not a magical effect."

"Yes."

"Your own external work is a third problem."

"Yes."

"Say it without lying."

I frowned.

"I wasn't lying."

"You were making them sound like one thing."

"That's theatre."

"No. That is irritating."

I laughed.

Hessa did not.

I tried again.

"I want to know if I can make a smaller external change than we were
trying before."

There.

Hessa looked at me for several seconds.

"That is a question."

"I had a question before."

"You had weather, a fox, a goose, an instrument fitting, a lamp, and an
opinion."

"The opinion was good."

"The question is better."

She stood.

I looked toward the shelf with the suspended-thread apparatus.

Hessa said, "No."

"I didn't say anything."

"You looked at it."

"I can look."

"Not at that."

She moved past the shelf and opened a low cabinet.

"What time do you need to leave?"

"Four."

"What happens at four?"

"Teren becomes angry."

"Useful measurement."

"Show tonight."

"Doing what?"

"Shopkeeper."

"Of course."

She took out a shallow wooden box.

Inside were little squares of thin paper, two flat pieces of clear
glass, chalk, a narrow wooden frame, and several small metal washers.

None of it looked magical.

I liked that.

"What is that?"

"Things."

"That is not a category."

"It is in my room."

"Unfair."

"Sit."

She set the wooden frame on the table.

It was about the length of my hand and twice as wide. She laid one piece
of glass across the top, then slid two small folded paper tabs
underneath it on separate chalk marks. The glass did not touch the tabs.
It rested on the frame above them, making a low clear roof.

"Breath shield," I said.

"Yes."

"I knew that."

"You are breathing."

"Professionally."

"Stop."

She put one washer on each corner of the frame.

"Table movement?"

"Partly. Also because you touch things."

"I don't."

She looked at me.

"I touch some things."

"Both tabs are cut from the same sheet. Same size. Same fold. One
target, one control."

She marked a small circle beside the left tab.

"Why not glass all around?"

"Because I have an hour, not a workshop."

"I have more than an hour."

"You have until four."

"I could be late."

"No."

That surprised me.

Hessa looked at me.

"You have work."

"Yes."

"Then go to work at four."

"Three forty-five."

"Three thirty."

"Why?"

"Because you walk."

"Rude."

"Accurate."

She pulled my old chair into place.

"We are not proving your theory."

"I don't have a theory."

"Excellent. Keep it that way."

"What are we proving?"

"Nothing."

"That's inspiring."

"We are asking whether you can produce a small external displacement
under a cleaner condition than your previous attempts."

"That's what I said."

"No."

"It is."

"You said goose."

"Related."

"No."

I smiled.

She did not.

Then the smile went away because she said, "Draw."

The word changed the room.

Not dramatically.

Nothing glowed.

No prepared object sang.

I had simply not heard Hessa tell me to do that in weeks.

I put my hands flat on my thighs.

Breathed.

Not too much.

I knew what reaching felt like now.

I also knew what not reaching felt like.

The first few times with Hessa, I had expected mana to arrive like
something entering a room.

It did not.

It was closer to finding a pressure I had been standing inside the whole
time and learning which part of myself was allowed to answer it.

I drew minimally.

Hessa watched.

"Enough."

I stopped.

The draw was clean.

Not impressive.

Not difficult either.

That bothered me more than difficulty would have.

Weeks on the road, no practice, and my body still knew the shape of the
instruction.

Hessa wrote something.

"Twenty-one?" I asked.

"Yes."

I had not meant to sound pleased.

I did anyway.

"Again?"

"No."

"Why?"

"Because we are testing something else."

She pointed at the target tab.

"Shape toward that."

"Move it?"

"Not yet."

"What am I shaping?"

"The smallest directed form you can hold without spilling it."

"That sounds like moving it."

"It is not."

I breathed again.

The mana was already gone from the draw. I drew minimally a second time
only after she told me to, then held it under her instruction and tried
to narrow what I was doing.

Hessa stopped me twice before I had anything.

"Too broad."

Again.

"You're pushing."

"I'm not."

"You are."

"How can I push if nothing is moving?"

"With enthusiasm."

"That's not a magical term."

"It is today."

Third time, I found something narrower.

Not a line.

Not a thread.

I was not going back to thread.

A direction, maybe.

That was too pretty.

A preference.

That was worse.

I held it.

Hessa watched my wrist.

Then my face.

Then the tab.

"Stop."

I released.

"That was good."

I looked at her.

"Actually?"

"Cleaner."

"Seventeen?"

"Yes."

That pleased me more.

Then Hessa moved the entire apparatus away.

"What?"

"Rest."

"I'm fine."

"I know."

"Then why?"

"Because you have started wanting the paper to move."

"That is the test."

"Later."

I hated her.

For six minutes.

During the six minutes, I remembered Lyssa's letter.

I took it from my bag.

Hessa was writing.

"Can I read?"

"Can you do it quietly?"

"No."

"Then no."

I opened it anyway.

Lyssa's letter was shorter than mine.

That seemed rude.

She said she was glad I had reached Dast without being eaten by
anything, which I had never suggested was a possibility. She said Marra
had finally admitted the gray cloth was wrong and they were replacing
it. She said the woman downstairs had started asking whether "the road
actor" was coming back, which explained yesterday.

Then:

You said you miss me. Good. Come back before I get used to having the
whole bed.

Below that:

Also stop being cruel to Marek about apples. I don't know him but I have
decided he deserved one.

I folded the letter.

Hessa said, "Bad news?"

"Terrible."

"Good."

"Lyssa has taken Marek's side."

"I don't know who Marek is."

"Nobody does."

Hessa moved the frame back.

"Ready?"

I put the letter away.

"Yes."

This time she marked the target tab's starting position with a fine
chalk line.

Then she marked the control.

"Your task is not to convince me it moved."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"Probably."

"No."

"Fine."

"Your task is to attempt one small directional influence on the marked
target. Nothing else."

"How far?"

"I don't care."

"That's suspicious."

"If it moves at all, we measure. If it does not, we record that."

"What if it almost moves?"

"It does not."

"That's harsh."

"Reality often is."

I settled.

Draw.

Minimal.

Shape.

Small.

The urge to perform the attempt was immediate.

That was new.

Not perform for Hessa.

Perform for the result.

I wanted the tab to twitch at the right moment. I wanted the still
control beside it. I wanted the clean little story.

Target moves.

Control does not.

Greg did magic.

Perfect.

I could see the scene before anything happened.

That made me distrust it.

I stopped.

Hessa said, "Why?"

"I was making it good."

She stared at me.

Then she leaned back.

"Explain."

"I wanted it to move right."

"There is no right."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"No."

She tapped the table once.

"Again."

I drew.

Shaped.

Held the smallest directed form I could manage.

Then tried to let it touch the world.

Nothing happened.

I did not push harder.

That felt like failure.

It also felt correct.

"Stop," Hessa said.

I stopped.

We both looked at the tabs.

Neither had moved.

"External attempt four," she said.

"Nothing."

"Correct."

I exhaled.

The target tab trembled.

I pointed.

"It moved."

"You breathed."

"I know."

"Good."

"I was joking."

"No, you weren't."

"Mostly."

Hessa wrote.

I looked at the paper.

I had expected disappointment to feel worse.

Instead I was annoyed by the tab.

That seemed healthier.

"Again?" I asked.

"No."

"One attempt?"

"One controlled external attempt today."

"We have time."

"We also have a useful failure."

"Those are cheap."

"They are if you waste them."

She took the glass roof off and picked up the target tab.

"You did two things better than before."

"Only two?"

"You kept the shaping smaller."

"Good."

"And you stopped when you noticed yourself constructing the result."

I looked at her.

"That's not magic."

"No."

"Then it doesn't count."

"It counts for me."

That was irritatingly close to praise.

I touched the failed throw blank.

"What about this?"

Hessa slid it toward me.

"Take your garbage."

"You don't want it?"

"I have better garbage."

"Can I bring it next time?"

"If you have a question about prepared structure."

"I do."

"Then write the question before you arrive."

"Why?"

"So I do not have to hear about geese."

"The goose is important."

"Ask your players."

That shut me up.

Mostly.

I put the blank back in its pocket.

"Next time?"

"Two days."

"I have theatre."

"At this exact hour?"

"I don't know."

"Find out."

Everyone was telling me that now.

"What are we doing?"

"Repeating this."

"The paper?"

"Something similar."

"Can we make it smaller?"

Hessa looked at me.

"The effect?"

"Yes."

"It was zero."

"Right."

"Hard to make smaller."

"You know what I mean."

"I do."

She closed the wooden box.

"We can make the question narrower."

That was probably what I meant.

It sounded worse when she said it.

I stood.

"Twenty-one draws. Seventeen shaping."

"Successful supervised minimal draws," Hessa said. "Successful
supervised deliberate shaping attempts."

"Yes."

"Four supervised external-effect attempts."

"With no established external effect."

"Correct."

"I remember."

"Say it anyway."

"No established external magical effect."

"Good."

"No spell."

"Correct."

"No Barrier."

"Correct."

"Independent work still prohibited."

"Very."

"I bought inert garbage instead."

"I am trying to reward that choice."

"You have an unusual face for reward."

"Go to work."

It was three twenty-seven.

I went.

East Market Hall smelled different when I came in through the side door.

Not actually.

Paint.

Old cloth.

Lamp oil.

Dust.

People.

But after Hessa's room, everything felt dishonest.

That was unfair to theatre.

Theatre was honest about being dishonest.

I was still deciding whether that sentence meant anything when Nessa
shoved a folded coat into my chest.

"Put that down."

"What?"

"Your bag."

I had carried it into the costume lane.

I moved it.

"Where?"

"Not there."

I moved it again.

"Greg."

"You're becoming Hessa."

"I don't know who that is."

"Good."

She took the coat back.

The hall was fuller than the touring company had been. Two men were
rigging a painted interior wall I remembered from before we left. A
woman I had seen once in the prop room was sorting cups by size. Another
actor was walking a line under his breath while Pell tried to get him to
lift one foot so he could retrieve a strap.

Marek was not eating.

That concerned me.

Teren found me.

"Shopkeeper. Second."

"Second what?"

"Piece."

"What first?"

"King."

"Who's King?"

"Not you."

"Good."

"You're also carrying the ledger on."

"That's not Shopkeeper."

"It is now."

"Why?"

"Because the person who was carrying it isn't here."

"Who?"

Teren had already turned away.

Home.

I changed.

The Shopkeeper coat fit differently after the road.

Or I did.

I found the ledger.

Then I noticed a small round hole low in the wall behind the side cloth.

I had seen it before.

I crouched.

A leather tube disappeared through it.

Pell appeared beside me.

"Don't."

"I'm looking."

"That's the ghost."

"The whole ghost?"

"The mouth."

I looked at him.

"Where's the other end?"

He pointed vaguely beneath the stage.

"Depends."

"On what?"

"Where Nessa puts it."

"Does Teren know you explain things like this?"

"No."

"Good."

Pell left.

I looked at the hole again.

Nothing magical.

A hole.

A tube.

A voice from somewhere it should not be.

Enough, if you did not know where to look.

"Greg!"

Teren.

I stood too fast and nearly hit my head.

"Here."

"Why are you on the floor?"

"Ghost."

He looked at the hole.

"Later."

That was becoming another category of education.

The show started.

King first.

I waited in the side corridor with the ledger under my arm.

The audience was quieter than Dast.

Quieter than the mill.

Quieter than the private house in a different way.

They knew where the stage was.

They had come to watch it.

Nobody was carrying turnips through the performance.

That should have made everything easier.

I entered too large.

Not physically.

The first line came out pitched for a market edge.

The room gave it back to me.

Too much.

Marek, playing a minor official, looked at me.

Not Greg.

Shopkeeper.

But I knew the look.

Smaller.

I adjusted.

Three lines later I rushed a pause because I expected someone to walk
away.

Nobody did.

The silence stayed.

I had forgotten audiences could wait.

That was embarrassing.

Then the scene settled.

The ledger was real wood and paper.

The debt was not real.

The irritation was real enough.

A woman in the second row leaned toward the man beside her before I had
finished a sentence. He whispered something. She covered a laugh.

I did not know what they thought was happening between us.

I did not need to.

Marek said, "I have already explained the circumstances."

"You explained circumstances," I said. "You have not explained money."

That landed.

Not huge.

Clean.

I let it.

Later, I nearly used the road version of a line that depended on a
constable who was not in this cut.

I felt it arrive.

Wrong room.

Wrong version.

I let it die.

Marek continued.

Good.

At the end, applause.

Not a lot.

Enough.

I came offstage and Teren said, "First entrance was shit."

"I know."

"Second half good."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"No."

He left.

I sat on a prop chest.

Pell was under the stage.

Somebody above me dragged a chair.

The ghost tube shifted beside my boot.

I thought about the paper tab.

Hessa had covered it with glass so my breath could not lie for me.

Here, we put a tube through a wall so a voice could.

That was not the same thing.

I knew that.

It still felt close enough to be annoying.

Rinna passed with a small cash box.

"You're in tomorrow."

"What?"

"Maybe."

"That's not in."

"Then you're learning."

She kept walking.

I took Lyssa's letter from my bag and read the line about the bed again.

Then I folded it and put it away before Pell could crawl out and ask
what I was smiling at.

He crawled out anyway.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"That's suspicious."

"Go be props."

"I am props."

"Exactly."

Someone called him.

He went.

I sat there another minute.

Magic had done nothing today.

The show had convinced a room of several things that were not true.

Neither fact made the other simpler.

At four tomorrow, I might be Shopkeeper again.

In two days, Hessa wanted another piece of paper not to move.

For once, both sounded like work.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 177

## THE STAGEHAND

The ghost had a kink in it.

I found that out because Pell said, "Talk."

I put my mouth near the wooden cup.

"What?"

From somewhere behind the painted wall, Pell shouted, "Not you."

"I am talking."

"Other end."

"You told me to hold this end."

"I told you to hold the ghost."

"Which end is the ghost?"

Nessa's voice came from under the stage.

"The end he didn't give you."

Pell looked offended.

"I was getting there."

"You were not."

It was morning.

East Market Hall had already become impossible.

A painted wall leaned against two braces in the middle of the floor.
Someone had hung three shirts from the balcony rail. A woman I did not
know was arguing with one of the lamp men about whether a prepared
warming stone belonged in costumes or properties. He said properties
because it was a stone. She said costumes because it went inside a coat.

Neither asked me.

Teren crossed behind them carrying a stool.

"Ghost in the third," he said.

Then he kept walking.

Pell looked at me.

"You heard him."

"I heard words."

"Tube."

"Why me?"

"You have arms."

"I have one leg."

"The tube doesn't."

That was unfortunately reasonable.

The ghost was twenty feet of narrow leather tube with a wooden
mouthpiece at one end and a flatter wooden opening at the other. The
leather was old enough to have opinions. It wanted to bend where it had
always bent and nowhere else.

Pell had given me the mouthpiece.

Nessa wanted the flat end.

I passed it down.

"Where?"

"Here."

Her hand appeared between the stage boards.

I gave her the end.

"No."

"You said here."

"I meant me."

"That is here."

"Greg."

I lowered it farther.

She took it.

Pell crouched beside me and fed the tube through the low hole I had
noticed yesterday.

"Don't twist it."

"I'm not."

"You are."

"That's the tube."

"Tube doesn't twist itself."

I looked at him.

He looked at me.

We both looked at the tube.

It had twisted itself.

"Fine," Pell said.

We fed more through.

The third piece was something called The Mourning House.

I had never seen it.

Apparently everyone else had.

That was becoming normal.

A woman named Veya played a widow who had inherited a house from an
uncle she hated. Marek played the uncle in the first scene and then
died. This pleased him because it meant he could spend most of the piece
backstage.

The dead uncle spoke twice after death.

That was the ghost.

"Why not just put Pell behind the wall?" I asked.

"Because the wall moves," Nessa said from below.

"Why not put him under the stage?"

"Because the audience can hear under the stage."

"Why can't they hear the tube?"

"They can."

I waited.

Nessa's head appeared through a gap beside the steps.

"They hear the wrong part."

That did not help.

Pell said, "It's obvious."

"Then explain it."

"No."

"Because you can't."

"Because Nessa will yell."

"I can hear you," Nessa said.

Pell whispered, "See?"

We routed the tube behind the painted wall, down through the low hole,
under the stage, and back up beside a dark hanging on the opposite side.

I thought the outlet should go farther.

"If it comes from over there," I said, pointing toward the rear corner,
"then it will sound more impossible."

Nessa looked at the corner.

"No."

"Why?"

"Mud."

"What?"

"Sound."

"That's not mud."

"It will be."

She took the flat outlet from me and fixed it behind the hanging less
than eight feet from where Veya would stand.

"That's too close."

"Good."

"How is close better?"

"Listen."

Pell went behind the wall.

Veya came onto the stage holding a cup.

She was maybe forty. I had seen her yesterday sorting nothing and
assumed she was crew.

She looked at the room.

"Where's my chair?"

Nobody answered.

"Where is my chair?"

A man on the balcony said, "King."

Veya looked up.

"Why?"

"King needed another."

"My dead uncle needs it."

Marek called from backstage, "I can die standing."

"You die in the first scene."

"I can do it."

"You're already dead in the third."

"Then I definitely don't need the chair."

Veya closed her eyes.

This problem had existed before I arrived.

Good.

Someone found another chair.

Pell said through the tube, "Veya."

His voice came from the hanging.

It sounded exactly like Pell speaking through a tube.

I laughed.

Pell emerged from behind the wall.

"What?"

"That was terrible."

"It was a test."

"You sounded like yourself in a bucket."

"It's leather."

"Leather bucket."

Nessa adjusted the outlet.

"Again."

Pell disappeared.

Veya stood beside the chair.

"Veya."

Still Pell.

Less bucket.

Veya turned toward the hanging before he finished saying her name.

Nessa said, "No."

Veya looked at her.

"What?"

"You're early."

"I heard him."

"So did everyone."

"That's why I looked."

"After."

Veya sighed.

Again.

Pell said, "Veya."

Veya waited.

Then turned.

It was better.

Not good.

Better.

Nessa lowered the nearest lamp.

The hall changed.

Only a little.

The hanging became less brown and more black.

She moved Veya's chair half a pace toward center.

Then she told Pell, "Less."

"Less what?"

"You."

"That's all I have."

"Find less."

Pell muttered something.

"Again."

This time the voice was quieter.

"Veya."

Veya did not turn immediately.

She stopped moving.

That was different.

She had been folding a cloth. Her hands stopped with the cloth half
open.

Then her eyes went toward the dark hanging.

Not her head.

Her eyes.

"Uncle?"

Pell did not answer.

Nothing happened.

I looked at the hanging.

There was nothing there.

I knew there was nothing there.

I had put the fucking tube there.

Still, for about half a second, the space beside it had somebody in it.

Then Pell coughed under the stage.

The person disappeared.

Veya said, "Excellent."

Nessa kicked the boards.

Pell said, "Sorry."

I was still looking at the empty space.

Nessa noticed.

She did not smile.

"Tube."

"What?"

"You're standing on it."

I moved my crutch.

I had been.

That afternoon I learned three more things about ghosts.

The first was that leather hated corners.

I routed the tube too tightly behind a brace because it hid better
there. Pell tried the line and sounded like a dying kettle.

Nessa made me pull the whole section loose.

"Visible," I said.

"To who?"

I stepped into the audience.

From the seats, the tube disappeared behind the painted edge.

From backstage, it looked obvious.

I had hidden it from the wrong people.

The second thing was that the outlet could not touch cloth.

It buzzed.

Not magically.

Just badly.

The third was that actors were part of the mechanism.

Veya got tired of waiting for Pell's second line and started
anticipating it.

Every time she did, the ghost got worse.

"You know it's coming," Nessa told her.

"Because we've done it six times."

"They don't."

She pointed at the empty seats.

Veya looked at them.

Then at Nessa.

"Fine."

The seventh time, she let herself not know.

That was better too.

Nobody explained why.

They had work.

By three, the hall had acquired an audience of people who did not pay.

A carpenter sat in the back while waiting for somebody to move the
painted wall.

Two costume women watched from the side.

A boy delivering lamp oil stayed through most of Mourning House until
someone realized he had not delivered the lamp oil.

The prepared warming stone was eventually declared costume property.

I never learned who won.

At some point Rinna found me under the stage with Pell.

"Greg."

"Yes."

"Two copper."

"For what?"

She held them out.

"Yesterday."

I took them.

"Show?"

"Show."

"Company share?"

"Your local rate."

I put them away.

"What about tonight?"

"If you do it."

"Helpful."

She looked at Pell.

"You owe me a copper."

Pell said, "No."

"You broke the latch."

"It was already weak."

"You made it two pieces."

"That's how we found out."

Rinna held out her hand.

Pell stared at it.

I crawled away before the economics became violent.

Outside, Carrow had decided to be warm.

A fruit seller had a shallow cooling plate under cut melon. The plate's
worked edge glimmered once when she set a fresh tray on it, then
stopped. Beside her, a man sold warm beer because apparently not
everyone made good decisions.

I bought bread.

Marek found me.

"Food?"

"You have eyes."

"Share."

"No."

"Lyssa says I deserved the apple."

He stopped.

"Who is Lyssa?"

"Nobody."

"You said Lyssa."

"I did not."

"You did."

I walked away.

He followed.

"Who told Lyssa about the apple?"

"Lyssa."

"That doesn't answer anything."

"Good."

He bought his own bread.

Back inside, Teren had written the evening bill on a board.

SHORT KING

MOURNING HOUSE

SHOPKEEPER

A fourth line had been written and crossed out so hard I could not read
it.

I pointed.

"What was that?"

"No."

"What?"

"Exactly."

"Am I Shopkeeper?"

"Yes."

"Anything else?"

"Ghost."

"I'm not the ghost."

"You're carrying it."

"That's not acting."

Teren looked at me.

"I didn't say it was."

Good.

I carried the tube.

We reset it for the evening.

This time Nessa made me place the outlet.

I put it where she had put it.

She looked.

"Too low."

"It was there."

"No."

"It was."

"The hanging moved."

I looked.

Someone had retied it two fingers higher.

"That's ridiculous."

"Fix it."

I moved the outlet.

"Too far."

I moved it back.

"Stop moving it like you're angry."

"I am angry."

"At leather?"

"Currently."

She crouched, touched the outlet, and rotated it slightly toward the
plaster side wall.

"Why?"

"Because that wall gives some back."

"The room."

"What?"

"Nothing."

Nessa looked at me.

"Varo?"

"Yes."

"She charges too much."

"One silver six."

"For a basic throw?"

"Yes."

"Too much."

"Pell said it was fair."

"Pell buys broken hinges."

"I heard that," Pell said.

He was under the stage.

"Good."

The doors opened.

The audience came in.

Not huge.

East Market Hall was not new to them.

They talked.

Found seats.

Moved seats.

One man objected to a post and then sat behind it anyway.

A child touched the painted wall until her mother stopped her.

The first piece began.

I was crew.

That felt different from waiting.

During King, I moved the ghost tube farther from a costume basket
because someone had put the basket on it.

Then I held a door flat while a hinge pin went back in.

Then I was supposed to be ready at the tube for Mourning House.

I was not the voice.

Pell was.

I only had to make sure nothing crushed it.

That was easy.

Until the lamp-oil boy came back.

He put two cans exactly where the tube crossed behind the wall.

I moved them.

He moved them back.

"No."

He looked at me.

"What?"

"Not there."

"Why?"

"Ghost."

He looked at the floor.

"Where?"

"Exactly."

He picked up the cans.

I liked him.

Mourning House began.

Marek died well.

Too well.

He added a hand twitch after the fall.

Veya stepped on it.

The audience laughed.

He stayed dead.

Professional.

Then the house became quiet.

Not actually quiet.

Someone coughed.

A bench creaked.

A child whispered.

But the piece wanted quiet, so the room began cooperating.

Veya sat.

Folded the cloth.

Stopped.

Pell spoke.

"Veya."

The voice came from the dark side.

I knew where he was.

I knew the tube path.

I knew the outlet.

I had adjusted it.

A woman in the third row turned toward the hanging.

Then the man beside her did.

Veya's hands stopped.

Her eyes moved.

The empty place filled.

Not with a ghost.

With everyone's attention.

That was enough.

"Uncle?"

Pell waited.

The pause held.

Then his second line came from the same place.

I watched the audience instead of the hanging.

That was my mistake.

Nessa hit my shoulder.

"Tube."

The costume basket had shifted again.

I caught it before it settled onto the leather.

Work.

The ghost continued without me.

After Mourning House, I had eight minutes to become Shopkeeper.

I used six.

The coat button was wrong.

Not broken.

Wrong hole.

I fixed it.

Then I heard applause and thought I had more time than I did.

Teren appeared.

"Go."

"What?"

"Go."

I grabbed the ledger.

My entrance was late.

Not terribly.

Enough.

Marek was already onstage waiting.

He covered.

"At last."

I came in.

"You say that like I wanted to see you."

The audience laughed.

That line was not supposed to be there.

Marek looked pleased.

I hated him.

The rest went fine.

Better than yesterday's first half.

Worse than yesterday's second.

I lost one word and replaced it with another that meant almost the same
thing.

Teren noticed.

Nobody else seemed to.

At the debt turn, a man near the aisle said, "Don't lend him anything."

I looked at Marek.

"Even he understands."

That got more than it deserved.

Afterward, Teren said, "Late."

"I know."

"Why?"

"Ghost."

He looked at me.

"Did it work?"

"Yes."

"Then next time be late for a worse reason."

I laughed.

He didn't.

Maybe a little.

Rinna paid me two copper for the night.

Four copper across two local shows.

That felt small after company silver and large after buying bread.

Money was becoming irritating that way.

Pell got paid too.

Then Rinna took one copper back for the latch.

He protested for three minutes.

Nobody helped him.

I helped Nessa coil the ghost.

That was harder than installing it.

Leather remembered every wrong bend.

"Loose," she said.

"I am loose."

"The coil."

"I know."

"You don't."

I loosened it.

She took the first loop, showed me once, and handed it back.

No speech.

I did the rest.

When we finished, the ghost looked like rope.

That was disappointing.

"Where does it live?" I asked.

"Wall chest."

"With magic?"

"No."

"Why not?"

"Because it's a tube."

"Good."

She looked at me.

"What are you doing?"

"Nothing."

"You're doing the thing."

"What thing?"

"Thinking at props."

"I don't think at props."

"You bought broken magic."

"Pell told you."

"Pell tells everyone everything."

From across the room Pell said, "No I don't."

Nessa ignored him.

I said, "Hessa wants me to write a question."

"Who?"

"Guild."

"The woman?"

"Yes."

"What question?"

"Prepared structure."

Nessa put the ghost into the wall chest.

"Ask someone who makes it."

"I did."

"Then why ask Guild?"

"Different question."

She closed the chest.

"Good."

That was all I got.

Outside, it was properly dark.

The street lamps were lit.

One of the prepared globes near the market had gone green again before
settling yellow. A lamp tender stood beneath it with a long pole and
swore at the fixture.

I walked toward Lyssa's.

She was not there.

The woman downstairs was.

"Road actor."

"Greg."

"Same."

"She's out."

"Where?"

The woman looked at me.

"I don't know."

That answer felt healthy.

"When back?"

"Didn't ask."

Also healthy.

I went upstairs.

Lyssa had told me I could.

That still felt strange.

I ate the end of yesterday's bread.

Then I found paper.

Hessa wanted a question.

I wrote:

HOW MUCH OF THE EFFECT HAS TO BE MINE?

I stared at it.

Wrong.

The blue lamp had gotten into the question again.

I crossed it out.

I wrote:

WHAT IS THE SMALLEST THING I CAN MOVE?

That sounded like a child challenging furniture.

Crossed out.

I wrote:

CAN I PRODUCE A REPEATABLE EXTERNAL CHANGE SMALL ENOUGH TO ISOLATE?

I hated the word isolate.

It sounded like Hessa.

I left it.

Then, underneath:

IF YES, HOW LITTLE OF IT HAS TO CHANGE BEFORE IT COUNTS?

That was worse.

Maybe better.

I did not cross it out.

The door opened downstairs.

Footsteps.

Not Lyssa's.

Someone laughed.

A door closed.

I waited.

Nothing.

I looked at the questions.

Then I remembered Veya's hands stopping around the cloth.

The tube had been real.

Pell's voice had been real.

The dark hanging had been real.

The empty space had contained nothing at all.

I had known that.

I had still looked.

I turned the paper over before I could write something stupid about
ghosts.

Tomorrow I had theatre.

The day after, Hessa had paper.

For now, that was enough.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 178

## THE ENSEMBLE PLAYER

Lyssa came home with somebody else's shoes.

Not wearing them.

Carrying them by the laces.

I was still at the table with Hessa's question facedown when the door
opened and Lyssa came in sideways, one shoulder against the frame, a
paper parcel under one arm and a pair of brown shoes dangling from two
fingers.

She stopped when she saw me.

"You live here now?"

"Apparently."

"Terrible."

"Whose shoes?"

"Jessa's."

"Why?"

"Because she went home barefoot."

"Why?"

Lyssa put the shoes on the table.

"Because her feet hurt."

"That doesn't answer why you have them."

"She left them at Marra's."

"That still doesn't."

"I am returning them tomorrow."

"Now we have a story."

She looked at the paper in front of me.

"What is that?"

"Nothing."

"Guild nothing?"

"Yes."

She reached for it.

I put my hand on top.

"No."

"Then definitely Guild nothing."

"It's a question."

"To who?"

"Hessa."

"The woman who makes you not do magic?"

"She lets me do magic."

"While making you not do magic."

"That's unfair."

"Did anything move?"

"That was yesterday."

Lyssa nodded.

"So no."

"Correct."

She put the parcel beside Jessa's shoes and started unpinning her hair.
The brass leaves were not in it tonight. I noticed that and then felt
stupid for noticing.

"Where were you?"

"Marra's. Then Jessa's sister's. Then the dyer."

"At night?"

"The dyer closes when the work is done."

"What work?"

"Blue."

"That's not work."

"It was six lengths of blue."

"More work."

She opened the parcel.

Inside was cheese.

I respected the parcel more.

"Did you buy that?"

"No."

"Steal it?"

"Payment."

"For blue?"

"For carrying the blue because Jessa took her shoes off."

I looked at the shoes.

"This city has complicated trade."

"You came home with broken magic."

"Educational garbage."

"Where is it?"

I pointed toward my bag.

Lyssa went to the bag.

"No."

She stopped.

"You said it doesn't do anything."

"It doesn't."

"Then why no?"

"Because Hessa said don't alter it."

"I was going to look."

"That's how it starts."

Lyssa stared at me.

Then she laughed.

"You're scared I'll accidentally do magic."

"No."

"You're scared I'll make your trash less educational."

"Yes."

She left the bag alone.

We ate cheese.

Later, she found the question anyway because I forgot it on the table
when I washed.

She read it upside down.

"Can I produce a repeatable external change small enough to isolate?"

"Stop."

"What does that mean?"

"I don't know."

"Good question."

"Give it back."

She did.

Then she read the second line before letting go.

"How little does it have to change before it counts?"

"That's not exactly what it says."

"It's exactly what it says."

"It has more words."

"Why?"

"Hessa."

"Does she charge by the word?"

"No."

"Then you're doing that yourself."

I folded the paper.

"Tomorrow is theatre."

"Today was theatre."

"Tomorrow is also theatre."

"Do you get a day off?"

"I had several before I met them."

"Those don't count."

She was right.

That was annoying.
