In bed, I found out she had been using my side for folded clothes.

I moved them.

She moved two back.

"Those are clean."

"So?"

"Your road coat touched the floor in four towns."

"More."

"Exactly."

I put the road coat on the chair.

She moved the clean clothes.

Compromise.

I slept better than I had on the road.

I also woke with Lyssa's elbow in my throat.

Home.

East Market Hall had lost a room overnight.

Not literally.

The room still existed.

A group of six men with rolled papers had rented it.

Rinna was standing in the corridor arguing with one of them.

"I was told noon."

"You were told the room was yours after noon."

"It is after noon."

"It is eleven forty."

Rinna looked toward me.

"What time is it?"

I stopped.

The man looked at me too.

This was dangerous.

"Almost noon."

Rinna smiled.

The man did not.

"Greg," she said, "go away."

I did.

Inside the hall, Pell was repairing the latch.

He had removed it entirely.

"That seems worse."

"It's temporary."

"Door doesn't close."

"That's why it's temporary."

Nessa walked past carrying a painted column.

"Don't talk to him."

"I wasn't."

"You were."

Pell said, "He started it."

Nessa kept walking.

The painted column was stone from ten feet away and wood from two.

I followed it.

Not Nessa.

The column.

She set it beside a shallow doorway built into a painted wall.

The doorway bothered me.

It looked wrong.

The painted wall had lines that narrowed toward the back. The doorway
itself was only deep enough for a person to stand inside and turn
sideways. Somebody had painted another door beyond it.

Up close, the second door was obviously paint.

The floor between them was paint.

The little shadow under the far lintel was paint.

"That's bad," I said.

Nessa looked at me.

"What?"

"The door."

"What door?"

"The back one."

"There is no back one."

"Exactly."

"Good."

"No. It looks fake."

"From here."

She walked away.

I stayed.

Then I went into the seats.

The back door became a door.

Not a good door.

A door.

The real front frame cast an actual shadow across the painted floor. The
painted shadow farther back continued it. The real column hid one edge.
The narrowing lines did the rest.

I moved three seats left.

Worse.

Three seats right.

Better.

Pell appeared beside me.

"What are you doing?"

"Door."

"What?"

I pointed.

He looked.

"That's been there forever."

"I know."

"You've seen it."

"I know."

"Why are you looking now?"

"Go fix your latch."

He left.

I went back to the stage.

There was a wooden crate in front of the column.

I moved it.

The doorway looked more real from here.

Nessa came back.

"Why?"

"Why what?"

"The crate."

"It was blocking the column."

"Put it back."

"Why?"

"Because from the house it blocks the bottom."

"The bottom is real."

"Yes."

"Why hide the real part?"

"Because it looks wrong."

That offended me.

I went back into the seats.

The crate hid where the real floor met the painted floor.

Without it, the seam made the whole thing shallow.

With it, the seam disappeared.

The fake door got deeper.

I put the crate back.

Nessa said nothing.

That was worse than being told.

The day's bill was not yesterday's.

Teren had crossed Shopkeeper out.

I stared at the board.

"What?"

"Not tonight."

"Why?"

"Veya wants the room."

"Veya is not Shopkeeper."

"No."

"What am I?"

"Third Man."

"What is Third Man?"

"Third man."

"How many lines?"

"Seven."

"That's not a role."

"It has a name."

"What name?"

"Third Man."

I looked at him.

He was already reading something else.

"Anything else?"

"Shopkeeper tomorrow."

"Probably?"

"Probably."

I had been demoted by a woman who was not even taking my part.

The piece was called The Petition.

I had seen part of it before we left, but not enough to matter.

Third Man entered with two other petitioners, argued about who had been
waiting longest, delivered a complaint about a goat, and left.

The goat was not present.

Good.

My seven lines were easy.

The problem was that my fifth line was a cue.

Nessa told me that.

Not Teren.

"Don't change it."

"I don't change lines."

She looked at me.

"Not that one."

"Why?"

"Door."

"What door?"

"Side."

She pointed.

A young actor named Sellen was supposed to enter on the word "neighbor."

My line was:

My neighbor's goat has eaten half my fence and all my patience.

Sellen entered on neighbor.

"That's obvious," I said.

"Good."

"Why not enter after goat?"

"Because then he crosses Veya."

"After fence?"

"Music."

"What music?"

"You'll hear it."

I did.

There was a three-note sting from the balcony after fence.

Not magic.

A little reed.

Everything was already full.

We ran it once.

I said the line.

Sellen entered on neighbor.

The reed sounded after fence.

Veya turned.

Nobody hit anyone.

Teren said, "Again."

We did.

Then somebody needed the stage for the rented room's chairs, which did
not make sense until I learned they were borrowing ours.

The six men with rolled papers came through.

One of them pointed at the painted doorway.

"Can that move?"

Nessa said, "No."

"It has wheels."

"No."

"It visibly has wheels."

"No."

They took chairs.

The doorway stayed.

I liked Nessa.

The afternoon broke into pieces.

I carried chairs.

Then costumes.

Then a bucket of paint with a prepared lid that tightened itself when
the rim was pressed twice. Pell pressed it three times and could not
open it.

Nessa made him carry it to the paint woman.

I did not help.

Marek arrived, changed his shirt, ate something from his pocket, and
left again.

"Where are you going?"

"Back."

"Back where?"

He pointed behind himself.

"That's not a place."

"It is if you're going there."

He disappeared through the side door.

I did not see him again until the show.

Serra came in once, spoke to Rinna, took a wrapped bundle from the
office, and left.

She saw me.

"Back?"

"Apparently."

"Good."

That was all.

I wanted to ask where she had been.

I did not.

At four, Lyssa came through the hall carrying Jessa's shoes.

I was holding a painted bench.

"What are you doing?"

"Returning shoes."

"Here?"

"Jessa's sister is meeting me by the west market."

"This is east."

"I know where markets are."

"Why are you here?"

"Shortcut."

She looked at the bench.

"What are you doing?"

"Acting."

"That looks heavy."

"It's a demanding role."

Nessa said from behind me, "Greg."

Lyssa smiled.

"I like her."

"You don't know her."

"I know enough."

She left through the opposite door.

Did not stay.

Did not ask about the show.

Good.

I carried the bench.

By evening, The Petition had changed one chair, two cups, and a coat.

My seven lines had not changed.

I knew them.

That was the problem.

The audience was good.

Not loud.

Interested.

The first petitioner got a laugh I had never heard in rehearsal.

The second got another.

I came in.

We argued.

Veya, playing the clerk, asked what business could possibly justify
three grown men shouting in her office.

The first petitioner answered.

The second answered.

Then me.

"My neighbor's goat has eaten half my fence and all my patience."

Sellen entered.

Perfect.

The audience laughed at the goat.

I should have stopped.

Instead, because the laugh was there and the road had taught me what to
do with a laugh, I looked toward the side door and added:

"And apparently he's followed me."

Bigger laugh.

Good laugh.

Sellen stopped.

Bad.

He had entered as the neighbor's son.

His first line was:

My father sent me because the goat is innocent.

Except I had just implied he was the goat.

The audience looked at him.

Sellen looked at me.

There were several things he could do.

Most were bad.

He chose one.

"My father sent me because the goat is innocent," he said.

The audience laughed again.

Different laugh.

Sellen kept going.

The reed missed its entrance because the balcony player was laughing
too.

Veya waited.

The pause stretched.

Then she slapped the desk.

"Your goat may defend itself after the people."

That was not her line.

It fixed the order.

Sellen moved.

The reed player found the three notes late.

The scene continued.

It worked.

That was the worst part.

Backstage, I was pleased for almost thirty seconds.

Then Sellen came off.

"Don't."

"It worked."

"For you."

There it was.

He was not angry enough to fight.

That would have been easier.

"You entered."

"Yes."

"You covered."

"Yes."

"The audience liked it."

"Yes."

"So..."

He stared at me.

"So I had to become a goat."

I laughed.

He did not.

"Sorry."

"Don't be sorry. Say the line."

"Right."

He walked away.

Teren appeared.

"Good laugh."

I smiled.

"Don't do it again."

Smile gone.

"It worked."

"Sellen already told you why it didn't."

"Yes."

"Good."

He left.

I stood there.

Pell walked past.

"Goat."

"Fuck you."

He laughed.

The next piece used the painted doorway.

I was not in it.

I helped shift the crate.

Then I watched from the side.

Up close, the painted hall beyond the doorway was terrible.

One brushstroke made a wall.

Another made a shadow.

The far door was four dark lines and a brass-colored dot.

An actor crossed through the real frame, stopped where the real floor
ended, and turned as if somebody farther inside had spoken.

He looked into painted space.

The audience looked with him.

Nobody laughed.

The room behind him did not exist.

The crate covered the seam.

The real frame cast the first shadow.

The actor supplied the rest.

I knew that.

I still wanted to see who was in the painted room.

That was becoming a problem.

After the show, Rinna paid me one copper.

"One?"

"Third Man."

"Seven lines."

"Exactly."

"I carried a bench."

"Free."

"Ghost yesterday."

"Different day."

"Door."

"What door?"

I gave up.

One copper.

Still money.

Sellen got paid too.

I considered apologizing again.

Then decided he had specifically told me not to be sorry.

I said, "Neighbor."

He looked at me.

"Goat."

"Fair."

That seemed to fix enough.

Pell was still working on the latch.

The door now closed.

It did not open.

Progress.

Nessa had received a folded note sometime during the second piece. She
read it, put it in her pocket, and left before cleanup finished.

Nobody told me why.

Teren and Veya were arguing quietly near the office.

Not about me.

I could tell because neither looked at me.

That was relaxing.

I moved cups.

Stacked chairs.

Put the crate back where it belonged.

Not where it looked best from the stage.

Where it looked best from the seats.

I was learning which direction mattered.

Outside, Marek was waiting with food.

"For me?"

"No."

He ate it.

"Why are you waiting?"

"Not for you."

"Good."

A woman came around the corner.

Marek handed her a folded paper.

She handed him a small wrapped parcel.

Neither introduced me.

They left in different directions.

I went home.

Lyssa was there this time.

Jessa's shoes were gone.

"Successful?"

"What?"

"The shoes."

"Yes."

"Good."

She was sitting on the floor with cloth spread over her knees, picking
stitches out of one seam.

I put my one copper on the table.

"Rich."

"Third Man."

"What's that?"

"Apparently one copper."

"Good role."

"I was a goat."

She looked up.

I explained.

Not all of it.

Enough.

She laughed harder than the audience had.

"You're horrible."

"It got a laugh."

"At him."

"Yes."

"You're horrible."

"I said sorry."

"Did that help?"

"No."

"Good."

I sat.

The question paper was where I had left it.

Lyssa had put a cup on the corner so it would not curl.

She had not written on it.

I appreciated that.

Tomorrow was Hessa.

I read the question again.

CAN I PRODUCE A REPEATABLE EXTERNAL CHANGE SMALL ENOUGH TO ISOLATE?

Still ugly.

Still probably useful.

I thought about adding something about the doorway.

I did not.

The doorway was not Hessa's problem.

The fact that four painted lines could become a room if one real frame
told the truth first was Nessa's problem.

Maybe nobody's problem.

Maybe just a door.

Lyssa held up the seam she was unpicking.

"Does this look straight?"

"No."

"Good."

"Why good?"

"Because I'm taking it out."

I looked again.

The stitches were very straight.

The cloth underneath them was not.

"Then the stitches are straight."

"Wrong place."

"Oh."

She kept cutting.

I did not say anything else.

Tomorrow Hessa wanted something real to move.

Tonight Lyssa was removing perfectly good stitches because they made the
dress wrong.

At the theatre, a real floor had made a fake room worse until we hid
part of it.

I was beginning to suspect that being technically correct was not as
useful as I had been promised.

That sounded like something Hessa would hate.

I did not write it down.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 179

## THE TESTER

Lyssa was gone before I woke.

There was bread on the table, half a pear, and a note under the cup that
had been holding down my question.

PAPER DAY.

Under that:

DON'T BECOME A GOAT.

I ate the pear.

The question went into my coat.

The failed throw blank did not. I had considered bringing it, then
decided I had already shown Hessa the garbage. Carrying the same useless
piece of metal back to her felt less like research and more like needing
somebody to admire a purchase.

The Guild rooms were busy enough that nobody noticed me for several
minutes.

A man I did not know was standing in the front passage with a cracked
white plate held between both hands. A narrow copper line ran through
its center and stopped at the crack.

"It held yesterday," he said.

A clerk behind the desk said, "It is cracked today."

"Yes."

"So it did not hold today."

"I can see that."

"Good."

I liked the Guild.

Hessa's door was open.

She was not waiting for me.

She had three narrow boxes on her table and a stack of papers under one
elbow. One box was sealed with red wax. One had a little brass tag tied
to it. The third was open and contained six black stones arranged in two
rows.

A woman in a gray Guild coat stood beside her.

"No," Hessa said.

The woman tapped the paper.

"It is the same mark."

"It resembles the same mark."

"How many differences do you need?"

"One useful one."

The woman looked toward me.

"Yours?"

"No," Hessa said.

"Good."

She gathered two papers and left.

Hessa watched her go.

Then she looked at me.

"You have the question?"

I took it out.

She held out her hand.

I gave it to her.

She read the first line.

Then the second.

Then the first again.

"Why are there two?"

"The second is part of the first."

"No."

"Related?"

"Yes."

"That's better."

She put the paper flat on the table.

"Can I produce a repeatable external change small enough to isolate,"
she read. "That is a question."

"Good."

"Do not look pleased."

I stopped.

She tapped the second line.

"If yes, how little of it has to change before it counts."

"Also a question."

"A worse one."

"Why?"

"Counts as what?"

"An effect."

"Observable?"

"Yes."

"Repeatable?"

"Yes."

"Caused by you?"

"Yes."

"Magical?"

I hesitated.

"Hopefully."

Hessa looked at me.

"Those are not one threshold."

"Right."

"You keep trying to make one sentence do several jobs."

"I've been acting."

That came out before I meant it to.

Hessa leaned back slightly.

"How long?"

"What?"

"How long were you with the players?"

"Several weeks."

"And now?"

"Still with them."

"I know."

She pushed the paper back toward me.

"You have spent several weeks being rewarded when people reach the
intended conclusion."

"Sometimes."

"Sometimes the intended conclusion is that Marek is dead."

"That happened."

"Was he dead?"

"No."

"Then stop bringing me conclusions."

I almost laughed.

She did not.

"I wasn't."

"You wrote 'counts.'"

"That's not a conclusion."

"It is asking permission for one."

I folded the paper once.

"Sometimes more real makes something worse."

Hessa's eyes narrowed.

I knew immediately that I should have left that at home.

"Worse at what?"

There it was.

"A play."

"Then ask a player."

"No. I mean, if you're making something look right."

"To an audience."

"Yes."

"Then ask a player."

"Fine."

"Good."

She stood.

"Today we are making something boring."

"I expected that."

"Good."

She moved the three boxes to the far shelf.

"Do not touch those."

"I wasn't going to."

"You were looking."

"I look at things."

"I know."

The apparatus from the last session was not on the table.

Hessa had changed it.

The shallow wooden frame remained, but the two folded paper tabs were
gone. In their place were two narrow paper fins, each folded once at the
bottom so it could stand upright. They sat between paired wooden guides
no wider than my little finger. Each guide had three ink marks along its
edge.

The glass shield was taller.

It covered the whole frame.

Four little wedges held it off the table.

"What happened to the tabs?"

"They were bad."

"I liked them."

"They were bad."

"Why?"

"Too much surface. Uneven folds. One leaned."

"The target?"

"The control."

"Did that matter?"

"It could have."

"So you changed them."

"Yes."

She put a finger on one paper fin.

"These can move only forward or back without hitting the guides."

"How far?"

"If we are lucky, not at all."

"Right."

"Sit."

I sat.

She turned the frame around.

Then again.

"What are you doing?"

"Annoying you."

"Working."

"That too."

She took two small wooden squares from a cup. One had a dot on the
underside.

She mixed them in her hands and placed one beneath each side of the
frame where I could not see.

"Which is target?"

"You tell me."

"I don't know."

"Good."

"How am I supposed to affect it?"

"You aren't yet."

She lowered the glass.

"First, you draw."

That part had become familiar enough to be dangerous.

I put my hand where she indicated.

Feet settled.

Shoulders loose.

No reaching.

No pushing.

No trying to make the room interesting.

I drew.

The mana came cleanly.

Not large.

Never large.

It gathered with the same internal wrongness that had stopped feeling
entirely wrong. I held the smallest useful amount and stopped.

Hessa watched my face, then my hand.

"Good."

Twenty-two.

I did not say it.

She probably had it written somewhere.

"Now shape."

"Toward what?"

"Nothing."

That was irritating.

I shaped anyway.

Deliberately.

The familiar asymmetry appeared. The wrist edge wanted to become more
definite than the other side. I did not chase it. I held the shape as
evenly as I could.

Hessa walked around the table.

"Again."

"I thought that was one."

"It is."

"Then why again?"

"Because I said again."

I adjusted.

She stopped me before I could rebuild the whole thing.

"Better."

Eighteen.

Maybe.

I still did not say it.

Hessa lifted the glass, reached under the frame, and checked the wooden
squares.

Then she turned the entire frame a quarter turn.

She replaced the glass.

"The left fin."

"That's target?"

"Yes."

"Why hide it before?"

"Because you spent the last session watching paper until you nearly
invented a result."

"I didn't invent it."

"You stopped yourself before you did."

"That's different."

"Yes."

I liked that answer less than I expected.

She pointed to the left fin.

"One direction only. Away from you. Do not move it sideways. Do not lift
it. Do not make it tremble. Do not make it interesting."

"How far?"

"One mark would be excellent."

The marks were tiny.

"That's all?"

Hessa looked at me.

"Move it first."

Fair.

I settled again.

The mana was already there.

I shaped toward the paper.

Not the whole paper.

Not a shove.

That was the problem with thinking move. Move was large. Move contained
success.

I tried to make the intention smaller.

Forward.

Barely.

The room was quiet except for somebody dragging a chair in the passage.

The sound stopped.

I waited.

Nothing happened.

The paper stood between the guides.

I kept the shape.

Nothing.

My leg began to ache from how I was sitting.

I adjusted without thinking.

Hessa said, "Stop."

I stopped.

"What?"

"You moved."

"Me."

"Yes."

"Not the paper."

"Correct."

"Can we try again?"

"We are still trying."

She inspected both fins without touching them.

Neither had moved.

Then she checked the wedges beneath the glass.

"Again."

I reset.

The second time I did not think about the paper.

That was impossible, obviously.

I thought about the space between its front edge and the first ink mark.

Smaller.

The mana held.

The shaping held.

Forward.

The left fin moved.

I saw it.

It did not jump.

It did not fall.

Its bottom edge slid along the wood with a tiny dry sound.

Less than the width of my smallest fingernail.

But it moved.

I stopped breathing.

Hessa said, "Stop."

I stopped everything.

She did not look at me.

She looked at the glass.

Then the right fin.

Then the table.

Then the floor.

"It moved."

Hessa lifted one finger.

I shut up.

She crouched.

Checked the wedges.

Pressed the table with two fingers.

Looked at the paper from the side.

Then she stood.

"Did you touch the table?"

"No."

"Did your knee?"

"No."

"Foot?"

"No."

"I didn't move."

"I know you believe that."

"I know where my foot is."

"Good."

She marked something on the page.

"What did you write?"

"Movement."

"That's it?"

"Yes."

"Target movement?"

"Yes."

"Control?"

"No visible movement."

I felt something open in my chest.

Not mana.

Worse.

Hope.

Hessa saw it.

"Again."

The next attempt did nothing.

Of course.

I held the same shape.

Or I thought I did.

The paper did not move.

The control did not move.

Nothing moved.

"Again," I said.

"No."

"What?"

"Release fully."

"I can do another."

"You can release."

I released.

The mana went.

I hated that.

Hessa waited.

Then she lifted the glass and swapped the fins.

Not the wooden squares.

The fins themselves.

"What are you doing?"

"Seeing if one likes to move."

"Paper doesn't like things."

"Good."

She checked the folds.

One was slightly flatter at the base.

Not much.

Enough that I could see it once she pointed.

"Was that the target?"

"Yes."

My chest closed again.

"So it moved because it was easier."

"I did not say that."

"It could have."

"Yes."

"Then it doesn't count."

Hessa looked at me.

"Counts as what?"

I sighed.

She almost smiled.

Almost.

She turned the frame again.

Then she switched which wooden square sat beneath which side.

I watched.

"Now I know."

"Yes."

"So what's the point?"

"The point is that we are not doing another external attempt."

"What?"

"Not today."

"That was one movement."

"Yes."

"And one failure."

"Yes."

"Which means we need another."

"Which means I need to know whether the apparatus is lying before I ask
you to draw again."

"The apparatus can't lie."

Hessa looked at me.

I thought about painted doors.

"Fine."

"It can mislead."

"Better."

She wrote again.

I leaned.

She covered the page with her hand.

"That's childish."

"Sit back."

I sat back.

"What did you write?"

"Possible directional movement during supervised external attempt. Not
repeated. Apparatus asymmetry identified after attempt."

"Possible."

"Yes."

"It moved."

"Yes."

"Under the glass."

"Yes."

"Control didn't."

"Correct."

"And I was shaping toward it."

"Correct."

"That sounds like magic."

"It sounds like a reason to build a better frame."

I stared at her.

"You hate joy."

"No."

"Evidence?"

"Frequently."

Someone knocked.

Hessa said, "Come."

The woman in the gray coat returned without waiting.

"The mark is on two more."

Hessa stood immediately.

"Where?"

"South storage."

"Both?"

"One crate. Two seals."

"Who opened it?"

"No one."

Hessa looked at me.

"We are done."

"What?"

"You heard her."

"I have theatre later."

"Excellent."

"That's not related."

"I know."

She was already gathering two papers.

"What about next time?"

"Not until I replace the fins."

"When?"

"I will tell you."

"Two days?"

"No."

"Three?"

"Greg."

"Right."

She stopped at the door.

"Do not reproduce this at home."

"I know."

"Do not use different paper."

"I know."

"Do not decide that because one paper moved, you can move paper."

"I wasn't going to."

She waited.

"I was going to a little."

"I know."

The gray-coated woman looked between us.

"Is this the paper man?"

"No," Hessa said.

I said, "Apparently."

Hessa pointed at the door.

I left.

At the front desk, the man with the cracked white plate was gone. The
plate was not. It sat in a shallow tray with a scrap of paper tied to
one corner.

DO NOT USE.

Under that, in different writing:

OBVIOUSLY.

I stopped long enough to read both.

The clerk looked up.

"Yours?"

"No."

"Then keep moving."

I did.

Outside, the day had become offensively normal.

A courier passed with a brass seal at his shoulder that flashed once
when the receiving clerk touched it. A woman was arguing over onions.
Somebody had dropped a basket of laundry in the street.

I had possibly moved paper.

Possibly.

That word was unbearable.

I walked to East Market Hall.

Pell had fixed the latch.

I knew because the door opened.

"Look," he said.

"Congratulations."

"It closes too."

"Magic."

"No."

"Better."

The painted doorway was still there.

The crate was still in front of the seam.

I did not touch it.

Teren had tomorrow's bill half written.

Tonight was mostly rehearsal and a shorter public piece later. I was not
in the public piece.

Good.

Sellen was onstage with The Petition pages.

He saw me.

"Goat."

"Neighbor."

Nessa was not there.

Veya was.

She looked at me.

"You're third again tomorrow."

"Seven lines?"

"Unless you earn fewer."

"Fair."

We ran the entrance.

Veya asked what business justified three grown men shouting in her
office.

First petitioner.

Second petitioner.

Me.

"My neighbor's goat has eaten half my fence and all my patience."

Sellen entered on neighbor.

The reed sounded after fence.

I said nothing else.

Sellen's eyes flicked toward me.

That was all.

The scene continued.

It felt smaller.

It also worked for everyone.

Afterward, Pell asked why I kept staring at my hand.

"I might have moved paper."

He waited.

"With magic."

He waited longer.

"Maybe."

Pell nodded.

"Good."

"That's it?"

"What do you want?"

"I don't know."

"How far?"

I held my fingers close together.

"Less."

He looked at the gap.

"That's bad magic."

"Apparently."

"Still magic."

"Maybe."

He shrugged.

Then he went to get a coil of rope because somebody had called his name.

I stood alone for perhaps five seconds.

Then Veya shoved a stack of pages into my chest.

"Office."

"What?"

"Take those to Teren."

I took them.

Work.

The public piece that night used no ghost, no blue lamp, no painted
room. It was two people, a table, a bad marriage, and a bowl of onions.

I watched from the side.

The audience laughed in the right places.

One woman cried near the end.

Nothing magical happened.

I thought about the paper anyway.

That was probably why Hessa had sent me away.

At home, Lyssa was not there yet.

I put the question paper back on the table.

Under the second line, I wrote:

ONE MOVEMENT.

Then I stared at it.

I added:

NOT REPEATED.

Then:

ONE FIN WAS EASIER TO MOVE.

That looked worse.

More accurate.

Worse.

I left it.

Lyssa came in while I was taking off my boot.

"Paper day?"

"Yes."

"Did anything move?"

I looked at her.

She stopped.

"Something moved."

"Maybe."

"That's annoying."

"Extremely."

She put down a bundle of dark cloth.

"How much?"

I showed her with my fingers.

She leaned closer.

"That's nothing."

"I know."

She smiled.

"You're happy."

"No."

"Greg."

"Possibly."

She laughed and went to wash her hands.

I looked at the three lines again.

ONE MOVEMENT.

NOT REPEATED.

ONE FIN WAS EASIER TO MOVE.

At the theatre, I could have made a room out of less.

Hessa would not even let me make a result.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 180

## THE THIRD MAN

Lyssa had the dark cloth spread across the table when I woke.

It covered breakfast.

"Is there bread under that?"

"No."

"Was there bread under that?"

"Yes."

"What happened to it?"

"I ate it."

I sat up.

Lyssa had pinned one edge of the cloth to itself and was measuring
something with a length of cord. The brass leaves were not in her hair.
They were on the shelf beside the washbasin with two pins through them.

"What is it?"

"Skirt."

"For you?"

"No."

"Marra?"

"No."

"Jessa?"

"No."

She looked at me.

"Am I allowed to know?"

"When I know whether I hate it."

"That seems fair."

She folded the cloth back and uncovered a heel of cheese.

"Breakfast."

"That's not bread."

"You slept."

Apparently that was my fault.

I ate the cheese while she marked the cloth with chalk.

After a while she said, "So paper moved and Hessa says maybe you
didn't."

I stopped chewing.

"That's a hostile summary."

"Is it wrong?"

"The paper definitely moved."

"And maybe you did it."

"Yes."

"Good."

"Why is that good?"

"Because yesterday you said maybe seven times."

"I did not."

"You did."

"You counted?"

"No. I got tired."

She folded the cloth again.

"What does Hessa think?"

"That the frame needs fixing."

"So she thinks the frame moved the paper."

"No."

"She thinks you moved it."

"No."

"She thinks something moved it."

"The paper moved."

Lyssa looked at me.

I pointed at her.

"Exactly."

She laughed.

I finished the cheese.

By the time I left, she had the cloth rolled under one arm and was going
south, not north. I did not ask where. She kissed me once at the door,
told me not to become a magician before supper, and walked away before I
could explain that this was precisely the disputed point.

East Market Hall had acquired a sign.

GREG MOVED PAPER.

It was written in charcoal on the wall beside the repaired latch.

I stood there.

Pell came through the door carrying three wooden bowls.

"Morning."

I pointed.

He looked.

"Oh."

"Did you write that?"

"No."

"Who did?"

"Don't know."

"You told someone."

"Yes."

"Who?"

He thought.

"Several people."

"Why?"

"You moved paper."

"Maybe."

"It moved."

"Yes."

"You were doing magic."

"Yes."

"So."

"No."

Pell shifted the bowls into one hand.

"I don't understand what part you don't understand."

"I don't understand what part you understand."

"Paper moved."

"Yes."

"While you were trying to move it."

"Yes."

"With magic."

"Possibly."

He nodded toward the sign.

"That's too long."

Then he went inside.

I rubbed at the charcoal with my thumb.

It smeared.

The words remained readable.

I rubbed harder.

"Leave it."

Rinna was behind me.

I turned.

"Why?"

"Because somebody will write it again and I don't want charcoal
everywhere."

"It's not true."

"Did paper move?"

"Yes."

"Did you move it?"

"Maybe."

"Then it's badly written."

"Thank you."

"Move chairs."

There were twenty-four folding chairs stacked near the side wall.

I moved chairs.

The hall was busier than it had been on the road and less organized than
I remembered. Two actors I had seen before but never traveled with were
arguing over a coat. A woman with paint on both wrists was repainting
the edge of a window flat because somebody had stored it face-down. Veya
was onstage with Sellen and another man, working through the office
scene without us.

Teren was at the front table talking to a baker.

Not about bread.

"Four evenings," the baker said.

"Three."

"Four."

"Three and the afternoon."

"That's four."

"No."

The baker stared at him.

Teren stared back.

I carried chairs around them.

Nobody asked whether I had moved paper.

That lasted six minutes.

A woman I knew only as one of the costume workers caught my sleeve.

"Pell says you finally did magic."

"No."

Her eyebrows rose.

"Paper moved."

"Yes."

"With magic."

"Maybe."

She looked disappointed.

"What did you do before?"

"Nothing."

"That's worse."

She let go and kept walking.

I found Pell backstage.

"You told her I finally did magic."

"I said you moved paper."

"She heard finally did magic."

"That sounds better."

"It isn't better."

"For a story."

I stopped.

Pell was tying a cord around a bundle of wooden spoons.

He did not notice.

Or he did and did not care.

"For a story," I repeated.

"Yes."

"Hessa would hate you."

"Who?"

"Never mind."

Nessa still was not there.

Her absence had become a practical problem rather than a mystery. Two
costume questions were waiting on a bench with nobody answering them. A
torn cuff had a note pinned to it. The painted doorway needed a strip of
cloth along the back edge, and nobody knew where she had put the right
gray.

Veya knew where the gray was.

"Third shelf."

Pell looked.

"Which room?"

Veya closed her eyes.

"Paint."

"Ah."

He left.

The hall survived.

That was useful to know.

Around noon, Teren put me at the front door with Sellen.

"Why?"

"Because you can speak."

"So can he."

"Not to strangers."

Sellen said, "I can."

Teren looked at him.

Sellen said, "I don't want to."

"See?"

We had a board with the evening bill painted on it.

THE PETITION.

THE WIDOW'S ROOM.

A SHORT MUSICAL PIECE I had never seen.

Two copper at the door for the full bill. One for children. The first
twenty people got the better benches, which seemed less like an
advertisement and more like a threat.

A man stopped.

"Is this the one with the ghost?"

"No," I said.

Sellen said, "Tomorrow."

The man looked interested.

"Real ghost?"

"Yes," I said.

Sellen turned his head.

The man said, "Really?"

"Pell."

"What?"

"The ghost is Pell."

The man looked less interested.

Sellen waited until he had walked away.

"You are bad at this."

"I told the truth."

"You told all of it."

"Apparently that's bad."

"At a door? Yes."

A woman with two children stopped.

"Any animals?"

Sellen said, "A goat."

"There is no goat," I said.

"There is a goat."

"There is discussion of a goat."

"That's a goat."

The children wanted to see the goat.

We sold three seats.

I decided not to interfere.

Later, I helped set the table for The Petition.

The papers on Veya's desk were fake.

Mostly.

The top sheet had six actual lines of writing.

The sheets beneath it had marks that became words from a few paces away
and nothing at all up close.

I picked one up.

"Who writes these?"

Sellen said, "Who cares?"

"Somebody."

"Probably Nessa."

"Nessa writes fake petitions?"

"She does everything."

I put the paper down.

One corner had a real wax seal.

Not a prepared seal.

Just wax.

From the house, the seal made the entire stack look official.

I knew the rest was nonsense.

It still looked more official with the seal.

I did not touch it again.

Before the doors opened, we also had to find a missing bench.

Not repair one. Find one.

Rinna's count said twelve. The hall contained eleven.

Pell counted twice and got thirteen the second time.

"How?"

"I counted that one twice."

"Why?"

"It looked useful."

Sellen found the missing bench in the costume room with three baskets of
hats on it. Nobody knew who had put it there. The hats had to go
somewhere else, which meant a shelf had to be cleared, which meant a box
of old hand props came down.

I ended up holding a wooden knife, two false keys, and a loaf of bread
made from painted cloth.

The bread looked terrible in my hand.

From ten paces away, beside a real bowl and a real knife, it looked like
bread.

I squeezed it.

"Don't," Veya said.

"I'm not hurting it."

"You're making it bread-shaped wrong."

"It is already bread-shaped."

"Not if you crush it."

I put it down.

The real knife on the prop table was dull enough to be safe and heavy
enough to make the fake loaf look more convincing.

I hated noticing that.

"Do we ever use real bread?"

"Yes."

"Why not here?"

"Because this loaf has been dinner for six years."

That was a better answer than anything I had.

We found room for the hats. The bench went out. The audience would never
know any of this had happened, which seemed to be the normal condition
of theatre.

Before the doors opened, Pell had amended the charcoal sign.

GREG MAYBE MOVED PAPER.

That was worse.

"Why did you add maybe?"

"You complained."

"I don't know if this is better."

"It's more accurate."

Rinna passed us.

"Move."

We moved.

The first piece went badly for somebody else.

A stool leg cracked during an entrance and the actor sitting on it
managed to remain upright by grabbing the other actor's sleeve. The
audience laughed. The scene was not funny.

Backstage, nobody cared why they had laughed.

The stool went out.

Another came in.

Work.

Then The Petition.

I stood in the wing and listened to the first petitioner complain about
a drainage ditch.

The second had a pig.

Then Veya called for the third.

I entered.

The local audience was quieter than the road crowds. I knew that now. I
did not throw the first line at them.

Veya looked at me as if I were already wasting her afternoon.

"What grievance?"

"My neighbor's goat has eaten half my fence and all my patience."

Sellen entered on neighbor.

The reed sounded after fence.

There was a laugh.

Small.

Smaller than the laugh I had gotten when I called Sellen a goat.

I felt the old line waiting.

And apparently he's followed me.

It would work.

I knew exactly where to put it.

I did not.

Sellen crossed in, offended.

"My father sent me because the goat is innocent."

The audience laughed harder.

Not at me.

Sellen held the pause.

Then he added, perfectly serious, "My father is less certain."

The laugh got bigger.

Veya looked down at her papers so the audience would not see her mouth
move.

I hated him.

The scene worked.

The reed player hit the next cue.

Veya got her business.

I got my next line.

Nobody had to repair anything.

When we came off, Sellen said, "Better."

"Your father line isn't written."

"No."

"You improvised."

"Yes."

"You told me not to."

"I told you not to ruin my entrance."

"That's different?"

"Very."

He walked away.

I considered killing him.

Not seriously.

Mostly.

Teren caught my shoulder before I could leave the wing.

"Good."

"Sellen improvised."

"I heard."

"He got a bigger laugh."

"Yes."

"I hate this job."

"No, you don't."

He was right, which made it worse.

The Widow's Room used the painted doorway.

I was crew for the change.

The crate stayed where it belonged.

I knew that without being told.

The fake stack of petitions went off. A low table came on. Someone
scattered dust across only the audience-facing half of an old coat and
hung it beside the painted doorway.

I looked at the clean back.

"Why only half?"

The woman with paint on her wrists said, "Dust costs time."

That was all.

From the house, the coat looked abandoned.

From backstage, it looked like somebody had gotten tired halfway through
making it dirty.

The scene did not use the ghost tube.

It did not use magic.

An actor stood beside the painted doorway and spoke into the room that
did not exist.

Nobody answered.

She waited.

The audience waited with her.

Then she closed the real doorframe against the painted dark.

It should not have worked.

It did.

After the bill, Rinna paid me one copper.

"Third."

"Thank you."

She was already counting someone else's share.

"Rinna."

"What?"

"Did Pell tell you I did magic?"

"Yes."

"I didn't."

"Good."

"I might have."

"Bad."

"Why?"

"Because if you can do magic, somebody will eventually ask me whether
you can do it in a show."

"I can't."

"Then don't."

"That's what I said."

"Good."

She pushed a chair toward me with her foot.

"Stack."

I stacked.

The charcoal sign lasted through cleanup.

By then it had changed again.

GREG MOVED PAPER WITH MAGIC MAYBE.

I stared at it.

Pell stood beside me.

"That one wasn't me."

"Who writes maybe at the end?"

"Someone careful."

"No."

He grinned.

A young actor passing with two lamp stands read it aloud.

"Oh. You did magic?"

"No."

He kept walking.

"Pell says you did."

"I said maybe."

The actor called back, "Congratulations."

I looked at Pell.

He raised both hands.

"I didn't say congratulations."

Nessa came in during the last half hour.

Nobody announced her.

She had a wrapped parcel under one arm and looked tired.

Veya immediately met her with the torn cuff.

Rinna had two questions.

The paint-wrist woman had three.

Nessa put the parcel down and said, "One at a time."

Nobody asked where she had been.

Neither did I.

She answered the cuff first.

By the time I left, the hall was still working.

Sellen was practicing his father line with Veya.

Pell was trying to convince Rinna the charcoal sign increased morale.

Nessa was cutting gray cloth.

Teren and the baker were still arguing about whether three evenings and
an afternoon were four bookings.

I went home.

Lyssa was there.

The dark cloth was not.

"Did you sell it?"

"No."

"What happened?"

"I took it where it was going."

"Where was it going?"

"West."

I took off my coat.

She was eating an apple.

I looked at it.

"No."

"I didn't say anything."

"You looked."

"Marek has damaged me."

"Good."

I put my copper on the table.

"Paid?"

"Third Man."

"Goat?"

"Still innocent."

She bit the apple.

"Did paper move today?"

"No."

"You tried?"

"No."

"Good."

I sat.

She looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"What?"

"Pell told people."

"That paper moved?"

"That I moved paper."

"Did you?"

"Maybe."

She chewed.

"Then he told them the exciting version."

"Yes."

"Do you like the exciting version?"

"No."

She kept looking.

"Maybe."

"Greg."

"I know."

That was the problem.

I liked it.

Not enough to lie.

Enough to understand the temptation.

Hessa had written three ugly lines that made the event smaller every
time they got more accurate.

At the hall, somebody had written six words in charcoal and made me a
magician by moving maybe to the end.

I went to the table.

My question paper was still there.

ONE MOVEMENT.

NOT REPEATED.

ONE FIN WAS EASIER TO MOVE.

I did not add anything.

Lyssa said, "You want supper?"

"Yes."

"I didn't make any."

"Then no."

"We can get something."

I folded the paper and put it away.

We stopped at a street stall two corners from home.

The woman running it had a shallow iron pan over a prepared heat tile.
The tile showed one dull orange line along the rim. She slapped flat
dough onto the pan, turned it, filled it with beans and chopped greens,
and charged us two copper for three.

"Why three?" I asked.

Lyssa said, "Because I know her."

The woman said, "Because the third one tore."

It had.

She folded the torn side inward and handed it to me.

"Still food."

"That's a good business model."

"It is if you stop talking."

We ate standing under the edge of an awning.

Lyssa knew the woman. She also knew a man who stopped to ask whether
Marra still needed the blue thread, and apparently knew that Jessa's
sister had changed her mind about a hem. None of those facts involved
me.

I ate my torn supper and listened.

When the man left, I said, "Blue thread?"

"Tomorrow."

"What happens tomorrow?"

"I carry blue thread."

"Important."

"More useful than moving paper."

"Possibly moving paper."

"Sorry."

She was not sorry.

Outside, somebody shouted at a cart.

A street lamp clicked brighter as the lamplighter touched the prepared
catch at its base.

Lyssa found her shoes.

I found my crutches.

By the time we reached the corner, I had stopped thinking about paper.

Mostly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 181

## THE CALLER

Lyssa was gone before I woke.

There was blue thread on the table.

Not all of it. One loose piece, maybe the length of my hand, had escaped
whatever bundle she was carrying and caught beneath the cup.

I picked it up.

It was blue.

I had no further useful observations.

I left it under the cup.

Outside, Carrow had already decided to be loud. A cart wheel complained
somewhere toward the market. Somebody was selling hot cakes badly enough
that I could hear him from the end of the lane. Two women were arguing
over a basket. A boy ran past with three prepared lamp wicks bundled
under one arm and nearly hit me.

He apologized without slowing.

East Market Hall's charcoal sign was gone.

Mostly.

GREG remained as a gray stain beside the latch.

I rubbed it once with my thumb.

"Don't start."

Rinna was inside the door.

"I wasn't."

"You were touching it."

"That's not starting."

"Good. We need you."

That was rarely good.

"What am I?"

"Calling second and third."

"What happened to whoever calls second and third?"

"Not here."

"Who?"

"Jori."

"Do I know Jori?"

"No."

"Then how do I know his job?"

"You don't."

She handed me a folded page.

I looked at it.

There were lines.

There were marks beside the lines.

There were names I knew and names I didn't.

"Rinna."

"Yes."

"I don't know this."

"I know."

"That's comforting."

"You're not calling first."

"Why?"

"Because first is complicated."

"Also comforting."

She pointed toward the stage.

"Pell will show you second. Veya knows third. Do not invent anything."

"I don't invent things."

Rinna looked at me.

"At work."

She left.

Pell was under the stage.

I knew because his voice came through the ghost tube.

"Greg."

I looked toward the dark corner of the hall.

"Under here."

I looked down.

There was a square opening beside the stage steps.

"Why are you under there?"

"Tube."

"Why?"

"Ghost."

"I understand the nouns."

His head appeared.

"We moved the outlet."

"Why?"

"People could see it from the left benches."

"I thought they couldn't."

"They could."

"Did someone complain?"

"No. Nessa sat there."

That was worse.

He disappeared again.

I lowered myself onto the stage edge and then down one step at a time.
Crutches were useless for the first part. Pell took one without asking
and leaned it against a beam.

The space beneath the stage was high enough for Pell to crouch.

It was not high enough for me to do anything gracefully.

Dust stuck to my palms.

"Second piece," he said.

"What is second?"

"The Dead Brother."

"That's cheerful."

"Ghost is the brother."

"Who is dead."

"Usually."

"Usually?"

"Don't worry about it."

I worried about it.

Pell showed me the page.

There were four marks that mattered.

Curtain open.

Lamp lower.

Ghost.

Door.

"That's it?"

"That's it."

"Why does Rinna have a whole page?"

"Other people."

"Ah."

He tapped ghost.

"When Nessa says, 'I heard him on the stair,' you point at me."

"Why?"

"So I talk."

"You need me to point at you?"

"I can't hear her well from here."

"Then how do you know when to talk normally?"

"Someone points."

"Jori."

"Usually."

"Who isn't here."

"Yes."

I looked at the tube.

"So my job is pointing."

"Second piece."

"Excellent."

"And curtain."

"Less excellent."

Pell grinned.

We climbed out.

The curtain was a problem.

It was not heavy. It was awkward.

The pull ran along the wall beside the stage, then around a wooden wheel
overhead. Jori apparently stood there, watched the stage, watched the
side door, listened for Nessa, and somehow did not let actors walk into
the curtain.

I tried once.

I let the curtain out too quickly.

It slapped the stage.

Everyone stopped.

Nessa looked up from the coat she was pinning.

"No."

"I noticed."

"Again."

Pell reset it.

I tried again.

Too slow.

The curtain crawled.

Sellen, waiting behind it, said, "I will die before the scene begins."

"You're not in this one."

"I'll die anyway."

"Quiet," Nessa said.

We tried again.

This time the curtain opened at a speed nobody commented on.

Apparently that was success.

My right shoulder already hurt.

"You pull with both hands?" I asked.

Pell said, "Jori does."

"I don't have both hands if I'm standing."

"You can sit."

There was a low box beside the wall.

I sat.

That changed the angle enough that I could brace my good foot and pull
without fighting the crutches.

"Better," I said.

Pell shrugged.

Nobody congratulated me for solving sitting down.

That was also good.

The third piece was The Petition.

Veya took over.

"You know your own entrance."

"Yes."

"You're not in it tonight."

I stared at her.

"What?"

"You're calling."

"But I'm Third Man."

"Not tonight."

"Why?"

"Because Jori isn't here."

"Can I be both?"

"No."

"I could."

"No."

"I know the scene."

"Good. Then you know when Sellen enters."

I looked at the page.

There was a mark beside my old line.

NEIGHBOR.

"You want me to call Sellen."

"I want you to point at Sellen."

"Why is all theatre pointing?"

"Because if you shout his name the audience hears you."

That was fair.

Sellen was across the backstage passage putting on the neighbor coat.

He looked at me.

I pointed.

"Not now."

"I was practicing."

"Don't."

Veya took the page from me and drew a small line.

"Watch me. When I put the petition down, point to the reed. After the
reed, Sellen. Do not anticipate."

"I don't anticipate."

Sellen laughed.

"Nobody asked you."

"You're not in the scene."

"I know."

That hurt more than it should have.

Before we opened the doors, Nessa made me walk the backstage route once
without the page.

Not for education. She needed to know whether I could get from the
curtain box to the side gap quickly enough without blocking the costume
change.

I could, barely.

The narrowest place was between a scenery brace and a basket of folded
cloth. My left crutch fit. My right one caught.

"Move the basket," I said.

"No."

"Why?"

"Quick change."

"Move the brace."

"No."

"Why?"

"Wall."

I looked at the passage.

"So I don't fit."

"You fit differently."

That was not inspiring. It was also true.

I turned sideways, planted both crutches ahead, and moved through in two
short hops.

Nessa watched.

"Do that."

"I hate that."

"Do it anyway."

So I did.

By the third trip my palm was sore where the grip rubbed. I wrapped a
strip of scrap cloth around it and kept going.

The hall filled around us.

Nessa had the wrapped parcel from yesterday open on a table. It
contained three narrow rolls of pale cloth and a packet of black hooks.

That was all.

No mystery.

She was arguing with the paint-wrist woman about whether the hooks were
too bright.

Teren had won something from the baker.

I could tell because there were trays of small rolls in the back room.

"Four bookings?" I asked.

"Three evenings and an afternoon," he said.

"That's four."

He pointed at me.

"Don't."

I took a roll.

He slapped my hand.

"After."

"You're cruel."

"Work."

At the front door, a woman asked me whether the ghost was real.

I had been sent to help for ten minutes while Rinna found change.

I looked at her.

Her daughter was holding her hand.

Behind them, three men were arguing about whether two copper was too
much.

Yesterday I would have said Pell.

Today I said, "You'll hear him."

The girl looked delighted.

The woman bought two tickets.

I felt guilty for almost half a second.

Then one of the men asked, "Is it frightening?"

"Not very."

Rinna, behind me, kicked my crutch.

"Ow."

"Sell."

"It's not frightening."

"People like frightened."

"Do you want me to lie?"

"No. Stop finishing every answer."

The men bought tickets anyway.

One said, "If it's bad, I'm blaming you."

"That's fair."

Rinna sighed.

Someone behind us said, "Move the ticket box with magic."

I turned.

The young actor from yesterday was carrying two lamp stands.

"No."

"Bad magic."

"Yes."

He kept walking.

That was the entire consequence of my possible breakthrough.

The first piece began.

I was not calling it.

Jori's replacement for first was a woman named Hara who had apparently
done the job before. She stood where I would stand later, barely moved,
and somehow knew what everyone needed.

I watched her instead of the play.

She did not look at the page much.

That was annoying.

At the end, she handed me the cord.

"Don't wrap it around your wrist."

"Why?"

She showed me a pale scar across hers.

"Ah."

Then she left to change costume.

I did not ask why the caller was also acting.

Apparently everyone was everything.

Second piece.

The Dead Brother.

I sat on the low box.

Crutches leaned within reach.

Page on my knee.

Pell was under the stage.

Nessa was onstage in a dark dress I had seen hanging from a nail that
morning.

The room quieted.

Curtain.

I pulled.

Good enough.

Lamp.

The lamp boy lowered the left lamp after I pointed.

Too far.

Nessa's face nearly vanished.

I pointed up.

He stared at me.

I pointed up harder.

He raised it.

Nessa kept speaking.

Nobody died.

Not yet.

A chair crossed.

Door closed.

Nessa stopped beside the painted stair.

"I heard him on the stair."

I pointed at Pell.

Nothing.

I pointed again.

Nothing.

My stomach dropped.

Then I realized I was pointing at the floor.

Pell was under the stage.

He could not see through wood.

There was a narrow gap beside the curtain.

That was where Jori pointed.

I leaned.

Too far.

My crutch tip slid into the edge of the curtain.

The fabric twitched.

Nessa looked toward the dark stair.

Not at me.

I got the crutch free.

I shoved my hand into the gap and pointed down.

The ghost spoke.

"Nessa."

I knew it was Pell.

I knew exactly where he was.

I knew the leather tube ran beneath my feet and ended behind the dark
flat beside the stair.

My eyes went to the stair anyway.

Nessa froze.

Not before.

After.

The room froze with her.

"You're dead," she whispered.

Pell answered through the tube.

"I know."

Someone in the audience made a small sound.

Not a scream.

More like they had forgotten to breathe and remembered badly.

Then I remembered the door.

I pointed.

The door operator did not move.

I pointed again.

Wrong person.

The operator was on the other side.

I had been told that.

I had also forgotten it.

I reached across and tapped the wooden frame twice.

That was apparently not the cue.

The door stayed open.

Nessa crossed toward it.

She was supposed to close it on the next line.

It was already open too wide.

For one terrible second, I could see the whole mechanism behind the
painted stair from where I sat.

The audience could not.

Probably.

Nessa reached the door, caught it herself, and slammed it.

The sound was better than the planned one.

The audience jumped.

Pell whispered through the ghost tube.

"Good."

I wanted to kill him.

The rest of the piece worked.

When the curtain closed, Nessa came offstage and walked directly to me.

"Wrong side."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"Now."

"Good."

She kept walking.

That was my review.

Pell crawled out from under the stage.

"You pointed at the floor."

"You were under the floor."

"Yes."

"So it was reasonable."

"No."

"I hate theatre."

"No, you don't."

"Everyone keeps saying that."

"Because you keep lying."

Third piece.

The Petition.

I was still annoyed that I was not in it.

The new Third Man was one of the actors I had seen arguing about a coat
yesterday. His name was Tovin.

He had my goat.

Not physically.

The goat remained theoretical.

I sat with the page.

Veya began.

First petitioner.

Drainage.

Second petitioner.

Pig.

Then Veya put the petition down.

I pointed at the reed.

The reed sounded.

I pointed at Tovin.

He entered.

"My neighbor's goat has eaten half my fence and all my patience."

Wrong.

He had reversed it.

It was still a sentence.

Sellen looked at me from the wing.

I almost laughed.

Tovin continued.

Sellen entered on neighbor anyway.

The scene worked.

Different.

Not broken.

I had spent two days learning exactly how the cue fit and now somebody
else had said it wrong and the building had not fallen down.

I was offended.

Sellen did not use the father line.

He used another line instead.

The audience laughed.

Less.

Then Veya got a bigger laugh with a look.

I sat behind the curtain and pointed when I was supposed to point.

At some point I realized I was enjoying myself.

That seemed unfair.

After the third piece, my shoulder hurt enough that I stopped pretending
it didn't.

I leaned both crutches against the wall and rubbed it.

Davin appeared beside me.

I had not seen him all day.

"Pulling?"

"Curtain."

He looked at the cord.

"Bad angle."

"I sat."

"Better."

"Thank you."

He touched the wooden wheel overhead, frowned, and walked away.

"Are you fixing it?"

"Tomorrow."

"What's wrong with it?"

"Worn."

"Was it worn yesterday?"

"Yes."

"Why tomorrow?"

He looked back.

"Because today is today."

Then he disappeared toward the rear yard.

I accepted this.

Cleanup took longer because someone had spilled lamp oil near the prop
shelf.

Nothing caught fire.

That was the good news.

The bad news was that Nessa made everyone stop carrying cloth through
the area until it was sanded and wiped.

The rolls came down.

The hooks went back in the parcel.

The fake loaf went somewhere I did not see.

Rinna paid me one copper.

"Caller."

"I was bad."

"You were adequate."

"I missed the ghost."

"It arrived."

"I missed the door."

"It closed."

"Nessa closed it."

"Yes."

"That means I was bad."

"That means the show happened."

She put the copper in my hand.

"Jori back tomorrow?"

"Maybe."

I stared at her.

She smiled.

"Don't."

Pell had not rewritten the sign.

Instead, somebody had drawn a tiny piece of paper beside the gray GREG
stain.

It had little lines around it like it was flying.

I left it.

Outside, Carrow was cooling.

I found Lyssa two streets from home carrying a bundle of blue thread.

Not one bundle.

Six.

They were looped over her arm.

"You carried blue thread."

"I told you."

"I didn't understand the scale."

"Move."

I moved.

She shifted two bundles onto me.

"I have crutches."

"You have an arm."

"Pell said that about a tube."

"Who?"

"Nobody important."

We walked home.

"What did you do?"

"Called."

"Called what?"

"Ghost."

She stopped.

"You summoned a ghost?"

"No."

"Good."

"It was Pell."

"I don't know who that is."

"Exactly."

She started walking again.

I carried blue thread.

At home there was a note under the door.

Guild paper.

I knew before I opened it.

Lyssa set down her bundles.

"Paper?"

"Different paper."

I unfolded it.

Hessa's handwriting.

TOMORROW. AFTER MIDDAY.

Below that:

NEW FINS.

Then:

DO NOT BRING PELL.

I stared.

Lyssa leaned over my shoulder.

"Who is Pell?"

"I may have mentioned him."

"To Hessa?"

"Possibly."

"Why?"

"I don't remember."

She took the note.

"She knows you."

"Unfortunately."

Lyssa handed it back.

I put it beside my question paper.

One movement.

Not repeated.

One fin easier.

Tomorrow, new fins.

My shoulder hurt.

There was blue thread on the table.

Somewhere at East Market Hall, Pell was probably still under something.

I had spent the day making a ghost arrive late, failing to close a door,
and watching another man say my line wrong.

Tomorrow Hessa wanted me to try not to move paper incorrectly.

Both sounded like work.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 182

## THE SUBJECT

Davin had the curtain wheel on the floor.

I stopped in the East Market Hall doorway.

The wheel looked smaller there.

Most things did when somebody took them apart.

Davin sat on an overturned bucket with the wooden wheel between his
knees, working a narrow metal pin out of its center. The curtain cord
hung uselessly from above. A second man I did not know was on a ladder,
scraping old wax from the bracket.

"Today is tomorrow," I said.

Davin looked at me.

"Yes."

"Good."

He went back to the pin.

That concluded our conversation.

Jori was back.

I knew because a thin man with a crooked nose was standing at my low box
with the cue page folded in half.

"Are you Jori?"

"Yes."

"I did your job."

"I heard."

"I was adequate."

He looked at the curtain cord hanging from the ceiling.

"Apparently."

Then he walked away.

I had expected to feel replaced.

Instead I felt relieved.

Rinna caught me before I could steal one of the baker's rolls.

"Third Man tonight."

"My goat?"

"Your goat."

"Tovin said it wrong."

"He says most things wrong."

"Why did you let him have it?"

"You were busy."

That was also apparently the entire theory of casting.

I ate the roll.

Rinna saw me.

She did not stop me.

That worried me more than being caught.

"Guild after midday," I said.

"I know."

"How?"

"You told Teren."

"I did?"

"You tell people things."

I thought of Hessa's note.

DO NOT BRING PELL.

"I should work on that."

"Yes."

She pointed toward a stack of chairs.

I moved chairs until noon.

Lyssa did not appear.

Neither did Pell, which made keeping him away from Hessa considerably
easier.

After midday I went to the Guild.

Hessa was not there.

Her room was open, but a gray-coated man had three wooden boxes on her
table and was comparing seals against a page. I recognized none of the
marks. He did not look at me.

I sat outside.

People went past.

A woman carrying a tray of small prepared glass beads stopped at the
room, saw the boxes, swore quietly, and kept going. Two Guild workers
argued at the end of the corridor about whether something belonged in
south storage or had only been found there. One of them said, "If it was
logged east, it stays east until someone changes the page."

The other said, "The crate is south."

"Then the crate is wrong."

I liked him.

Hessa arrived carrying six paper fins in one hand and looking irritated.

"You're here."

"You told me to be."

"Good."

She looked into her room.

The gray-coated man looked up.

"Five minutes."

"You said that ten minutes ago."

"I wasn't here ten minutes ago."

He considered this.

"Five minutes."

Hessa sat beside me.

I looked at the fins.

They were all the same pale paper.

"New fins."

"Yes."

"Did you make them?"

"No."

"Who did?"

"Someone who folds paper better than you."

"That could be anyone."

"Yes."

She had not brought a book.

She had not brought my old notes.

For five minutes she sat beside me and watched Guild workers go past.

I wanted to ask about the boxes.

I did not.

At six minutes, Hessa stood.

The gray-coated man came out carrying two boxes. He left the third on
her table.

Hessa stopped him.

"No."

He looked at the box.

"I need the table."

He took it.

Hessa went inside.

I followed.

"Do not touch anything."

"I know."

"You touched the glass last time."

"After."

"You touched it."

I sat.

The wooden frame from our last test was gone.

The glass shield remained.

So did the washers.

Hessa brought out a different base. It was a flat board with two shallow
grooves cut parallel into the surface. Each groove had three ink marks
beside it.

"New?"

"Mostly."

"Mostly?"

"The board is old."

"From what?"

"Not relevant."

That meant I would never know.

She set the six fins in a row.

They were small folded pieces of paper, each with a flat foot and an
upright face. The folds looked sharper than the ones we had used before.

Hessa picked up the first.

"Look."

"I am."

"The base."

I looked.

"Flat."

She set it down.

Second.

"Flat."

Third.

"Flat."

By the sixth I understood the activity.

"Flat."

"Good."

"Was that a test?"

"No."

"Good."

She took a narrow piece of wood and pressed it along the fold of each
fin.

"Same edge," she said. "Same paper. Same fold."

"Same person?"

"Yes."

"Who?"

"No."

I leaned back.

Hessa placed two fins into the grooves. One in each.

She slid the glass shield over them.

"Nothing yet."

"I know."

She checked the table with the same small wooden wedges she had used
before. One leg got a thin sliver beneath it.

Then she tapped the table.

Both fins stayed still.

She walked around it.

Both stayed still.

She opened the glass, switched the fins, closed it, and tapped again.

Nothing.

"You're making this very boring."

"That is the intention."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"Usually."

She looked at me.

"Why did you write not to bring Pell?"

"Who?"

I stared at her.

Hessa's mouth moved.

Barely.

"You remembered."

"Unfortunately."

"Why?"

"Because you described a man under a stage speaking through leather."

"That is Pell."

"I gathered."

"He would have liked this."

"No."

"He likes garbage."

"No."

"Fair."

Hessa sat opposite me.

"Hands."

I put my hands on the table.

She checked them.

Then my wrist.

Then the old familiar questions.

Pain.

Numbness.

Tingling.

Heat.

Anything unusual since the last session.

No.

No.

No.

No.

No.

"Draw."

I did.

The mana came easier than it had before the road, though I no longer
trusted easy as a useful word. It was familiar. That was different.

I held the minimal draw where she had taught me to hold it.

Hessa watched.

"Stop."

I stopped.

"Again."

I looked at her.

"Again?"

"Baseline."

I drew again.

The second was smaller.

Cleaner.

The old unevenness along the wrist edge was there. Not stronger. Not
gone.

Hessa touched two fingers lightly against the inside of my wrist.

"Stop."

I stopped.

She wrote.

"Two?"

"Two."

"So twenty-four."

"Yes."

I had been keeping count.

Apparently so had she.

"Shape."

"No paper?"

"Not yet."

I shaped the draw without trying to send anything anywhere.

The asymmetry came back almost immediately.

It felt like leaning toward a door that was not there.

I corrected too hard.

Hessa said, "No."

"I know."

"Then stop."

I stopped.

She waited.

"Again."

The second shaping was better.

Not good.

Better.

I held it for three breaths.

"Stop."

I stopped.

Hessa wrote again.

"Twenty."

"Yes."

I flexed my hand.

"So now paper."

"Now paper."

She opened a small cloth bag.

Inside were six little wooden counters.

Three had black dots.

Three were blank.

"What are those?"

"Not magic."

"I assumed."

"You shouldn't."

She shook two counters into her closed hand.

"Choose."

"Why?"

"Choose."

"Left."

She opened her left hand.

Black dot.

She placed the black counter beside the left groove.

"Target?"

"Yes."

"You could have just said left."

"Then you would know I chose left."

"I know now."

"Yes."

I hated this.

She closed the glass.

"One attempt."

"Only one?"

"One, then we inspect."

I settled.

The room was quiet except for voices somewhere in the corridor and the
scratch of somebody dragging something heavy across stone.

I drew.

Not much.

I shaped.

The target fin was on the left.

I tried not to look at its edge.

That was impossible.

I looked at its edge.

I wanted it to move.

I wanted it so badly that I could feel myself beginning to turn wanting
into evidence.

I stopped thinking about the fin.

That did not help.

I shaped toward the space in front of it.

The familiar wrist-edge tendency pulled sideways.

I corrected.

Too much.

Back.

Smaller.

The fin moved.

I stopped breathing.

It had moved.

Not far.

Less than last time, maybe.

Forward.

Across the first ink mark.

The right fin had not moved.

"It moved."

"Stop."

I stopped.

Hessa did not look at me.

She looked at the table.

Then at my hands.

Then at the glass.

Then at the fin.

She walked around the table.

I waited.

She opened the shield.

"Don't touch."

"I wasn't."

She checked the target base.

Then the control.

Then the groove.

Then the ink mark.

She switched the fins.

The moved fin went to the right.

The control went left.

Then she shook the counters again.

"Choose."

"Right."

Blank.

She put the blank counter beside the right groove.

"Target?"

"Right."

"Again."

"Isn't that the same fin?"

"Yes."

"So if it moves again, we know the fin is easier."

"No."

"Why not?"

"Because that is not the only explanation."

"Right."

I hated her.

I drew.

The second attempt felt worse immediately.

Not painful.

Crowded.

The shape would not sit where I wanted it.

I tried to force it narrower.

Hessa said, "Don't chase."

I loosened it.

The right fin did not move.

The left fin did not move.

I held.

Nothing.

"Stop."

I stopped.

Hessa wrote.

"That doesn't help."

"It does."

"How?"

"It didn't move."

"That's not helpful."

"It is information."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"No."

She let me rest.

I rubbed my palm.

The cloth I had wrapped around the crutch grip had left a faint line
across the skin.

Hessa noticed.

"What's that?"

"Curtain."

She looked at me.

"That answer is not useful."

"I pulled a curtain."

"Better."

"I called a ghost."

"No."

"Fine."

She waited until I stopped smiling.

Then she changed both fins.

Two unused ones.

She placed them in the grooves.

She checked the bases.

Glass down.

Counters.

"Choose."

"Left."

Blank.

Target right.

I did not like not choosing the target.

That was probably why she was doing it.

Third attempt.

I drew.

The shape came cleaner.

Not easy.

Cleaner.

I found the wrist edge, let it be there, and worked around it instead of
trying to erase it.

Hessa did not speak.

The right fin stood beyond the glass.

I shaped toward it.

Nothing.

I kept the shape small.

Nothing.

Then the fin gave a tiny jump.

Not forward.

Sideways.

Its upright face twisted a fraction toward the groove wall.

I stared.

The left fin did not move.

Hessa said, "Stop."

I stopped.

She checked everything again.

"That wasn't forward."

"No."

"Does it count?"

"As movement."

"Caused by me?"

She looked at me.

"Wait."

I waited.

She removed the right fin and set it on the table.

It stood.

She tapped the board.

It trembled but did not twist.

She replaced it.

Then she switched the two fins.

"Again?"

"No."

"What?"

"Rest."

"I can do another."

"I know."

"Then why rest?"

"Because your hand is shaking."

I looked.

It was.

Barely.

Still enough.

I put it in my lap.

Hessa wrote.

I tried to read upside down.

She covered the page with her hand.

"Hostile."

"Rest."

We waited.

The room did not become dramatic.

Someone outside laughed.

A cart rattled in the street.

Hessa got up, went to the shelf, and came back with water.

I drank.

"How many external attempts is that?"

"Three today."

"So eight."

"Yes."

"And two movements."

"Today."

"Three total."

"Observed movements during external attempts, yes."

"That sounds good."

"It sounds like three movements."

"You're impossible."

"Good."

After several minutes she put the fins back.

Not the same pair.

She chose two others.

This time she put the counters in her hands before I could say anything.

"Choose."

"Right."

Black.

Target right.

"Last."

"Only?"

"Last."

I settled again.

My shoulder hurt from yesterday.

My palm hurt.

My wrist did not.

That mattered more.

I drew.

The mana sat where it sat.

I shaped.

The right fin waited.

I did not imagine the audience.

I did not imagine Pell.

I did not imagine a ghost.

I tried to make one stupid piece of paper move a stupidly small distance
while one woman watched and refused to be impressed.

The fin moved forward.

Not much.

Enough to cross the first ink mark.

I let the shape go immediately.

"Stop."

"I stopped."

"Hands away."

I pulled them back.

Hessa checked.

Glass.

Table.

Fin.

Control.

Groove.

Base.

She switched the fins.

She checked the board.

She looked at the wedges.

Then she sat.

I waited.

She wrote for a long time.

"Well?"

"No."

"No what?"

"Do not make me answer while I am writing."

I waited.

She finished.

Then she turned the page toward me.

There were four lines for today.

First: left target, forward movement.

Second: right target, none.

Third: right target, lateral movement.

Fourth: right target, forward movement.

Below that she had written:

THREE DIFFERENT FINS MOVED ACROSS TWO POSITIONS.

I read it twice.

"Three?"

"The first, the third, the fourth."

"The second was the same fin as first."

"Yes. It did not move."

"So three different fins moved."

"Yes."

"While I was shaping."

"Yes."

"Targets."

"Yes."

"Controls didn't."

"No visible control movement."

I looked at her.

"Did I move paper?"

Hessa leaned back.

I could see her deciding how much she hated the question.

"Under this setup," she said, "during supervised deliberate shaping
toward a designated paper target, we have now observed small movement of
multiple target fins without visible movement of the paired controls."

I waited.

"That is a terrible sentence."

"It is an accurate sentence."

"Did I do it?"

"We have removed the easiest explanation from last time."

"That isn't what I asked."

"I know."

"Hessa."

She looked at the page.

Then at the fins.

Then at me.

"Yes."

Nothing happened.

No light.

No sound.

No pressure.

No revelation.

I sat there.

"Yes?"

"Within the limits I just stated."

"I moved paper."

"You produced a repeatable external response under this apparatus."

"Paper."

"Do not make me regret this."

I smiled.

I could not help it.

Hessa pointed at me.

"No."

"I'm not doing anything."

"You are expanding the claim in your head."

"I am not."

"You are."

I was.

I stopped.

Mostly.

"What does it mean?"

"That we have a result."

"What can I do?"

"This."

She pointed at the paper.

"That's pathetic."

"Yes."

I laughed.

She did not.

Then she almost did.

I saw it.

"Can we try something heavier?"

"No."

"Farther?"

"No."

"Different direction?"

"Not today."

"Tomorrow?"

"No."

"Why?"

"Because you have done two minimal draws, two deliberate shaping
baselines, and four external attempts."

I counted.

"Twenty-four draws. Twenty shaping. Nine external."

"Yes."

"Nine?"

"Four today."

I had forgotten the last one while celebrating it.

Hessa folded the page.

"You are done."

"But now we know."

"Now we know one thing."

"One good thing."

"One small thing."

"Same."

"No."

I looked at the fins.

"What next?"

"Direction."

"Forward?"

"Whether forward is yours or the apparatus."

That took some of the smile out of me.

"How?"

"Different orientation. Different target direction. Same fins. Not
today."

"Because hand shaking."

"Among other things."

She gathered the counters.

"What other things?"

"You have somewhere to be."

I looked toward the window.

The light had shifted.

"Shit."

"Yes."

"Rinna."

"Probably."

I grabbed my crutches.

Hessa said, "Greg."

I stopped.

"Restrictions remain."

"I know."

"Say them."

"No independent draw. No shaping. No testing. No trying paper at home.
No trying anything else because paper worked."

"Good."

"It worked."

"Leave."

I left.

I was halfway down the corridor when I went back.

Hessa looked up.

"What?"

"Can I tell Lyssa I moved paper?"

Hessa stared at me.

"Leave."

I took that as yes.

At East Market Hall, Davin had the curtain wheel back up.

Jori was calling.

Nobody cared that I had returned from the Guild.

Rinna pointed at the coat rack.

"Third Man."

I put on the coat.

Sellen was already waiting.

"You're late."

"I moved paper."

He looked at me.

"Good."

"With magic."

"Better."

"Hessa says under a controlled setup during supervised deliberate
shaping toward a designated paper target, we observed small movement of
multiple target fins without visible movement of paired controls."

Sellen stared.

"Did you move paper?"

"Yes."

"Why didn't you say that?"

I hated everyone.

The Petition began.

I waited for my entrance.

Veya put down the petition.

The reed sounded.

Jori pointed at me.

I went.

"My neighbor's goat has eaten all my patience and half my fence."

Sellen came in exactly where he was supposed to.

The audience laughed.

Not huge.

Enough.

I did not add anything.

Afterward, Rinna paid me one copper.

"Pell says congratulations."

"Where is Pell?"

"Under the stage."

"Of course."

I found Lyssa after the show at home with the blue thread spread into
smaller bundles.

She looked up.

"Paper?"

"Yes."

"Moved?"

"Yes."

"On purpose?"

"Yes."

"More than once?"

I put my crutches against the wall.

"Yes."

Lyssa sat back.

"Oh."

That was better than cheering.

I sat opposite her.

"Hessa said yes."

"Actually yes?"

"With a terrible sentence around it."

"That sounds like Hessa."

"I have a result."

"What can you do?"

"Move very small pieces of paper a very small amount under a glass cover
while Hessa watches."

Lyssa considered this.

"Useful."

"You're mocking me."

"A little."

"I did magic."

"You've been doing magic."

"I did magic outside me."

She stopped sorting thread.

That was the part that reached her.

"Ah."

"Yes."

She looked at my hand.

"Does it hurt?"

"No."

"Good."

Then she picked up the thread again.

"What happens next?"

"Different direction."

"Why?"

"To see if I moved it or the table likes forward."

Lyssa nodded as if this were reasonable.

It was.

I put the copper from the show on the table.

One copper.

One result.

Six bundles of blue thread.

Lyssa had apparently spent the day turning six into twelve.

Tomorrow the hall had another show.

Hessa did not want me tomorrow.

That felt rude now.

I wanted to move something else.

I wanted to move the cup.

The thread.

The copper.

Anything.

I did not.

I sat on my hands for a moment instead.

Lyssa noticed.

"Good."

"Don't."

She smiled.

The paper had moved.

This time, maybe had become yes.

It was a very small yes.

It was enough.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 183

## THE WORKER

I woke up looking at the corner of a piece of paper.

It was sticking out from under Lyssa's book.

I stared at it.

The paper did not move.

That was because I was not doing anything.

I knew this.

I continued staring at it.

Lyssa came in carrying a cup and stopped.

"No."

"I am not."

"You are looking at it."

"Looking is allowed."

"Is it?"

"Yes."

"Did Hessa say?"

I looked at Lyssa.

She drank from the cup.

"Hostile."

"You moved paper yesterday."

"Yes."

"Go to work."

She had already dressed. The blue thread from last night was gone except
for three short lengths on the table, all tied around small folded
scraps of cloth. I did not know what the scraps meant.

"Where is the thread?"

"Mostly not here."

"I can see that."

"Good."

"Where is it?"

"With people who needed blue thread."

That seemed intentionally unhelpful.

Lyssa picked up two of the folded scraps.

"Marra?"

"Some."

"Jessa?"

"One."

"Who are the others?"

She kissed my forehead.

"People."

Then she left.

I sat for another minute.

The paper corner was still there.

So was the cup.

So was one copper from last night.

The copper seemed heavier than it had before.

Not actually heavier.

I knew that too.

I put my hands on my knees, stood, got my crutches, and went to work.

At East Market Hall, Pell was waiting for me beside the repaired latch.

That was suspicious.

"You did magic."

"Yes."

He grinned.

It was the first time I had been able to answer that without immediately
correcting the sentence.

"Do it."

"No."

His grin vanished.

"Bad magic."

"Yes."

"What can you move?"

"Paper."

He picked up a torn corner of an old handbill from the floor and held it
out.

"Move this."

"No."

"You just said paper."

"Under glass."

Pell looked at the handbill.

"Put glass over it."

"No."

"Why?"

"Hessa."

"She isn't here."

"That is the problem."

Pell thought about this for perhaps half a second.

"Bad magic."

"I already agreed."

He dropped the handbill.

"Can you move a feather?"

"I don't know."

"A string?"

"I don't know."

"A fake petition?"

"I don't know."

"Things?"

"No."

"You can move paper but not things."

"Paper is a thing."

"Then you can move things."

"No."

Pell looked genuinely offended by my categories.

I understood Hessa a little better.

Nessa came through carrying a painted wooden bracket.

"Pell."

"Yes?"

"Tube."

He left immediately.

Apparently I ranked below tube.

Rinna arrived with a small wooden box under one arm and a folded sheet
in her hand.

"Afternoon."

"I know what time it is."

"Show."

"Oh."

The baker's afternoon.

I had forgotten.

Rinna handed me the sheet.

It was not a cue page.

It was a bill.

THE LITTLE KING.

THE MILLER'S SON.

THE RED DOOR.

Under that, in smaller writing:

SHORT SONG IF CHILDREN BEHAVE.

I looked at her.

"Do children behave?"

"No."

"Then why write it?"

"Hope."

Teren came out from behind the stage carrying a length of rope.
