"Greg."

"Yes?"

"Can you do the paper thing on cue?"

"No."

"Can you do it here?"

"No."

"Can you do it without the Guild woman?"

"No."

"Can you move anything larger than paper?"

"No."

He nodded once.

"Good."

"Good?"

"Then it isn't my problem."

He handed me the rope.

"Doorframe."

That was how my first established external magical effect entered the
theatre.

I carried rope.

The red doorframe had split at the lower joint.

It was not the same painted doorway from The Widow's Room. This one was
narrower, red on the audience side, bare wood on the back, and built to
stand by itself with two feet that stuck out behind it.

One foot had cracked.

The frame leaned.

Nessa was kneeling beside it with the broken foot in her lap.

"Don't lift it."

"I wasn't."

"You were about to."

"I was going to look."

"Look lower."

I sat on the floor.

The crack ran through one of the old peg holes.

"Can Davin fix it?"

"Yes."

"Where is Davin?"

"Not here."

"Can you fix it?"

"Enough."

She took the rope from me.

"What do you need me to do?"

"Hold that."

She pointed at the upright.

I held it.

For the next fifteen minutes, my contribution to theatre consisted of
keeping a fake red door vertical while Nessa bound a replacement block
against its foot.

My shoulder still hurt from the curtain work. Holding the frame was not
heavy, but it was awkward. I shifted my grip twice.

"Stop moving."

"My arm hurts."

"Then sit closer."

I moved closer.

That helped.

Nobody congratulated me.

A girl carrying a basket of costume belts stepped over my good leg
without apologizing.

Sellen came past wearing a green coat and stopped.

"I heard you can move objects with magic."

"No."

"Pell says."

"Pell says I moved paper."

"He said objects."

"He's wrong."

Sellen considered the doorframe I was holding.

"Can you move that?"

"No."

"Then that's disappointing."

"Thank you."

He left.

Nessa pulled the rope tighter.

"You told Pell?"

"He already knew."

"How?"

"Rinna."

Nessa looked toward the front.

"Rinna."

"What?"

"Nothing."

The repaired block held when she let go.

She stood.

"Now lift."

I lifted my side.

A man I did not know took the other.

We carried the doorframe six paces to its mark.

The new curtain wheel worked.

I noticed because Jori pulled the curtain while we were setting the
door, and it opened without the old scrape and hitch.

That was all.

Davin had fixed it.

The curtain worked.

Nobody mentioned it.

The afternoon audience began arriving before we were ready.

They were louder than the evening people.

Children came in pairs and groups, some with adults and some with older
siblings who had apparently been told to keep them alive until supper.
Market workers arrived still wearing aprons. One baker came with flour
up both forearms.

Rinna put me at the door because she had not learned.

"Two copper full bill," I said. "One for children."

A woman with three children pointed at the painted sign.

"Magic?"

I looked.

Someone had added a small star beside THE LITTLE KING.

"I don't know why that's there."

The oldest child looked at me.

"Are you the magician?"

"No."

"Pell says you are."

Of course he did.

"I moved paper."

The child waited.

"With magic," I added.

"Can you make something disappear?"

"Yes."

His face changed.

I took the handbill from his hand, put it behind my back, and handed it
to Rinna.

The child stared at me.

Rinna stared at me.

"That's not magic," he said.

"No."

He seemed disappointed.

His mother laughed and paid four copper for all of them.

Rinna waited until they were inside.

"That was terrible."

"They bought tickets."

"Do it again."

"I hate this job."

"No, you don't."

I hated when people knew that.

The afternoon problem was not the children.

It was the lamp.

The Little King used a small prepared lamp with a pale blue glass cap.
Not the same blue-lamp piece I had hung before. This one was supposed to
brighten briefly when the king opened a wooden box.

It did not.

The first test gave a weak gray flicker.

The second gave nothing.

Pell found me.

"Magic."

"No."

"Fix."

"No."

"Bad."

"Find Nessa."

Nessa was already there.

She took the lamp from the boy holding it, checked the worked line under
the cap, then called for Rinna.

Rinna touched the prepared strip with one finger.

Nothing.

"Spent," she said.

"Can it be charged?" I asked.

"Yes."

"Now?"

"No."

Pell looked at me.

I pointed at Rinna.

"See?"

"Your magic is still bad."

"My magic has nothing to do with this."

Nessa removed the blue cap.

"Plain lamp."

Pell said, "But the king's box."

"Plain lamp."

"What about the flash?"

"No flash."

"What if Greg moves paper?"

Nessa looked at him.

Pell left.

The piece ran with a plain lamp.

The king opened the box.

Nothing brightened.

A little girl in the front row still gasped because the actor looked
into the box as if he had seen something wonderful.

I was carrying a stool behind the side cloth and almost stopped to
watch.

Nessa tapped the stool.

"Move."

I moved.

The Miller's Son was next.

I had one line.

Not Third Man.

Not Shopkeeper.

Not anything I had performed before.

I was a clerk.

Teren had given it to me twenty minutes before the audience came in.

My entire job was to enter with a folded page, tell the miller's son
that the north wheel belonged to the widow until the debt was paid, hand
him the page, and leave.

"Which widow?" I had asked.

"The widow."

"From the other piece?"

"No."

"Does she have a name?"

"No."

"Why does she own a wheel?"

"Debt."

That had been enough for me.

I liked the clerk.

He knew what he was doing.

I entered.

The miller's son was played by Hara.

She looked younger than she had yesterday because someone had put her
hair loose and given her a badly fitted brown coat.

I knew she was Hara.

She looked seventeen.

That was annoying.

I gave her the page.

"The north wheel belongs to the widow until your father's debt is paid."

Hara stared at me.

I waited.

She was supposed to say, "My father is dead."

She did not.

A child coughed.

Hara looked down at the page.

Then back at me.

"My father is dead."

Too late.

I had already started turning.

I stopped.

My crutch squeaked on the floor.

A boy laughed.

I turned back.

"That does make collection difficult."

The audience laughed.

Hara's eyes changed.

Not angry.

Interested.

"Will you tell the widow?"

"No."

Bigger laugh.

That was not the scene.

I knew it immediately.

I had done it again.

Hara folded the page.

"Then I'll tell her myself."

That got us back.

I left.

Backstage, Teren was waiting.

"It worked," I said before he could speak.

"For you."

I closed my mouth.

He had not been there for the last version of this conversation, but
apparently theatre had one answer.

Hara came off two minutes later.

"You left."

"You forgot your line."

"I remembered it."

"After I left."

"You were supposed to wait."

"I did wait."

"You turned."

"Because you didn't say anything."

"That was my silence."

"It was a long silence."

"It was my silence."

Teren pointed between us.

"Both."

Hara frowned.

"Both what?"

"Both wrong."

Then he walked away.

I looked at Hara.

She looked at me.

"Your father is dead," I said.

"I know."

We both started laughing.

The Red Door used the repaired frame.

That was its entire reason for being called The Red Door as far as I
could tell.

A woman came home.

The door was locked.

Her brother was inside.

He would not open it.

They argued through an empty frame that had no wall attached to it.

From backstage, it looked ridiculous.

From the side gap, I could see the brother standing three feet behind
the red frame with nothing between him and his sister.

From the audience, the frame and a strip of painted cloth made a house.

The repair held.

Halfway through, one of the children yelled, "Go around!"

The woman onstage stopped.

The brother stopped.

The audience laughed.

She looked at the painted wall.

Then at the child.

"I've tried."

The child accepted this.

The play continued.

The short song happened because the children had not behaved and Teren
apparently wanted them tired.

Afterward, the hall looked like a meal had exploded.

Cups under benches.

A heel of bread behind the third row.

One child's scarf tied around the leg of a chair.

A wooden horse that belonged to nobody in the company.

Rinna held it up.

"Whose?"

Three children shouted, "Mine."

She put it on the ticket table.

"Fight later."

We cleaned.

Pell found the old magic sign stain and added a second tiny paper beside
the first.

This one had legs.

"Why?"

"It can move."

"Paper does not have legs."

"Yours does."

"No."

He added a hat.

"Stop improving it."

"Magician."

"I'm not a magician."

"You did magic."

"Yes."

"You moved a thing."

"No."

He put down the charcoal.

"You moved paper."

"Yes."

"Paper is a thing."

I looked at him.

He smiled.

I did not have Hessa's patience.

Rinna paid me one copper for the afternoon clerk role and crew work.

"One?"

"One."

"I also did door."

"You sold tickets."

"I repaired scenery."

"Nessa repaired scenery."

"I held scenery."

"One."

I took it.

"Fair."

"Yes."

"Are we paid tonight too?"

"If you work tonight."

"What am I?"

"Third Man."

"My goat."

"Your goat."

That made two shows in one day.

The afternoon crowd left.

The hall did not empty completely.

A few company people lay down backstage. Hara ate half an onion with
bread. Sellen disappeared. Jori sat on the low box with his cue page
over his face.

I went outside.

Carrow was still doing everything else.

A fish seller poured meltwater from a shallow cooling tray into the
gutter. A delivery boy pushed a handcart too fast around a corner and
lost three cabbages. Two women argued over a bolt of yellow cloth. A
prepared bakery stone showed a dull orange line beneath a pan of rolls.

Nobody knew I had moved paper.

That was good.

I bought one roll.

The baker did not ask me to move it.

Also good.

When I returned, Teren had changed the evening bill.

The Petition was gone.

Third Man was gone with it.

I stared at the board.

"What happened to my goat?"

Teren did not look up.

"Tomorrow."

"You told me tonight."

"I was wrong."

"What am I doing?"

"House."

"Door?"

"House."

"What does that mean?"

"Seats. Late people. Don't let anyone through the left passage during
the second piece."

"Why?"

"Costume change."

I had become less important in under three minutes.

I worked the house.

It was worse than acting.

People wanted aisle seats after buying center tickets. A man arrived
during the first piece and whispered that he had paid yesterday. A woman
insisted the left passage was where she had entered last week.

"No."

"Yes."

"Not tonight."

"Why?"

"Costume change."

"Whose?"

"I don't know."

That was the correct amount of information.

She went around.

During the second piece, I stood at the back wall and watched a scene I
had never seen before. Sellen played a physician. Veya played a woman
pretending not to know him.

I did not know why.

It was good.

Nobody needed me.

Then a bench leg shifted.

I caught the end before it tipped.

The man sitting on it looked at me.

"Thank you."

"Don't move."

He froze.

I found a folded scrap of wood, shoved it under the short leg, and let
go.

The bench stayed.

The scene continued.

That was my largest practical accomplishment of the day.

No magic.

After the evening show, Rinna gave me another copper.

"House."

"Bench."

"House."

"I saved four people."

"You stopped a bench wobbling."

"It was going."

"Two copper total today."

I put both coins in my pocket.

Pell came past carrying the ghost tube.

"Can you move coins?"

"No."

"Bad magic."

"Go away."

He did.

Lyssa was not home when I got there.

There was a note on the table.

BACK LATE. EAT.

Under it sat half a loaf and a small bowl of beans.

I ate.

Then I found paper.

Not the paper I had stared at that morning.

A different piece.

I wrote:

FORWARD?

Then underneath:

MY FORWARD OR BOARD FORWARD?

I looked at it.

That was ugly enough to be useful.

I did not draw.

I did not shape.

I did not put anything under glass.

I folded the paper and set it beneath Hessa's old note.

Then I put the two copper from the day beside yesterday's copper.

Three.

The coins did not move.

Neither did the paper.

Lyssa came in while I was washing the bowl.

She carried no blue thread.

"Where is it?" I asked.

"Where is what?"

"The thread."

"Gone."

"All of it?"

"Most."

"What happened?"

"People took it."

"Who?"

Lyssa looked at me.

"Still people."

I dried the bowl.

"I worked two shows."

"Good."

"I was a clerk."

"Good."

"I moved no paper."

"Very good."

"I held a door."

"That sounds more useful."

"It was."

She took off her shoes.

"How was the magic?"

"I told you. No paper."

"I mean yesterday."

"Oh."

She smiled.

I leaned against the table.

"It is still good."

"Good."

"Everyone keeps asking what I can do."

"What can you do?"

"Move paper."

"Then tell them."

"I do."

"And?"

"They ask what else."

"What else?"

"Nothing."

Lyssa nodded.

There was no cruelty in it.

That made it worse.

I looked at the folded question.

Tomorrow Hessa did not want me.

Tomorrow the hall did.

I had one small piece of real magic and no use for it.

I had a repaired curtain, a red door that stood if nobody kicked it, two
copper from a day of work, and a question about which direction paper
preferred.

That seemed like enough things to own at once.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 184

## THE RUNNER

Lyssa asked me for a favor before I had finished chewing.

That should have warned me.

"You're going east?"

"Eventually."

"Good."

She put a parcel on the table.

It was wrapped in gray cloth and tied twice with blue thread.

I looked at it.

"No."

Lyssa stopped.

"What?"

"I am not moving it."

"I want you to carry it."

"Oh."

She stared at me.

"Your life has become strange."

"Recently."

The parcel was not heavy. It was about the size of two folded shirts and
soft enough that I could wedge it under my arm.

"Where?"

"Marra's."

"I know Marra's."

"Do you?"

"Green door."

"Good."

"Not Sen's."

"Very good."

"I made that mistake once."

"You nearly made that mistake once."

"That still counts as learning."

Lyssa tore bread in half.

"Give it to Marra. Tell her the left side is marked. Do not untie it."

"Why would I untie it?"

"I know you."

"That is not an answer."

"It has worked so far."

I took the parcel.

"Anything else?"

"Yes. If Jessa is there, tell her I said the narrow one, not the wide
one."

"The narrow what?"

"She'll know."

"I don't."

"You don't need to."

This was apparently what trust looked like.

I finished breakfast with the parcel against my leg.

My right palm was still tender. The scrap cloth I had wrapped around the
crutch grip after calling the show had shifted overnight and bunched
under my hand. I retied it.

Lyssa watched.

"You should replace that."

"It works."

"It is dirty."

"Those are different questions."

"You've been spending too much time with Hessa."

I smiled before I meant to.

Lyssa noticed.

"Still pleased?"

"Yes."

"You moved paper."

"Yes."

"A very small amount."

"Yes."

"Under glass."

"Yes."

"While supervised."

"Yes."

"Good."

"Why are you doing this?"

"Because you're smiling at bread."

I stopped smiling.

Mostly.

Lyssa picked up her bag.

"I'll be west until midday. Maybe longer."

"People?"

"People."

"Blue thread?"

"Not today."

"What today?"

She kissed me.

"Work."

Then she left.

I had the parcel, my crutches, three copper on the table, a theatre call
before midday, and no reason to go near the Guild.

It seemed manageable.

That was my second warning.

Marra's was not on the way to East Market Hall.

It was only a few streets wrong.

A few streets on crutches was still a few streets.

I went north first, cut across the cloth lane, and found the green door
open.

Marra was inside with one sleeve pinned around a wooden arm and a mouth
full of pins.

I held up the parcel.

"Lyssa."

Marra pointed at a table.

I put it there.

"The left side is marked."

Marra removed two pins from her mouth.

"I know."

"Good."

"Did she tell you that?"

"Yes."

"Then why did you tell me?"

"Because she told me to."

Marra looked at me for a moment.

"Useful."

"Thank you."

"Not you."

She cut the blue thread.

I watched the knot fall loose.

Inside was dark cloth.

Not the same dark cloth from Lyssa's table, unless all dark cloth looked
like dark cloth to me, which seemed possible.

Marra unfolded one edge.

A row of tiny chalk marks ran along it.

"Jessa here?"

"No."

"I have a message."

"Then she's not here."

"I understand the concept."

Marra put two pins back in her mouth.

"She'll be at Sen's."

I stared at her.

"Red door."

Marra nodded.

"Of course."

"Tell her narrow, not wide."

"Yes."

I had delivered one parcel and somehow acquired the rest of the errand.

Sen's red door was two lanes back.

I had almost reached it when someone called my name.

I kept going.

"Greg."

I stopped.

Nessa was standing outside a shop with three coils of cord over one
shoulder and a small paper packet in her hand.

"Hall."

"I'm going."

"Now."

"I have an errand."

"So do I."

She handed me the paper packet.

I looked at it.

"No."

"What?"

"Nothing."

The packet was full of something hard and small.

"What's this?"

"Hooks."

"Where?"

"Hall."

"You're going to the hall."

"No."

"Where are you going?"

Nessa looked past me toward the next street.

"Somewhere else."

Then she left.

I now had a message for Jessa and a packet of hooks for the theatre.

Neither was heavy.

Together they were irritating.

I went to Sen's.

The red door was closed.

I knocked.

A man opened it.

"Jessa?"

"No."

"Is she here?"

"No."

"Do you know where she is?"

"Yes."

I waited.

He waited.

"Where?"

"Marra's."

I looked back toward the lane I had just crossed.

"No."

He shrugged.

"She was going there."

"When?"

"Before."

"How long before?"

He thought.

"Some."

I hated Carrow.

I went back to Marra's.

Jessa was there.

She was standing exactly where I had put Lyssa's parcel.

Marra was not.

I pointed at her.

"Narrow, not wide."

Jessa nodded.

"Good."

"Do you know what that means?"

"Yes."

"Excellent."

She looked at the packet under my arm.

"What is that?"

"Hooks."

"For what?"

"I don't know."

She smiled.

"You are useful today."

"Apparently."

I left before she could give me anything.

By the time I reached East Market Hall, my palm hurt and I was late
enough that Rinna was standing in the doorway.

She looked at me.

I looked at her.

"I have hooks."

"You're late."

"I also had cloth."

"Do you still have cloth?"

"No."

"Then I don't care."

I handed her the packet.

She opened it.

"These aren't ours."

I stared.

"Nessa gave them to me."

"These are costume hooks."

"Yes?"

"She needed curtain hooks."

"They are hooks."

Rinna looked at me.

I understood how Pell felt around Hessa.

"Where is Nessa?"

"Somewhere else."

"Helpful."

"I asked."

"Did you ask what kind of hooks?"

"No."

Rinna handed the packet back.

"Take those to costumes."

"Where are the curtain hooks?"

"With Nessa, apparently."

I carried the wrong hooks twelve paces into the building and gave them
to a woman sewing a brown coat.

She looked inside.

"Good."

"Are they?"

"Yes."

That improved nothing.

Teren was onstage.

"Greg."

"Yes."

"Third Man."

"My goat?"

"Your goat."

Finally.

"Then after, take this."

He handed me a folded note.

I did not take it.

"Where?"

"South market. Lamp oil seller beside the cooper."

"Why?"

"Tell him six small tins tomorrow, not four. Rinna will pay on
delivery."

"Why me?"

"You're going that way."

"I'm not."

"You are now."

I took the note.

"I have a show."

"Yes."

"When am I supposed to go?"

"After."

"After the show?"

"After your piece."

"There's more show after my piece."

"Correct."

"Do I come back?"

"If you want."

This was not a schedule.

It was weather.

I put the note inside my coat.

The Petition ran that afternoon.

I got my goat back.

I stood behind the side cloth, listened to Jori call the first entrance,
and waited for the line before mine.

The curtain moved smoothly.

I noticed again.

Then I stopped noticing.

Sellen said, "My neighbor has complained to half the street and all the
watch."

That was not my cue.

I waited.

Veya answered.

Sellen crossed.

Then came the line.

"My neighbor says the animal has damaged his property."

Jori pointed.

I went.

"My neighbor's goat has eaten all my patience and half my fence."

Sellen turned.

"My father sent me because the goat is innocent."

The audience laughed.

I did not add anything.

Sellen continued.

I continued.

The scene worked.

It was almost disappointing.

Afterward, Teren caught me at the side gap.

"Good."

"That's all?"

"What do you want?"

"I don't know."

"Then good."

He shoved the red doorframe toward me.

"Move."

I moved it.

The repaired foot held.

The curtain worked.

The fake petition went back into its box.

Nobody asked me about magic.

For almost an hour, I forgot I had any.

Then Pell passed carrying a painted bucket.

"Magician."

"Props."

He kept walking.

That was the entire conversation.

I liked it better.

I left for the south market after my piece.

The lamp seller beside the cooper was farther south than Teren had
implied.

Everything was farther when somebody else described it.

I had made it halfway when the cloth around my right crutch grip twisted
again.

I stopped beside a cobbler's stall and fixed it.

The cobbler watched.

"That's terrible."

"It was free."

"Still terrible."

He had a basket of leather scraps under the bench.

I looked at it.

He looked at me.

"How much for a strip?"

"What size?"

I showed him the grip.

He took my crutch before I could object, turned it once, then pulled a
narrow brown strip from the basket.

"This."

"How much?"

"One copper."

"That's too much for scrap."

"It's good scrap."

"It's in a basket on the ground."

"Then use your cloth."

I looked at the cloth.

The cloth looked back.

It was not going to improve.

"Half."

"No."

"Half and I don't tell people you charge full copper for rubbish."

"One and I wrap it."

"Half and you don't."

"One."

I paid one copper.

He wrapped it.

That changed the argument.

The leather went around the grip tight and smooth, with the seam away
from my palm. He tied it under itself and cut the end.

I put weight on the crutch.

Better.

Annoyingly better.

"Good scrap," he said.

"I dislike you."

"Walk on it."

"I don't walk on that end."

He laughed.

I left.

The lamp seller was beside the cooper.

Teren had been right about that part.

I gave him the note.

He read it.

"Six?"

"Yes."

"Tomorrow?"

"Yes."

"Not four?"

"Apparently this is important."

"It is if he wants six."

"Do you have six?"

"Tomorrow."

"Good."

He folded the note.

"Tell Teren I want the old tins back."

"Why?"

"Because they're mine."

"That seems fair."

"Tell him."

I had become a message with crutches.

On the way back, I passed the Guild street.

I did not need to go there.

I kept going.

Then a boy in a gray Guild vest came out of the side entrance and
called, "Greg?"

I stopped.

This was becoming a problem.

He held a folded paper.

"For you."

"From Hessa?"

He looked at the front.

"Yes."

I took it.

"Do I need to go in?"

"No."

"Good."

I opened it on the street.

DAY AFTER TOMORROW. AFTER MIDDAY. BRING THE QUESTION. NO TESTING BEFORE.

Under that, in smaller writing:

THIS INCLUDES PAPER.

I read it twice.

The boy was still there.

"Does she usually add that?"

"I don't know."

"Good answer."

He went back inside.

Two workers were carrying a long shallow crate through the side
entrance. One of them complained that it had been marked for east
storage. The other said something about south.

I kept walking.

Hessa had scheduled direction.

Not tomorrow.

The day after.

I folded the note and put it with Teren's lamp message, then remembered
I had already delivered Teren's lamp message.

My coat was becoming an office.

I reached the hall during the last piece.

Nobody had missed me.

That was useful information.

Rinna was counting coins.

"Six tins tomorrow," I said. "He wants the old tins back."

"Good."

"I bought leather."

"I can see."

"One copper."

"Why are you telling me?"

"I don't know."

She looked at my hand.

"Better?"

"Yes."

"Then stop complaining."

"I wasn't."

"You were preparing."

She was right.

I helped clean.

A costume sleeve had torn under the arm. The woman with the brown coat
was already fixing it using one of the hooks Nessa had given me.

So the hooks had not been wrong.

They had merely been wrong for Rinna.

That felt familiar.

Jori rolled his cue page.

Sellen stole the last baker roll.

Hara accused him.

He denied it while chewing.

The hall had another evening show.

I did not.

Rinna told me I was done.

"Paid?"

She gave me one copper.

It replaced the one I had spent on leather.

That felt less like earning money than moving it through myself.

"Tomorrow?"

"Morning setup. Evening maybe."

"Role?"

"Maybe."

"Don't."

She smiled.

I left.

Lyssa was not home.

I was beginning to suspect she had a job.

I put Hessa's note on the table beside my folded question.

FORWARD?

MY FORWARD OR BOARD FORWARD?

The note looked like an answer to a different question.

DAY AFTER TOMORROW.

I had tomorrow first.

There was still one copper from the previous days on the table, plus the
copper I had just earned. I had spent one on the grip, so the pile had
not changed much.

I touched the new leather.

Worth it.

Then I realized I had forgotten to tell Jessa anything except narrow,
not wide.

That was exactly what Lyssa had told me to say.

So perhaps I had succeeded.

Lyssa came home after dark carrying a basket.

"Did you take it?"

"Yes."

"To Marra?"

"Yes."

"Did you tell her left side?"

"Yes."

"Jessa?"

"Eventually."

Lyssa stopped.

"What happened?"

"She wasn't at Marra's."

"She was supposed to be."

"She went to Sen's."

"Why?"

"I don't know. Then she went back to Marra's."

Lyssa closed her eyes.

"I found her."

"Did you tell her?"

"Narrow, not wide."

"Good."

"That is all I know."

"That is all you needed to know."

I pointed at her.

"Exactly."

She put the basket down.

Inside were onions, a small wrapped piece of cheese, and two things that
might have been turnips.

"What's that?"

"Food."

"I know what food is."

"Do you?"

"I had beans yesterday."

"That is evidence."

I took the basket to the table.

"Hessa sent a note."

"When?"

"I passed the Guild."

"You weren't going to the Guild."

"I didn't."

"Then how did you get a note?"

"They found me."

Lyssa looked at the paper.

"Day after tomorrow."

"Yes."

"Direction?"

"Probably."

She read my question.

"MY FORWARD OR BOARD FORWARD?"

"Yes."

"That's ugly."

"Thank you."

"What does it mean?"

"I don't know yet."

"Good question."

I looked at her.

She started cutting an onion.

"You sound like Hessa."

"Hostile."

"Accurate."

I sat.

My palm still hurt, but the crutch grip no longer rubbed the sore place
when I leaned it against the table.

Lyssa noticed the leather.

"New?"

"One copper."

"Good."

"The man was a thief."

"Is it better?"

"Yes."

"Then maybe not."

"He charged me for scrap."

"He wrapped it."

I hated that everyone understood this except me.

We ate late.

The turnips were turnips.

Neither of us had expected the other to have food ready, so the meal was
bread, onion, cheese, boiled turnips, and the last of yesterday's beans.

It was fine.

Lyssa's day had involved three people changing what they wanted after
cloth had already been cut.

Mine had involved carrying her parcel to the correct green door, walking
to the red door anyway, carrying Nessa's hooks, performing a goat
complaint, buying leather, carrying Teren's message south, receiving
Hessa's message while not visiting Hessa, and returning to a theatre
that had continued perfectly well without me.

"Whose was worse?" I asked.

"Mine."

"You didn't hear mine."

"I lived mine."

"Unfair."

"Yes."

I ate cheese.

Afterward I put tomorrow's theatre time on a scrap beside Hessa's note.

MORNING HALL. EVENING MAYBE.

Under that:

DAY AFTER TOMORROW. HESSA. QUESTION.

I looked at the two pieces of paper.

Neither moved.

I did not ask them to.

Tomorrow I had theatre.

The day after, I had magic.

Tonight I had dishes.

I did those first.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 185

## THE REGULAR

The new leather grip was already dirty.

I decided that meant it belonged to me.

It was also better.

My palm still had a sore patch from the curtain cord, but the crutch no
longer twisted a wad of cloth into it every time I leaned. I noticed
this on the way to East Market Hall because I was carrying nothing.

This lasted until the door.

Rinna handed me three empty lamp tins.

"Morning."

"Good morning."

"Find the other three."

I looked at the tins.

"Where?"

"If I knew, I would have six."

The hall was already awake.

Someone had opened the rear doors, and a pale strip of morning crossed
the floor through dust and paint smell. Jori was onstage with the
curtain half open. Hara stood in one stocking beside a costume basket,
arguing that two brown stockings were not the same brown. Veya was
reading a page while somebody pinned the back of her dress. Pell's legs
were visible beneath a table.

I stepped around them.

"Why do we need six?"

"The oil man is coming."

"I know."

"Then why did you ask?"

"I was hoping the number had changed."

"It hasn't."

Three tins knocked together under my arm.

I knew where the lamp shelf was.

That was new enough that I noticed it, then annoying enough that I
stopped.

Two more old tins sat behind the blue lamp pieces, both empty except for
a greasy smell and one dead moth.

Five.

"Five," I called.

"Six," Rinna called back.

"I understand counting."

"Then find six."

Pell's legs disappeared under the table.

I looked at the stage.

The sixth tin could have been anywhere.

That was the problem with a place where everything became something
else. A crate was a seat until it was a wall. A bowl was supper until it
was a crown. A lamp-oil tin was probably lamp oil until Pell saw it.

"Pell."

Nothing.

"Pell."

"What?"

"Where is the sixth oil tin?"

"Which one?"

"The sixth."

His head appeared beneath the table.

"That's not a description."

"The small square ones. We have five."

"We have more than five."

"Excellent. Where?"

He disappeared again.

I waited.

A hand emerged holding a wooden wheel.

"Not a tin."

"I know."

"Then why did you give it to me?"

"I didn't."

I put the wheel on the table.

Nessa came through carrying a folded painted cloth.

She handed one end to me without stopping.

I took it.

"Where?"

"Back rail."

I knew the back rail.

I followed.

The cloth was painted with pale stone blocks on one side. Nessa walked
backward, guiding it around a bench.

"Not on the floor."

"I know."

"Then lift."

I lifted.

We got it onto the rail.

She tied one corner, looked at my side, and said, "Higher."

I raised it.

"Other higher."

I raised the wrong hand.

"No."

"I know what other means."

"Apparently not."

We got the cloth hung.

She left.

I looked at the five tins still under my arm.

I had forgotten I was holding them.

That seemed dangerous.

I put them beside Rinna's table.

A young man I had seen twice but never spoken to came through the side
door carrying the fake loaf.

"Where?"

"Prop shelf. Second level, left."

He went.

Nessa's voice came from behind me.

"No."

I closed my eyes.

The young man stopped.

"Where?"

"Kitchen box today," Nessa said.

He turned around.

I pointed at Nessa.

"She changes things."

"It was on the shelf yesterday," I said.

"Yesterday it wasn't in The Empty Table."

"What is The Empty Table?"

"Third piece."

I looked at the young man.

"Kitchen box."

He went.

Nessa looked at me.

"I was right yesterday."

"Very useful today."

Then she left.

I knew enough to be wrong faster.

That was progress of a kind.

The oil seller arrived before we found the sixth tin.

He came through the front with a wooden carrier holding six sealed tins
and the expression of a man who had been told he would receive six old
tins.

Rinna met him.

"Five now," she said.

"Six old."

"Yes."

"Six new."

"I can see them."

"Six old."

Rinna looked toward me.

I disliked being included in this.

"Looking."

The seller put the carrier down but kept one hand on it.

"No old, one copper extra."

"For the tin?"

"For not returning it."

"It's my tin."

"Then return it."

Rinna looked at me again.

I went to find Pell.

He was no longer under the table.

The table had acquired a woman sewing a hat.

"Where's Pell?"

She pointed down.

I looked.

No Pell.

"Not there."

"He was."

"Everyone was."

I went backstage.

Jori was testing the repaired curtain wheel. It rolled quietly enough
that the cloth moved without the old scrape.

"Seen Pell?"

"Rear."

I went rear.

Davin was crouched beside a wagon wheel with a hammer and a block of
wood.

"Seen Pell?"

"Yes."

"Where?"

Davin pointed toward the hall.

I had just come from the hall.

"Recently?"

"No."

"Thank you."

He glanced at the new leather grip.

"Better."

"Yes."

That was the whole conversation.

I went back inside.

My right shoulder had started to complain before my palm did. This
seemed unfair but predictable.

Hara was now wearing both stockings.

They were not the same brown.

Nobody had died.

"Have you seen Pell?"

"Yes."

"Where?"

"He asked me for red powder."

"When?"

"Morning."

"It is morning."

"Earlier morning."

"What did he want red powder for?"

Hara shrugged.

That was enough.

Red powder meant props or paint or fake blood, depending on which person
had said it.

I checked the prop shelf.

No Pell.

I checked the side table.

No Pell.

Then I saw a square metal corner beneath a stack of folded rags.

I pulled them aside.

The sixth lamp tin sat open on the table.

It was full of nails.

I stared at it.

Pell appeared behind me.

"Those are mine."

"The nails?"

"Yes."

"The tin?"

"No."

"Good."

He reached for the nails.

I stopped him.

"Where do they go?"

"In the tin."

"Not anymore."

"Then where?"

I found a cracked wooden cup.

Pell looked offended.

"That's the blood cup."

"Is there blood in it?"

"No."

"Then it's the nail cup."

"It leaks."

"Nails don't."

He considered this.

"Fine."

We poured the nails into the cup.

One fell through the crack.

Pell picked it up.

"See?"

"It lost one."

"You found it."

"Still."

I took the tin.

"Rinna is waiting."

"Tell her I needed it."

"You didn't."

"I needed something like it."

"That's worse."

The oil seller got his sixth tin.

Rinna got six new ones.

Nobody paid an extra copper.

The entire crisis had lasted long enough for Jori to finish checking the
curtain, Hara to change stockings again, Nessa to hang two cloths, and
Teren to decide the afternoon bill did not need The Empty Table after
all.

The fake loaf moved back to the prop shelf.

The young man who had asked me where it went looked at me.

I pointed.

"Don't."

He laughed.

By midday I had swept the left passage, carried two benches, taken a
coat to costumes, returned the coat because it was the wrong coat, and
moved the ghost tube before someone put a basket on it.

Nobody told me to move the tube.

I just did.

Pell came around the corner carrying the basket.

He stopped.

"Where'd it go?"

"Tube."

"Oh."

He put the basket somewhere else.

That felt better than magic.

Not more important.

Just more useful before lunch.

Teren found me sitting on the low curtain box with my crutches against
my knee.

"Evening."

"Maybe?"

"Yes."

"That means yes?"

"It does now."

"Role?"

He handed me four pages.

"Witness."

"In what?"

"Third."

Then he walked away.

I stared after him.

"Third what?"

He did not answer.

Jori did.

"The Empty Table."

I looked toward the prop shelf.

The young man with the fake loaf was already laughing.

"Of course."

The Empty Table turned out to be about an inheritance.

There was a dead aunt, three cousins, a missing will, a servant who knew
too much, and a table nobody was allowed to touch because the aunt had
supposedly died beside it.

The table was not empty.

It had a fake loaf, a wooden knife, a cup, two folded papers, and a bowl
with one real onion in it.

I pointed this out.

Veya said, "The title is old."

"Was the table empty before?"

"No."

"Then why?"

"Greg."

"Yes?"

"Read."

I read.

The Witness had six lines.

I had seen the piece once from the back wall, but I had not known it was
called The Empty Table because nobody had needed me to know.

My job was to enter after the second cousin accused the servant, say I
had seen the aunt alive after sunset, identify which cousin had been at
the rear gate, then leave after everybody decided I was lying.

I liked the Witness.

He knew one thing.

Everyone hated him for it.

Simple.

We ran the entrance once.

Jori called it.

I entered from the wrong side.

Veya stopped.

"Other."

"I know."

"You said that this morning."

"That was cloth."

"This is you."

I went around.

The second entrance worked.

During the break I went outside for air.

Carrow was busy in the ordinary way that had nothing to do with me.

A fish seller was throwing gray water into the gutter. Two boys rolled a
barrel downhill until a woman shouted at them. A wagon blocked half the
lane while somebody argued over sacks. Across the market, I saw Lyssa.

She was talking to a woman I didn't know.

The woman held a folded strip of yellow cloth. Lyssa had one hand on her
hip and the other pointing toward the cloth as if the cloth had
personally caused trouble.

Lyssa looked up.

She saw me.

I raised a hand.

She raised two fingers.

Then the woman said something, and Lyssa turned back to her.

I went inside.

I did not know who the woman was.

I survived.

The baker rolls arrived before the evening show.

Teren stood beside the tray.

I approached carefully.

"No."

"I haven't done anything."

"You were going to."

"That is not evidence."

"It is experience."

He turned away to answer Jori.

I took a roll.

Nobody stopped me.

I stood there with it in my hand, suspicious.

Hara walked past.

"You look guilty."

"I succeeded."

"At bread?"

"Yes."

"Congratulations."

She took one too.

The evening crowd came in slowly.

I worked the door until Rinna told me not to.

A man asked where the privy was.

I knew.

A woman asked whether the left passage was open.

"No."

"Why?"

"Quick change."

"Whose?"

"I don't know."

She went around.

That was apparently the correct amount of truth.

A boy carrying two tickets asked me where the ghost was.

"Not tonight."

"Tomorrow?"

"I don't know."

He looked disappointed.

"Paper?" Pell said from behind me.

"Go away."

The boy looked at Pell.

"What paper?"

"Nothing," I said.

Pell went away.

The rumor was dying.

I appreciated his effort to save it less than he probably intended.

The first piece was a short comedy I did not know.

I carried a stool on, carried it off, and missed nothing.

The second was The Red Door.

The repaired frame held.

A child did not tell anyone to go around.

This felt like a loss.

Then came The Empty Table.

I waited on the correct side.

The leather grip had darkened under my hand from sweat and dust, but it
stayed smooth.

Jori pointed.

I entered.

Veya, playing the oldest cousin, turned on me.

"You were at the lane."

"I was."

"You saw her?"

"After sunset."

"Alive?"

"Angry."

A laugh.

That line was written.

Good.

"Who else was there?"

I looked at the younger cousin.

He looked guilty.

This was also his job.

"Him."

The younger cousin stood.

"You're lying."

"No."

"You've hated me since spring."

"I met you this morning."

That got a bigger laugh.

That line was also written.

I liked this play.

The servant crossed behind the table.

Veya said, "Then why were you at the rear gate?"

I answered.

"Because your aunt paid me to watch it."

The younger cousin came toward me.

That was where I was supposed to back away.

I did.

My crutch hit the edge of the table.

The fake loaf fell.

It landed on the floor.

For one very long moment, everyone looked at it.

The loaf was painted cloth over something light. From the house it
looked acceptable.

On the floor, upside down, it looked like a dead pillow.

The younger cousin looked at it.

I looked at it.

He said, "Even the bread wants out."

The audience laughed.

I bent automatically.

Veya said, "Leave it."

I stopped.

The scene continued.

The loaf stayed on the floor for another two lines until the servant
kicked it under the table without looking.

Backstage, Nessa was waiting.

"I know."

"What?"

"Don't hit the table."

"No."

I blinked.

"No?"

"Don't pick up the loaf."

"I didn't."

"You started to."

"It fell."

"The audience saw it fall. If you stop the scene to fix it, they watch
you fix it."

I looked toward the stage.

The servant was accusing Veya of hiding the will.

The loaf was gone.

"Right."

Nessa handed me a folded cloth.

"Costumes."

I took it.

"Which chest?"

"Wall."

I hesitated.

She looked at me.

"Actually wall?"

"Yes."

"Today?"

"Greg."

I went.

The rest of my work was ordinary.

That was the part I noticed most.

I knew where the folded cloth went.

I knew not to use the left passage during Hara's change.

I knew which stool had the bad leg and put it against the wall before
anyone sat on it.

I knew the lamp boy needed the long taper, not the short one, for the
last piece.

I knew the blue lamp was not a lamp anyone should light for ordinary
light.

I knew where Pell would be when he wasn't where he was supposed to be.

Usually.

I was wrong twice.

Once about a coat.

Once about a rope.

The rope had moved to the rear peg because tomorrow's setup needed the
front peg clear.

I said, "It was here."

Rinna said, "Yes."

That was all.

The building changed while I learned it.

Apparently that was allowed.

After the show, Rinna paid me one copper.

"Witness and crew."

"I dropped bread."

"You hit a table."

"The bread fell."

"Yes."

"The audience laughed."

"Not because you were good."

"I didn't say that."

"You were going to."

I put the copper away.

"Tomorrow?"

"No morning."

I waited.

"After midday," she said. "Maybe evening."

"I have Hessa after midday."

Rinna looked at me.

"Paper?"

"Direction."

"Is that better?"

"I don't know."

"Then come after."

"If we're done."

"With paper?"

"Yes."

She nodded.

"Come after paper."

That was the entire scheduling negotiation.

Magic had become something I had to tell work about.

I was not sure how I felt about that.

Mostly I felt tired.

When I left, the hall still had people in it.

Nessa and the brown-coat woman were arguing about a hem. Jori was
writing on tomorrow's cue page. Pell had reclaimed the cracked wooden
cup for nails and was pretending this had always been the plan. Teren
was eating the last baker roll.

I pointed at him.

"You stopped me yesterday."

"Yesterday was yesterday."

I hated this place.

I went home smiling.

Lyssa was already there.

That was unusual enough that I checked the room as if I might have
entered the wrong one.

She was sitting at the table with her shoes off and a wet cloth around
one ankle.

"What happened?"

"Nothing."

"That's wet."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"My ankle hurts."

"What did you do?"

"Worked."

I put my crutches down.

"Hostile."

"Accurate."

There was bread on the table.

I sat.

"Hessa tomorrow."

"I know."

"How?"

"You left the note under the cup."

"Right."

Lyssa looked at my coat.

"You smell like oil."

"Six tins."

"Of oil?"

"Yes."

"Why?"

"Because there were five."

She waited.

I realized that did not explain anything.

"There were supposed to be six old tins. Pell put nails in one."

"Of course."

"You don't know Pell."

"I know enough."

I ate bread.

"My grip works."

"Good."

"One copper."

"You told me."

"It still works."

"Excellent."

"I was a Witness."

"To what?"

"An inheritance."

"Did you inherit anything?"

"One copper."

"Good inheritance."

"I also dropped bread."

"Real?"

"Fake."

"Then you didn't drop bread."

I thought about Hessa.

"I dropped the representation of bread."

Lyssa stared at me.

"No."

"Fair."

I got up to wash.

My coat had a pale streak of stage dust along one sleeve. There was
something black under my thumbnail, probably charcoal or paint. The
leather grip was dirty.

Tomorrow's note was still under the cup.

AFTER MIDDAY. BRING THE QUESTION.

I took out the question.

FORWARD?

MY FORWARD OR BOARD FORWARD?

I did not improve it.

Today I had found a lamp tin, been wrong about a loaf, been wrong about
a door, been right about a passage, carried a stool, played a Witness,
knocked fake bread onto the floor, and earned one copper.

Tomorrow I was going to ask paper which way forward was.

I put the question back under the note.

Then I went to bed before anything else could need carrying.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 186

## THE TESTER

Lyssa's ankle was still wrapped when I woke.

Not badly. She was already standing on it.

I pointed.

"No."

"You don't know what I was going to say."

"Sit down."

"That wasn't it."

"It was close."

She put bread on the table and sat long enough to cut it.

I had Hessa's note beside my cup and my question under it.

FORWARD?

MY FORWARD OR BOARD FORWARD?

Lyssa read it again.

"Paper today?"

"Direction."

"Which direction?"

"That's the problem."

She nodded as if this were a reasonable answer.

"Are you working?"

"Yes."

"With the ankle?"

"Yes."

"Hessa would object."

"Hessa doesn't supervise cloth."

"She should expand."

Lyssa gave me bread.

I was still smiling sometimes for no reason.

Not at paper anymore. I had learned that staring at paper made Lyssa
hostile.

I smiled at the bread instead.

She saw.

"Very small amount."

"Yes."

"Under glass."

"Yes."

"While supervised."

"Yes."

"You are still pleased."

"Extremely."

"Good."

Then she left before me.

I did not go to the hall.

That felt wrong.

I had spent enough mornings there that walking past the turn toward East
Market made me feel as if I had forgotten something. I checked my coat,
my question, and the copper in my pocket.

Nothing forgotten.

The Guild had me after midday.

Until then, I had nowhere I was required to be.

This was almost suspicious.

I bought a meat bun and sat near the lower market long enough to eat it
while it was still hot.

Nobody handed me anything.

Nobody asked where Pell was.

Nobody needed a fake loaf.

It was peaceful.

I disliked it after about ten minutes.

By the time I reached the Guild, Hessa was not ready.

Of course.

The clerk at the front knew me now.

That was not necessarily good.

"Wait."

"I didn't ask."

"You were going to."

"I hate when people do that."

"Sit."

I sat.

The chair was against the wall near the same long table where people
left things they did not want to hold while arguing. Today it had two
wrapped bundles, a cracked prepared plate in a shallow tray, and a box
with three seals hanging from strings.

The cracked plate had acquired another note.

DO NOT REPAIR UNTIL CLEARED.

Someone had written beneath it:

I WASN'T.

I liked the Guild slightly more.

The gray-coated woman passed through carrying a stack of papers.

She saw me.

"Paper man."

"No."

She kept walking.

That was worse than Pell.

Hessa appeared several minutes later with ink on two fingers and
irritation on her face.

"Come."

"Good afternoon."

"No."

I followed her.

"Bad afternoon?"

"Unfinished."

"That seems normal here."

She looked back at me.

"Do you want to wait?"

"No."

"Then don't improve it."

The room was not the same one we had used last time.

The old table was there, or one much like it, but the wall behind it had
shelves with shallow boxes, folded cloth, weights, and a stack of wooden
frames. Hessa had cleared the center.

The apparatus sat on the table.

I recognized it and didn't.

The paired wooden guides remained. The glass shield remained. The paper
fins were new again, cut from the same pale sheet and folded at the
bottom. Hessa had added a flat square board beneath the guides.

There were four black marks on the board, one near each edge.

One was a line.

One was two lines.

One was a dot.

One was a cross.

"Directions?"

"Marks."

"Those are directions."

"They will be if I tell you they are."

I put my crutches against the wall.

"That's annoying."

"Good."

She held out her hand.

I gave her my question.

She read it.

Then she read it again.

"Better."

I stared at her.

"This is the ugliest question I've brought you."

"Yes."

"And this is better."

"Yes."

"Why?"

She put the paper beside the board.

"What is your forward?"

I pointed away from my chest.

"That."

"What is board forward?"

I pointed toward the black line.

"That."

"If I turn the board?"

"The line turns."

"If you move?"

"My forward turns."

"Good."

She looked at the question.

"It asks two things I can separate."

"I liked my other questions."

"They were prettier."

I was offended because she was right.

Hessa checked the table legs.

Then the wedges.

Then the glass.

She removed the shield and set two fins into the guides.

"Do not touch the table."

"I know."

"Do not touch the chair after I set it."

"I know."

"Do not move your crutches once we begin."

"They're against the wall."

"Good."

She placed the chair.

I sat.

The table was slightly too far away.

I shifted the chair.

Hessa waited.

"Now?"

"Yes."

She moved it half a hand closer.

"Now?"

"Yes."

"Then stay."

I put my good foot flat.

The missing leg did what it always did, which was not participate.

Hessa looked down.

"Can you hold that position without bracing on the table?"

"Yes."

"Show me."

I held it.

My shoulder objected mildly.

"Fine."

She put the glass shield down.

The fins stood beneath it.

One on the left.

One on the right.

Tiny.

Ridiculous.

Real.

I wanted one to move so badly that I had to look at the table edge for a
moment instead.

Hessa mixed two small wooden squares beneath the table and set one
beside each guide with the marked sides hidden.

Same as before.

I would not know which fin she had designated until she showed me.

"Minimal first."

I nodded.

The draw came cleanly.

It was still small.

Still supervised.

Still familiar.

I had spent days not touching it, and the sensation returned with an
almost insulting lack of ceremony. A narrow inward gathering. The same
difficult-to-name awareness along the wrist edge. The same sense that
one side of the shape was easier to find than the other.

I held.

Hessa watched.

"Release."

I released.

She wrote.

That made twenty-five successful supervised minimal draws.

"Again. Shape only. No external target."

I drew again.

The deliberate shape took longer.

The wrist-edge asymmetry was there.

I kept myself from leaning toward it.

Hessa saw something in my face.

"Don't chase."

"I'm not."

"Good."

I formed the shape as evenly as I could.

Held.

Released.

Twenty-one successful supervised deliberate shaping attempts.

Hessa wrote again.

Then she lifted the wooden square beside the left guide.

A black mark underneath.

"Left target."

I looked at the left fin.

"Direction?"

"Line."

The black line on the board pointed away from me.

Board forward and my forward were the same.

"That's not helpful."

"It is first."

"Right."

She checked the glass again.

"Begin when settled."

I drew.

Shaped.

The target sat beneath the glass.

Forward.

Barely.

Not move.

Not jump.

Not slide across the table.

Forward.

I tried to make the intention smaller than the thing itself.

The familiar asymmetry sharpened at the wrist edge.

The paper moved.

It was tiny.

A dry little scrape.

I opened my mouth.

Hessa raised one finger.

I shut it.

She leaned over the glass without touching it.

The left fin had shifted forward perhaps half the width of my smallest
fingernail.

The right fin had not visibly moved.

Hessa checked the wedges.

She checked the board.

She checked the guide.

She crouched to look at my foot.

"I didn't move."

"I know."

"Then why are you looking?"

"Because knowing is not checking."

I shut up.

She marked the board beside the fin.

Then she lifted the glass, removed both fins, and examined their bases.

"Nothing obvious."

"Good?"

"It means nothing obvious."

She wrote.

That was the tenth supervised external-effect attempt.

One movement.

In the intended direction.

Also away from me.

Also board forward.

It proved almost nothing about the question.

I hated useful preparation.

Hessa turned the entire square board.

The black line now pointed to my left.

The guides turned with it.

The chair did not.

"Same target side?"

"Different fin. Different assignment."

She changed both fins.

Mixed the wooden squares again.

This time the right fin was target.

"Direction?"

"Line."

I looked at the line.

My left.

Board forward.

Not my forward.

"Try."

I drew.

The effort felt the same until it didn't.

I shaped toward the line.

Left.

The wrist-edge sensation wanted to become important.

I refused to decide what it meant.

The fin did nothing.

I held until Hessa said, "Release."

Nothing.

Control nothing.

Eleventh supervised external-effect attempt.

Hessa inspected anyway.

"Again?" I asked.

"No."

She rotated the board back.

"Why?"

"Because I want a different question."

She stood behind me.

"Get up."

I reached for the crutches.

"Careful."

"I know how to stand."

"Not without shaking my table."

That was fair.

I stood without touching it.

Hessa moved the chair to the opposite side of the table.

This took longer than the magical part.

I had to get around the table without hitting the board, the glass, the
chair, the shelf, or Hessa. My crutch tip caught the chair leg once.

Hessa said, "Stop."

I stopped.

She moved the chair herself.

"This is humiliating."

"This is furniture."

"Same thing sometimes."

When I sat on the opposite side, the board's black line pointed toward
me.

Board forward had not changed.

My forward had.

"Now they're opposite."

"Yes."

She changed the fins again.

New assignment.

Left target.

"Line again?"

"Line."

I stared at the target.

To move board forward, it would have to move toward me.

That felt wrong before I even drew.

I did not know if that mattered.

I drew.

Shaped.

The familiar asymmetry returned.

I tried to aim through it toward the line.

Toward me.

Nothing happened.

I held.

Nothing.

"Release."

I released.

Twelfth supervised external-effect attempt.

No movement.

Hessa inspected.

Nothing.

I leaned back.

"So it doesn't like toward me."

"No."

"It moved away from me before."

"Once today."

"And before."

"Under different arrangements."

"It moved forward twice before."

"Board forward."

"Which was also away from me."

"Yes."

I smiled.

Hessa did not.

"Don't."

"I didn't say anything."

"You were going to."

Everyone had become unbearable.

Hessa rotated the board again.

Now the line pointed to my right.

From my new seat, my forward was toward the opposite wall.

The line was sideways.

"Different intended direction," I said.

"Yes."

"Still board forward."

"Yes."

She changed the target assignment.

Right fin.

I settled.

My shoulder had begun to ache from holding myself too carefully. The
mana itself was not painful. The attention was worse. Every tiny thing
in the room had become a possible explanation.

My foot.

My breath.

The glass.

The table.

The paper base.

The board.

My crutch against the wall.

Hessa's sleeve.

I understood why she was annoying.

This did not make her less annoying.

I drew.

Shaped toward the line.

Right.

The paper moved.

Not right.

Away from me.

A tiny forward slide relative to my body.

Which, from the board's perspective, was sideways.

I saw it.

Hessa saw it.

Neither of us spoke.

She inspected.

Control unchanged.

Wedges unchanged.

No contact.

The target fin had moved less than the first one, but enough to see
against the ink mark.

Hessa marked it.

Thirteenth supervised external-effect attempt.

I waited.

That was difficult.

Finally I said, "That wasn't the line."

"No."

"It went away from me."

"Yes."

"So my forward."

"Once."

"Twice today if you count the first."

"The first cannot distinguish them."

"Right."

"And the failed attempt with the line sideways?"

"Nothing."

"And the attempt with board forward toward you?"

"Nothing."

I looked at the paper.

"Again."

Hessa looked at me.

"Please."

"No."

"Why?"

"You're tired."

"I'm not."

"Your shoulder has moved three times since you sat down."

I looked at my shoulder as if it had betrayed me.

"It hurts."

"Yes."

"That's not mana."

"No."

"Then it shouldn't count."

"It counts as you moving."

I hated her.

She removed the glass.

I watched the target fin as she lifted it.

It had moved perhaps a few grains' width.

That was all.

Enough to make my heart beat harder.

Not enough to make Hessa let me do it again.

She laid the fins side by side.

"What can I say?"

"About today?"

"Yes."

"You produced two observed movements during four external attempts."

"Both away from me."

"One was away from you and board forward."

"The other was away from me and not board forward."

"Yes."

"And the two failures were directions that weren't away from me."

Hessa looked at me.

"One was sideways relative to you. One was toward you."

"So."

"So today suggests movement may be easier away from your position."

I waited.

"That's it?"

"That is more than you knew this morning."

"Can I say direction follows me?"

"No."

"Can I say I can push away?"

"No."

"Can I say it prefers away?"

"Not yet."

"What can I say?"

She took my ugly question paper and wrote beneath it.

POSSIBLE BIAS: AWAY FROM GREG.

NOT ESTABLISHED.

I read it.

"That's terrible."

"It's accurate."

"It sounds weak."

"It is weak."

"I moved it twice."

"Yes."

"With magic."

"Yes."

That still worked on me.

The irritation fell away for a moment.

"Yes," I repeated.

Hessa capped the ink.

"Do not become stupid because I agreed with one word."

"I moved paper twice."

"Under this setup."

"Yes."

"In two arrangements."

"Yes."

"With two failures."

"Yes."

"And today's evidence suggests, but does not establish, that movement
may be easier away from your position."

"Yes."

"Good."

I looked at the board.

"What about the wrist thing?"

"No."

"I didn't even ask."

"You were going to connect them."

"They both have a side."

"Everything has a side if you describe it badly enough."

I laughed.

Hessa did not.

She wrote the counts.

Twenty-five successful supervised minimal draws.

Twenty-one supervised deliberate shaping attempts.

Thirteen supervised external-effect attempts.

I pointed.

"Only one shaping?"

"One isolated shaping before external work. The external attempts are
already deliberate external shaping."

"Right."

"Do not inflate your own record."

"I wasn't."

She looked at me.

"At work," I added.

That almost got something from her.

Almost.

Hessa took a fresh scrap of paper.

She wrote:

IS THERE AN EASIER DIRECTION?

Then below it:

TEST AWAY FIRST.

I frowned.

"I want to know if I can choose."

"I know."

"That seems more useful."

"Later."

"Why?"

"Because if one direction is easier, I want to know that before you
spend six sessions failing to prove you can do something harder."

"That sounds reasonable."

"Yes."

"I don't like it."

"I know."

She handed me the paper.

"When?"

"Not tomorrow."

"Of course."

"I have other work."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"The gray woman called me paper man."

"She has other work too."

"I noticed."

Hessa began clearing the fins.

"Restrictions remain."

"No independent draw."

"Yes."

"No shaping."

"Yes."

"No paper."

"Yes."

"No testing whether things move away from me."

"Correct."

"What if Pell moves away from me naturally?"

Hessa stopped.

"Go to the theatre."

"That's where Pell is."

"Then suffer."

I left before she could improve the instruction.

East Market Hall was already in the middle of something when I arrived.

The front doors were open.

A bench sat sideways in the aisle. Two costumes hung from the ticket
table. Somebody was singing behind the curtain, badly and with
confidence.

Rinna saw me.

"Paper?"

"Complicated."

"Can you work?"

"Yes."

"Good. Chairs."

She pointed.

I moved chairs.

That was it.

Nobody asked whether I had discovered a fundamental property of magic.

I put six chairs against the right wall, moved two benches forward, and
carried a basket to costumes.

Pell found me halfway through the basket.

"Paper?"

"Yes."

"Better?"

"Maybe."

"Can you move it sideways?"

"Maybe."

He grinned.

"Better magic."

"Nessa needs you."

"Does she?"

"I don't know."

He looked toward backstage.

Then went anyway.

Useful.

Jori handed me a folded page.

"House tonight."

"Role?"

"House."

"That's not a role."

"It is if people keep sitting where they shouldn't."

Fair.

I worked the door.

A woman wanted the aisle seat because her husband had a bad knee.

I moved two people.

A man wanted to know whether The Red Door was on.

It wasn't.

A girl dropped a ribbon.

I picked it up.

The evening passed without requiring me to move anything with magic.

I earned one copper.

When Rinna paid me, she asked, "Direction?"

I looked at her.

"Paper may prefer away from me."

Rinna put the copper in my hand.

"Reasonable."

"What does that mean?"

"Most things do."

Then she called Jori over because tomorrow's bill had changed.

I went home.

Lyssa was not there yet.

I put Hessa's new paper under the cup.

IS THERE AN EASIER DIRECTION?

TEST AWAY FIRST.

Under my old question, Hessa's answer looked annoyingly small.

POSSIBLE BIAS: AWAY FROM GREG.

NOT ESTABLISHED.

I sat.

My shoulder hurt.

My palm hurt less.

The room contained paper, cups, coins, bread, cloth, a chair, and
several other things I was not allowed to attempt to move away from
myself.

I behaved.

Lyssa came in later carrying a bundle under one arm.

"Paper?"

"Yes."

"Which direction?"

"Maybe away from me."

She put the bundle down.

"Can you make it come back?"

"No."

"Then don't lose it."

I stared at her.

"That's almost exactly the problem."

"Good."

She started untying the bundle.

I looked at Hessa's question again.

Tomorrow the hall wanted me.

Hessa did not.

After that, apparently, we were going to find out whether my magic had a
favorite direction.

For now, it had moved two pieces of paper less than a fingernail each.

That was enough to keep me awake longer than it should have.

Not long enough to test anything.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 187

## THE SUBSTITUTE

We had no bread.

This was Lyssa's fault because I had thought she was buying bread.

It was also my fault because she had thought I was buying bread.

We established both facts before either of us had properly dressed.

"I bought it last time," she said.

"I don't remember that."

"You ate it."

"That doesn't establish who bought it."

"It establishes you were present."

Her ankle wrap was still on, though looser than yesterday. She stood
with most of her weight on the other foot while tying her hair back.

I pointed at the ankle.

She pointed at my crutches.

We abandoned that argument.

"I'll get bread," I said.

"Good."

"If I'm near Marra's, I am not carrying anything."

"I didn't ask you to."

"You were going to."

"I was going to tell you Jessa said your coat button is loose."

I looked down.

The second button was loose.

"That's worse."

"How?"

"I was prepared for a parcel."

Lyssa smiled.

She had work west again. I had the hall.

Hessa's papers remained under the cup.

POSSIBLE BIAS: AWAY FROM GREG.

NOT ESTABLISHED.

And beneath that:

IS THERE AN EASIER DIRECTION?

TEST AWAY FIRST.

I put the cup back over them.

Nothing moved.

Good.

Outside, a shop door opened away from me.

I noticed.

Then I was annoyed that I had noticed.

By the time I reached East Market Hall, I had bought bread, eaten part
of it, and stopped assigning directions to doors.

Rinna was waiting inside with a coil of narrow cord over one arm.

"You're late."

"I'm early."

"Good. You're here."

She handed me the cord.

"What's this?"

"Back drop."

"Today?"

Rinna looked at me.

"Yes."

That felt like progress.

Nessa was already on the rear platform with a folded length of blue-gray
cloth. She saw the cord in my hand and pointed upward.

"Back rail."

"I know."

"Today."

"I know that too."

She gave me one end of the cloth.

We raised it.

I got the first corner right.

The second sagged.

"Other peg," Nessa said.

I moved it.

"Not that other peg."

"There are too many pegs."

"There are six."

"Exactly."

She fixed it while I held the cloth.

Nobody explained what the drop was for.

I did not ask.

Across the hall, Jori was checking the curtain line. Hara stood in one
stocking and one bare foot, arguing with a costume worker about whether
brown meant brown or the other brown. Veya sat on the stage edge reading
a page while somebody pinned the side of her dress.

Pell was nowhere visible.

This should have worried me.

It did not yet.

Rinna passed me on her way toward the front.

"Tell Pell narrow tube tonight. Not long."

"Narrow tube."

"Tonight."

"Yes."

She kept walking.

I repeated it once to myself.

Narrow tube tonight.

Then Jori called, "Greg."

I looked over.

A young woman I had seen twice before was holding the fake petition
stack.

"Where does this go?"

I almost answered.

Then I remembered the loaf.

"Today?"

Jori looked pleased in a way I distrusted.

The young woman said, "The Petition."

"Prop box by left wing."

Jori nodded.

I pointed.

"Bottom shelf. Wax side up."

She carried it away.

I had become dangerously competent.

Nessa handed me a broom.

That corrected the feeling.

I swept the left passage.

I moved two benches.

I took a red coat from a chair to costumes and was told it belonged on
the chair.

"Today?" I asked.

"Today," the costume worker said.

I returned it.

Someone asked where the blue lamp was.

"Upper prop shelf, wrapped."

It was.

Someone asked where the bad stool was.

"Which bad stool?"

"The one with the loose back."

"Rear wall."

It was not.

Pell had moved it.

I found him under the stage with his feet sticking out.

"Narrow tube tonight," I said.

He slid halfway out.

"What?"

"Narrow tube. Tonight."

"Why?"

"Rinna."

"For what?"

"I don't know."

"Ghost?"

"Probably."

"Which narrow tube?"

I stared at him.

There were two.

Of course there were two.

"The narrow one."

"They're both narrow."

"One must be narrower."

"Yes."

"Use that one."

Pell considered this.

"Good."

I left.

That was when Hara called me to hold a costume basket.

Then Jori needed the second stool.

Then Teren arrived carrying three folded pages and said, "You're in
second if Evin isn't here."

I forgot about the tube.

"Who is Evin?"

"Clerk."

"In what?"

"Debtor's Uncle."

"I don't know Debtor's Uncle."

"You've seen it."

"Once."

"Good."

Teren handed me a page.

There were eight lines marked in charcoal.

I read the first.

"I have no authority to release the chest."

I looked at Teren.

"This is a terrible role."

"It's a clerk."

"Exactly."

"Learn it."

"What if Evin comes?"

"Then he does it."

Teren walked away.

I looked at the page.

Nobody had asked whether I wanted the role.

That was also progress.

Debtor's Uncle turned out to be a short comedy about a man who inherited
a chest from an uncle who owed money to everyone in the district. The
chest contained almost nothing. This did not stop six people from trying
to claim it.

The clerk existed to tell everyone no.

I liked him immediately.

Veya found me reading beside the left wing.

"Entrance after second knock."

"Which side?"

"Right."

"Today?"

She looked at me.

"Yes, Greg."

"I am learning."

"Slowly."

She walked away.

I read the lines again.

The second knock.

Right side.

No authority.

Chest remains sealed.

Receipt first.

No, your cousin cannot sign.

Eight lines.

Easy.

Which meant something else would go wrong.

At midday, Evin still had not arrived.

Rinna had not seen him.

Jori had not seen him.

Teren had apparently expected this because he did not look surprised.

"Why is he late?"

"His sister's boy is sick," Hara said while eating an apple.

"How do you know?"

"He told me yesterday."

"Did he tell Teren?"

Hara looked toward Teren.

"Apparently not."

Teren heard.

"He told me he might be late."

"That seems relevant."

"It was."

"Did you tell me?"

"I just did."

Fair.

We ran the entrance once.

I came in on the right.

The first knock sounded.

I started.

Veya said, "Second."

"I know."

"You moved."

"I didn't enter."

"You leaned."

"That's not entering."

"Do it again."

The second time I waited.

Second knock.

Enter.

I made it to the desk.

The chest was a square wooden box with iron-colored paint at the
corners. It was light enough that Sellen had carried it one-handed five
minutes earlier.

I was not supposed to touch it.

That helped.

My first line was to Veya.

"I have no authority to release the chest."

She answered.

I gave the second.

Sellen came in too early.

Veya told him to go back out.

He did.

Nobody treated rehearsal as sacred.

Somebody hammered backstage through half of it.

Nessa crossed behind us carrying a rolled painted wall.

Pell shouted something about a hinge.

Jori called, "Again from the knock."

We did.

By the third time, the clerk existed.

Not much.

Enough.

During the break, I went to find Pell.

He was not under the stage.

I remembered Rinna's message.

Narrow tube tonight.

Good.

I had delivered it.

Mostly.

At the rear wall, one of the tubes was already out.

It was the longer one.

I stared at it.

Pell came through the side door with a handful of chalk.

"Why is that out?"

"Ghost."

"Rinna said narrow."

"That is narrow."

"The other narrow."

He looked at me.

"You said narrower."

"Yes."

"This one is narrower than the long one."

"There are three?"

"Yes."

I closed my eyes.

Pell pointed toward the prop shelves.

"Long, narrow, narrower."

"Why?"

"Different rooms."

"Rinna said narrow tube, not long."

"That's narrow."

I had delivered exactly the words.

I had also known he had asked which one.

I had decided I was done.

That part was mine.

"Wait."

I found Rinna near the ticket table.

"Which narrow tube?"

She looked at me.

"The short one."

"Pell has the middle one."

"I told you narrow, not long."

"There are three."

"I know."

"I didn't."

"You do now."

"Do you want the short one?"

"Yes."

"Good."

I turned.

Rinna said, "Greg."

I looked back.

"I told you this morning."

"Yes."

That was all.

I went back.

"Pell. Short one."

"That's narrower."

"I don't care what it's called."

"Then how will I know which one?"

"Short."

"Good."

He put the middle tube away.

Nothing had broken.

Nobody died.

We lost perhaps four minutes.

I had been relied upon to carry six words across one building and had
managed to make them insufficient.

This seemed unfair.

It was not.

I went outside for bread.

The market was loud enough that the hall noise disappeared after twenty
steps.

A fish seller was shouting prices. Two boys rolled an empty barrel
between them and nearly hit a woman carrying eggs. A wagon had stopped
crooked beside a stack of sacks, and three men were arguing about
whether the wagon or the sacks had been there first.

I saw Lyssa across the street.

She was with the woman from yesterday, the one with the yellow cloth.

Today the woman had green cloth.

This seemed like a development.

Lyssa saw me.

I lifted the bread.

She looked at it, then at me.

I pointed at myself.

She nodded approval.

Neither of us crossed the street.

I did not know who the woman was.

I survived again.

Back at the hall, Evin still had not arrived.

Teren saw the bread.

"Where did that come from?"

"I bought it."

He looked disappointed.

"Why?"

"Because yesterday you oppressed me."

"The baker arrangement ended."

I stopped.

"What?"

"No rolls today."

Behind me Pell said, "What?"

Rinna said, "Paid work ended."

Pell came around the curtain.

"We're still working."

"Different problem," Rinna said.

Pell looked genuinely betrayed.

I tore my bread in half.

He held out his hand.

"No."

"You're cruel."

"You called me magician for three days."

"That was praise."

"It was inaccurate."

"Half."

"No."

He wandered away.

I ate both halves.

This was one of my better performances.

The first piece went on without me.

I moved a stool before it and moved the same stool back afterward.

Nobody applauded.

Evin had still not arrived.

Teren found me.

"Clerk."

"Yes."

"Second knock."

"Yes."

"Right."

"Today?"

He stared at me.

"Go."

The house was not full, but it was good enough that the room changed
when the curtain opened.

That still happened.

Empty hall became audience.

Painted wall became a room.

Sellen became a man with a dead uncle and six creditors.

Veya became his cousin, who claimed the chest contained family property
despite never having seen it.

I waited behind the right side.

First knock.

I stayed.

Second knock.

I entered.

The clerk's coat was too wide through the shoulders and slightly too
short in the sleeve. Nobody had altered it for me because I was not
supposed to own the role.

I crossed to the desk.

Veya demanded the chest.

"I have no authority to release the chest."

"Then find someone who does."

"I have no authority to find someone who does."

That got a laugh.

Not a large one.

Enough.

The scene continued.

Sellen tried to sign for his dead uncle.

"No, your cousin cannot sign."

"He's not my cousin."

I looked at Veya.

"I met you this morning."

The audience laughed harder.

That line belonged to Evin.

I had heard him do it once.

He did it better.

Mine still worked.

A creditor entered.

Then another.

The chest acquired more owners without moving.

My job was mostly to prevent everyone else from progressing.

I understood bureaucracy spiritually.

Near the end, Sellen put both hands on the chest.

I said, "Receipt first."

He said, "For my own uncle?"

"Especially for your own uncle."

That got another laugh.

Then Veya took the scene away from me with a long complaint about how
the dead man had owed her three spoons, a blanket, and an apology.

She was better.

The audience followed her.

Good.

I stood behind the desk and looked annoyed.

Also good.

The piece ended.

Backstage, Teren said, "Fine."

"Fine?"

"The show happened."

"I got laughs."

"So did the chest."

The chest had not said anything.

I chose not to argue.

Evin arrived during the next piece.

He was thin, red-faced from hurrying, and angry before anyone spoke to
him.

"Boy's fever broke," he said to Hara.

"Good."

"Cart wheel split."

"Bad."

"Took the south road."

"Worse."

He saw me in his clerk coat.

"Oh."

"Hello."

"Did you do it?"

"Yes."

"How bad?"

"Teren said fine."

Evin nodded.

"Good."

That was all.

For the evening repeat, Evin took the coat back.

Obviously.

I still felt a small, stupid disappointment when he did.

Then I watched him run the clerk scene and understood why it was his.

He did less.

That was the irritating part.

He barely moved behind the desk. He let everyone come to him. His first
"no" was almost bored. By the time he said, "I met you this morning,"
the audience was already waiting for him to refuse something.

His laugh was bigger than mine.

I hated him for approximately six seconds.

Then Jori handed me a cue page.

"Hold."

I held it.

"Not there."

I moved.

"Other side."

I moved again.

The evening continued.

The ghost used the short tube.

It worked.

Pell did not mention magic.

I noticed this halfway through the piece and was offended.

Then he whispered, "Move."

I looked at him.

"What?"

"You're on my cord."

I moved my crutch.

He pulled the cord free.

That was better.

Later, Nessa handed me a gray cloth.

"Back rail."

"Today?"

"Tomorrow."

I stopped.

She nodded once.

"Good."

I put it on the marked shelf instead.

That felt suspiciously like learning.

Then I carried the wrong rope to Jori.

"It was there yesterday," I said.

Jori pointed to the front peg.

"Today."

"Yes."

The building kept changing while I learned it.

By the end of the evening, my shoulder hurt, my right palm was tender,
and the new leather grip had another dark mark across it.

It still did not twist.

Worth one copper.

Rinna paid me two.

I looked at the coins.

"Two?"

"Morning, clerk, evening crew."

"I was only clerk once."

"You were only paid for it once."

"Good."

"Did you want less?"

"No."

She closed her box.

I put the coins away.

"Do you need me tomorrow?"

"Afternoon."

"Role?"

"Maybe."

"Don't."

Rinna smiled.

"Tell Pell the short tube goes back on the upper shelf."

I looked toward Pell.

He was six paces away.

"PELL."

He looked over.

"SHORT TUBE. UPPER SHELF."

Rinna said, "Excellent."

"I've developed a system."

Pell shouted, "WHICH UPPER SHELF?"

I looked at Rinna.

She closed her eyes.

I went home.

Lyssa was already there.

Her ankle wrap was off.

The ankle itself looked slightly swollen.

I pointed.

She said, "Don't."

"Better?"

"Yes."

"Good."

"Your button is worse."

I looked down.

The loose button was now hanging by one thread.

"That also seems like work."

"Sit."

I sat.

She took the coat.

"How was paper?"

"Yesterday."

"I know. I wanted to see if you remembered."

"You're becoming cruel."

"Work."

She found a needle.

I watched her repair the button.

"Busy day?"

"Yes."

"Bad?"

"No."

I thought about it.

"Busy."

She nodded.

"Mine too."

"Yellow cloth woman had green cloth today."

Lyssa looked up.

"You saw us?"

"Across the market."

"That isn't her cloth."

"Whose is it?"

"Someone else's."

"Good."

She returned to the button.

I waited.

Nothing else came.

I had no idea who the woman was.

Still alive.

"I was a clerk."

"At the theatre?"

"Yes."

"What did you do?"

"Told everyone no."

"Good casting."

"I was excellent."

"How excellent?"

"Teren said fine."

Lyssa laughed.

"The real clerk came back."

"And?"

"He was better."

"That's rude."

"Very."

She bit the thread and handed me the coat.

"What did you earn?"

"Two copper."

"Better than fine."

I put the coat beside me.

On the table, Hessa's paper was still under the cup.

Nothing had moved.

I had thought about away twice during the day.

Once at the door.

Once when Pell finally walked away from me carrying the correct tube.

Neither counted.

I did not test anything.

Tomorrow the hall wanted me in the afternoon.

Hessa had not asked for me at all.

That was fine.

Probably.

I put one copper beside the bread money and kept the other.

Lyssa leaned back and stretched her sore ankle.

I stretched my shoulder.

Neither of us said anything useful about that.

People had needed me all day.

Cord.

Cloth.

A message.

A clerk.

A cue page.

A rope.

A tube.

A place to put something.

I had gotten some of it right.

I had gotten some of it wrong.

The show happened anyway.

That felt less impressive than moving paper.

It was considerably more tiring.

I went to bed before anyone could ask me where the short tube belonged.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 188

## THE HOUSEMAN

Lyssa was gone before I woke.

There was bread.

This was an improvement.

There was also a bowl on the table that did not belong to us.

I knew this because ours had a chip on the rim and this one did not. The
