bowl contained nothing. Beside it was a folded scrap of paper.

MARRA.

That was the entire note.

I ate bread while looking at the bowl.

Then I looked at the door.

"No."

Nobody answered.

I finished eating.

The bowl was still there.

I carried it to Marra's.

This was how they got you.

The morning was cool enough that the leather on my right crutch did not
immediately grow damp under my palm. The soreness was better than
yesterday. Not gone. Better. The grip stayed where the cobbler had put
it, seam turned away from the tender place.

I passed the Guild street without looking toward it.

Mostly.

Hessa had not sent for me.

There was no reason to go in.

I had no paper.

I had no glass.

I had no permission.

A cart wheel rolled away from a boy in the street and struck a wall.

Away.

I kept walking.

Marra's green door was open.

Marra was kneeling beside a low stool with three skirts hanging from
pegs behind her. Jessa stood on the stool in her shift while another
woman pinned a dark hem around her.

I held up the bowl.

Marra looked at it.

"Good."

"Is that all?"

"Yes."

Jessa looked down at me.

"Your button?"

"Repaired."

"Show me."

"No."

"Then why did I tell Lyssa?"

"So she could repair it."

Jessa seemed dissatisfied by the successful completion of her own
instruction.

I put the bowl on a shelf.

Marra said, "If you see Lyssa, tell her west after second bell."

I stared at her.

Marra smiled.

"No."

"Why?"

"I came here to return a bowl."

"And now you know something."

"I refuse."

"Fine."

Jessa said, "Tell her west after second bell."

I left.

I had become a message with crutches again.

The hall did not want me until afternoon.

This left me with time.

I bought an onion.

I stood beside a fruit stall and considered buying an apple, decided
against it, then bought one because I had already spent too long
considering it.

I sat on a low wall near the lower market.

Nobody needed me.

A man repaired a basket across the street. Two women argued about fish.
A dog slept under a cart until somebody moved the cart, at which point
the dog moved three feet and went back to sleep.

I ate the apple.

Nobody handed me a rope.

Nobody shouted my name.

Nobody asked which tube was narrow.

It was peaceful.

I lasted perhaps fifteen minutes.

Then I went to the hall early.

Rinna was at the front table counting small coins into stacks.

She looked up.

"Afternoon."

"It is almost afternoon."

"It isn't."

"I can leave."

"Don't."

I leaned my crutches against the table.

"Role?"

"No."

I waited.

Rinna kept counting.

"That's all?"

"Unless something goes wrong."

I considered this.

"That sounds like a role."

"It isn't."

"It sounds like one."

"Carry the wall."

There was a wall.

Of course there was.

It was a narrow painted flat with a window on it, leaning against the
left side of the stage. Pell had one end.

I took the other.

"Where?"

"Rear."

"Today?"

Pell looked at me.

"Why do you keep saying that?"

"Experience."

We carried it rear.

The painted window showed a strip of dark blue sky and one pale square
that might have been another building. Up close, the paint was streaked
and the square looked crooked.

"Which piece?"

"The Miller's Son."

"I've seen that."

"Good."

"Is it still the same?"

Pell stopped.

"What?"

"Today."

He stared at me.

Then he laughed hard enough that the wall shook.

"Don't."

We set it down.

Nessa was at a worktable with a small lamp opened in front of her.

Not the blue lamp.

This one had a brass frame, cloudy glass, and a thin prepared strip set
into the base. The strip was dark at one end.

I knew enough to stop two steps away.

"It isn't lighting," Hara said.

She stood beside Nessa with one sleeve rolled up and a smear of paint on
her wrist.

"Did you change the oil?" Nessa asked.

"Yes."

"Wick?"

"Yes."

"Catch?"

"Twice."

Nessa touched the wooden side of the lamp, not the prepared strip.

"Who moved it?"

Hara pointed at Pell.

Pell pointed at me.

"I just arrived."

"Then not Greg," Nessa said.

This was the nicest thing anyone had said to me all day.

I leaned closer.

"Can I help?"

"No."

"Good."

Nessa looked at me.

"Get Sava."

"Who is Sava?"

"Rear yard. Gray apron."

I went.

Sava was a broad woman with a shaved strip above one ear and both hands
blackened with lamp soot. I had seen her before without knowing her
name.

"Nessa wants you."

"Why?"

"Lamp."

"Which?"

"Brass. Cloudy glass. Prepared strip dark on one end."

She wiped her hands on the gray apron.

"Good."

That was apparently enough.

I brought the right person.

This felt suspiciously mature.

Sava looked at the lamp, swore once, and asked for a narrow blade.

I left before anyone could mistake my presence for competence.

Jori found me near the curtain.

"Tonight you're rear."

"Rear what?"

"Rear."

"That's not a job."

"It is now."

He handed me a small wooden block.

I looked at it.

"What does this do?"

"Door."

"Which door?"

"The Miller's Son."

I looked toward the painted wall.

"The fake one?"

"The real fake one."

"Good."

Jori pointed behind the rear hanging.

There was a short board on the floor, another upright board, and a metal
latch fixed to nothing I could see.

Pell came through carrying a bucket.

"He's crowd."

Jori said, "You're crowd."

"I thought I was rear."

"Same place."

"How many jobs are in rear?"

"All the ones the audience shouldn't see."

That seemed excessive.

The Miller's Son had a scene I remembered badly. A young miller owed
grain to three men, money to two women, and an apology to his mother.
Near the end, people gathered outside his house while he tried to
convince Veya, playing his sister, that leaving through the window was
reasonable.

Apparently the people outside were mostly Pell.

"How many?" I asked.

"Seven," Pell said.

"How many people?"

"Two."

"Who's the other?"

"You."

I looked at Jori.

He was already reading his cue page.

Pell showed me the arrangement.

The rear side of the stage had two strips of flooring. One was bare
board. One had an old woven runner nailed down. There was a hanging door
panel that the audience saw from the other side. Beside it, a loose
shutter rested against the wall. A tin cup sat on a shelf.

Pell pointed.

"Three steps on board. Stop. Knock."

"Me?"

"You."

"Then what?"

"Move to runner. Different voice."

"What voice?"

"Not yours."

"I have several voices."

"No."

"You haven't heard them."

"I have."

That was probably true.

Pell crossed the boards with heavy steps.

He knocked twice.

Then he moved behind the hanging, changed the angle of his body, and
called, "Open up, Len!"

It sounded like one man.

He stepped onto the runner, softened his feet, leaned toward the
opposite side of the hanging, and said in a higher, irritated voice, "We
know you're in there."

Different man.

Not completely.

Enough.

Then he rattled the loose shutter while striking the wall once with his
heel.

From where I stood, it was obviously Pell making noise.

Jori said, "Greg, board."

I crossed three steps.

"Too even."

"I'm walking."

"You're counting."

"I was told three."

"Don't sound like three."

I tried again.

Apparently I had been walking like a man demonstrating the concept of
footsteps.

Pell shook his head.

"Angry."

I walked harder.

"Now you're a horse."

"Pick a species."

"Person."

I did it again.

Better.

"Knock," Jori said.

I knocked.

Veya, onstage beyond the hanging, turned toward the door.

I watched her.

"Greg."

I knocked again.

Jori looked at me.

"What?"

"Late."

"She looked at the door."

"That was your warning."

"I thought that was the cue."

"No. She looks. Then Sellen says the line. Then knock."

Pell said, "Not when they look. After."

"I understand."

"Good."

"Today?"

Pell started laughing again.

We reset.

Veya looked toward the door.

Sellen said, "Nobody knows I'm here."

Jori lifted two fingers.

I knocked.

Veya flinched.

The knock sounded better because she flinched.

That was annoying.

Pell immediately crossed behind me, gave two heavy steps from farther
left, and called, "Miller!"

Then I moved to the runner.

"Open up," I said in a low voice.

Pell stopped.

"No."

"What?"

"Never that voice."

"It was different."

"It was a dying cow."

"I don't know what cows sound like here."

"The same."

Jori said, "Use your voice. Turn away."

"That isn't a different person."

"Audience can't see you."

I turned my head toward the rear wall.

"Open up."

It sounded different.

Not much.

Enough.

Pell nodded.

"Better cow."

We continued.

He rattled the shutter.

I struck the wooden block against the upright board once.

Veya crossed away from the door.

Sellen looked at the window.

The two of them made the room feel crowded before we made another sound.

I noticed that.

Then Jori snapped his fingers at me because I had missed my next step.

"Work."

"Yes."

The lamp problem took longer.

Sava had the prepared strip out on a cloth. Nessa held the lamp body.
Hara stood nearby, increasingly impatient.

"Can it run tonight?" Hara asked.

"Not like this," Sava said.

"What does that mean?"

"It means no."

"What if we use the other catch?"

"No."

"What if we use the blue lamp?"

Nessa said, "Wrong light."

I had an idea.

This was dangerous.

I kept it.

Then Nessa looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Good."

Sava asked me to fetch a plain taper lamp from the upper shelf.

I knew where that was.

I brought it.

Nessa set it behind a thin cream screen, moved it twice, and looked from
the house.

"Closer."

Hara moved it.

"Too close."

They moved it again.

The broken prepared lamp stayed on the worktable.

The ordinary taper became the replacement.

I did not know exactly what the prepared one had been meant to do.

Nobody explained.

The show was going to happen anyway.

At the front, a woman asked me whether The Red Door was on tonight.

"No."

"What is?"

"The Miller's Son, The Widow's Room, and something short after."

"What's short?"

"I don't know."

She looked at me as though I worked there.

This was unreasonable.

"Is it funny?"

"Probably."

Rinna, behind the table, said, "Yes."

I looked at her.

She said, "Sell the seat."

I looked back at the woman.

"Yes."

She bought two.

I was learning commerce.

Poorly.

Before the house opened, I remembered Marra.

I had not seen Lyssa.

I found a scrap of paper.

WEST AFTER SECOND BELL.

I wrote LYSSA above it.

Then I realized I had no reliable way to get it to her.

I put it in my pocket.

This was not useful.

The house filled enough that I stopped thinking about it.

I worked the aisle first.

A man wanted to move three seats because his wife could not see around a
tall hat.

The woman wearing the tall hat objected to being described as a hat.

I moved the man and his wife instead.

A boy dropped a wooden animal under a bench.

I retrieved it.

An older woman asked whether the hall was always this warm.

"Only when people come."

She stared at me.

I decided I should not work the house.

Then Jori called from the side.

"Rear."

Better.

The first piece did not need me.

I stood behind the hanging and listened.

Audience laughter came through cloth differently. Softer. Less like
people and more like weather.

Pell was repairing a strap beside me.

"Paper," he whispered.

"No."

"Didn't ask."

"You were going to."

"I was going to ask if you had paper."

"Why?"

He held up the strap.

"Need a shim."

I gave him a folded scrap from the prop shelf.

He tore it.

"Thanks."

That was the entire magic conversation.

The Miller's Son began.

I took my place.

The painted window was six feet from me and looked terrible.

From the house it had looked like night.

The replacement taper behind the cream screen made a pale square across
one side of the set. It was not the same as the prepared lamp. I could
tell because Hara had complained twice.

The audience did not know what had been planned.

The scene moved.

Veya and Sellen argued.

The miller lied.

His sister did not believe him.

Offstage, Pell held up one finger.

Not yet.

Veya looked toward the door.

Sellen said, "Nobody knows I'm here."

Jori's hand lifted.

I crossed three hard steps.

Not counting.

I knocked.

Veya flinched.

A murmur went through the house.

Pell moved left.

"Miller!"

I moved onto the runner and turned away.

"Open up."

Different enough.

Pell struck the shutter.

I hit the upright with the block.

Someone in the audience laughed.

Onstage, Sellen backed toward the painted window.

Veya caught his sleeve.

"No."

"They're at the door."

"There are six of them."

There were two of us.

Pell made another voice from farther right.

I moved behind the hanging and stamped once on bare board.

Veya turned toward that sound before I made it.

For half a second, I felt late.

Then I remembered.

After.

I waited.

Her head turned.

Sellen said, "The back."

I struck the wall.

The audience's attention shifted.

I could hear it.

Not a sound exactly.

A change.

Pell rattled the shutter.

The room outside the fake house filled with people who did not exist.

I nearly missed my last knock because I was listening to them.

Jori touched my sleeve.

I knocked.

The scene continued.

When it ended, Pell grinned.

"You were four."

"Four what?"

"People."

"I was at least five."

"No."

"Why?"

"Bad cow only counts half."

"I didn't use the cow."

"It remains."

We reset the block.

No one in the audience had seen me.

I had enjoyed that more than I expected.

The Widow's Room used the painted doorway but not the blue lamp. The
ordinary taper replacement stayed in Miller's Son storage.

The short final piece turned out to be Hara and Evin arguing over a
missing shoe.

It was funny.

I had no role.

I watched from the side until Nessa handed me a basket and said,
"Costumes."

I carried it.

Afterward, the hall became itself again.

People stood.

Benches scraped.

Coins clicked at the front.

Pell carried the short tube toward the wrong upper shelf.

I pointed.

"Other."

He changed direction without arguing.

That was disturbing.

Sava had wrapped the bad prepared strip separately and written something
on the cloth.

I did not ask what.

Hara was already complaining about tomorrow.

Jori rolled his cue page.

Veya took off one shoe and walked around in the other.

Teren was nowhere I could see.

Rinna paid me one copper.

I looked at it.

"Rear?"

"House and rear."

"I was four people."

"Then split it with them."

I closed my hand.

"One is fine."

"Good."

She reached under the table.

"For you."

It was a folded note.

My name was on the outside in Hessa's writing.

I opened it.

DAY AFTER TOMORROW.

AFTER MIDDAY.

AWAY FIRST.

Below that, smaller:

SAME RESTRICTIONS.

I read it again.

Rinna said, "Paper?"

"Day after tomorrow."

"Good."

"Why is that good?"

"You can work tomorrow."

I looked at her.

She had already turned away.

Of course.

Outside, it was fully dark.

I had forgotten Marra's message.

I remembered it halfway home.

Second bell had been hours ago.

I stopped in the street.

"Excellent."

A man passing me said, "What?"

"Nothing."

Lyssa was home.

I knew before opening the door because light showed at the bottom and I
could hear her moving something inside.

She was sitting on the floor with a basket between her knees.

Her ankle was wrapped again.

I held up one finger.

She said, "No."

"I haven't said anything."

"You were going to."

"Marra said west after second bell."

Lyssa stopped.

"When?"

"This morning."

She stared at me.

"I remembered."

"When?"

"Now."

"Greg."

"I wrote it down."

"Where?"

I pulled the paper from my pocket.

She took it.

"Very useful."

"I had work."

"So did I."

"Did you need the message?"

"No. Jessa found me."

"Good."

"At third bell."

"Less good."

Lyssa put the paper in the basket.

"What did you do?"

"I was four people outside a door."

She looked at me.

"How many were you?"

"One."

"That sounds dishonest."

"It was theatre."

"Same thing."

"Not according to Teren."

"Who were the other three?"

"Pell."

"All three?"

"Some of him."

She nodded as though this clarified it.

I showed her Hessa's note.

"Paper?"

"Day after tomorrow."

"Away?"

"First."

"Then what?"

"I don't know."

"Good."

"You say that too much."

Lyssa returned the note.

"What did they pay you for being four people?"

"One copper."

"Did the other three get paid?"

"I hope not."

We ate bread, onion, and the last piece of cheese.

My coat smelled faintly of dust and lamp oil even though I had not
touched the bad lamp.

There was black on the side of my hand from the wooden block.

My right palm still hurt.

Lyssa's ankle still hurt.

Tomorrow the hall wanted me.

Day after tomorrow Hessa wanted me.

Somewhere in between, Marra would probably want a bowl carried again.

I put Hessa's note under the cup.

DAY AFTER TOMORROW.

AFTER MIDDAY.

AWAY FIRST.

SAME RESTRICTIONS.

Nothing on the table moved.

At the theatre, two men had become a crowd.

At home, one onion remained one onion.

I did not ask it to go anywhere.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 189

## THE SHADOW

Lyssa was wrapping her ankle when I woke.

Not because it was worse.

I knew this because she told me before I asked.

"It's better."

"I didn't say anything."

"You looked."

"I have eyes."

"So do I."

She pulled the cloth snug, tied it, stood, and put most of her weight on
the foot before I could object.

I looked again.

She pointed at my crutches.

This argument had developed rules.

I ate bread.

Lyssa drank water and sorted three folded pieces of cloth into a basket.
None were yellow or green. I did not ask whose they were.

This was growth.

She put the basket beside the door.

"If Marra tells you anything today, don't bring it home after dark."

"I wrote it down."

"That wasn't the problem."

"I was working."

"So was Jessa. She still found me."

"Jessa has two legs."

Lyssa stared at me.

"That's what you're using?"

"No."

"Good."

I tore another piece of bread and wrapped it in cloth with half an onion
and a little salt.

Lyssa watched.

"Food?"

"The rolls are gone."

"You knew they would be."

"I knew the agreement ended. I didn't know that meant the food would end
emotionally."

"That's usually what ending means."

I put the food in my bag.

The Hessa note was still under the cup.

DAY AFTER TOMORROW.

AFTER MIDDAY.

AWAY FIRST.

SAME RESTRICTIONS.

Except it was not day after tomorrow anymore.

It was tomorrow.

I knew this without touching the paper.

I left it there.

Nothing moved.

Outside, Carrow was already noisy.

A wagon blocked half the street near the cooper. Someone had dropped a
basket of pale roots, and three people were collecting them while a
fourth argued that they were doing it wrong. A boy ran past me with a
long strip of red cloth tied around his shoulders.

I did not think about direction.

I thought the cloth was going to catch on something.

It did.

He stopped hard enough to nearly sit down.

I kept walking.

East Market Hall had both front doors open.

That usually meant work or smoke.

Today it was work.

Nessa was onstage with a coil of cord around one arm. Jori stood in the
house staring upward. Pell was behind a painted wall with his feet
sticking out. Rinna had a chalk board propped on the ticket table.

My name was on it.

Not large.

Not important.

Still there.

GREG: PORTER / REAR.

I read it twice.

Rinna said, "You can read."

"I like confirmation."

"Then confirm the rear window is still on the rear rack."

"Today?"

She looked at me.

"Yes."

I went.

The rear window was not on the rear rack.

This pleased me more than it should have.

I came back.

"It isn't."

Rinna stopped writing.

"Where is it?"

"I don't know."

"Less useful."

"But correct."

"Find it."

I found it behind the left hanging, where Pell had moved it because the
rear rack was needed for two wall flats.

"I moved it," Pell said from under the wall.

"I know."

"How?"

"You move everything."

"Not everything."

"Where's the bad stool?"

"Which?"

I pointed at him.

"Exactly."

He slid farther under the wall.

I carried the window back toward the stage.

It was not really a window.

It was a wooden frame with stretched pale cloth, painted around the
edges to suggest stone. From the front it could be a high window in a
house, a low window in a tower, or possibly a very disappointing
painting depending on what they put around it.

Nessa saw me.

"Not there."

"I was told rear rack."

"Later."

"Where now?"

"Stage left."

"Today?"

"Greg."

"Yes."

I put it stage left.

Teren came through the side door carrying a bundle of pages and a heel
of bread in his mouth.

He pulled the bread out.

"You're Porter."

"I saw."

"Six lines."

"How many things do I carry?"

"One."

"That seems low."

"You complain about carrying things."

"I complain about unpaid carrying."

"Good. This is paid."

He handed me a page.

The piece was called The Borrowed House.

I had not seen it.

My role was a porter delivering a small chest to the wrong house.

This caused a woman to believe her husband had bought jewelry, the
husband to believe the woman had bought poison, and a neighbor to
believe both of them were leaving town.

My six lines were not difficult.

"I was told this house."

"By whom?"

"A man."

"What man?"

"The one who told me this house."

I liked the Porter.

He was an idiot with procedural integrity.

Teren pointed at the right entrance.

"Second piece."

"Which side?"

"Right."

"Today?"

Teren chewed.

"Keep doing that."

I narrowed my eyes.

He walked away.

I rehearsed the lines while carrying the window again because Nessa had
changed her mind.

Or, more accurately, because I had misunderstood "stage left" as its
final location instead of where she wanted it while she measured
something.

She did not explain this distinction.

She just said, "Back."

I carried it back.

Then she gave me a coat on a stick.

I looked at it.

It was an old black coat tied across a short wooden crosspiece. Above
the shoulders, another piece of wood rose into a battered round hat.
There was no head.

One sleeve had been stuffed lightly with cloth. The other hung empty.

I looked at Nessa.

"No."

"What?"

"Whatever this is."

"Man."

I looked at the coat.

"No."

"Tonight."

I looked again.

"That's a man tonight?"

"Window."

She pointed.

The pale-cloth window was now upright behind part of the set for The
Borrowed House.

I understood less.

Pell emerged from behind the wall and took the coat-stick from me.

"He's too close."

"I haven't done anything."

"Not you."

He carried the coat behind the window.

Nessa had placed a plain lamp several feet farther back.

Pell stood between lamp and cloth.

A dark shape appeared on the pale window.

From where I stood beside it, the shape was obviously a coat hanging on
wood.

Nessa walked into the house.

"Back."

Pell stepped backward.

The shape softened.

"More."

He stepped again.

The shoulders changed.

The hat stopped looking like a hat balanced on a stick and became the
top of a head I could not see.

Nessa said, "Lower."

Pell lowered it.

"Stop."

I moved into the house beside her.

There was a man behind the window.

Not a good man.

Not a detailed man.

A man.

I went back.

Coat.

House.

Man.

Back.

Coat.

I did this three times.

Pell said, "Are you broken?"

"Maybe."

Nessa said, "Greg holds it tonight."

"Why?"

"Pell changes coat."

Pell pointed at himself.

"In the scene."

"You are in this?"

"I'm the neighbor."

I looked at the coat.

"Who is he?"

"No one."

"Then why is he there?"

Nessa said, "Because Veya sees him."

That was apparently the entire explanation.

The scene had the husband and wife arguing near the end. Veya, playing
the wife, looked up toward the window and saw someone outside. The
husband turned. The shadow moved away.

That was it.

Four seconds.

Maybe five.

I took the stick.

It was not heavy.

It was awkward.

I could not stand behind the cloth safely while holding it with both
hands because I needed one hand for a crutch. Nessa looked at me, looked
at the space, and dragged a low stool into position.

"Sit."

"I can stand."

"Sit."

I sat.

My crutches went against the rear wall.

With both feet placed badly, I shifted.

Nessa pointed at my good foot.

"Flat."

I put it flat.

The coat-stick rested lightly against the floor beside my knee.

This was much easier.

"Up," Nessa said.

I raised it.

The shadow appeared.

"Back."

I moved the stick backward.

"Not you."

I stopped.

"Move the bottom."

I angled the base away while keeping the shoulders roughly in place.

The shadow changed.

"Too much."

I corrected.

Pell stood in the house.

"Stick."

"What?"

"I can see the stick."

I looked at the shadow.

The lower vertical line showed beneath the coat.

"How do I hide it?"

"Lower coat."

"If I lower the coat, the man gets shorter."

Pell shrugged.

"Then shorter man."

I lowered it.

Nessa said, "Good."

Apparently we had sacrificed height for having legs that were not one
wooden pole.

We ran the scene.

I waited behind the window.

Veya and Hara argued onstage.

I could hear them clearly through the cloth.

Veya said, "Then why was it delivered here?"

Hara said, "Because the porter is an idiot."

I took this personally.

That was not my cue.

I waited.

Veya crossed.

She looked toward the window.

I raised the coat.

Too early.

Her eyes had not landed yet.

The shadow was already standing there when she found it.

Nessa said, "Down."

I lowered it.

Veya stopped.

"Again."

We reset.

"What's the cue?" I asked.

Nessa said, "Her."

"She looked."

"Not enough."

This was becoming familiar.

Veya heard us.

She said, "I turn. I see it. Then you give it to me."

"That's three things."

"Yes."

"Which one?"

"The seeing."

"How do I know when you see something that isn't there?"

Veya smiled.

"You'll know."

I disliked actors.

We ran again.

Veya turned.

Nothing.

Her eyes rose.

Nothing.

Then her body stopped.

Not much.

Just enough.

I lifted the coat.

The shadow appeared in the place she was already looking.

"Oh," I said.

Nessa said, "Don't."

"What?"

"Talk."

"During rehearsal?"

"Practice."

We did it again.

I got the timing right.

Then I moved the shadow away.

Smoothly.

Too smoothly.

Pell, watching from the house, said, "Board."

"What?"

"It slides."

"It is on a stick."

"Man doesn't know that."

"How does a man leave?"

Pell stood and took three steps sideways.

His shoulders moved a little. His height changed a little. His head
shifted.

"Walk it."

I tried.

The coat bounced like a drunk scarecrow.

Pell covered his face.

"Less man."

"You said walk."

"Not a parade."

Again.

Small rise.

Small settle.

Pause.

Then out.

From the house, it was enough.

Not good.

Enough.

I had a role to rehearse too.

The chest was real wood and mostly empty. I carried it onstage with one
hand while using a crutch in the other.

Teren stopped me.

"No."

"What?"

"You're working too hard."

"I'm carrying a chest."

"Porter does this every day."

"He has two legs."

"So?"

I stared at him.

Teren pointed toward the entrance.

"Use both hands. Sellen brings it to the mark."

Sellen was playing a servant in the first scene. He could carry the
chest to just inside the wing before my entrance. I could brace, put
both hands on it, and take the last four steps without a crutch.

I tried.

It worked.

Not elegantly.

Better.

My first line came while I was still holding the chest.

"I was told this house."

Veya said, "By whom?"

"A man."

"What man?"

"The one who told me this house."

She stared at me.

I stared back.

Someone behind the set laughed.

Teren said, "Don't wait for it."

"I wasn't."

"You were."

"I was breathing."

"Faster breathing."

The next run was cleaner.

At midday, I ate my bread and onion sitting on the rear step.

Pell sat beside me with nothing.

I looked at him.

He looked at my bread.

"No."

"I didn't ask."

"You were going to."

"I was going to ask what kind."

"Bread."

"What kind?"

"Mine."

He sighed.

"Rolls were better."

"Paid work ended."

"We're still working."

"Different problem."

He looked offended.

I had been waiting to use that.

The afternoon disappeared into small work.

A buckle broke.

Not mine.

A paint pot spilled.

Also not mine.

Jori could not find a cue page because he was holding it.

Hara changed stockings twice.

Sava came in, collected the wrapped prepared strip from yesterday, and
left with it. Nobody asked me to help.

The plain taper remained in use.

The audience began arriving before sunset.

I worked the front for ten minutes, then Teren called me to dress.

Porter had a brown coat with a patched elbow and a cap that smelled like
someone else's hair.

I put it on.

The first piece went without me.

Then The Borrowed House began.

I waited right.

Sellen brought the chest to the mark.

He said, "Yours."

"Today?"

He looked at me.

"Forever."

"That seems unlikely."

My entrance came.

I set the crutch aside where it would not fall, braced, took the chest
with both hands, and walked the four steps.

The audience saw a porter carrying a chest.

They did not see Sellen move it most of the distance.

"I was told this house."

Veya looked at the chest.

"By whom?"

"A man."

"What man?"

"The one who told me this house."

A laugh.

Not huge.

Enough.

I liked it.

The husband entered.

The misunderstanding grew.

I had three more lines, one of which was simply, "I don't know."

That got the best laugh.

I left.

Sellen handed me my crutch.

"Good."

"Which part?"

"You left."

I hated actors.

I stripped the cap off and went rear.

Pell was already changing into the neighbor's coat.

The fake man waited against the wall.

Coat.

Stick.

Hat.

Nothing else.

I sat on the stool.

Crutches against wall.

Good foot flat.

The lamp was lit.

The pale window glowed.

Onstage, Veya and Hara argued about the chest.

The audience laughed.

I held the stick loosely.

Not yet.

Veya crossed.

Not yet.

She turned.

Not yet.

Her eyes rose.

Then she saw him.

I lifted.

Someone in the audience stopped laughing.

A small sound came from the front.

Not quite a gasp.

Close.

Hara turned toward the window.

The shadow stood there.

A man.

I knew there was no man.

I could see the stuffed sleeve hanging six inches from my hand.

Veya stepped backward.

"Who's that?"

I moved the bottom of the stick.

Too much.

The shadow leaned strangely.

I corrected before it became obvious.

Then I walked it away.

Small rise.

Settle.

Pause.

Out.

The audience made another sound.

Gone.

I lowered the coat.

My shoulder immediately complained.

Four seconds.

Maybe five.

Pell came behind the hanging in his neighbor's coat.

"Did it work?"

"Yes."

"Good."

"How do you know?"

"They shut up."

Then he went onstage.

I stayed behind the window and grinned at a coat.

Jori appeared.

"Why are you smiling?"

"Man."

He looked at the coat.

"That's not a man."

"Tonight."

Jori looked toward the stage.

"Fair."

Then he handed me a rope.

"Hold."

I held it.

The rest of the show did not care that I had just been a Porter and a
man who did not exist.

There was a missed entrance in the final piece.

Not mine.

A cup rolled off a table and did not break.

Veya forgot a glove and used the wrong hand for an entire scene.

Nobody died.

The audience laughed.

Afterward, I carried benches.

The fake man came apart.

Hat onto shelf.

Coat into basket.

Crosspiece against wall.

The man disappeared faster than the audience.

Nessa checked the pale cloth for soot.

Pell complained about food again.

Rinna counted money.

She paid me one copper.

"Porter and rear."

"I was also a man."

"One copper."

"I was two visible people."

"One of them was a coat."

"The audience disagreed."

"Ask them for money."

I took the copper.

Tomorrow was Hessa.

The thought arrived without warning.

Not day after tomorrow.

Tomorrow.

Away first.

I looked at the fake man's crosspiece leaning against the wall.

Then at my hand.

Then stopped.

That was not paper.

That was not the apparatus.

That was not anything.

I put the copper in my pocket.

On the walk home, my shoulder hurt more than my palm.

The right grip still did not twist.

Worth one copper.

Possibly the best financial decision I had made in Carrow.

Lyssa was home before me.

Her ankle was unwrapped.

She was standing at the table cutting thread.

I looked down.

She did not look up.

"It's better."

"I didn't say anything."

"You looked."

"You're developing magic."

"Mine works."

I sat.

She glanced at my coat.

"How was theatre?"

"I delivered a chest to the wrong house."

"On purpose?"

"Professionally."

"Good."

"Then I was a man in a window."

Lyssa stopped cutting.

"Were you?"

"No."

She waited.

"It was a coat."

"That sounds less impressive."

"Audience thought it was a man."

"Did you wear the coat?"

"No."

"Was anyone wearing the coat?"

"No."

She looked at me.

"So you were a coat."

"I was operating a man."

"That's worse."

"It worked."

"Did they pay the man?"

"One copper."

"Good for him."

I put the coin on the table.

She slid it back toward me.

"Yours."

"Hessa tomorrow."

"That's not money."

"No."

She looked toward the cup.

The note was still underneath.

I pulled it out.

DAY AFTER TOMORROW.

AFTER MIDDAY.

AWAY FIRST.

SAME RESTRICTIONS.

The first line was wrong now.

I found charcoal and crossed out DAY AFTER TOMORROW.

I wrote TOMORROW above it.

Lyssa watched.

"Scientific."

"Very."

"Does Hessa know you changed her note?"

"No."

"Good."

I put it back under the cup.

Tomorrow, Hessa would put paper under glass and ask whether away was
easier.

Tonight there was a wooden crosspiece against a theatre wall that had
been a man for five seconds because a lamp, a coat, Veya's eyes, and my
hand had agreed to lie at the same time.

I did not write that down.

My shoulder hurt.

Lyssa's ankle was better.

There was bread for morning.

That was enough work for one day.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 190

## THE MEASURE

Lyssa was gone before I finished changing Hessa's note.

Not because she had written it wrong.

Because time kept attacking the accuracy.

TOMORROW.

AFTER MIDDAY.

AWAY FIRST.

SAME RESTRICTIONS.

I crossed out TOMORROW and wrote TODAY.

The paper now had three different versions of the first line on it.

This seemed scientifically important.

Lyssa had seen me doing it while tying her shoe.

"Your science keeps changing."

"The science is fine. The calendar is unstable."

"That's worse."

Her ankle was unwrapped. She still favored it for the first few steps,
then less once she had moved around. I noticed without saying anything.

She noticed me noticing without saying anything.

We were improving.

She left with a cloth bag over one shoulder and told me she would
probably be late.

"Where?"

"Out."

"Excellent detail."

"You'll survive."

She kissed my cheek and left.

I ate bread.

The note stayed under the cup.

Nothing moved.

Today it would.

Maybe.

That word had become expensive.

I got to East Market Hall early enough to be useful and late enough that
Rinna did not accuse me of arriving yesterday.

The chalk board had changed.

GREG: SET / FRONT UNTIL MIDDAY.

No role.

I looked at Rinna.

"Paper," she said.

"Today."

"After midday?"

"Yes."

"Then you're mine until food."

This was apparently how scheduling worked when two institutions wanted
pieces of me.

Nessa had the pale window down on the floor. The man from last night was
no longer a man. His coat was in a basket. His hat was on a shelf. The
wooden crosspiece had been tied into a bundle with three other pieces of
scrap wood.

I looked at it once.

Then Nessa handed me a bucket.

"Water."

I got water.

The morning was mostly walls.

One wall went up.

Another came down.

A narrow painted arch had to move from rear storage to the right side
without scraping the fresh edge. Pell and I carried it together.

"Your end up," he said.

"My end is up."

"More up."

"Then yours is down."

"Correct."

We reached the turn.

The arch did not.

We backed out.

"Other way," Pell said.

"You said this way."

"I was wrong."

"That was easy."

"I practice."

We turned the arch and tried again.

It fit.

Jori had me check three stool positions for the afternoon bill, then
changed one after I checked it. I asked whether he wanted me to check
again.

"No."

"How will we know?"

"I moved it."

"That has failed before."

He pointed at the front doors.

"Go sell something."

I worked the front until the smell of somebody's fried onions outside
became stronger than my loyalty.

A man asked whether The Borrowed House was playing again.

"Tomorrow."

"Is the porter the same?"

I paused.

"No."

He looked disappointed.

This was flattering for almost half a breath.

Then he said, "Good."

I sold him a seat anyway.

At midday Rinna pushed a copper-colored token across the ticket table.

"Food."

"What is this?"

"Marker. Bring it back."

"Why?"

"Because it is mine."

I looked at the token.

"Does it buy food?"

"No."

"Then this is a terrible food system."

"It means I know you left."

"Why do you need to know I left?"

"So I know you're gone."

I took the marker.

"Very advanced."

She ignored me.

I ate bread and a small piece of cheese in the lower market, returned
the marker, collected my crutches from behind the ticket table, and left
for the Guild.

Rinna called after me.

"Greg."

I turned.

"Paper."

"Yes."

"Don't be late tomorrow because paper happened."

"I don't know what paper is going to do."

"Neither do I. That's why I'm telling you now."

This was unreasonable and probably useful.

The Guild front clerk saw me and raised one finger before I spoke.

I stopped.

"I hate that."

"Wait."

"I haven't asked anything."

"Good."

I waited.

The front room smelled of dust, old wood, and something sharp from the
corridor to the left. A woman I had seen before was arguing with a clerk
over a bundle of prepared cord.

"I brought six."

"You brought five."

"I tied six."

"There are five."

"Then one is somewhere."

"Yes."

This did not appear to satisfy either of them.

The cracked prepared plate was not on the shelf where I had seen it
before. A chalk mark remained on the wood beneath the empty space.

The note was gone too.

I did not ask.

A gray-coated woman came through carrying two narrow boxes.

"Paper Man."

"No."

She kept walking.

I had lost this fight permanently.

Hessa appeared from the opposite corridor with a folded board under one
arm and a cup in the other.

She looked at me.

"Shoulder?"

I blinked.

"Hello."

"Shoulder."

"Sore."

"Why?"

"I was a man."

She stopped.

"At the theatre."

"That did not improve it."

"I held a coat on a stick behind a window."

Hessa looked at me for a moment.

"Of course you did."

"It worked."

"Your shoulder?"

"The man worked."

"Sit."

This was becoming a theme in my life.

The room was not the same one as last time.

It was smaller and had one high window, two shelves of boxed pieces,
folded cloth, iron weights, and three empty wooden frames stacked
against the wall. The table was broad enough for the apparatus but left
little room around it.

Hessa set down the board.

"Today is not whether you can move paper."

"I can."

"Yes."

I enjoyed that.

She took a drink.

"Today is whether one requested direction produces the response more
reliably than another."

"Which way works."

"If you need to make it worse."

"I do."

"Which way works."

I liked Hessa.

She did not always deserve it.

The apparatus had changed.

The square board was gone. In its place was a long pale board marked
with a center line and three shallow positions. One nearest me. One
farther away. One crossing the center at right angles.

Hessa had paired guides for each position, target and control, with
enough space between them that the fins would not touch.

The glass shield was the same.

Or looked the same.

"Same glass?"

"Yes."

"Today?"

Hessa stared at me.

I smiled.

She checked the table legs, pressed two corners, then wedged the rear
left leg with a thin piece of wood.

"Chair."

I put it where I thought it belonged.

"Back."

I moved it.

"More."

I moved again.

"Stop."

My good foot sat flat. My other leg rested where it did not press the
table. The crutches went against the wall.

Hessa touched my shoulder lightly, then had me lift the arm.

"Pain?"

"Muscle."

"That was not the question."

"Yes. A little."

"Does it change if you hold here?"

I moved.

"Yes."

"Then don't."

She made a mark beside the chair leg.

"You're not bracing on the table."

"I know."

"You're tired."

"I'm always tired."

"Useful."

"How?"

"It means I don't have to ask."

She laid out the fins.

They were small, folded from pale paper, matched as closely as I could
tell. She made me inspect the bases.

Flat.

Edges similar.

No obvious crease differences.

Then she took six little wooden counters from a pouch.

Three had black marks.

Three did not.

"Order?" I asked.

"Mine."

"Why?"

"Because if you choose, you'll choose away."

"That's the point."

"The point is to compare it."

She closed the counters in her hand.

I disliked science again.

First came the draw.

I settled.

Breath.

The familiar inward gathering came slowly, then narrowed.

The same slight wrongness at the wrist edge.

Nothing new.

Nothing dramatic.

Hessa watched my hand.

"Hold."

I held.

"Release."

I released.

She made a mark.

"Twenty-six."

I knew.

I did not say it.

That felt like another kind of progress.

Then shaping without a target.

No paper under glass.

Just the familiar deliberate attempt to make the narrow gathered thing
become something more directed without letting it run away from me.

The wrist edge crowded first.

I wanted to correct harder.

"Don't chase."

I didn't.

The shape held for two breaths, rough but deliberate.

"Release."

I did.

"Twenty-two."

Then the paper came out.

Hessa placed the first pair in the straight guides.

Target assignment by counter.

Left.

She set the black-marked counter beside it.

"Requested direction?"

"Away."

"Say it once."

"Away."

The target fin sat between us and the far end of the board.

I drew.

Shaped.

This time the shape did feel different.

Not stronger.

Cleaner was too generous.

Less crowded, maybe.

Like there was one fewer thing in the way.

I held the idea of away.

The fin moved.

Barely.

A tiny forward slip, less than the width of my smallest fingernail.

The control did not visibly move.

I breathed out.

Hessa's finger rose.

I closed my mouth.

She inspected the glass.

Then the board.

Then the guide.

Then the fin.

She checked the wedge under the table.

"Movement."

"I know."

"Good."

"That sounded almost kind."

"It wasn't."

Attempt fourteen.

Movement.

Away.

The second pair went into the same guides.

New target assignment.

Right.

Hessa drew another counter.

"Toward."

I looked at her.

"You hate me."

"Toward."

I drew.

Shaped.

The feeling was not painful.

Not blocked.

Just worse.

Crowded sooner.

I tried to hold the requested direction without pushing harder.

Nothing moved.

I released.

Hessa inspected anyway.

Attempt fifteen.

No movement.

"Again?" I asked.

"Different."

She moved the guides to the cross position.

Now the target and control sat sideways relative to me.

New fins.

New counter.

Left target.

"Requested direction?"

"Away."

I frowned.

"The guide is sideways."

"Yes."

"So if it moves away, it leaves the guide."

"Possibly."

"That's rude."

"Shape."

I did.

The first breath felt messy.

The second settled.

Away.

The target twisted.

Not much.

Its front edge shifted out of the shallow guide and stopped.

The control stayed where it was.

I looked at Hessa.

Her finger was already up.

I had not even opened my mouth.

"I wasn't going to say anything."

"You were."

She inspected.

The fin had not traveled forward along the guide.

It had moved partly out of it, in the direction farther from me.

Hessa marked the page.

"Movement."

"Away."

"Observation."

"Away."

"Yes."

Attempt sixteen.

Movement.

Away.

Something warm moved through my chest that had nothing to do with mana.

Hessa replaced everything.

"Water."

"I'm fine."

"Water."

I drank.

She waited longer than I wanted.

The room had a high narrow window. Somewhere outside it, someone dropped
metal and swore. A cart rolled over stone. Two people passed the door
arguing about a frame number.

Hessa read something on another sheet while I sat there.

Her day continued even during mine.

"Ready?" she asked.

"Yes."

"Say that after you move your shoulder."

I moved it.

It hurt.

"Less yes."

"I can do another."

"I know."

She set the next pair.

Straight guides.

Target right.

"Requested direction?"

"Sideways. Left."

"That's not away."

"Correct."

I drew.

Shaped.

Tried to keep left.

The shape wanted to smear.

That was the only word I had for it.

I corrected once.

"Don't chase."

I stopped correcting.

The target gave a tiny tremble.

Or I thought it did.

Then one corner shifted.

Not left.

Slightly away.

Hessa leaned closer.

"Release."

I released.

She inspected.

"Movement?"

I asked.

"Maybe."

"Direction?"

"Not left."

"Away."

"Possibly."

She wrote longer this time.

Attempt seventeen.

Possible movement.

Requested sideways left.

Observed displacement too small for clean directional claim, with
possible away component.

I hated the sentence before she finished it.

"That's disgusting."

"It happened."

"Maybe."

"Yes."

"You enjoy this."

"No."

I did not believe her.

Attempt eighteen was toward.

Nothing moved.

Not the target.

Not the control.

The shape felt crowded almost immediately. My shoulder wanted to lift.
Hessa stopped me before I did.

"Release."

I did.

She checked the apparatus.

No movement.

Toward.

Failure.

I stared at the fin.

"I don't like toward."

"Noted."

"That was a joke."

"I know."

"You wrote it."

"I wrote that you reported increased difficulty maintaining the
requested shape."

"That is not what I said."

"It's what I heard."

I considered arguing.

She was right enough to be irritating.

"One more," she said.

"Only one?"

"Yes."

"Away?"

She showed me the counter after drawing it.

"Away."

The final pair went into the far position.

Still along the same line from me, but farther from the edge of the
table than the first away attempt.

I noticed.

"Distance."

"Not today."

"You changed it."

"I know."

"Then it matters."

"It may. Which is why I am recording it."

I wanted to ask three questions.

I asked none.

Draw.

Shape.

Away.

The first breath was bad.

The second was better.

The familiar wrist-edge asymmetry sat there, annoying and known.

I left it alone.

Away.

The target moved.

A tiny slip.

Then stopped.

Not farther than the first.

Maybe less.

Still visible.

Control unchanged.

My whole body wanted to lean toward it.

I did not.

Hessa raised no finger this time.

I stayed still anyway.

She looked at me.

"Good."

That was worse than the finger.

She inspected everything.

Attempt nineteen.

Movement.

Away.

Hessa sat.

I kept looking at the paper.

Three away requests.

Three movements.

Two toward requests.

No movements.

One sideways request.

Something too small and wrong-directed to call cleanly, maybe away.

I knew what I wanted to say.

Hessa knew too.

She started writing before I could.

"So away is easier."

"Probably."

I stopped.

That was not one of her usual words.

"What?"

"Probably."

"You said probably."

"I know."

"Write that."

"No."

"Why?"

"Because I'm writing what happened."

"What happened is probably."

"What happened is three requested-away trials produced visible target
movement today. Two requested-toward trials did not. The sideways trial
produced an ambiguous small displacement that did not follow the
requested sideways direction."

"And went away."

"Possibly."

"Mostly."

"Possibly."

I leaned back.

My shoulder objected.

Hessa pointed at it.

"Also that."

"That is theatre."

"That is your body."

"Different problem."

"Not while your body is part of the apparatus."

I hated when she did that.

She finished writing.

I tried to read upside down.

She turned the page.

AWAY RESPONSE REPEATED UNDER MULTIPLE TARGET POSITIONS.

TOWARD RESPONSE NOT OBSERVED TODAY.

DIRECTIONAL PREFERENCE RELATIVE TO GREG'S POSITION SUPPORTED.

NOT GENERALIZED.

I read it twice.

"Supported."

"Yes."

"Not possible."

"It remains possible in the larger sense."

"You changed the word."

"Because we have more evidence."

I looked at the fins again.

They were pathetic.

Tiny pale folded pieces under glass.

Nothing about them looked like an achievement.

"So away is easier."

Hessa rubbed ink from the side of one finger.

"That is currently the better explanation."

I smiled.

"Don't."

"I'm not doing anything."

"You are."

"Can I practice away?"

"No."

"That was fast."

"No independent draw. No independent shaping. No paper testing. No
coins. No thread. No trying larger objects. No trying to discover
whether every object in your room dislikes you."

"I wasn't going to."

"You were."

"I was going to think about it."

"You may think."

"Generous."

"Quietly."

I looked at the page again.

"Does this mean the wrist edge..."

"No."

"You let me get farther that time."

"No."

"Everything has a side."

"Everything has many sides if you describe it badly enough."

"That sounds familiar."

"It should."

She pulled a fresh sheet toward herself.

"Next question."

"How hard can I push?"

"No."

"How far?"

"Closer."

I waited.

She drew two short lines on the page.

One near.

One farther.

"Does distance from you change the response if the requested direction
remains away?"

I looked at the far line.

"You already moved the last pair farther."

"Yes."

"And it moved."

"Yes."

"So distance doesn't matter."

Hessa stared at me.

I sighed.

"Fine."

"Good."

"You're going to make me fail at two distances."

"I'm going to compare them."

"Same thing with better handwriting."

She wrote:

AWAY ONLY.

NEAR / FAR.

I pointed at it.

"When?"

"Not tomorrow."

"Of course."

"I have other work."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"People keep saying that."

She gathered the counters.

I looked at the record one more time.

"Twenty-six."

"Yes."

"Twenty-two."

"Yes."

"Nineteen."

"Yes."

"And away is probably easier."

Hessa paused.

"Supported as a directional preference in the current setup."

"Probably."

She gave me the cup.

"Leave."

I drank the last of the water first.

Then I left.

The gray-coated woman was in the front room.

She looked up.

"Paper Man."

"Away."

She frowned.

I kept walking.

This was a victory.

East Market Hall was still open when I returned.

I had not planned to go back.

My feet apparently had.

Rinna saw me.

"Paper?"

"Away."

Pell was carrying a basket behind her.

He immediately took one step backward.

"Working."

I hated him.

Rinna said, "Can you carry chairs?"

"Yes."

"Better."

I carried chairs.

Not with magic.

There were six.

Pell carried four at once and made a point of it.

I carried two.

At home, Lyssa had beaten me back.

She was sitting with one foot up on the other chair, ankle bare.

Better.

Actually better.

I put Hessa's new paper under the cup.

Lyssa watched me.

"Paper?"

"Yes."

"Did it move?"

"Three times."

Her eyebrows went up.

"Away."

"All three?"

"All three away attempts."

"Did the other ways move?"

"Toward didn't. Sideways did something stupid."

"Like you."

"Very much like me."

She held out her hand.

I gave her the sheet.

She read Hessa's wording.

"DIRECTIONAL PREFERENCE RELATIVE TO GREG'S POSITION SUPPORTED," she
said.

"See?"

"That sounds important."

"It sounds terrible."

"Does Hessa agree?"

I sat down.

"More than before."

Lyssa nodded once and gave the paper back.

That landed better than congratulations would have.

I put the sheet under the cup.

Beside it I put Hessa's next note.

AWAY ONLY.

NEAR / FAR.

Not tomorrow.

No date yet.

The room contained bread, a cup, two chairs, a table, thread, my copper,
Lyssa's basket, and several other things that could theoretically be
farther from me than they currently were.

They remained exactly where they were.

I was getting very good at magic.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 191

## THE WITNESS

Lyssa was gone before I woke properly.

There was bread on the table, half an apple beside it, and a strip of
paper under the cup.

Not Hessa's paper.

LYSSA: DON'T FORGET THEATRE BECAUSE PAPER HAPPENED.

I stared at it.

Rinna had said almost exactly the same thing.

This was either evidence of a conspiracy or evidence that I had become
predictable.

I ate the apple first because it seemed less judgmental.

Hessa's actual sheet remained under the cup.

AWAY ONLY.

NEAR / FAR.

No date.

Nothing I was allowed to do about it.

I left it there.

On the way to East Market Hall, a carter shouted at his boy to move a
sack away from the wheel.

The word caught.

I hated that.

The boy dragged the sack with both hands.

I kept walking.

East Market Hall had both front doors open and three different people
trying to occupy the same patch of floor.

A rolled hanging blocked half the entry. Two benches stood outside.
Someone had left a basket of costume shoes directly where nobody could
avoid it.

I stepped over the basket and looked at the chalk board.

KING: MAREK / HARA / SELLEN BORROWED HOUSE: VEYA / HARA / EVIN / PELL
THE LETTER BOX: VEYA / SELLEN / GREG / NESSA REAR: JORI / PELL FRONT:
RINNA

I read my name.

Then I read it again.

GREG: WITNESS.

No if.

No maybe.

No missing person.

No little mark beside it that meant somebody else had failed to arrive.

Rinna came past with a roll of tickets in one hand.

"You're on time."

"You threatened me."

"I scheduled you."

"Same thing."

She pointed at the board.

"I saw."

"Good."

"What is The Letter Box?"

"Piece you're in."

"Useful."

"Pages are on the table."

She kept moving.

That was it.

I stood there for another second.

Nessa put a folded green cloth into my hands.

"Right table."

I took it.

Theatre had apparently decided I had experienced enough emotion.

The Letter Box was a short domestic comedy about a locked wooden box
that belonged to nobody until everybody wanted it.

Veya played Mara, the woman whose dead aunt had left the box in her
room.

Sellen played Corren, her brother, who claimed the aunt had promised him
everything worth stealing.

Nessa played the landlady, who claimed anything left in the room after
rent was late belonged to the house.

I was a municipal witness.

My job was to stand there, record who said what, and repeatedly refuse
to decide anything.

I liked him immediately.

There were eighteen lines.

Not forty-three.

Not eight.

Eighteen.

Enough that I had to learn them. Not enough that I needed to reconsider
every decision that had brought me to Carrow.

The important object was not the box.

That was the first problem.

The important object was a little brown purse on the table beside it.

The purse contained the key.

The audience was not supposed to know that until late.

I knew because the page said so.

This became a problem almost immediately.

Teren arrived while I was reading.

He had bread in his mouth and two pins stuck through the cuff of his
shirt.

"You're Witness."

"I gathered."

"Know it?"

"I've seen part."

"Then see the rest."

He pulled one pin from his cuff and used it to point.

"Entrance after Nessa says, 'Then let the town hear it.' Left side. You
have ledger. You don't touch box."

"Today?"

He looked at me.

"Yes."

"Good."

"Keep doing that."

Then he walked away.

I looked after him.

That might have been praise.

I decided not to ruin it by checking.

Rehearsal started with a missing ledger.

The ledger was eventually found under the folded cloth I had moved to
the right table.

This was somehow not my fault.

The first run lasted less than a minute before Teren stopped us.

"Greg."

I had entered correctly.

I had my ledger.

I had said the first two lines correctly.

I looked at him.

"What?"

"Stop looking at the purse."

I looked at the purse.

Then I realized I had looked at the purse.

"I'm not."

Veya laughed.

Teren pointed at me.

"You just did it again."

"Because you said purse."

"Before that."

"I was looking at the table."

"At the purse."

"The purse is on the table."

Sellen said, "He's got you there."

Teren ignored him.

"Your Witness doesn't know the key is in it."

"I know."

"That's the problem."

"I am aware of what my character doesn't know."

"Your face isn't."

I looked at Veya.

She was standing close enough to the purse that her sleeve nearly
touched it.

She had not looked at it once.

I knew it was there.

Because I knew it mattered, I kept seeing how carefully she did not see
it.

This was deeply irritating.

Teren reset us.

"Again."

We went again.

Nessa entered as the landlady and demanded the box.

Sellen accused her of theft.

Veya accused Sellen of being cheap enough to steal from the dead.

Nessa said, "Then let the town hear it."

I entered with the ledger.

"I was told there was a dispute."

"There is," Veya said.

"There isn't," Sellen said.

Nessa pointed at both of them.

"There."

I opened the ledger.

"Good. A dispute."

Small laugh from Pell, who was not the audience and should have been
working.

I continued.

"Names."

They all spoke at once.

I looked down to write.

Then my eyes flicked to the purse.

Teren clapped once.

"Greg."

"Damn it."

"Again."

On the third run, I solved it by staring determinedly at the box.

Teren stopped us.

"Now the box is guilty."

"It is the subject of the dispute."

"You are making it look like it contains a body."

"What do you want me to look at?"

"The people."

This seemed unreasonable.

I tried the people.

Veya was much harder to accidentally reveal.

Sellen was impossible to make look unimportant, but that was his
problem.

We got through the scene.

At the reveal, Veya finally picked up the purse, opened it, and removed
the key.

The action felt larger because she had spent the previous part of the
scene treating the purse like cloth.

I noticed.

Then Teren said, "Greg, line."

I had missed it.

Of course.

"I object to the opening."

Sellen looked at me.

"You object now?"

"Municipally."

Pell laughed again.

Teren rubbed his face.

"That's not the line."

"I know."

"Then use the line."

"I had it."

"Find it."

The actual line was, "I have not witnessed consent to open the box."

Less funny.

Probably better.

We reset.

The hall kept working around us.

A shoe buckle snapped during the next run. Nessa left the scene, fixed
it while still wearing her landlady shawl, and came back before we
reached her next entrance.

Someone spilled a little red paint near the rear wall.

Pell stepped in it.

He spent the next ten minutes leaving half a red footprint everywhere
until Jori noticed and made him clean both the floor and his shoe.

Hara changed stockings because the first brown pair had a run at the
ankle.

Then she changed back because the second pair were apparently the wrong
brown.

I asked what wrong brown meant.

She told me to become older.

I did not ask again.

By midday I had most of the Witness in my mouth.

Not good.

Present.

There was a difference.

I ate bread outside with Pell and EvIn.

Pell had food today.

This disappointed me.

EvIn was reading the Porter pages from The Borrowed House while eating a
cold potato.

"You're Porter?" I asked.

"No."

"Who is?"

He pointed with the potato.

A young man I had seen carrying benches was practicing my old lines
beside the wall.

I watched him.

"I was told this house," he said.

"By whom?" EvIn called.

"A man."

"What man?"

"The one who told me this house."

Pell looked at me.

"Better."

"He hasn't performed it yet."

"Still."

The young man had less trouble with the chest because he had two good
legs and no need to arrange the final four steps around a crutch.

I resented this unfair advantage.

Rinna came outside.

"Greg."

"I am eating."

"After."

"Then why say my name now?"

"So you know after exists."

She went back in.

Pell nodded.

"Good system."

"I hate all systems."

"Paper."

"Don't."

He took another bite of bread.

That was the entire conversation.

After food, Rinna had me move two benches away from the front wall.

Away.

I noticed the word.

Then I moved the benches with my hands because I was not an idiot.

Mostly.

The afternoon rehearsal got better.

I stopped looking at the purse.

Then I started avoiding looking at the purse so aggressively that I
turned my body away from the table every time I crossed.

Veya stopped me.

"Now you hate the purse."

"I don't look at it."

"You move around it."

"I am not touching it."

"Exactly."

She took my place.

"Watch."

She entered.

She crossed the room.

She spoke to Sellen.

She put one hand on the table beside the purse.

She shifted the ledger.

She took the chair.

She never looked at the purse.

She also never avoided it.

It existed.

That was all.

She gave me my place back.

I tried again.

Better.

Not good.

Better.

Teren said, "Fine."

I took it.

Then I ruined something else.

During Sellen's long complaint about the dead aunt promising him the
box, I turned toward him too fully and blocked Veya from the house.

"Greg."

I moved.

"Other way."

I moved too far.

"You're not furniture."

"I have been furniture here."

"Not today."

"Today?"

Teren pointed at the floor mark.

I found it.

The next run worked.

No one applauded.

A cart outside lost a board with a crash loud enough that everyone in
the hall stopped.

Jori went to the front door.

"Not ours."

We continued.

By late afternoon, the floor had been swept twice and was dirty again.

The hall smelled of warm bodies, old paint, lamp oil, damp wool from
coats, and the onion someone backstage had cut without permission.

Rinna opened the house.

People came in.

The man who had asked about the Porter came back.

I saw him take a seat near the left aisle.

He saw me at the side curtain.

His expression changed.

I could not tell whether this was good.

I was in the Witness coat.

Gray-brown, plain, narrow collar.

The ledger was real enough to be heavy.

My shoes were mine.

Nessa had looked at my crutches, looked at the entrance, and moved my
waiting position half a pace closer to the wing without comment.

The Borrowed House played first.

I watched the new Porter from behind the side hanging.

He entered with the chest.

"I was told this house."

The audience laughed earlier than they had for me.

I disliked him.

"By whom?"

"A man."

"What man?"

"The one who told me this house."

Bigger laugh.

I hated him for approximately four seconds.

Then he missed the next line.

I liked him again.

The piece continued.

He recovered.

The audience man near the aisle laughed.

Good.

Fine.

Whatever.

Then came The Letter Box.

I stood left.

Ledger.

Crutches placed where I could reach them after exit.

The purse sat on the table.

I did not look at it.

I knew exactly where it was.

That was worse.

Nessa entered.

Sellen entered.

Veya entered.

The argument built.

The audience laughed when Sellen claimed the dead aunt had always loved
him best.

Veya said, "She called you a damp boot."

"Affectionately."

Bigger laugh.

Nessa stepped between them.

"Then let the town hear it."

My cue.

I entered.

No stumble.

No wrong side.

"I was told there was a dispute."

"There is," Veya said.

"There isn't," Sellen said.

Nessa pointed.

"There."

I opened the ledger.

"Good. A dispute."

The audience laughed.

Not huge.

Enough.

"Names."

They spoke over each other.

I looked at them.

Not the purse.

Sellen tried to hand me the box.

I stepped back.

"I have not witnessed transfer."

"I'm transferring it."

"I have witnessed an attempt."

"That's the same thing."

"It is written differently."

That got a laugh I had not expected.

I did not wait for it.

Teren had trained that out of me by violence.

Metaphorical violence.

Mostly.

The scene moved.

Veya crossed near the table.

Her hand passed within an inch of the purse.

Nothing.

It was just a purse.

Sellen accused Nessa of hiding the key.

Nessa accused him of swallowing it.

I wrote this down because the Witness wrote everything down.

Then Sellen said, "Ask her where she was when the aunt died."

Veya went still.

That was the turn.

The audience quieted.

I knew the purse was about to matter.

My eyes wanted it.

I kept them on Veya.

She looked at Sellen.

Then at Nessa.

Then down at the table as though the table had only just occurred to
her.

Her fingers touched the purse.

The audience followed.

There.

Now it mattered.

She opened it.

The key came out.

A small sound moved through the room.

Not a gasp.

Recognition.

Sellen said, "You had it."

Veya said, "I had her purse."

"With the key."

"I didn't know."

I had my line.

"I have not witnessed consent to open the box."

Sellen turned on me.

"You have witnessed the key."

"Yes."

"Then open it."

"No."

"Why?"

"I have no authority."

The audience laughed.

Sellen stared at me.

"What do you have?"

I looked at the ledger.

"Excellent notes."

That was scripted.

I wanted everyone to know.

The laugh was mine anyway.

The box opened later.

It contained three old letters, a broken comb, and a receipt proving the
aunt had already sold the valuable thing everyone thought was inside.

Veya got the final line.

"She left us the argument."

She was better than all of us.

The audience went quiet for the line, then laughed after.

I stood there and let her have it.

This was harder than it sounded.

We exited.

Sellen handed me my crutch.

"Fine."

"That word is destroying me."

"You want bad?"

"No."

"Then fine."

I had no answer.

Backstage immediately became work.

Jori needed the narrow cord.

Pell had put it on the correct shelf, which made me suspicious.

A costume basket had to move.

Someone had lost a glove.

The red paint footprint returned because apparently Pell had not cleaned
the edge of his sole.

Nessa saw it.

Pell said, "Impossible."

She pointed.

He cleaned it again.

The last short piece had no Greg.

I watched half of it until Rinna gave me a stack of used tickets to
count.

I counted wrong.

"Again," she said.

"I can move paper."

"Not that paper."

I counted again.

Thirty-seven.

She checked.

Thirty-seven.

"See?"

"You needed two tries."

"Repeatable."

She pushed the stack away from me.

I looked at her.

She looked at me.

"Don't."

"I didn't."

"You did."

I hated everyone.

Cleanup took longer than the last piece.

The audience left dirt, two apple cores, one ribbon, and a wooden button
under a bench.

Nobody claimed the button.

Nessa claimed the ribbon for repairs.

Pell claimed one apple core was not his.

Nobody had accused him.

Rinna paid me one copper.

"Witness," she said.

"And front."

"One copper."

"And tickets."

"One copper."

"And I moved benches."

"Do you want less?"

"No."

"Good."

She turned to the board.

"Tomorrow."

I looked.

My name was not written yet.

"What tomorrow?"

"Work."

"Role?"

"Maybe."

"That's how this started."

"What?"

"Nothing."

She erased part of the board.

I put the copper away.

Outside, Carrow had gone blue with evening.

Shops were closing in pieces. One shutter down, another still open. A
woman swept flour from a doorway. Two boys argued over a hoop in the
road. Somewhere farther off, somebody was singing badly and confidently.

I went home.

Lyssa was not there.

I was first.

This felt unusual enough that I stood in the room for a moment as if I
had entered the wrong house.

Then I put bread on the table, set my copper beside the others, and took
off the Witness coat.

No.

My coat.

The Witness coat belonged to the hall.

This was how it happened.

I sat.

Hessa's sheet waited under the cup.

AWAY ONLY.

NEAR / FAR.

No date.

I did not touch it.

Lyssa came in after dark carrying a narrow bundle wrapped in pale cloth.

I looked at the bundle.

She looked at me looking.

"No."

"I didn't ask."

"You looked."

"This is becoming oppressive."

She put the bundle against the wall.

"How was theatre?"

"I was a municipal witness."

"Did you witness anything?"

"A purse."

She waited.

"I wasn't supposed to."

"Then why did you?"

"I knew it mattered."

"Did it?"

"Later."

"So you were right."

"Incorrectly."

Lyssa took off her shoes.

Her ankle looked almost normal.

I did not look long enough to get caught.

Probably.

"What did the witness do?" she asked.

"Told everyone I had no authority."

"Good casting."

"I've already had this joke."

"Then stop earning it."

I told her about the purse.

About Teren telling me to stop looking at it.

About Veya standing beside it without making it exist until she needed
it.

Lyssa listened while unwrapping the pale bundle.

Inside was dark cloth.

Not yellow.

Not green.

Not mine.

I did not ask.

"Did you get it right?" she asked.

"In the show."

"Then good."

"Fine."

"What?"

"Teren said fine."

"You said good."

"I am improving the review."

She smiled.

I showed her the copper.

"One."

"For witnessing?"

"And front. And tickets. And benches."

"Underpaid."

"Rinna asked if I wanted less."

"Did you?"

"No."

"Then expertly negotiated."

We ate bread and the last of the cheese.

Later, Lyssa moved the dark cloth to the chair.

I noticed that it went farther from me.

I noticed that I noticed.

Then I noticed that I was an idiot.

Hessa's paper remained under the cup.

Twenty-six draws.

Twenty-two shapings.

Nineteen external attempts.

Away was probably easier.

The purse had been important all afternoon.

The best thing I had done with it was pretend I did not know.

I did not write that down either.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 192

## THE SELLER

The dark cloth was gone in the morning.

So was Lyssa.

There was bread.

This was enough continuity for one household.

I ate, put Hessa's paper back under the cup after checking that it still
did not contain a date, and left for East Market Hall early enough that
Rinna could not accuse me of being late.

She accused me of something else.

"Move those."

I had barely entered.

"Good morning."

"Those."

She pointed at the rear benches.

There were six of them.

"Why?"

"Because nobody bought them."

That answered a different question, but I knew better than to ask for
the first one again.

The hall looked wrong.

Not empty. It was too early for empty to mean anything. But the benches
had been laid for a larger house, and the spaces between them made the
room feel stretched. A whole section near the rear wall had no chalk
marks on the ticket board.

Rinna was erasing seat numbers.

"Bad sales?" I asked.

"Thin."

"How thin?"

"Move the benches."

I moved the benches.

Pell arrived while I was on the second one and took the other end
without being asked.

"Closer," Rinna said.

I was grateful for the word.

We carried the bench forward.

"Closer."

Again.

By the fourth bench, the rear of the house had become open floor. Rinna
had us turn the last two sideways against the wall.

"Now what?" Pell asked.

"Nothing."

"Good."

He left.

I stayed.

Rinna looked at me.

"What?"

"You can also leave."

"I was told work."

"Board."

The board had changed.

KING: MAREK / HARA / SELLEN SHOPKEEPER: VEYA / GREG / HARA LETTER BOX:
VEYA / SELLEN / GREG / NESSA SHORT: EVIN / HARA FRONT: RINNA / GREG
REAR: JORI / PELL

I looked at Shopkeeper.

I had not played it since the road.

Not here, anyway.

The part felt old enough that I knew where the first line lived before I
found the pages.

"Both?" I asked.

Rinna nodded.

"Shopkeeper and Witness?"

"Yes."

"Front too?"

"Until house."

"One copper?"

"If you're lucky."

"I've learned not to negotiate with you."

"No, you haven't."

That was true.

The Shopkeeper rehearsal was barely a rehearsal.

Veya wanted the counter moved six inches because the new bench layout
changed the sightline from the left side.

Hara could not find the narrow brown scarf and used a gray one instead.

Teren came in, watched three minutes, and said, "Again from debt."

We did.

The scene was familiar.

Not memorized like a prayer. Better than that. I knew where Veya would
move when she became angry. I knew Hara liked to take half a beat before
the line about interest. I knew the counter edge caught my sleeve if I
stood too close.

I also knew the joke that usually got a laugh.

That knowledge became a problem later.

For now, it was useful.

"You're less annoying," Veya said after the run.

"Thank you."

"That wasn't praise."

"It was comparative."

She considered that.

"Fine."

Everyone had become infected.

The Letter Box needed less work.

I entered.

I looked at people.

The purse existed without becoming the most important object in the
world.

Teren watched once.

"Fine."

I stared at him.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Good."

He left to argue with Jori about whether The King needed the second
stool.

It did not.

Then it did.

Then Hara needed it for the short piece, so The King lost it again.

The stool survived all of this without opinion.

By midday, Rinna had sold nineteen seats.

I knew because she made me count.

"Twenty," I said.

She tapped the board.

"Nineteen."

"One man paid for two."

"Two seats."

"Then twenty."

"He hasn't chosen the second."

"That's still a seat."

"Not until someone sits in it."

I looked at her.

"This is a terrible accounting system."

"Sell another."

She handed me the ticket roll.

The market outside was busy enough to make the hall's thin sales
insulting.

People passed with baskets, bolts of cloth, fish wrapped in leaves, hot
food, children, dogs, arguments, and absolutely no urgent need to see
theatre.

I stood at the door.

A woman slowed.

"What's playing?"

"The King, The Shopkeeper, The Letter Box, and a short piece."

"Is The King sad?"

"Sometimes."

She kept walking.

Rinna leaned around the door.

"Sell the seat."

"I answered."

"Poorly."

A man stopped.

"Funny?"

"Some of it."

He kept walking.

Rinna closed her eyes.

"What?"

"Do you want them inside?"

"Yes."

"Then tell them why."

"They asked questions."

"Yes."

Another pair approached.

I tried again.

"The Shopkeeper is funny."

Rinna made a small sound behind me.

I ignored her.

"The Letter Box is also funny."

The older of the pair asked, "The King?"

"Less funny."

"Good."

They bought two seats.

I turned.

"See?"

"You found people who wanted less funny."

"I identified the market."

"Go eat."

I ate bread on the rear step.

Pell had an onion and nothing else.

"That's bleak," I said.

"It's an onion."

"Yes."

He bit it.

I moved farther away from him.

Not magically.

Hara came out carrying one shoe.

"Anyone seen the other?"

"No," I said.

Pell shook his head.

She looked at his feet.

"I don't have it," he said.

"I didn't say you did."

"You looked."

Hara went back inside.

Pell frowned.

"People are becoming unreasonable."

I ate my bread.

A few more seats sold.

Not many.

By house, Rinna had twenty-seven people for a room that could take far
more.

She closed the rear completely.

A family tried to sit there.

"Forward," she said.

"We like the back."

"Not today."

The father looked at the empty benches against the wall.

"Why?"

"Better seats."

He accepted this because Rinna said it like a fact.

They moved forward.

Another woman wanted the aisle.

A boy wanted to sit beside the wall.

A tired-looking man said he did not care where he sat and then rejected
two places.

I helped until Jori called me back.

From behind the hanging, the house sounded strange.

Twenty-seven people made more individual noises than a crowd.

One cough belonged to a specific man.

A child whispered and could be heard.

Someone unwrapped something dry and crackling.

A woman cleared her throat three times.

There was no broad murmur to cover any of it.

The King went first.

Marek entered.

The opening line usually got a small laugh.

Nothing.

He continued.

Hara came in.

Nothing.

Sellen's first complaint landed into a silence so clean I could hear a
cart outside.

I looked at Pell.

Pell was checking a strap.

He did not seem concerned.

Onstage, Marek got smaller.

Not quieter exactly.

Closer.

He stopped throwing the lines at the back wall because there was nobody
at the back wall.

Hara did the same.

They played to each other.

The audience watched.

They were not restless.

They simply did not laugh.

Then a man near the front laughed alone at a line I had never heard get
much before.

Nobody joined him.

Marek continued.

At the end, the applause was modest but real.

"Bad?" I whispered when Hara came off.

"No."

"They didn't laugh."

"It's The King."

"They usually laugh more."

Hara was already taking off the wrong brown scarf.

"Then they usually laugh more."

That was all I got.

The Shopkeeper was next.

I put on the coat.

My right palm was almost normal now, but the leather grip stayed. I had
paid for it. It could continue being useful.

Veya adjusted the counter.

"Don't shout."

"I don't shout."

She looked at me.

"I project."

"Don't project at twenty-seven people like they're seventy."

That seemed like a distinction invented to hurt me.

We went on.

The room was visible.

That was the first difference.

With a full house, faces became a mass beyond the first rows. Tonight I
could see the man who had rejected two seats. I could see the child
leaning against his mother's arm. I could see a woman in a yellow
headcloth who looked tired enough to sleep sitting upright.

I could also see the man who laughed alone during The King.

This became important.

The opening worked.

Veya accused me of cheating her brother.

I denied it.

Hara entered with the account.

I said, "That account is honest."

Veya said, "Your handwriting bends around the truth."

Usually a laugh.

Tonight, two people made small sounds.

Not silence.

Almost worse.

We continued.

I was fine.

Then came the debt line.

It was one of mine.

"If your brother wanted mercy, he should have borrowed from a priest."

The lone-laughing man laughed.

A real laugh.

Sharp.

Immediate.

Mine.

The rest of the house gave me a little more.

I felt it.

That was the problem.

My next line was not a joke.

It was supposed to be irritated.

"Debt does not disappear because you dislike the number."

I gave it more.

More voice.

More face.

More Shopkeeper.

The line died.

Not quietly.

It died in a room where I could see every person who had refused to save
it.

Veya looked at me.

Not Greg.

Shopkeeper.

Her expression said I had become embarrassing.

Which worked for the scene.

This was unfair.

She stepped closer.

"Then perhaps the number should learn to be likable."

Small laugh.

She had not pushed.

I hated her.

We continued.

For the next few lines, I could feel myself wanting the room.

I wanted another laugh to prove the dead line had been an accident.

Sellen was not in this piece, so he could not tell me to stop being
stupid.

Veya could.

She did not.

She just played the scene.

Eventually I had to play it with her.

The room came back.

Not much.

Enough.

At the end, the lone man laughed again.

This time I did not try to marry him.

Backstage, Teren was waiting.

"You chased it."

"I didn't."

"You did."

"I said the line."

"At them."

"It was for them."

"Leave them alone."

Veya passed us.

"That's what I said."

"You said don't shout."

"Same thing."

"It is not."

Teren pointed toward the stage.

"Letter Box."

I had no time to defend myself.

Good.

The Letter Box started with a dropped cup.

Not in the script.

Nessa set it on the table badly. It rolled off during Sellen's entrance
and hit the floor.
