One woman in the audience laughed.

Sellen looked down.

"Even the crockery is leaving."

That got the best laugh of the day.

Nessa picked up the cup.

"Rent is due from it too."

Another laugh.

I waited in the wing.

The audience had apparently decided pottery was superior to actors.

Fine.

Then the scene settled.

The purse was on the table.

I did not look at it.

This was easier today.

Not easy.

Easier.

"Then let the town hear it," Nessa said.

I entered.

"I was told there was a dispute."

"There is," Veya said.

"There isn't," Sellen said.

Nessa pointed.

"There."

I opened the ledger.

"Good. A dispute."

Yesterday, laugh.

Today, nothing.

I felt the silence.

I did not fix it.

"Names."

They all spoke.

We continued.

The tired woman in the yellow headcloth was watching now.

The child had stopped leaning against his mother.

The man who laughed alone was quiet.

Sellen tried to hand me the box.

"I have not witnessed transfer."

Nothing.

"I'm transferring it."

"I have witnessed an attempt."

A small laugh from somewhere left.

"That's the same thing."

"It is written differently."

Yesterday, good laugh.

Today, one cough.

I wanted to sharpen it.

I did not.

The scene moved.

Veya reached the turn.

"Ask her where she was when the aunt died."

She went still.

The room went still with her.

That part worked.

Not because anyone laughed.

Nobody was supposed to.

The purse became important when Veya let it become important.

The key came out.

The tired woman leaned forward.

Sellen said, "You had it."

Veya said, "I had her purse."

"With the key."

"I didn't know."

"I have not witnessed consent to open the box," I said.

The lone man laughed.

Wrong place.

I nearly looked at him.

I didn't.

Sellen turned on me.

"You have witnessed the key."

"Yes."

"Then open it."

"No."

"Why?"

"I have no authority."

The child laughed.

One bright laugh.

Then his mother did.

Then three more people.

Not huge.

Enough.

Sellen said, "What do you have?"

I looked at the ledger.

"Excellent notes."

The laugh was smaller than yesterday.

It was still there.

I let it go.

At the end, Veya said, "She left us the argument."

Silence.

For half a breath I thought the room had lost her.

Then the tired woman laughed softly.

Someone else did.

The applause came.

Twenty-seven people could still make applause.

It just sounded like twenty-seven people.

Backstage, Sellen took the box from me.

"You were loud in Shopkeeper."

"I know."

"Good."

"Teren already told me."

"Then why are you telling me?"

"I didn't start this conversation."

"You looked conversational."

I walked away.

The short piece was delayed because Hara's missing shoe had finally been
found inside the costume basket under two aprons.

Nobody knew how.

Hara blamed Pell.

Pell said, "I don't even wear that size."

"That isn't a defense."

"It should be."

EvIn missed his first entrance because he was helping move a bench for a
late-arriving couple.

Jori filled the silence by knocking twice from behind the side wall as
though someone in the scene was at the door.

Hara turned toward it.

"Not now."

The audience laughed.

EvIn came in.

The scene survived.

By the end, the house had warmed a little.

Or we had.

I could not tell.

Afterward, Rinna counted coins at the front table.

There were fewer than yesterday.

I knew that without counting.

Pell came up beside me.

"Bad house."

Rinna did not look up.

"They paid."

Pell considered this.

"Good house."

"Go clean."

"Bad Rinna."

"Go."

He went.

I helped collect cups.

There were fewer cups.

Less dirt.

One child had left a length of string tied around the leg of a bench.

I untied it.

The lone-laughing man stopped at the door.

"You were the shopkeeper."

"Yes."

"Funny."

"Thank you."

He left.

I stood there.

Rinna looked up.

"Don't."

"What?"

"Whatever you're about to become."

"I wasn't becoming anything."

"Good."

She gave me one copper.

"Shopkeeper, Witness, front."

"That sounds like at least three copper."

"One."

"I was also benches."

"Do you want less?"

"No."

"You're learning."

Teren came past carrying the ledger.

"Tomorrow's not set."

"Work?"

"Probably."

"Role?"

"Probably."

I waited.

He looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

He left.

Fine.

Outside, the market was nearly done.

I bought an onion because apparently Pell had damaged me.

Then I went home.

Lyssa was there.

The pale wrapping from yesterday was folded on the chair.

The dark cloth was gone.

I put the onion on the table.

She looked at it.

"Why?"

"Food."

"That's one onion."

"It remains one onion."

She looked at me again.

"What happened?"

"The audience hated me."

"All of them?"

"Twenty-seven."

"You counted?"

"Rinna did."

Lyssa cut the onion.

"They paid to hate you?"

"Apparently."

"Good business."

"They didn't laugh."

"At anything?"

"At a cup."

"Was the cup funny?"

"Very."

She put half the onion in the pan.

I told her about The Shopkeeper.

About getting one laugh and trying to get another one too hard.

About Veya making the next line work by not doing that.

Lyssa stirred the onion.

"So they didn't hate you."

"They were quiet."

"That's different."

"I know that now."

"Did they clap?"

"Yes."

"Then stop insulting your customers."

I sat.

Hessa's paper was still under the cup.

AWAY ONLY.

NEAR / FAR.

No date.

I slid it back where it had been without reading it a second time.

Lyssa saw.

"Nothing?"

"Nothing."

"Good."

"Why does everyone say that when nothing happens?"

"Because you keep making nothing difficult."

The onion cooked.

Twenty-seven people had watched us.

Some had laughed.

Some had not.

One man had laughed at nearly everything except the parts I expected.

Tomorrow I would probably work.

At some point Hessa would decide how far away to put the paper.

Tonight the onion stayed in the pan.

I left the audience alone.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 193

## THE DINER

Lyssa was still home when I woke.

This felt suspicious.

She was sitting at the table with one knee up, eating the last piece of
bread and reading something that did not belong to me. The pale wrapping
from yesterday had disappeared. So had the dark cloth. In their place
were two onions.

I looked at them.

Lyssa looked at me.

"No."

"I didn't say anything."

"You bought one onion."

"Yes."

"Now there are two."

"That seems like growth."

"I bought the other one."

"Then we're both contributing."

She tore the bread in half and gave me the smaller piece.

"Your contribution was worse."

I ate it anyway.

Her ankle did not have a wrap on it. I noticed because I had eyes. She
noticed me noticing because apparently she had developed a professional
interest in my eyes.

"It's fine."

"I didn't ask."

"You looked."

"Everyone keeps accusing me of looking."

"Stop being visible."

"That's not how looking works."

She folded the paper she had been reading.

"What are you doing today?"

"Theatre. Probably."

"When?"

I stopped.

That was a useful question.

"Teren said tomorrow."

"That's not a time."

"He also said probably."

"That's worse."

I considered going to the hall immediately.

Lyssa saw that too.

"No."

"What?"

"Don't go there at breakfast because somebody might need you at supper."

"I wasn't."

"You were."

"I was thinking."

"Poorly."

She stood, put the folded paper into the pocket of her skirt, and took
one onion.

"That's mine."

"You bought the other one."

"I bought this one."

"Prove it."

She left with my onion.

I sat at the table with the remaining onion and Hessa's note.

AWAY ONLY.

NEAR / FAR.

Still no date.

I did not read it twice.

This was becoming a skill.

I had no reason to be at the hall before midday.

I knew this because I went there to check.

Rinna was at the front table with her hair tied back and a cup beside
one hand. She looked up when I entered.

"No."

"I haven't asked anything."

"Good."

"What time?"

"After third bell."

I looked toward the board.

It was blank except for old chalk smears.

"Role?"

"After third bell."

"That isn't a role."

"It's also not now."

I stood there.

Rinna drank from her cup.

"Are you going to make me assign you something so you'll leave?"

"No."

"Good."

I left.

This was humiliating.

I had several hours.

Carrow was already busy. The lower market had opened fully, and the
morning traffic had settled into the part of the day where everybody
seemed to know where they were going except me.

I went to the cobbler first.

Not because anything was wrong.

That was new.

The leather grip on my right crutch had darkened where my palm sat. The
seam still stayed where it belonged. It had not twisted once. My hand
was nearly healed.

The cobbler glanced at it when I came in.

"Still there."

"Yes."

"Good."

"I came to tell you."

"No, you didn't."

"I could have."

He went back to a boot sole.

I looked around.

There was nothing I needed.

"How much for soap?"

He looked up.

"Wrong shop."

"I know."

"Do you?"

I left.

The soap seller was three stalls down.

I bought a small hard square for one copper after arguing with myself
longer than I argued with the seller.

It was soap.

I had paid for magic garbage for the same price.

This seemed unfair to soap.

Then I bought a meat bun.

That cost less thought.

I carried both to the lower market and sat on the same low wall where I
had once discovered I could tolerate peace for about fifteen minutes.

Today I had food.

This improved peace.

A dog slept under a cart with one eye open. A woman repaired the bottom
of a basket by threading fresh reeds through the old broken edge. Two
fish sellers argued about whether one of them had moved a bucket.
Neither mentioned magic.

A boy chased a hoop past me.

An old man sat at the far end of the wall and removed one shoe.

I ate the bun.

Nobody asked me where Pell was.

Nobody handed me a message.

Nobody told me to move a bench.

I finished eating and stayed.

The dog changed sides.

The basket got a new bottom.

The fish argument ended without agreement.

The old man put his shoe back on.

I stayed long enough that I stopped measuring it.

That was probably because I was tired.

Eventually a bell rang.

Not third bell.

I knew this because I was not completely useless.

I got up and went nowhere important.

There was a public pump two streets over. I washed my hands, then used
the new soap because I had bought it and wanted evidence that the
purchase had not been stupid.

The water ran gray from my fingers.

Paint.

Dust.

Lamp soot.

Something brown that I decided was food.

The soap smelled faintly of pine and strongly of soap.

I washed my face too.

A woman waiting behind me said, "You missed a spot."

"Where?"

She pointed at my ear.

I washed my ear.

"Other one."

I stared at her.

She smiled.

I washed the other one.

By the time third bell was close enough to be arguable, I went to the
hall.

Rinna looked up.

"Better."

"I was exactly on time."

"You're early."

"Close enough."

"Board."

There was writing now.

KING: MAREK / HARA / SELLEN PETITION: VEYA / SELLEN / GREG / EVIN WIDOW:
VEYA / HARA / NESSA SHORT: HARA / EVIN FRONT: RINNA REAR: JORI / PELL
GREG: THIRD MAN / SET

I read it.

Third Man.

Again.

No emergency.

No explanation.

Just work I already knew.

"Goat?" I asked.

Sellen was behind me.

"Don't."

"I asked one word."

"You asked the wrong one."

"Is it the same piece?"

"Today?"

I looked at him.

He looked at me.

"Yes," he said.

"Good."

"You're getting worse."

Nessa handed me a rolled brown hanging.

"Back wall."

"Today?"

"Yes."

Sellen laughed.

I carried the hanging.

The afternoon setup was boring in the best possible way.

The Petition used the same table but a different chair because the old
chair had developed a loose front rung. Pell had tied it once. Davin had
untied it and written BAD on the seat in chalk.

Someone had still moved it back toward the stage.

Nessa caught it before it got there.

"Who?"

Nobody answered.

Pell said, "Could be anyone."

"It has your cord on it."

"Many people use cord."

"Your knot."

Pell looked offended.

"My knots are not signatures."

Davin walked past.

"They are."

Pell carried the chair away.

I helped hang the brown wall, moved the petition stack to the correct
shelf, then moved it again because Veya wanted more room on the table.

The fake loaf was not in tonight's bill.

I checked anyway.

It was in the kitchen box.

Correctly.

This bothered me.

At rehearsal, The Petition took twelve minutes.

I knew the entrance.

I knew the line.

I knew Sellen was not a goat.

This was useful.

Teren watched from a bench.

"Again from Greg."

I entered.

"My neighbor's goat has eaten all my patience and half my fence."

Sellen came in.

"Your fence was mostly hope."

A laugh existed only in our memory because there was no audience.

I said the next line.

We continued.

Teren stopped us once because EvIn was too far upstage.

He stopped me once because I had set my crutch where Veya needed to
cross.

"Sorry."

"Move it."

I moved it.

That was the entire correction.

No one explained what it meant for my future.

I appreciated this.

Then Teren left.

He had somewhere else to be.

I did not know where.

Nobody told me.

Sellen sat on the edge of the stage and took a small wrapped packet from
his pocket.

"What is that?"

"Food."

"What kind?"

"Mine."

"I wasn't asking to have it."

"You looked."

I hated everyone.

He opened the packet.

Dried fish.

I changed my mind.

"You can keep it."

"I was going to."

We ate before house.

Not together exactly.

Near each other.

I had another piece of bread from a stall outside. Sellen had dried
fish. Pell had acquired an egg.

"Cooked?" I asked.

He cracked it against the edge of a box.

It was cooked.

I felt disappointed.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You expected raw."

"No."

"You did."

"You're becoming predictable."

He peeled the egg.

Hara came through in a clean blue overdress with one sleeve pinned but
not yet sewn.

"Nessa wants you."

Pell stood.

"Why?"

"Didn't ask."

He went.

Sellen watched him leave.

"He's good with the shutters."

"I know."

"That's why Nessa wants him."

"I know."

Sellen ate another piece of fish.

"You sound upset."

"I'm not."

"You looked upset."

I considered leaving the theatre forever.

Instead, I asked, "Do you live near here?"

Sellen glanced at me.

"Why?"

"No reason."

"Then no."

"That doesn't answer."

"It answered the question you should've asked."

"What question?"

"Can you come bother me after work?"

"I wasn't going to."

"Then we're done."

I ate bread.

After a moment, he said, "South side."

That was all.

I did not ask where.

It felt like winning something I had not entered.

House was better than yesterday.

Not full.

Better.

Rinna had opened one more row.

People came in carrying the day's heat with them. The hall warmed
quickly. Someone had tracked dry straw onto the floor. A little girl
wore a paper crown that kept slipping over one eye.

I had no front work.

This felt luxurious.

I stood backstage and did almost nothing for four whole minutes.

Then Jori handed me a stool.

"King."

Of course.

The King went cleanly.

The audience laughed more than yesterday.

Marek did not seem relieved.

Hara did not seem surprised.

Sellen missed one word, replaced it with another, and the world did not
end.

I watched from the wing until Nessa told me to stop standing where she
needed to pass.

The Petition was next.

I put on the Third Man coat.

It smelled like somebody else.

Probably because it belonged to everybody.

The petition stack had the real wax seal on top and nonsense beneath.
The chair was the good chair. My crutch was where Veya would not hit it.

I waited.

The scene began.

Veya wanted the road repaired.

EvIn wanted the town to admit the road belonged to somebody else.

Sellen wanted everybody to stop saying his goat had caused anything.

Then my cue came.

I entered.

"My neighbor's goat has eaten all my patience and half my fence."

A decent laugh.

Not huge.

I did not ask it to become one.

Sellen entered.

"Your fence was mostly hope."

Bigger laugh.

I looked at him.

As Third Man.

Annoyed.

Correct.

The scene moved.

There was a point later where I had to hand Veya the petition stack.

I handed it to her upside down.

She looked at it.

I looked at it.

The seal was now at the bottom.

For half a second, my brain tried to fix reality.

Veya did it for me.

She turned the stack over and said, "At least the signatures know which
way the road goes."

The audience laughed.

I said, "More than the council does."

That was not the line.

It was also not terrible.

Sellen made a small sound through his nose.

Veya continued.

The scene survived.

Backstage, Sellen said, "That was fine."

"Which part?"

"The wrong papers."

"I gave them upside down."

"I noticed."

"Veya fixed it."

"Yes."

"I added a line."

"Yes."

"It worked."

Sellen looked at me.

"For everyone."

I stopped.

He had done that on purpose.

"You've been waiting months to say that."

"Days."

"It feels longer."

"That's because you talk."

Nessa came through carrying a basket.

"Move."

We moved.

Widow's Room used the painted doorway.

I had seen it enough times that the false depth barely interested me
from backstage anymore. It was cloth, frame, paint, floor seam, crate.
From the house, people still looked into a room that was not there.

I did not need to learn anything about it today.

I carried a costume basket instead.

The short piece lost a spoon.

This became a problem for approximately six minutes.

The spoon was required for Hara to accuse EvIn of stealing it.

Without the spoon, the accusation became philosophically difficult.

Everyone searched.

I checked the prop shelf.

Pell checked under the stage.

Nessa checked the kitchen box.

EvIn checked his own pocket twice.

Hara said, "Use the knife."

"The knife changes it," EvIn said.

"Into what?"

"Murder."

"Fair."

Eventually Jori found the spoon inside the cup from The Letter Box.

Nobody knew why.

The Letter Box was not even playing tonight.

"Yesterday was yesterday," I said.

Nessa looked at me.

"Don't become Teren."

"I don't know where he is."

"Good."

The short piece happened with the spoon.

After the show, Rinna paid me one copper.

"Third Man. Set."

"I was also stool."

"One copper."

"Petition recovery."

"Veya recovered it."

"I assisted."

"By causing it?"

"Essential."

"One copper."

I took it.

There was no immediate rush to go home.

This was partly because Pell said, "Food?"

It was not a question for me specifically.

It became a group.

Rinna did not come.

Nessa said no before anyone finished asking.

Hara had somewhere to be and left with her blue overdress half unlaced
at the back.

EvIn went with her for the first block, then turned east.

Jori disappeared.

Teren was still absent.

That left me, Pell, Sellen, and eventually Marek, who joined because he
had heard the word food from across the hall.

We went to a stall near the south edge of the market where a woman sold
bowls of beans with chopped greens and small pieces of pork if you paid
extra.

I paid extra.

This was reckless wealth.

The bowl cost enough that I noticed and not enough that I changed my
mind.

We sat on low stools around a table that leaned toward Pell.

"It likes me," he said.

"It's broken," Sellen said.

"Same thing."

Marek ate quietly.

For a while nobody talked about theatre.

This was strange.

Pell complained about a landlord who had raised the price of a room
because the roof had been repaired.

Sellen said that was the point of repairing the roof.

Pell said the old hole had been free.

Marek asked if anyone knew a cheap cart going north in three days.

"Why?" I asked.

He looked at me.

"Going north."

I waited.

Nothing else came.

Apparently this was allowed.

Sellen owed Pell a copper.

I learned this when Sellen put a copper on the table.

Pell immediately handed it to Marek.

Marek put it in his pocket.

"What just happened?" I asked.

"Debt," Sellen said.

"For what?"

"No."

That was the entire explanation.

I ate my beans.

They were good.

Better because I had bought them after work instead of receiving them
because someone else had negotiated food into a job.

Not much better.

Enough.

A group at the next table started arguing about whether the cider was
watered.

The stall woman told them it was, and if they wanted stronger they could
pay for stronger.

The argument ended.

This seemed like excellent governance.

Pell told a story about falling through a chicken-house roof when he was
fourteen.

I did not believe half of it.

Sellen believed less.

Marek believed none.

The story improved under these conditions.

By the time we left, the market lamps were lit.

Sellen went south.

Now I knew that meant something.

Pell went east after remembering he had promised to return a latch.

Marek went north, perhaps because he was practicing.

I went home.

Lyssa was not there.

That was normal.

There was a folded paper under the cup.

Not Hessa's old paper.

A new one.

I opened it.

THREE DAYS.

AFTER MIDDAY.

AWAY ONLY.

NEAR / FAR.

SAME RESTRICTIONS.

I read it once.

Then I put it beneath the old note.

Three days.

Good.

I had time to do absolutely nothing about it.

Lyssa came home while I was taking off my coat.

She carried no mysterious cloth.

This was almost disappointing.

"How was theatre?"

"Fine."

She stopped.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You said it wrong."

"I was Third Man."

"Again?"

"Yes."

"Goat?"

"Everyone knows too much."

She put a small wrapped bundle of greens on the table.

I told her about the upside-down petitions.

She laughed before I got to Veya's line.

"That's not the funny part."

"It is from here."

"I recovered."

"Veya recovered."

"I assisted."

"By causing it?"

I stared at her.

"Do you speak to Rinna?"

"No."

"Suspicious."

I told her I had eaten after work.

"Without me?"

"You stole my onion."

"I bought that onion."

"You cannot prove that."

She unwrapped the greens.

I showed her the new Hessa note.

"Three days," she said.

"Yes."

"Good."

"Apparently."

"What happens then?"

"Near and far."

"Both away?"

"Yes."

"How far?"

"I don't know."

"How near?"

"I don't know."

She nodded.

"You know a lot."

"I moved paper."

"Three days ago."

"Recently."

She pushed the greens toward me.

"Cut those."

I cut them.

No theory emerged.

The soap sat in my pocket until I remembered it and put it by the basin.

Lyssa picked it up.

"You bought soap."

"Yes."

"For us?"

I had not thought that far ahead.

"Obviously."

She smelled it.

"Good."

That one I accepted.

We ate the greens with what was left of the onions.

Tomorrow the hall would probably want me again.

In three days Hessa wanted paper farther away and paper nearer.

Sellen lived somewhere south.

Marek needed a cheap cart north.

Pell had once fallen through a chicken-house roof, unless he had not.

I had bought soap.

It was not a dramatic day.

I liked it anyway.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 194

## THE HAND

The soap was already wet.

I stood at the basin holding it.

Lyssa was still asleep.

This meant either she had used it before bed or somebody had broken into
our room during the night to wash.

I chose Lyssa.

I washed my face, my hands, and both ears without supervision.

Then I put the soap back exactly where it had been.

This was adulthood.

There was bread on the table. Not much. I cut it in half and left one
piece under a cloth for Lyssa. Beside it I put a note.

THEATRE.

That seemed sufficient.

I considered adding PROBABLY.

I did not.

Hessa's two papers stayed under the cup.

THREE DAYS had become two without either of us doing anything.

I liked that kind of progress.

The East Market Hall was already making noise when I arrived. Hammering
came from inside in an irregular pattern that suggested either repair or
murder.

It was repair.

Davin was on one knee near the left edge of the stage with a short pry
bar under a floorboard. Jori held a lamp low. Nessa stood above them
with both arms full of folded costumes.

"Don't step there," Davin said.

I had not stepped there.

"Good."

A chalk cross marked one board.

"What happened?"

"Splinter."

"To who?"

"Board."

I looked at him.

Davin looked at me.

"Also EvIn."

EvIn was sitting on a bench pulling a long pale splinter from the heel
of his shoe.

"Not me," he said.

"Good."

"Through the sole."

"Less good."

Nessa pushed the folded costumes into my arms.

"Rail."

"Which?"

"Costume."

"There are two."

"Left."

"Today?"

She stared at me.

"Yes."

I carried them away.

The board had already been written.

KING: MAREK / HARA / SELLEN PETITION: VEYA / SELLEN / GREG / EVIN WIDOW:
VEYA / HARA / NESSA SHORT: HARA / EVIN GREG: THIRD MAN / SET

Yesterday.

Almost exactly.

I looked at Rinna.

"Did you forget to erase it?"

"No."

"So I'm Third Man."

"For now."

I did not like those words.

"How long is now?"

"Until it isn't."

This was not an answer, but it was accurate enough that Hessa might have
approved.

I went back to the costume rail.

One of the wooden pegs had pulled halfway out of the wall. Nessa had
apparently decided the solution was to put fewer clothes on it and more
clothes on me.

"Hold that."

Davin had appeared beside me with a hammer.

"What?"

"The rail."

I held it.

He pulled the peg out, looked into the hole, made a dissatisfied sound,
and put the peg in his mouth.

"Tool."

"Which?"

He pointed with the hammer toward an open box.

There were seven things in it.

"That narrows it."

"Thin chisel."

I found the thin chisel.

Wrong one.

He took a narrower one.

"That's thinner."

"Yes."

"You could have said narrowest."

"I said thin."

"This is why civilization fails."

He scraped old wood from the hole.

I held the rail.

Nessa took two costumes off my shoulder without thanking me.

Then she put one back.

"Why?"

"Wrong rail."

"Whose fault is that?"

"Yours now."

I held the rail harder.

The first change came before Davin finished.

Marek walked in carrying a folded scrap of paper and said, "I have a
cart."

Rinna looked up.

"When?"

"Last bell before dark."

"Today?"

"Today to arrange it. Leaves in two days."

"How long?"

"An hour. Maybe."

Rinna looked at the board.

I looked at the board.

Marek looked at me.

"No," I said.

Nobody had asked.

Rinna erased MAREK from The King.

"Who?"

Hara was pinning the sleeve of a brown coat.

"Not me."

"You are already in it."

"I know."

Sellen said, "I can take the King."

Rinna erased something else.

"You are already in it."

"I know."

"I hate all of you."

Teren came through the side door at that moment, carrying a rolled page
and a small bag of nails.

"Good."

Rinna pointed at the board.

"Marek has to leave."

Teren looked at Marek.

"Cart?"

Marek nodded.

Teren looked at Sellen.

"King."

Sellen nodded.

"Hara?"

"Still Hara."

"Fine."

"What about his part?" I asked.

Everyone looked at me.

"Marek's part."

Teren said, "Sellen."

"Sellen was already Sellen."

"Not in The King."

I had forgotten that names were not roles.

This was getting complicated.

Rinna erased half the board and rewrote it.

KING: SELLEN / HARA / EVIN PETITION: VEYA / GREG / EVIN WIDOW: VEYA /
HARA / NESSA SHORT: HARA / EVIN GREG: THIRD MAN / SET

Sellen stared.

"Who am I in Petition?"

"Not in it," Teren said.

"Why?"

"Because you're King."

"Those happen at different times."

"Your coat doesn't."

Nessa said, "And I need the brown coat open."

Sellen looked at the coat.

The coat did not apologize.

Teren went to the stage.

"King first."

I kept holding the costume rail.

Davin tapped the new peg into place.

"Done."

I let go.

The rail stayed on the wall.

"Good."

"Yes."

"Do I get paid for this?"

"No."

"Then less good."

Davin moved back toward the floorboard.

Rehearsal became a sequence of people asking which version of today
existed.

Sellen knew the King well enough to take Marek's part with the page in
his hand for the first run. EvIn took Sellen's smaller place and
immediately complained that the hat smelled like Marek.

"It smelled like that before," Hara said.

"Then Marek smells like hat."

"Line," Teren said.

They continued.

I moved the petition table.

Then Rinna told me not to because The Petition might move later.

"Where?"

"Later."

"That's a time."

"Good."

I left it.

Marek went out to arrange his cart.

I caught him at the door.

"What are you taking north?"

He looked at me.

"Myself."

"That seems difficult to ship."

"I'm going with it."

"Why?"

"See my sister."

There it was.

A whole answer.

I was not prepared.

"Oh."

"She's having a baby."

"You're helping?"

"No."

"Then why are you going?"

Marek gave me the same look Lyssa gave me when I asked questions that
had already been answered.

"See my sister."

"Right."

He left.

I stood there for a moment.

Rinna called, "Greg."

I turned.

"Table."

Of course.

The second change came because Hara had to leave before evening.

This information arrived from a girl I did not know, who came through
the front doors and said, "Hara?"

Hara went outside.

She came back three minutes later.

"I have to go after Widow."

Rinna said, "Why?"

"Work."

"This is work."

"Other work."

"Better?"

"Different."

Rinna looked offended on behalf of employment.

Teren looked at the board.

Hara said, "I can do King and Widow. Not Short."

"Fine."

EvIn said, "I can do Short alone."

"No," three people said.

He looked hurt.

The Short disappeared from the board.

This created space.

Then it created a different problem.

Rinna had sold the evening as four pieces to at least six people.

"Add Letter Box," she said.

I looked at her.

"No."

"You like Witness."

"I do."

"Good."

"I didn't say yes."

"You are Witness."

The chalk changed again.

KING: SELLEN / HARA / EVIN PETITION: VEYA / GREG / EVIN WIDOW: VEYA /
HARA / NESSA LETTER BOX: VEYA / SELLEN / GREG / NESSA GREG: THIRD MAN /
WITNESS / SET

I read my line twice.

"You made it worse."

Rinna said, "I made it four."

"I have two coats."

Nessa said, "One coat."

"Third Man and Witness wear the same coat?"

"No. Witness wears gray."

"That's two coats."

"Third Man doesn't need the brown one today."

"He did yesterday."

"Today."

I closed my eyes.

"Good."

Nessa patted my shoulder once.

I think it was mockery.

We rehearsed The Petition first because everyone in it was present.

That was where I made the wrong mistake.

"My neighbor's goat has eaten all my patience and half my fence."

EvIn entered.

Not Sellen.

I knew that.

We continued.

Veya took the petition.

I said, "And if the council wishes to call that a road, perhaps the
council should walk it barefoot."

Teren said, "No."

I stopped.

"What?"

"Not that cut."

I looked at Veya.

She looked at me.

"What cut?"

"Road cut," Teren said.

"We're not on the road."

"I know where we are."

"Then why are you using it?"

"Because I know it."

EvIn said, "That's a strong defense."

"Thank you."

"It wasn't."

Teren held out his hand.

"Home cut. From the seal."

I knew the home cut too.

That was the problem.

I started again.

Veya held the petition stack.

I said, "The seal is real. That is more than I can say for the road."

"Yes," Teren said.

"Today?"

"Yes."

I pointed at him.

"See? Useful question."

"Keep going."

We kept going.

That was all.

Nobody gathered around to discuss the danger of knowing multiple
versions.

At midday, the floorboard was fixed.

Davin had cut the damaged edge back, set a narrow replacement strip, and
hammered it flush. The new wood showed pale against the old stage.

EvIn tested it with his shoe.

Davin said, "Don't."

EvIn stopped.

"Why fix it if I can't step on it?"

"Glue."

"Ah."

He stepped around.

Pell arrived late carrying a latch.

"Returned it."

"To who?" I asked.

"The person."

"Which person?"

"The latch person."

"That explains everything."

"It did to them."

He saw the board.

"Greg's two people."

"I'm always one person."

Pell looked unconvinced.

Marek returned with dust on his trousers and said the cart was arranged.

"Cheap?" Sellen asked.

"Cheap enough."

"North?"

"Still."

Rinna told him he was no longer King.

Marek looked at the board.

"Good."

I was offended.

"You don't care?"

"I have to pack."

"That's not the point."

"What is the point?"

I did not know.

He took a piece of bread from the table and left again to find Rinna's
string.

Apparently packing had already begun.

The third change was smaller.

The Widow's Room lost its pale shawl.

It had not disappeared.

Nessa had it in her hands.

It had torn under the arm.

"Use the dark one," Hara said.

"No."

"Why?"

"Wrong."

"How wrong?"

Nessa held the dark shawl against Hara.

We all looked.

Hara looked like a widow who had murdered her husband personally.

"Fair," Hara said.

Nessa repaired the pale shawl.

Nobody changed the board.

This felt like mercy.

By house, I smelled less like pine soap and more like old wool.

So the soap had lasted approximately half a day.

Still worth one copper.

The audience was normal.

I had forgotten normal could be noticeable.

Not full. Not thin. Not loud. Not strangely quiet.

People came in, sat down, talked until the lamps lowered, then mostly
stopped.

A baby cried once and was taken outside.

A man sneezed during The King.

Nobody built a chapter around it.

The King went first.

Sellen was good.

Not Marek-good in Marek's exact way. Sellen made the King's irritation
sharper and less tired. Hara adjusted without making it visible. EvIn
remembered the hat and most of the lines.

One audience member laughed where nobody usually did.

Sellen did not marry him.

I approved professionally.

Then The Petition.

I wore the right coat.

This mattered because I had nearly put on the gray Witness coat until
Nessa caught my sleeve.

"Later."

"I knew that."

"You had it on."

"Partly."

"Later."

I changed.

Onstage, the home cut stayed in my head.

"My neighbor's goat has eaten all my patience and half my fence."

EvIn entered.

"Your fence was mostly hope."

He did not say it like Sellen.

He said it like EvIn.

The audience laughed anyway.

I had a brief irrational objection.

Then Veya spoke and I had work.

The petition stack stayed upright this time.

I used the correct line about the seal.

Nobody applauded my accuracy.

The scene ended.

Backstage, I changed coats.

The gray Witness coat caught on the top of my crutch.

I pulled.

It caught harder.

Nessa slapped my hand away.

"Stop."

"I can get it."

"You're making it worse."

She lifted the cloth off the handle in one motion.

I put it on.

"Thank you."

"Go."

The Letter Box was already starting.

I had enough time.

That was all I needed.

Nessa's line came.

"Then let the town hear it."

I entered from the left with the ledger.

"I was told there was a dispute."

"There is," Veya said.

"There isn't," Sellen said.

"There," Nessa said.

I opened the ledger.

"Good. A dispute."

A laugh.

Normal.

I continued.

The purse sat on the table.

It was a purse.

I did not have to fight myself about it.

When the key came out later, the audience made the same small sound
audiences often made.

I gave the consent line.

Sellen argued.

I had no authority.

I had excellent notes.

The laugh was good.

Not enormous.

Good.

Veya got the last line.

"She left us the argument."

The audience laughed, then applauded.

I went offstage.

That was the whole performance.

I had done two roles.

Neither had changed my life.

I liked that too.

Hara left almost immediately after Widow's Room, still carrying the
repaired pale shawl over one arm.

"That's theatre property," Nessa called.

"I'm changing outside."

"Why?"

"Because I'm late."

"For what?"

Hara was already through the door.

Nessa looked at me.

"I don't know."

"I didn't ask."

"You looked."

This disease was everywhere.

Cleanup took longer than the show felt.

The floor collected scraps of thread, one crushed nut shell, two ticket
halves, and a small smear of something sticky near the third bench.

Pell touched it.

"Why?"

I asked.

He looked at his finger.

"Jam."

"How do you know?"

He licked it.

I walked away.

Davin checked the repaired floorboard.

The pale strip held.

Rinna counted coins at the front table.

There were more than yesterday.

I knew because the pile looked less insulting.

She paid me one copper.

"Third Man. Witness. Set."

"Two roles."

"One copper."

"Two coats."

"One copper."

"Rail."

"Davin fixed the rail."

"I held civilization together."

"Do you want less?"

"No."

"Good."

She pushed the copper toward me.

I took it.

On the board, tomorrow had already begun.

Not fully.

Just names and question marks.

I saw GREG once.

Then Rinna erased it.

I did not ask.

This required effort.

She noticed.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You look ill."

"I'm growing."

"Do it somewhere else."

I went home.

Lyssa was not there.

The bread I had left was gone.

My note was still on the table.

THEATRE.

Under it, in Lyssa's writing:

OBVIOUSLY.

I kept the paper.

I did not know why.

Hessa's note stayed under the cup.

Two days.

No new instructions.

No reason to touch it.

I washed my hands with the soap.

The water ran gray again.

The theatre had defeated cleanliness in less than one shift.

Lyssa came home after dark carrying a narrow wooden hoop and a bundle of
pale thread.

I looked at both.

She looked at me.

I looked away.

"Better," she said.

"How was work?"

"Changed."

"Bad?"

"No."

"Then?"

"Changed."

This was apparently an acceptable answer when other people used it.

I told her Marek was going north to see his sister because she was
having a baby.

"That's nice."

"He said he's not helping."

"With the baby?"

"Yes."

"Good."

"I asked why he was going if he wasn't helping."

Lyssa slowly put the wooden hoop on the table.

"What?"

"He said to see his sister."

"Yes."

"I understood eventually."

"Did Marek survive this conversation?"

"Barely."

She took off her outer layer and hung it.

I told her the board changed three times.

"How many people were you?"

"Two."

"That's too many Gregs."

"I said that."

"No, you didn't."

"I said I'm always one person."

"Different."

She was right, which was irritating.

I told her I had nearly worn the wrong coat.

"Did you?"

"Partly."

"Then you did."

"Nessa stopped me."

"Useful Nessa."

"Everyone is very useful when I'm wrong."

Lyssa smiled.

"Convenient."

We ate bread, cheese, and the last of the greens.

I did not mention the one copper until she asked whether I had been
paid.

"One."

"For two Gregs?"

"Exactly."

"Underpaid."

"Rinna offered less."

"Expertly negotiated again."

I pointed at her.

"That joke belongs to me."

"No."

After we ate, she took the wooden hoop and pale thread to the far side
of the room and began doing something with both.

I did not ask.

This also required effort.

Tomorrow the chalk board might say my name.

It might not.

Marek had a cart north in two days. Hara had other work nobody had
explained to me. Davin's floorboard needed another night before EvIn was
allowed to test it by standing on it. The pale shawl had survived.

Hessa wanted me after midday in two days.

Near.

Far.

Away only.

Nothing about today had moved because I wanted it to.

A surprising amount had changed anyway.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 195

## THE CARRIER

Lyssa had turned the wooden hoop into cloth.

Not all of it.

The hoop was still wood. The cloth had simply been stretched across it
so tightly that I could no longer understand why the thread had been
necessary.

I stood over her shoulder.

"What is it?"

"You lasted longer yesterday."

"I wasn't awake enough."

"Apparently."

Pale cloth filled the hoop. A torn place near one edge had been drawn
together with stitches so small I had to lean closer to see them.

Lyssa put two fingers against my forehead and pushed me back.

"You're breathing on it."

"I breathe most places."

"Not there."

I sat down.

Morning had gotten farther than usual before either of us left. Light
came through the window. Somebody below us was arguing about a bucket.
The soap sat beside the basin with one corner already rounded from use.

On the table, Hessa's note remained under the cup.

Tomorrow.

After midday.

Away only.

Near / far.

I knew what it said without lifting the cup.

That was convenient.

Lyssa cut the repaired cloth free from the hoop.

"Hold this."

She handed me the hoop.

Then the cloth.

Then a folded dark blue piece from the chair.

"Separate?"

"Yes."

I put the hoop on my lap and the two cloths beside each other.

She handed me a smaller pale bundle.

"Separate."

"From which?"

"Both."

"This system needs labels."

"This system has me."

"That seems fragile."

She ignored me and went to wash.

By the time she came back, I had four things.

"Where are we going?"

"Marra."

"We?"

"You have theatre?"

"Later."

"How much later?"

I had gone to the hall the previous night without asking tomorrow's
time. This had felt like personal growth until now.

"I don't know."

Lyssa stopped tying her hair back.

"You didn't ask?"

"No."

She looked impressed.

I did not like it.

"I can go ask."

"No."

"I need to know."

"You can ask after."

"After what?"

"Marra."

This was how I learned I was going to Marra.

Lyssa took the hoop from me and gave me a larger bundle.

"I thought I was holding that."

"You were."

"What happened?"

"Now you're holding this."

The theatre had prepared me for nothing.

We left after eating the heel of yesterday's bread and one piece of
cheese between us.

Lyssa carried the hoop under one arm. I had the large bundle tucked
against my side, one crutch under the opposite arm, and a smaller folded
piece balanced over my forearm.

Halfway down the stairs, she put another bundle on top.

"How many hands do you think I have?"

"The useful number."

"That's not a number."

"Keep walking."

We walked.

Carrow in the morning had already heated at the edges. Bakers had their
shutters open. A cart loaded with narrow boards blocked half a crossing
while three men discussed where the cart ought to have been. A woman
carrying flowers passed us going the other way, leaving a sharp green
smell behind her.

Lyssa adjusted her pace at the first crowded corner.

I adjusted mine.

Neither of us said anything.

At the next crossing she reached for the top bundle before I needed to
change my grip. I gave it to her, stepped around a basket seller, then
took it back on the other side.

That was apparently how we did streets now.

Marra's place was busy enough that nobody noticed us for almost a
minute.

I liked this.

Jessa stood on a low stool pinning the side of a green dress on a woman
who had both arms lifted and the expression of somebody regretting every
decision that had led to clothing.

Marra was behind the long table cutting dark fabric.

Another woman sat near the wall with a half-finished sleeve in her lap.

Lyssa walked in.

Marra said, "There."

Not hello.

There.

Lyssa put the hoop down.

I waited.

Jessa glanced over.

"You delivered him."

"I carried myself."

"Late?"

"No."

"Then somebody else did it."

The woman in green looked at me.

I looked at Jessa.

"That was one message."

"It was a memorable message."

"It was not."

"You wrote it down and still didn't deliver it."

"I eventually delivered it."

Lyssa put a bundle on the table.

"Hours later."

I looked at her.

"You were there."

"Yes."

"You're supposed to be on my side."

"I am. That's why I remember."

Marra pointed at me without looking up.

"Blue on the chair."

I looked down.

I was holding dark blue, pale, and something brown that had appeared
somewhere between our room and here.

"Which blue?"

"The blue."

"There are two."

Every woman in the room looked at me.

I checked again.

There were apparently not two.

One was blue.

The other was, according to Jessa, "blue-gray."

"That is blue."

"No."

"It contains blue."

"So does a bruise."

"That is not helping."

The woman in green laughed.

Jessa said, "Chair."

I put the actual blue on the chair.

"Other one?"

"Table."

I put the blue-gray on the table.

Lyssa immediately moved it six inches to the left.

"Why?"

"Pins."

There were pins where I had put it.

I had not seen them.

"This room is hostile."

Marra said, "Only to blood."

"That is not reassuring."

She finally looked at me.

"Hold."

A long piece of brown cloth came across the table.

I took it.

"How?"

"Up."

I held it up.

"More."

I raised my arm.

"Not you. Cloth."

I raised the cloth.

"Stop."

I stopped.

Marra and Lyssa looked at it.

Jessa looked at it from the stool.

The woman in green looked too, because she had nothing better to do
while wearing half a dress.

"Too warm," Lyssa said.

Marra nodded.

I looked at the brown cloth.

It was brown.

Jessa said, "Don't."

"I didn't say anything."

"You were going to."

"I was going to ask what warm brown means."

"Exactly."

"What does it mean?"

"No."

The woman in green laughed again.

I had become entertainment without pay.

Marra took the cloth.

Then she handed me another.

This one was also brown.

I decided to survive.

For the next half hour, my work consisted of holding things, moving
things, and not placing things where pins lived.

I failed the third one twice.

Lyssa repaired the pale cloth from the hoop at the table beside Marra.
It was not embroidery. It was a torn inner panel from some larger piece,
and the hoop had only kept the fabric stretched while she worked the
tear back together.

This made sense once somebody else explained it to Jessa.

I pretended I had understood already.

A customer came in and greeted Lyssa by name.

Then another.

The second asked whether she had finished "the narrow one."

Lyssa said, "Tomorrow."

Nobody told me what the narrow one was.

Marra sent Jessa into the back for black thread.

Jessa came out with black thread, a red ribbon, and a complaint about a
missing box.

Lyssa knew which shelf the box had been on last time.

Marra knew who had moved it.

The woman with the sleeve knew who had borrowed it.

None of them needed me.

I held brown cloth.

This was peaceful in a different way from the lower market.

Eventually Marra said, "Done."

I lowered my arms.

"With me?"

"With that."

She took the cloth.

Lyssa folded the repaired pale panel and put it with the blue-gray.

I picked up the blue.

"No."

I stopped.

"What?"

"That stays."

"You brought it."

"I did."

"So it goes back."

"No."

I looked at Lyssa.

She pointed at the blue-gray.

"That."

I picked it up.

Then the pale panel.

"No."

I stopped again.

"That stays too."

"Why did I carry things here if I'm not carrying them back?"

"Because that was the job."

"This work is badly designed."

Marra put a different bundle in my arms.

"Take this."

"Where?"

"Home."

"Whose?"

"Lyssa's."

I looked at Lyssa.

She was smiling.

"This is how you get furniture," I said.

"What?"

"You keep putting things on it."

Jessa said, "Furniture doesn't complain."

"Bad furniture."

The woman in green said, "He's more like a shelf."

"Thank you."

"That wasn't praise."

I was beginning to suspect this entire city had agreed on one sentence.

Lyssa had one more stop.

A thread seller two streets over.

I waited outside because the stall was narrow and because I had become a
shelf.

She came out with two small paper-wrapped spools.

"How much?"

"Not yours."

"I can contribute."

"You can carry."

"That's not currency."

"It is today."

We bought food after.

That part I was allowed to understand.

Bread, a small wedge of white cheese, and three carrots.

I paid for the carrots.

Lyssa let me.

This felt suspiciously ceremonial, so I did not mention it.

We ate one carrot raw while walking.

It was not good enough to justify doing this regularly.

At the turn toward East Market, Lyssa stopped.

"I go west."

"I go east."

"I know."

She took the smaller spool bundle from under my arm.

I handed it over before she asked.

She took half the bread too.

"That was mine."

"Was."

"You're becoming Rinna."

"No."

"Marra?"

"Worse."

She bit the carrot.

"See you tonight."

"Probably."

She pointed the carrot at me.

"Don't start."

I went east.

The hall board had my name.

It had apparently survived since last night.

GREG: SET / NEIGHBOR.

I stood in front of it.

Rinna came past with a stack of tickets.

"After fourth bell."

"What?"

"You're early."

"I went to Marra."

"Why?"

"I don't know."

"Good."

"What's Neighbor?"

She pointed at a rolled page.

"Four lines."

"New?"

"Old."

"Mine?"

"Today."

I picked up the page.

The piece was The Broken Gate, which I had seen but never performed.
Neighbor entered once to complain about a cart blocking the lane, left,
returned near the end to discover the gate had fallen down, and blamed
the wrong person.

Four lines.

I read them.

"That's it?"

Rinna stopped.

"Do you want more?"

"No."

"Good."

This was the most successful negotiation we had ever had.

Marek was near the rear door with a canvas bag, two shirts, and a length
of cord.

"Packing?"

"No."

I looked at the bag.

He looked at the bag.

"Yes."

"Need help?"

"Know where Pell put the short tying cord?"

"Upper shelf. Left of narrow tubes. Not the long narrow one."

Marek stared.

"What?"

"Nothing."

I found the cord.

It was exactly where it should be.

Pell was not there to witness this miracle.

Marek tied the bag.

"Leaving morning?"

"First bell."

"Back when?"

"Depends."

"On baby?"

"On sister."

"Right."

I had learned.

He pulled the knot tight.

"Tell them not to replace me."

"Who?"

"Everyone."

"They already replaced you yesterday."

"Then tell them badly."

"That I can do."

He nodded.

That was goodbye.

No one embraced.

No one promised anything.

He carried the bag out to wherever he was sleeping before morning.

I went to set.

The Broken Gate needed a gate.

We had one.

It was painted wood on a frame with a hinge that had been repaired
enough times to become mostly repair.

Davin was checking the bottom brace.

"Can I step on the floor now?"

He looked at me.

"Yes."

I stepped on yesterday's pale replacement strip.

Nothing happened.

"Good."

Davin said, "Yes."

"Strong day."

He went back to the gate.

Rehearsal for Neighbor took six minutes.

Teren was there.

He gave me an entrance, a place to stop, and one correction.

"Don't stand in the gate."

"I thought I'm complaining about it."

"From beside it."

"Why?"

"Because EvIn needs to come through."

"That seems selfish."

"Again."

We did it again.

I stood beside the gate.

EvIn came through.

Civilization survived.

That was all.

The rest of the afternoon I moved two benches, carried a lamp, fetched a
cup for Nessa, and helped Jori hang a narrow painted strip that had
nothing magical about it and did not become important later.

I appreciated this.

The audience was decent.

The Broken Gate ran second.

My first line was, "Whose cart is blocking my lane?"

EvIn said, "Not mine."

"It has your name on it."

"Then someone has stolen my name."

A laugh.

I waited where I was supposed to wait.

"My wife says move it."

EvIn said, "Tell your wife I am considering it."

"I did. She said consider faster."

A better laugh.

I left.

Later I returned.

The gate was down.

It was supposed to be down.

I looked at it.

Then at Hara.

Then at EvIn.

"I leave for ten minutes."

Hara said, "It was twelve."

"Then this is my fault."

The audience laughed.

I blamed Hara.

Hara blamed EvIn.

EvIn blamed municipal drainage.

The piece ended.

I went backstage.

Nobody corrected me.

Nobody said fine.

I almost went looking for somebody to do it.

Instead I carried the gate frame out of the way for the next piece.

This was healthier.

The last show ran a little late because a strap broke on a costume and
Nessa refused to let the actor go out with it hanging.

She fixed it.

The actor went out.

The audience never knew they had waited for thread.

Afterward, Rinna paid me one copper.

"Neighbor. Set."

"Gate."

"Set."

"Floor testing."

"No."

"Carrots."

She looked at me.

"Unrelated."

"You don't know my accounting."

"I know enough."

"One?"

"One."

I took it.

I did not stay for food.

Pell arrived as I was leaving and asked if I was coming.

"No."

"Why?"

"I have bread."

"That's not a reason."

"It was yesterday."

He accepted this.

Outside, the air had cooled.

I walked home with the remaining bread under one arm and the bundle
Marra had given me under the other.

I had carried the bundle through the entire theatre shift without
opening it.

This felt like evidence of character.

Lyssa was home first.

She had the hoop out again, but no cloth stretched across it.

She looked at the bundle.

"You still have it."

"Nobody told me to lose it."

"Good."

I put it on the table.

"What is it?"

"Mine."

"I know that."

"Then you're improving."

She opened it.

Two finished dark sleeves.

I stared.

"I carried sleeves all day?"

"Yes."

"They weigh nothing."

"Did you want heavier sleeves?"

"I wanted my labor to have shape."

Lyssa held one against her arm.

"It had shape."

"Not enough."

She laughed.

We ate bread, cheese, and cooked carrots because raw carrots had failed.

I told her I had been a Neighbor.

"Whose?"

"Apparently everyone's."

"Did you know them?"

"No."

"Bad neighbor."

"I was excellent."

"Did someone say that?"

"No."

"Then how do you know?"

"I wasn't corrected."

Lyssa considered this.

"Fine."

I pointed my knife at her.

"Don't."

She smiled.

After food, I finally lifted the cup.

Hessa's note was still there.

THREE DAYS.

It no longer meant three days.

Tomorrow.

After midday.

Away only.

Near / far.

Same restrictions.

I read it once.

Lyssa saw.

"Tomorrow?"

"Yes."

"Excited?"

I put the paper back.

"A little."

That was true.

"Nervous?"

"A little."

Also true.

"What do you do?"

"Sit where she tells me."

"Good start."

"Then draw if she tells me. Shape if she tells me. Ask the paper to move
away."

"Near and far."

"Yes."

"What does far mean?"

"I don't know."

Lyssa nodded.

"What does near mean?"

"I don't know."

"You know a lot again."

"I was hoping you'd forgotten that."

"No."

I put the cup back over the papers.

Nothing moved.

I did not ask anything to.

Marek would leave north at first bell.

Lyssa had work.

The hall would open whether I was there or not.

After midday, Hessa would put paper somewhere near me and somewhere
farther from me, and we would find out whether distance mattered inside
one very small thing I was actually allowed to claim.

Tonight I had carried cloth, sleeves, a gate, bread, and several objects
nobody had trusted to themselves.

That seemed like enough.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 196

## THE SITTER

Marek left north at first bell.

I knew this because the cart made enough noise to announce itself to
three streets.

Lyssa was already dressed when the first wheel struck something outside
and produced a wooden crack followed by a man's opinion of the road.

"That him?" I asked.

"Probably."

I went to the window.

The cart was long, low, and loaded with sacks, two barrels, a wooden
chest, and enough rope to make Pell emotional. Marek sat on the rear
edge with his canvas bag between his boots.

He looked up because I was leaning out the window.

"See your sister," I called.

"That was the plan."

"Don't get replaced."

He lifted one hand.

The cart moved.

That was goodbye.

Lyssa handed me bread.

"You weren't going down?"

"He was already moving."

"You could have."

"I said goodbye yesterday."

"Then why did you hang out the window?"

"Confirmation."

She ate.

I looked at the cup on the table.

She looked at me looking at the cup.

"After midday."

"I know."

"Good."

"I've been very good."

"At not touching paper?"

"At several things."

"Name two."

I ate bread.

Lyssa left before I did.

She had the narrow thing to finish.

I still did not know what the narrow thing was.

This had begun to feel deliberate.

I washed, used the soap, checked my right palm, and left the cup where
it was.

My palm had stopped being interesting. The skin was still newer where
the bad grip had rubbed it, but it no longer complained every time I put
weight through the crutch.

This was excellent.

Body parts should become boring whenever possible.

At the hall, Rinna was counting tickets that did not yet belong to
anyone.

"I have Guild after midday."

She kept counting.

"Fine."

"I don't know how long."

"Less fine."

"Do you need me tonight?"

"Probably."

"Role?"

"Probably."

I waited.

She looked up.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Good."

I had become extremely mature.

The board said:

KING: SELLEN / HARA / EVIN

BROKEN GATE: EVIN / HARA / GREG

WIDOW: VEYA / NESSA / HARA

GREG: NEIGHBOR / SET

Marek's name was gone.

Nobody had written a little memorial around the empty chalk.

Sellen was carrying a crown.

"You're king again."

"I can read."

"How does it feel?"

"Like a hat."

He put the crown on a shelf.

I worked until midday.

Nothing important happened.

This was not entirely true. Davin discovered that one of the rear bench
braces had cracked. Nessa discovered somebody had hung a damp shirt
among dry costumes. Jori discovered the lamp oil count was wrong by one
small tin.

All of these were important to the people holding them.

None of them changed my life.

I helped Davin turn the bench over.

The underside contained dust, a bent ticket, and one dried pea.

Davin tapped the cracked brace.

"Hold."

I held.

He removed two nails, replaced the brace with a shorter piece from
behind the work shelf, and nailed it in.

"Done?"

"Not yet."

He drove another nail.

"Done?"

"Yes."

We turned the bench back.

I sat on it.

Davin looked at me.

"Testing."

"You test everything by sitting?"

"Only things designed for it."

The bench held.

"Excellent."

At midday I ate the rest of the bread with a little cheese.

Rinna came past.

"Guild?"

"After."

"Go."

"I have time."

"Go slowly."

"I don't think that's how appointments work."

"It is if you leave now."

I left.

Hessa's room looked exactly like it had been waiting for me.

The table was clear except for the square board, the paper fins, the
glass covers, two small weights, Hessa's notes, and a piece of chalk.

There was also a chair.

I looked at the chair.

Hessa looked at me.

"Sit."

"I was afraid of that."

"Why?"

"I've developed a reputation."

"For sitting?"

"Apparently."

She pointed.

I sat.

The chair had been placed at one end of the table rather than the side.
A chalk line crossed the tabletop a little more than a forearm from the
edge nearest me. Another line crossed it near the far end.

The board rested beside Hessa, not on either mark.

"Eat?"

"Yes."

"Sleep?"

"Yes."

"Hand?"

"Mostly boring."

"Show me."

I held out my right hand.

She turned it once, pressed the healed skin near the base of my fingers,
then let go.

"Shoulder?"

"Fine."

"Wrist?"

"Fine."

"Any draw since last time?"

"No."

"Shaping?"

"No."

"External attempt?"

"No."

"Paper?"

"No."

"Coin?"

"No."

"Thread?"

"No."

She looked at me.

"I know."

"You asked."

"Good."

She sat opposite the side of the table, where she could reach the board
without standing.

I looked at the chalk lines.

"Near and far."

"Yes."

"Those?"

"Yes."

"Near is that near?"

"Today."

Of course.

Hessa put the board on the first chalk line.

The center of the target fin sat roughly a forearm and a hand beyond the
table edge in front of me. Far enough that I could not accidentally
breathe on it. Close enough that I could see the cut edge of the paper
clearly.

She set the glass cover over it, checked the two small control fins,
then marked something on her page.

Then she moved the entire board to the far line.

It was more than twice as distant. I could still see the target, but the
smallest cut marks disappeared into paper.

"Far," she said.

"That is definitely farther."

"Yes."

"Good experiment."

"Sit back."

I had leaned forward.

I sat back.

She moved the board near again.

"Your position does not change."

"At all?"

"Not intentionally."

"Comforting."

"Feet."

I adjusted my foot.

"Crutch."

I had leaned it against the table.

She pointed to the wall.

I moved it.

"Hands."

"Where?"

"Same place each attempt."

She had me rest my left hand on my thigh and my right hand open on the
other.

This felt like being arrested by furniture.

"Draw first," she said.

I stopped joking.

The familiar part was still not easy.

That bothered me less than it used to.

I settled my breathing and waited until Hessa told me to begin.

The draw came narrow.

Not smooth. Not pleasant. But narrow.

I found the small controlled pull without reaching for more. Heat
gathered under my ribs and behind my sternum, not enough to frighten me,
enough to make my shoulders want to join the work.

I kept them out of it.

"Stop."

I stopped.

Hessa watched my face.

"Again?"

"No."

I blinked.

"That was a question?"

"How do you feel?"

"Oh."

I checked.

"Fine. Warm."

"Where?"

I told her.

She wrote.

That made twenty-seven successful supervised minimal draws.

She waited until my breathing was ordinary again.

"Shape."

The shaping was worse.

It always wanted to become movement somewhere in my body instead of
remaining the small deliberate pressure Hessa had been making me
practice.

My wrist tightened.

"Release."

I did.

"Again?"

"You just said one."

"I asked how you feel."

"You're using the same word for too many things."

"How do you feel?"

"Wrist tight. Shoulder fine. Breathing fine."

She wrote again.

Twenty-three supervised deliberate shaping attempts.

Then she put the board on the near line.

My stomach tightened.

That was ridiculous.

It was paper.

Hessa checked the target fin, then the controls. She lifted the glass,
replaced it, and looked at me.

"Away only."

"Away from me."

"Yes."

"Not board-forward."

"Not board-forward."

"Not left, right, north, south, spiritually distant."

She waited.

"Away from me."

"Yes."

I looked at the target.

I did not imagine a hand.

I did not imagine a shove.

I did not imagine the paper flying across the table and proving
something much larger than it had ever proved.

I tried to ask for the same small external change we had already gotten,
in the direction away from where I sat.

The pressure narrowed.

My wrist wanted to tighten.

I let it stay small.

The paper fin moved.

Not much.

The upper edge gave a tiny turn away from me, enough that the cut shadow
beneath it changed.

I saw it.

Hessa did not react.

The control fins did not move.

"Stop."

I stopped.

She leaned in, checked the target, checked both controls, then wrote.

"How much?"

"Less than I'd like."

"Observed."

"Half a fingernail?"

"Less."

"That's insulting."

She ignored that.

External attempt twenty.

Near.

Response observed.

I knew better than to celebrate paper.

I still wanted to.

Hessa gave me water.

We waited.

Then she moved the board to the far line.

The same board.

Same fins.

Same glass.

Same direction relative to me.

The target looked smaller from here.

"Do I lean?"

"No."

"I thought not."

"Same position."

I put my hands where they had been.

Hessa checked them.

"Ready?"

"Yes."

"Away."

I asked.

Nothing happened.

The sensation was there. The small shaped pressure was there. My wrist
tightened a little earlier than it had near.

The paper did nothing.

I held too long.

"Stop."

I stopped.

Hessa checked the target.

Controls unchanged.

Target unchanged.

She wrote.

I stared at the far fin.

It looked smug.

"Don't."

"I didn't say anything."

"You leaned."

I sat back.

External attempt twenty-one.

Far.

No observed response.

"Rest."

"I'm fine."

"Rest."

I drank more water.

The room had a small high window. Somebody outside passed close enough
that their shadow crossed the lower wall and disappeared.

Hessa turned her page.

I looked at the far chalk line.

"So."

"No."

"I haven't said anything."

"You were going to."

"This is becoming a city problem."

She waited.

I did not say closer was easier.

This required effort.

After a few minutes she moved the board back to near.

She checked the fins again.

"Same."

"Same."

"Away."

The second near attempt felt worse.

Not dramatically.

Just enough that I noticed the first attempt had been cleaner.

My shoulder tried to lift.

I lowered it.

The pressure narrowed.

The target fin gave a small twitch.

Then, after a moment, a clearer turn.

Away.

Tiny.

Real.

The controls remained still.

Hessa stopped me almost immediately.

She checked everything.

"Observed?"

I asked.

"Yes."

"Good."

She wrote.

External attempt twenty-two.

Near.

Response observed again.

I smiled.

Hessa looked up.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You're smiling."

"I'm allowed."

"Yes."

This was generous of her.

She moved the board far.

The smile became less useful.

"Same?"

"Same."

I rested my hands.

The target was far enough away that I had to resist narrowing my eyes at
it.

Hessa waited until I stopped.

"Away."

I tried.

The first few breaths felt wrong.

I released before she told me.

Hessa said nothing.

"Again within the same attempt?"

"No."

I looked at her.

"No?"

"You released."

"I thought that was good."

"It was."

She checked my wrist.

"Pain?"

"No."

"Tight?"

"Yes."

"Shoulder?"

"Starting."

She wrote something.

"Are we done?"

"Not yet."

I looked at the far board.

She waited longer this time.

My shoulder settled.

My wrist did not entirely.

"One more external attempt," she said.

"Far?"

"Far."

"Then we're ending on the one that doesn't work."

"We are ending on the condition we have less evidence for."

"That is a much worse sentence."

"It is more accurate."

I put my hands back.

She checked my position.

The far target waited under glass.

"Away."

I tried again.

Nothing.

Then maybe something.

I stopped breathing for half a second.

The upper edge of the target seemed to tremble.

I could not tell whether it had actually changed position or whether I
had stared at it long enough to invent mercy.

Hessa said, "Stop."

I stopped.

She went to the board.

She did not immediately write.

That was worse.

"Did it move?"

"Maybe."

"That's not one of your usual words."

"It is when I am not sure."

She checked the control fins.

Then the target.

Then the glass.

"One control may have shifted also."

I leaned forward.

"How much?"

"Enough."

"So it doesn't count."

"It counts as an attempt."

"Of course it does."

She wrote.

External attempt twenty-three.

Far.

Uncertain target movement. Possible control movement. Not usable as
evidence of response.

I hated this.

It was exactly correct.

I hated it more.

"Again."

"No."

"One clean far."

"No."

"Because of the control?"

"Because your wrist is tightening earlier, your shoulder has joined
twice, and this would be the fifth external request after draw and
shaping."

"I can do one."

"Probably."

"Then."

"No."

I looked at the paper.

Hessa closed her notes.

That was unfairly final.

"Near worked twice."

"Yes."

"Far failed once."

"Yes."

"And far maybe did something useless."

"Yes."

"So near is easier."

"Here."

I looked at her.

"Today."

"Yes."

"In this arrangement."

"Yes."

I sighed.

She opened the notes again.

"I liked it better closed."

She wrote slowly enough that I could read upside down if I leaned.

I did not lean.

She turned the page toward me when she finished.

AWAY RESPONSE OBSERVED TWICE AT NEAR POSITION.

FAR RESPONSE NOT ESTABLISHED.

NEAR RESPONSE MORE RELIABLE THAN FAR RESPONSE TODAY.

POSSIBLE DISTANCE DEPENDENCE IN CURRENT APPARATUS.

NOT A RANGE.

NOT GENERALIZED.

I pointed.

"You wrote the part I was going to say."

"Which?"

"Near is easier."

"I did not write that."

"You wrote it with more words."

"No."

"It is emotionally the same."

"No."

"Fine."

She added beneath it:

REPEAT.

NEAR / FAR.

AWAY ONLY.

No date.

I noticed.

"When?"

"Not today."

"I know that."

"Good."

"When later?"

"I'll tell you."

"Tomorrow?"

"No."

"Day after?"

"I'll tell you."

"You're becoming Rinna."

Hessa stared at me.

"Never mind."

She checked my wrist again.

Then my shoulder.

"Same restrictions."

"All of them?"

"All."

"No paper."

"No."

"No coin."

"No."

"No thread."

"No."

"No external testing."

"No."

"No independent draw."

"No."

"No independent shaping."

"No."

"I remembered."

"I know."

That was almost praise.

I decided not to damage it.

"Twenty-seven draws," I said.

"Successful supervised minimal draws."

"Twenty-three shaping."

"Supervised deliberate shaping attempts."

"Twenty-three external."

"Supervised external-effect attempts."

"You make every number longer."

"That is because you shorten every claim."

I thought about that.

"Fair."

She looked suspicious.

"I can say fair."

"Go home."

"I have theatre."

"Then go there and do not test anything."

"I don't usually test things at theatre."

"Good."

I stood.

My right wrist complained when I picked up the crutch.

Not pain.

Just enough fatigue to make me shift the grip.

Hessa saw.

"Light work."

"Tell Rinna."

"I am telling you."

"Less effective."

"Your problem."

This was also fair.

The hall had moved on without me.

It had done this very successfully.

When I came in, Pell was carrying a stool upside down.

"Guild?"

"Yes."

"Good?"

"Paper."

He nodded as though that answered anything.

Maybe it did.

Rinna saw me.

"You came back."

"You said probably."

"I say many things."

"I've noticed."

She looked at my wrist.

"Hessa say anything?"

"Light work."

"House."

"That's light?"

"Compared to scenery."

I could not argue.

I spent the evening taking tickets, moving one stool, answering where
the privy was, and telling two people The Broken Gate was second.

It became third.

I told the next person third.

The performance happened without me.

This felt slightly strange.

Not bad.

Just strange.

I heard laughs through the door.

At one point I heard my Neighbor line delivered by somebody else.

I could not tell who from the front.

The audience laughed.

I objected privately.

Then a man asked whether he could bring a cup inside.

"No."

"Why?"

"I don't know."

He looked at me.

I looked toward Rinna.

She said, "No cups."

I looked back.

"No cups."

"Why?"

"Authority."

Rinna made a sound.

The man left the cup.

At cleanup she paid me one copper.

"House."

"Guild fatigue."

"Not my expense."

"I returned."

"That is why you got paid."

"Excellent system."

"Go home."

Everyone had become Hessa.

Lyssa was not home when I arrived.

I washed my hands and wrist in cool water.

The soap had become smaller again.

This was the problem with useful things.

I did not lift the cup.

There was no reason.

The old note underneath it was now wrong in every temporal sense and
still correct in every instructional one.

When Lyssa came in, she had no hoop.

She had a small wrapped parcel and a smear of something dark near one
thumb.

"Near or far?" she asked before taking off her shoes.

"Near."

She looked at me.

"Near here."

"Better."

"Far was worse."

"How worse?"

"Nothing once. Maybe something once, but a control may have moved too,
so Hessa refused to count it as evidence."

Lyssa put the parcel on the table.

"Near?"

"Twice."

"Both moved?"

"Yes."

"Far?"

"Not established."

She smiled.

"That sounds like Hessa."

"I said near was easier."

"What did she say?"

"Here."

Lyssa laughed.

"Then today."

"Yes."

"In this arrangement."

"Yes."

She laughed harder.

"I don't see what's funny."

"You."

"That's not useful."

"It is to me."

I sat.

My shoulder felt tired now that nobody needed it.

Lyssa unwrapped the parcel.

Inside was a piece of flatbread with onions folded into it.

I looked at her.

"Two?"

"One."

"For us?"

"Obviously."

That word had also become infected.

She tore it in half.

I ate.

After a while she asked, "Again when?"

"I don't know."

"Hessa doesn't know?"

"She probably knows. She hasn't told me."

"What next?"

"Same thing."

Lyssa paused.

"Again?"

"Near and far. Away only."

"No new thing?"

"No."

"Good."

I looked at her.

"Why good?"

"Because the last thing barely moves paper."

This was difficult to dispute.

I ate more flatbread.

Twenty-seven successful supervised minimal draws.

Twenty-three supervised deliberate shaping attempts.

Twenty-three supervised external-effect attempts.

Near had worked twice.

Far had not worked cleanly at all.

That was more than I had known this morning.

It was less than I wanted to know.

Hessa would have liked that sentence.

I did not tell her.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 197

## THE PETITIONER

My wrist was stiff in the morning.

Not hurt.

Stiff.

There was an important difference, and I spent several seconds proving
it by rotating my hand until Lyssa looked up from tying her hair.

"Stop."

"I'm checking it."

"You've checked it four times."

"That is how you establish repeatability."

"No."

I stopped.

She had already put bread on the table. There was also a narrow strip of
dark blue cloth beside her elbow.

I pointed at it.

"The narrow thing?"

Lyssa looked down.

"Part of it."

"What is it?"

"Binding."

I waited.

She ate.

"That's all?"

"What did you think it was?"

"I didn't know. That's why I asked."

"It's binding for a sleeve edge."

I stared at the cloth.

Three days of mystery had produced sleeve binding.

Lyssa watched my face.

"Disappointed?"

"No."

"You are."

"I had assigned it no importance."

"Good."

"I was still expecting more object."

She folded the strip and put it in her bag.

"Work?"

"Theatre."

"All day?"

"Probably."

"You know when?"

"Morning."

She nodded.

This was progress.

I ate.

The cup remained on the table.

There was no new paper under it.

I knew because the edge of the old note was still visible in exactly the
same place.

I did not lift the cup.

Lyssa noticed.

"Nothing?"

"Nothing."

"Good."

"Everyone keeps saying that."

"Because you keep checking."

"I didn't check."

"You looked."

"That is different."

She kissed the side of my head on the way past.

"Go to work."

This made it difficult to continue the argument.

Outside, Carrow had already warmed enough that the stone near the market
smelled dry.

A man was selling fried dough from a pan set over coals. I bought one
piece because bread had not entirely convinced me breakfast had
occurred.

The dough was hot, greasy, and folded around chopped greens.

It cost enough that I regretted it for one bite.

Then I stopped regretting it.

This was becoming financially dangerous.

At the next corner two men were arguing about whether a cart had damaged
a drain cover.

The cart was gone.

The drain cover was still there.

Neither man appeared to own either.

Carrow remained well governed.

I reached the hall with grease on two fingers and soap still faintly on
my wrists.

By the time I went inside, the hall removed both improvements.

Pell was sanding the edge of a painted frame.

Dust settled on my sleeve.

I looked at it.

"Morning," he said.

"You've ruined me."

"Already?"

"I was clean."

He looked at my coat.

"No."

"Cleaner."

"Maybe."

The board was short.

KING: SELLEN / HARA / EVIN

PETITION: VEYA / SELLEN / GREG / EVIN

WIDOW: VEYA / NESSA / HARA

SHORT: HARA / EVIN

GREG: PETITIONER / SET

Marek was still absent.

The company had survived the night.

I found this encouraging.

"Petitioner?" I asked.

Rinna was tying a stack of ticket slips with cord.

"Yes."

"Which petitioner?"

She looked at me.

I pointed at the board.

"There are several people petitioning in that piece."

"You're the fence."

"Third Man."

"No."

I looked again.

"Not Third Man?"

"No."

"Then which fence?"

"First petition. Two lines. Then you come back with the drainage
complaint."

I stared at her.

"That man has a drainage complaint?"

"Today."

"Did he yesterday?"

"No."

"Good."

Rinna stopped tying tickets.

"What?"

"I asked."

"Congratulations."

I found Teren near the rear wall with Davin and a door hinge.

The hinge belonged to a narrow painted door that had been removed from
its frame and laid across two benches.

Davin held the old pin between two fingers.

"It bends."

Teren said, "Then don't use it."

"I wasn't planning to."

"Good."

I waited.

Teren looked at me.

"Petitioner."

"Apparently."

"First petition. Fence line. Leave. Back after Sellen's tax line.
Drainage."

"How many lines?"

"Four."

"Entrance?"

"Same side as Third Man."

"Coat?"

"Nessa."

"Version?"

Teren looked at me.

"Today."

"Excellent."

He pointed toward the stage.

"Go ask Veya."

This was the entire meeting.

Nessa had three coats on a rail and one coat over her shoulder.

I knew two of them.

The third was Marek's king coat.

Sellen stood with his arms out while Nessa pulled the coat across his
back.

It did not want to be Sellen's coat.

Marek was broader through the shoulders.

Sellen was not.

The fabric gathered beneath the collar and the sleeves hung too low.

Nessa folded one cuff inward.

Sellen said, "That's uneven."

"So are your arms."

"My arms are not uneven."

Nessa looked at me.

"Are his arms uneven?"

"I don't know."

Sellen turned.

"Don't involve him."

"I was invited."

Nessa pinned the inside fold at the shoulder.

Sellen flinched.

"That is me."

"Then stop moving."

"I was stabbed."

"You were touched."

"With metal."

"Hold this."

She handed me a length of narrow cord.

I held it.

Sellen looked down.

"Why does he get the safe job?"

"Because I don't need him."

"That feels insulting."

"It is."

Nessa tied the back of the coat tighter, folded the second cuff, then
stepped away.

Marek's coat now looked less like Marek had left it behind and more like
Sellen had borrowed something expensive from a larger cousin.

"Fine," Nessa said.

Sellen lowered his arms.

"Can I breathe?"

"No."

"Good."

He walked away.

I still held the cord.

"Nessa."

She was already working on another sleeve.

"Nessa."

"What?"

"The cord."

"Rail."

I put it on the rail.

This was how objects migrated.

My petitioner coat was brown, short, and smelled faintly of old smoke.

I had worn it before in something else.

I could not remember what.

That seemed fair. The coat probably could not remember me either.

Veya was at the petition table with the stack of papers.

"Fence," she said.

"I have one."

"Not yours."

"I know."

"Do you?"

I took my place.

The new petitioner was not complicated.

I entered angry about a neighbor moving a boundary post.

Veya, as the official, did not care.

I left.

Later I returned angry about water running from the public lane into my
yard.

Veya cared even less.

This was apparently the entire man.

We ran it once.

"My neighbor moved the boundary post two feet into my garden."

Veya looked at the petition.

"Then move it back."

"I did."

"Why are you here?"

"He moved it again."

"Move it again."

I paused.

Teren said, "Don't wait."

"I thought she might help."

"She isn't going to."

"That seems bad government."

Veya looked at me.

"You're learning."

We continued.

Later I came back.

"The lane drain is pouring into my yard."

Veya said, "Then your garden is watered."

"It has my chair in it."

"Move the chair."

"Where?"

She looked at me.

"Inside."

Teren said, "Good."

That was rehearsal.

I liked the petitioner.

He had problems.

Nobody respected them.

This was familiar.

The rest of the morning was less theatrical.

Davin needed the door held upright while he fitted the new hinge pin.

I started to take the heavier side.

My wrist reminded me about yesterday.

Not pain.

Just a small tightness.

I shifted.

"Pell."

He looked over.
